A textbook companion · Lectures 1–13

Holomorphic Functions

A textbook built from the slides of a thirteen-lecture course in complex analysis. Part I asks whether a harmonic function is determined by, and can be found from, its boundary values, and answers with finite elements. Part II develops Cauchy's integral theory. Part III uses it to compute integrals and Fourier transforms and to prove the sampling theorem. Part IV studies entire functions through their zeros, ending with the Gamma function. Part V studies conformal maps and closes the circle: the solution of Part I's Dirichlet problem produces the Riemann map.

The main text follows the slides one by one, with every step justified. Background the slides take for granted is collected in a lettered appendix.

How to read this guide

Every numbered item is labelled by its logical status. A definition names something and cannot be wrong. A derived result is proved from earlier items. An assumption limits which situations the argument covers.

Defined A name or convention we choose.
Derived Proved here from earlier items.
Assumed A hypothesis on $\Omega$, the grid, or $g$.
Cited A standard result, used without proof; details in the appendix.

Three kinds of reference help you move around.

  • Lecture notation. Symbols the lecture defines, such as $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$, $\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}$, $\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w)$ or $m_n$, are tinted inside formulas. Hover over one to see what it means. Click it (or, on a touch screen, tap it and use the link in the box) to go to its definition.
  • Numbered results. Mentions of numbered items, such as Prop. 3.6.4 or §3.11, are links. Hovering shows the statement; clicking takes you there.
  • Background. A dotted link with a small box, such as Cauchy–SchwarzA.12, goes to the appendix.

Each lecture opens with an overview box: its goal, its main results, what it uses from earlier lectures and where it is used later. Exercises, where the slides have them, come with worked solutions that stay folded until you open them.

After any jump, the Back button in the corner returns you to where you clicked, one step at a time. Each appendix entry lists every place that cites it, and the outside references (Wikipedia and similar) are kept there.

How the course fits together

The course was taught as a sequence of self-contained lectures. Read as a book, it falls into five parts.

PartQuestionAnswer
I · Lectures 1–5Given continuous values $g$ on the boundary of a region, is there exactly one harmonic function with those boundary values?Yes, for regions made of grid squares: uniqueness by energy or the maximum principle; existence by finite elements, Weyl's lemma and a barrier (Theorem 5.1.1).
II · Lectures 6–7What does one complex derivative buy?Everything: Cauchy's formula, power series, derivatives of all orders, isolated zeros, residues, and counting zeros by an integral (Theorems 6.3.1, 6.4.1, 6.9.1, 7.3.1).
III · Lecture 8What do contour integrals say about real integrals and Fourier transforms?They compute them, and they match holomorphy of $f$ with decay of $\hat f$: Paley–Wiener and the sampling theorem (Theorems 8.5.2, 8.7.1, 8.10.1).
IV · Lectures 9–11How are an entire function's zeros related to its growth, and does a function factor over its zeros?Jensen's formula bounds zeros by growth; Weierstrass and Hadamard products rebuild the function; examples: the sine and $1/\Gamma$ (Theorems 9.5.1, 10.7.1, 10.11.1, 11.6.1).
V · Lectures 12–13Which regions can be mapped onto the disk by a holomorphic bijection, and what is such a map good for?It transports harmonic functions, so Dirichlet problems move to the disk. The disk's self-maps are known exactly (Theorem 12.15.1), and regions made of squares have a Riemann map, built from Part I's solution of the Dirichlet problem (Theorem 13.2.1).

Threads across the parts. The parts were taught separately, but they lean on each other:

  • Two views of one theory. The real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic (Prop. 2.8.1, Cor. 6.6.2), and the mean value property of Part I (Theorem 4.2.2) is Cauchy's formula of Part II (Theorem 6.3.1) at the centre of the circle.
  • Part I's tools reused in Part IV. Jensen's formula is the mean value property applied to $\log|f|$, the potential of point charges at the zeros (§9.3, Lemma 9.4.1, logarithmic potentialE.6); the maximum modulus lemma is Lecture 4's maximum principle (Lemma 9.6.1, Cor. 4.4.1).
  • Uniform limits. Harmonic (Cor. 4.11.1) and holomorphic (Theorem 10.3.1) functions survive uniform limits for the same reason: an integral formula with no derivatives in it.
  • Promises kept. Lecture 1 announced the identity theorem and isolated zeros (Theorem 1.3.1, Cor. 1.3.2): they are proved as Theorem 10.1.1 and Theorem 6.7.1. Standing assumption 1.9.2 (smooth parts) is proved as Cor. 6.6.2. The Gaussian integral used in §6.18 and §8.3 is Cor. 11.9.1; the Basel sum used in Lemma 6.13.2 follows from Euler's product (E.18).
  • The circle closes. Part I solved the Dirichlet problem on unions of squares (Theorem 5.1.1). Part V uses that solution, with boundary values $\log|z-z_0|$, to build the conformal map onto the disk (Theorem 13.2.1); conversely, a conformal map moves Dirichlet problems to the disk (Cor. 12.3.2). The harmonic conjugate of Lemma 12.2.1 is Lecture 1's stream function.
  • Counting zeros. The argument principle (Theorem 7.3.1) leads to Rouché's theorem (Theorem 11.10.1); Jensen's formula (Theorem 9.5.1) leads to Hadamard's theorem (Theorem 10.13.1).

Part I

Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem

Given a region $\Omega$ and continuous values $g$ on its boundary, is there exactly one function that is harmonic in $\Omega$ and equals $g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$? Lectures 1 and 2 introduce holomorphic and harmonic functions through fluid flow and electrostatics, and prove uniqueness. Lectures 3 to 5 prove existence for regions made of squares in three steps: a weak solution from finite elements, its smoothness from the mean value property, and its boundary values from a barrier.

L1 · Slide 2

1.1 What complex analysis is about

Complex analysis is the study of functions from $\mathbb C$ to $\mathbb C$ that can be differentiated. These functions are known by the fancy name of "holomorphic functions". Points are written $z=x+iy$ (complex notationC.1).

DefinedDefinition 1.1.1 (holomorphic). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be openC.2. A function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$ if at every $z_0\in\Omega$ the limit \[ f'(z_0):=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}{h},\qquad h\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}, \] exists. Openness guarantees that $z_0+h\in\Omega$ for all small $h$, in every direction.
DefinedDefinition 1.1.2 (complex analytic). $f$ is complex analytic if near each point $z_0$ it equals a convergent power seriesA.19 $\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-z_0)^n$.

Every analytic function is holomorphic (a convergent power series can be differentiated term by term). The converse is Theorem 6.4.1. So the two terms are interchangeable, although their definitions look different; see how the definitions meetE.2.

L1 · Slide 3

1.2 The main difference with real analysis

At first sight the only difference is that taking a derivative is more constraining.

  • On $\R$: two directions, two limits, required to match: \[ \lim_{h\to0^-}\frac{f(x_0+h)-f(x_0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{f(x_0+h)-f(x_0)}{h}. \]
  • On $\mathbb C$: left, right, top, bottom, and everything in between, all required to match. Writing $h=e^{i\theta}t$ with $t$ real and $\theta$ fixed picks a direction: \[ \lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(z_0+t)-f(z_0)}{t}=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(z_0+it)-f(z_0)}{it}=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(z_0+e^{i\theta}t)-f(z_0)}{e^{i\theta}t}. \]

And more: Def. 1.1.1 asks that the quotient converge as $h\to0$ along any path, not just straight lines. The next sections show that, for functions that are differentiable as maps $\R^2\to\R^2$, two directions already decide everything (Theorem 1.5.2).

L1 · Slide 4

1.3 This small difference is gigantic

The difference is very constraining. Two basic theorems that the course proves later:

CitedTheorem 1.3.1 (identity theorem). Let $f$ and $g$ be holomorphic on open sets $U$ and $V$, with $U\cap V$ connectedC.4. If $f=g$ on some nonempty open subset of $U\cap V$, then $f=g$ on all of $U\cap V$.
CitedCorollary 1.3.2 (isolated zeros). Let $f$ be holomorphic on a connected open set $\Omega$. If $f(z_n)=0$ for a sequence of distinct points $z_n\to z\in\Omega$, then $f\equiv0$ on $\Omega$.

Both are stated here and proved later: Cor. 1.3.2 as Theorem 6.7.1, and Theorem 1.3.1 as Theorem 10.1.1 (which also covers sequences with a limit point).

DerivedCorollary 1.3.3 (constant on a segment). A holomorphic function on a connected open set $\Omega$ that is constant on a nontrivial line segment contained in $\Omega$ is constant everywhere.
Proof. Say $f=c$ on the segment. Then $f-c$ is holomorphic and vanishes at infinitely many distinct points of the segment, for instance at points $z_n$ converging to one endpoint $z\in\Omega$. By Cor. 1.3.2, $f-c\equiv0$. ∎

Nothing like this holds for $C^\infty$ functions: a bump functionD.5 is smooth, zero on a whole half-plane, and not zero everywhere. Holomorphic is a much more restricted class.

L1 · Slides 6–10

1.5 The Cauchy–Riemann equations

DefinedDefinition 1.5.1 (complex functions as maps of the plane). A map $f:\R^2\to\R^2$, $f(x,y)=\big(u(x,y),v(x,y)\big)$, is identified with the complex function \[ f(x+iy)=u(x,y)+i\,v(x,y). \] $u$ is the real part and $v$ the imaginary part of $f$. Partial derivatives are written $u_x=\partial u/\partial x$ and so on.
DerivedTheorem 1.5.2 (Cauchy–Riemann). Let $f=(u,v)$ be differentiableA.1 at $(x_0,y_0)$ as a map $\R^2\to\R^2$, and $z_0=x_0+iy_0$. Then $f=u+iv$ is complex differentiable at $z_0$ if and only if \[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y},\qquad\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\qquad\text{at }(x_0,y_0). \] In that case $f'(z_0)=u_x+i\,v_x$.

The theorem says that for complex differentiability only two directions matter: top–bottom and left–right. If $f$ is differentiable as a real map, the derivatives in these two directions determine all the others, and Cauchy–Riemann is exactly the condition for them to fit together into a complex derivative.

Proof of (⇒). Suppose $f$ is complex differentiable at $z_0$. Then the limit defining $f'(z_0)$ can be taken along any direction; take two.
  • Left–right: $h=t\in\R$, $t\to0$. The quotient is $\frac{u(x_0+t,y_0)-u(x_0,y_0)}{t}+i\,\frac{v(x_0+t,y_0)-v(x_0,y_0)}{t}$, whose real and imaginary parts tend to the partial derivatives: \[ f'(z_0)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(z_0+t)-f(z_0)}{t}=u_x+i\,v_x. \]
  • Top–bottom: $h=it$, $t\in\R$, $t\to0$. Now the numerator changes $y$, giving $u_y+iv_y$ in the limit, and we divide by $i$, using $\frac1i=-i$: \[ f'(z_0)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(z_0+it)-f(z_0)}{it}=\frac{u_y+i\,v_y}{i}=v_y-i\,u_y. \]
The two must agree: $u_x+iv_x=v_y-iu_y$. Comparing real parts gives $u_x=v_y$; comparing imaginary parts gives $v_x=-u_y$. ∎
Proof of (⇐). Assume the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold at $(x_0,y_0)$; all partial derivatives below are evaluated there.
  1. Taylor expand, as real functions. Since $u$ and $v$ are differentiable at $(x_0,y_0)$ (A.1), for $(h_1,h_2)\to(0,0)$: \[ \begin{aligned} u(x_0+h_1,y_0+h_2)&=u(x_0,y_0)+h_1u_x+h_2u_y+o(|h|),\\ v(x_0+h_1,y_0+h_2)&=v(x_0,y_0)+h_1v_x+h_2v_y+o(|h|), \end{aligned} \] where $|h|=\sqrt{h_1^2+h_2^2}$ and $o(|h|)$ is an error that is small compared with $|h|$.
  2. Reinterpret as a complex function. Put $h=h_1+ih_2$, so that $z_0+h$ corresponds to $(x_0+h_1,y_0+h_2)$. Then \[ \begin{aligned} f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)&=\big[u(x_0+h_1,y_0+h_2)-u(x_0,y_0)\big]+i\big[v(x_0+h_1,y_0+h_2)-v(x_0,y_0)\big]\\ &=h_1(u_x+iv_x)+h_2(u_y+iv_y)+o(|h|). \end{aligned} \]
  3. Use Cauchy–Riemann. Substituting $u_y=-v_x$ and $v_y=u_x$, \[ u_y+iv_y=-v_x+iu_x=i(u_x+iv_x). \] So both coefficients are multiples of the same complex number $u_x+iv_x$: \[ f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)=(h_1+ih_2)(u_x+iv_x)+o(|h|)=h\,(u_x+iv_x)+o(|h|). \]
  4. Conclude. Divide by $h$: \[ \frac{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}{h}=(u_x+iv_x)+\frac{o(|h|)}{h}\longrightarrow u_x+iv_x \] as $h\to0$ from any direction, since $|o(|h|)/h|=o(|h|)/|h|\to0$. So $f$ is complex differentiable at $z_0$, with $f'(z_0)=u_x+iv_x$. ∎

Step 3 is where the two directions "fit together": a general real-linear map $(h_1,h_2)\mapsto h_1a+h_2b$ is multiplication by a single complex number exactly when $b=ia$. Geometrically, a complex derivative acts on small displacements as a rotation combined with a scaling.

L1 · Slides 11–14

1.6 The meaning of the Cauchy–Riemann equations: flows

The simplest interpretation is a two-dimensional fluid with velocity field $(x,y)\longmapsto\big(u(x,y),v(x,y)\big)$.

DefinedDefinition 1.6.1 (divergence and curl). For a planar vector field $(u,v)$, \[ \class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}(u,v):=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y},\qquad\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}(u,v):=\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}. \] In two dimensions the curl is a scalar: it is the $z$-component of the three-dimensional curl $\nabla\times(u,v,0)$, the only component that can be nonzero for a planar field. (More on flux and circulationA.5.)

To check the curl claim: \[ \nabla\times(u,v,0)=\big(\partial_y0-\partial_zv,\ \partial_zu-\partial_x0,\ \partial_xv-\partial_yu\big)=(0,0,v_x-u_y), \] because $u,v$ do not depend on the third coordinate.

DerivedProposition 1.6.2 (Cauchy–Riemann in the language of flows). The pair $(u,-v)$ satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations if and only if \[ \class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}(u,v)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}(u,v)=0. \] Equivalently: for $u,v$ of class $C^1$, $f=u-iv$ is holomorphic if and only if $(u,v)$ is divergence-free and curl-free.
Proof. Theorem 1.5.2's equations for real part $u$ and imaginary part $-v$ read $u_x=(-v)_y$ and $u_y=-(-v)_x$, that is $u_x+v_y=0$ and $v_x-u_y=0$: $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}(u,v)=0$ and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}(u,v)=0$. For the second sentence, $C^1$ functions are differentiable (A.1), so Theorem 1.5.2 applies at every point. ∎

The minus sign is forced. Cauchy–Riemann for $(u,v)$ itself would say $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$, which is neither $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}=0$ nor $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}=0$; flipping the sign of $v$ turns them into exactly those two. (See sign conventionsE.1.)

DerivedProposition 1.6.3 (incompressible and irrotational). Write $V=(u,v)$, of class $C^1$, and let $D$ be any small region with boundary $\partial D$, inside the domain.
(a) Incompressible: if $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}V=0$, then $\oint_{\partial D}V\cdot n\,ds=0$: as much fluid flows into $D$ as flows out. No sources, no sinks.
(b) Irrotational: if $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}V=0$, then $\oint_{\partial D}V\cdot t\,ds=0$: the circulation around $\partial D$ vanishes, so the fluid does not swirl around any point.
Proof. (a) By the divergence theoremA.6, $\oint_{\partial D}V\cdot n\,ds=\iint_D\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}V\,dA=0$. (b) By Green's theoremA.6, $\oint_{\partial D}V\cdot t\,ds=\iint_D\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}V\,dA=0$. ∎

$\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}V=0$ is conservation of mass for a fluid of constant density. Upshot: holomorphic functions $f=u-iv$ are the same thing as incompressible, irrotational plane flows.

DerivedExample 1.6.4 (which flows come from holomorphic functions?). Rotation $(u,v)=(-y,x)$: $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}=2\ne0$, and indeed $u-iv=-i\bar z$ is not holomorphic.
Source $(u,v)=(x,y)$: $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}=2\ne0$, and indeed $u-iv=\bar z$ is not holomorphic.
Stagnation point $(u,v)=(x,-y)$: $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}=0$ and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}=0$, and $u-iv=x+iy=z$ is holomorphic.
Proof. Rotation: $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}=\partial_x(x)-\partial_y(-y)=1-(-1)=2$, the fluid circulating in closed loops (vorticity); and $u-iv=-y-ix=-i(x-iy)=-i\bar z$. Source: $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}=\partial_xx+\partial_yy=2$, fluid pouring out of the origin; $u-iv=x-iy=\bar z$. Stagnation point: $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}=1-1=0$, $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}=\partial_x(-y)-\partial_y(x)=0-0=0$; $u-iv=x-i(-y)=z$. Finally, $\bar z=x-iy$ is not holomorphic: its real part $x$ and imaginary part $-y$ have $\partial_x(x)=1\ne-1=\partial_y(-y)$, violating Cauchy–Riemann everywhere; and $-i\bar z$ is not holomorphic either, since $\bar z=i\cdot(-i\bar z)$ would then be. ∎
L1 · Slide 15

1.7 A standard fact from vector calculus

CitedFact 1.7.1 (Poincaré lemma on a disk). Let $D$ be an open disk and $W=(W_1,W_2)$ a $C^1$ vector field on $D$ with $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}W=0$. Then $W$ is a gradient: $W=\nabla\varphi$ for some $\varphi:D\to\R$, unique up to an additive constant.

The slides call this a standard fact; a complete proof is in the Poincaré lemmaA.7. Not to be confused with Poincaré's inequality (Theorem 3.17.2), a different result by the same mathematician. The disk matters: §1.14 shows the lemma fails on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$.

L1 · Slide 16

1.8 The two potentials

DerivedProposition 1.8.1 (velocity potential, stream function, primitive). Let $f=u-iv$ be holomorphic on a disk $D$, with $u,v\in C^1$, so that the associated flow $V=(u,v)$ is curl-free and divergence-free. Then there are $C^2$ functions $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi},\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ on $D$ with \[ \nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=(u,v)\quad(\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x=u,\ \class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y=v),\qquad\nabla\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=(-v,u)\quad(\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x=-v,\ \class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_y=u), \] and $F:=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ is holomorphic on $D$ with $F'=f$.
Proof.
  1. Velocity potential. $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}(u,v)=0$ (Prop. 1.6.2), so the Poincaré lemma (Fact 1.7.1) gives $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}$ with $\nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=(u,v)$.
  2. Stream function. Rotate by $90°$: \[ \class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}(-v,u)=\partial_xu-\partial_y(-v)=u_x+v_y=\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}(u,v)=0. \] So the Poincaré lemma gives $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ with $\nabla\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=(-v,u)$.
  3. Put them together. Comparing, $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x=u=\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_y$ and $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y=v=-\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x$. These are the Cauchy–Riemann equations of Theorem 1.5.2 for $F=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$. Since $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi},\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ have continuous gradients, they are differentiable (A.1), so $F$ is holomorphic on $D$, and \[ F'=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x+i\,\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x=u-iv=f. \] ∎

So every holomorphic function on a disk has a holomorphic primitive (antiderivative). The disk is essential, through the Poincaré lemma; see §1.14.

L1 · Slides 17–18

1.9 Derivatives of holomorphic functions

The derivative of a holomorphic function is holomorphic. This is a deeper theorem in general, but easy under slightly stronger regularity.

DerivedProposition 1.9.1. Let $f=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ be holomorphic with $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi},\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}\in C^2$. Then $f'=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x$ is holomorphic, with $C^1$ parts.
Proof. By Theorem 1.5.2, $f'=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x$, and $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x,\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x$ are $C^1$. Differentiate the Cauchy–Riemann equations $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x=\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_y$, $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y=-\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x$ of $f$, using equality of mixed partialsA.2: \[ (\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x)_x=(\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_y)_x=(\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x)_y,\qquad(\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x)_y=(\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y)_x=(-\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x)_x=-(\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x)_x. \] These are the Cauchy–Riemann equations for $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x$ (real part $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x$, imaginary part $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x$), and $C^1$ parts are differentiable, so Theorem 1.5.2 applies. ∎
AssumedStanding assumption 1.9.2. From now on, holomorphic functions have $C^2$ (in practice, smooth) real and imaginary parts. That this is automatic is a theorem for later in the course: Cor. 6.6.2 proves it, assuming only $C^1$ parts (Convention 6.1.1).
L1 · Slide 19

1.10 Holomorphic functions as flows

DefinedDefinition 1.10.1 (complex potential and complex velocity). Take any holomorphic $f=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ and consider the flow with velocity field \[ \class{ntn-Vfl}{V}=\nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=(\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x,\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y). \] $f$ is the complex potential of the flow, and $f'$ its complex velocity. $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}$ is the velocity potential and $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ the stream function, as in Prop. 1.8.1.
DerivedProposition 1.10.2. $f'=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x-i\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y$. So $\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}$ is the flow associated to $f'$ in the sense of §1.6 ($f'=u-iv$ with $(u,v)=\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}$); the velocity vector is $\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}=\overline{f'}$, and the speed is $|f'|$.
Proof. By Theorem 1.5.2 and the Cauchy–Riemann equation $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x=-\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y$: $f'=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x-i\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y$. Its complex conjugate is $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x+i\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y$, which corresponds to the vector $(\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x,\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y)=\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}$. The speed is $|\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}|=|\overline{f'}|=|f'|$. ∎

Two things to explain: the curves $\{\operatorname{Im}f=c\}$ are the streamlines, the paths the particles follow (§1.11); and the flux across a curve from $A$ to $B$ is $\operatorname{Im}f(B)-\operatorname{Im}f(A)$ (§1.12).

L1 · Slide 20

1.11 Streamlines: the level sets of $\operatorname{Im}f$

Setup. $f=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ holomorphic, velocity $\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}=\nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=(\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x,\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y)$. By Cauchy–Riemann, $\nabla\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=(\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x,\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_y)=(-\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y,\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x)$ is $\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}$ rotated by $90°$ anticlockwise.

DefinedDefinition 1.11.1 (streamline). A streamline is the path of a fluid particle: a curve $\gamma(t)$ whose velocity is that of the fluid, \[ \gamma'(t)=\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}(\gamma(t))=\nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}(\gamma(t)). \]
DerivedProposition 1.11.2 ($\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ is conserved along streamlines). $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ does not change along a streamline. So a particle starting on $\{\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=c\}$ stays on $\{\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=c\}$: the level sets of $\operatorname{Im}f$ are the streamlines of the flow of $f'$.
Proof. By the chain rule, \[ \frac{d}{dt}\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}(\gamma(t))=\nabla\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}\cdot\gamma'(t)=\nabla\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}\cdot\nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=(-\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y,\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x)\cdot(\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x,\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y)=-\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x+\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y=0. \] A function with zero derivative on an interval is constant (mean value theoremA.3). ∎

So $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ is a conserved quantity of the motion. Geometrically: $\nabla\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}\perp \class{ntn-Vfl}{V}$, so the velocity is always tangent to the level curves of $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$.

L1 · Slide 21

1.12 How much fluid crosses a curve?

Pick a holomorphic $f=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$, with its flow $\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}=\nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}$ (the flow described by $f'$), and a curve $C$ from $A$ to $B$. How much fluid passes through $C$ per unit time? This is the flux of $\class{ntn-Vfl}{V}$ across $C$. With $(dx,dy)$ the tangent displacement and $n\,ds:=(dy,-dx)$ the normal (pointing to the right of the direction of travel; fluxA.5), \[ \text{flux}=\int_CV\cdot n\,ds=\int_C\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x\,dy-\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y\,dx. \]

DerivedProposition 1.12.1. The flux across $C$ is $\operatorname{Im}f(B)-\operatorname{Im}f(A)$: it depends only on the endpoints.
Proof. By Cauchy–Riemann, $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x=\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_y$ and $-\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y=\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x$, so the integrand is $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_y\,dy+\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x\,dx=d\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$, the change of $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ along the curve. Concretely, parametrize $C$ by $\gamma(s)$, $s\in[a,b]$; then \[ \int_C\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_x\,dx+\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}_y\,dy=\int_a^b\nabla\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}(\gamma(s))\cdot\gamma'(s)\,ds=\int_a^b\frac{d}{ds}\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}(\gamma(s))\,ds=\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}(B)-\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}(A) \] by the chain rule and the fundamental theorem of calculusA.9. ∎

Consequence. Between two streamlines $\{\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=c_1\}$ and $\{\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=c_2\}$ the flow rate is $c_2-c_1$, wherever you cut across. So where streamlines come closer together, the fluid moves faster.

L1 · Slides 22–23

1.13 Examples 1 and 2: uniform flow and a stagnation point

DerivedExample 1.13.1 ($f'(z)=1$). The flow. $f'=1=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x-i\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y$: velocity field $V=(1,0)$. Every particle moves to the right at unit speed.
The primitive. $f(z)=z=x+iy$, so $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=x$, $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=y$.
The streamlines. $\{\operatorname{Im}f=c\}=\{y=c\}$: horizontal lines.
The flux across the vertical segment from $A=(0,0)$ to $B=(0,h)$ is $h$, and $\operatorname{Im}f(B)-\operatorname{Im}f(A)=h-0=h$.
Check. $f'=1$ means $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x=1$, $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y=0$. $\nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=\nabla x=(1,0)=V$. Travelling up the segment, $(dx,dy)=(0,ds)$, so $n=(1,0)$ and $V\cdot n=1$ along a segment of length $h$: flux $h$, matching Prop. 1.12.1. ∎
DerivedExample 1.13.2 ($f'(z)=z$). The flow. $f'=x+iy=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x-i\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y$, so the velocity at $(x,y)$ is $V=(x,-y)$: away from the $y$-axis horizontally, toward the $x$-axis vertically. At the origin the velocity is $0$: a stagnation point.
The primitive. $f(z)=\frac12z^2=\frac12(x^2-y^2)+i\,xy$.
The streamlines. $\{\operatorname{Im}f=c\}=\{xy=c\}$: hyperbolas with the axes as asymptotes. A particle comes in along the $y$-axis direction, turns, and leaves along the $x$-axis direction.
Check. Matching real and imaginary parts in $x+iy=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x-i\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y$ gives $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x=x$, $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y=-y$. $z^2=(x+iy)^2=x^2-y^2+2ixy$, so $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=\frac12(x^2-y^2)$ and $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=xy$, and $\nabla\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}=(x,-y)=V$. This is the stagnation-point field of Example 1.6.4. ∎
L1 · Slides 24–26

1.14 Example 3: $f'(z)=1/z$, a source

DerivedExample 1.14.1 ($f'(z)=1/z$). The flow. $f'=\frac1z=\frac{x-iy}{x^2+y^2}$, so $V=\frac{(x,y)}{r^2}$ with $r^2=x^2+y^2$: radially outward, speed $1/r$. A source at the origin.
A primitive on a disk not containing $0$: choose a continuous branch of the angle $\theta$ and set $f(z)=\log z=\log r+i\theta$.
The streamlines. $\{\theta=c\}$: rays from the origin.
Check. $\frac1z=\frac{\bar z}{|z|^2}=\frac{x-iy}{r^2}$, so $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_x=x/r^2$ and $\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}_y=y/r^2$, and the speed is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}/r^2=1/r$. On a disk not containing $0$ the angle can be chosen continuously (branches of the logarithmE.3). $\nabla\log r=\nabla\tfrac12\log(x^2+y^2)=\frac{(x,y)}{r^2}=V$. The level sets of $\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}=\theta$ are rays. ∎

Compare Lecture 2: there the same $1/z$, scaled by $\frac1{2\pi}$, is the electric field of a unit point charge (Def. 2.4.1). Here it is the velocity of a fluid source of strength $2\pi$.

DerivedProposition 1.14.2 ($1/z$ has a genuine singularity at $0$). (a) The flux of the flow of $1/z$ out of any circle $|z|=\rho$ is $2\pi$. (b) $1/z$ has no holomorphic extension to a disk containing such a circle.
Proof. (a) Across $|z|=\rho$ the fluid moves outward at speed $1/\rho$, perpendicular to the circle, along a curve of length $2\pi\rho$: the flux is $\frac1\rho\cdot2\pi\rho=2\pi\ne0$. Fluid is being created at the origin.
(b) Suppose $1/z$ had a holomorphic extension $g$ to a disk containing the circle (with $C^2$ parts, Standing assumption 1.9.2). Then $g$ would have a primitive $f$ on that disk (Prop. 1.8.1), and by Prop. 1.12.1 the flux across the circle, a closed curve from $A$ back to $B=A$, would be $\operatorname{Im}f(B)-\operatorname{Im}f(A)=0$. But $g=1/z$ on the circle, so the flux is $2\pi$. So there is no such disk: the origin is a genuine singularity. ∎

The vortex $f'=-i/z$ tells the same story with flux replaced by circulation: $-\frac iz=\frac{-y-ix}{r^2}$ gives $V=\frac{(-y,x)}{r^2}$, so the streamlines are circles around the origin, and the circulation around any of them is $\frac1\rho\cdot2\pi\rho=2\pi$.

DerivedProposition 1.14.3 (no global primitive on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$). $1/z$ has no holomorphic primitive on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$.
Proof. $\operatorname{Im}\log z=\theta$ increases by $2\pi$ once around the circle, so $\log z$ is not single-valued on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. Any other primitive would differ from a local branch of $\log z$ by a constant (the difference has derivative $0$, so it is constant on connected pieces), so it would have the same $2\pi$ jump. Equivalently, by Prop. 1.12.1, a primitive $f$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ would give flux $\operatorname{Im}f(A)-\operatorname{Im}f(A)=0$ around the unit circle, contradicting Prop. 1.14.2(a). ∎

This is why the Poincaré lemma (Fact 1.7.1) was stated on a disk: on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, the curl-free field $(-v,u)$ for $V=(x,y)/r^2$ is not a gradient.

L1 · Slides 27–28

1.15 Example 4: flow past a cylinder

DerivedExample 1.15.1 ($f(z)=z+1/z$). This time start from the primitive. $f(z)=z+1/z$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and \[ \operatorname{Im}f=y-\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}=y\Big(1-\frac1{r^2}\Big). \] The streamlines are the curves $y\,(1-1/r^2)=c$.
– $c=0$ gives the unit circle $r=1$ (together with the $x$-axis). So the unit circle is a streamline: no fluid crosses it. The flow does not notice whether the disk is full of fluid or a solid cylinder.
– For large $r$, $\operatorname{Im}f\approx y$: far away, the uniform flow of Example 1.13.1.
Check. $\frac1z=\frac{x-iy}{r^2}$ has imaginary part $-y/r^2$, so $\operatorname{Im}f=y-y/r^2$. It is zero when $y=0$ or $r=1$. As $r\to\infty$, $y/r^2\to0$ relative to $y$. ∎
DerivedProposition 1.15.2 (where is the fluid fast?). The velocity is $\overline{f'(z)}$, with $f'(z)=1-\frac1{z^2}$; the speed is $|f'(z)|$. On the circle $z=e^{i\theta}$, $\ |f'|=|1-e^{-2i\theta}|=2|\sin\theta|$.
– It vanishes at $z=\pm1$: stagnation points at the front and back of the cylinder. The fluid comes to rest there and splits to go around.
– At the top, $z=i$: $f'(i)=1-1/i^2=2$, and likewise at the bottom. The fluid moves at twice the far-field speed there.
Proof. Velocity and speed: Prop. 1.10.2. On the circle, $z^2=e^{2i\theta}$, so $\frac1{z^2}=e^{-2i\theta}$ and \[ |1-e^{-2i\theta}|=|e^{-i\theta}|\,|e^{i\theta}-e^{-i\theta}|=1\cdot|2i\sin\theta|=2|\sin\theta|, \] using $e^{i\theta}-e^{-i\theta}=2i\sin\theta$. This is $0$ at $\theta=0,\pi$ ($z=\pm1$) and $2$ at $\theta=\pm\pi/2$ ($z=\pm i$). Directly, $i^2=-1$ gives $f'(i)=1+1=2$. ∎

Look at the picture: above and below the cylinder the streamlines are squeezed together. That is the flux proposition at work (Prop. 1.12.1): the same amount of fluid has to pass through a narrower channel, so it speeds up.

L1 · Slide 29

1.16 Four flows

Streamlines $\{\operatorname{Im}f=c\}$, and level sets $\{\operatorname{Re}f=c\}$ of the velocity potential, for four complex potentials:

  • $z^2$: flow into a corner. Stagnation point at $0$: streamlines spread apart, speed $0$. (Example 1.13.2, doubled.)
  • A branch of $\log z$: source. A branch of $-i\log z$: vortex, since $\operatorname{Im}(-i\log z)=\operatorname{Im}(-i\log r+\theta)=-\log r$, whose level sets are circles. Neither extends holomorphically across $0$: the flux out of (respectively the circulation around) a circle about $0$ is $2\pi\ne0$, impossible for an incompressible, irrotational flow on a disk containing $0$ (Prop. 1.14.2).
  • $z+1/z$: uniform flow past the unit disk; the circle $|z|=1$ is itself a streamline ($\psi=0$).

The level sets of $\operatorname{Re}f$ and $\operatorname{Im}f$ always cross at right angles where $f'\ne0$, because $\nabla\psi$ is $\nabla\varphi$ rotated by $90°$ (§1.11). Lecture 2 reinterprets the same pictures as electric fields.

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 1.16.1 (a holomorphic flow; Homework 1, Problem 1). Consider the complex potential $F(z)=\frac{z^3}3$, with velocity field $V=\overline{F'(z)}$ (Prop. 1.10.2).
  1. Write $V=(u,v)$ explicitly in terms of $x$ and $y$.
  2. Verify directly that $V$ is divergence-free and curl-free.
  3. Find an equation for the streamlines, and sketch the streamline $\operatorname{Im}F=0$ with several nearby streamlines. Indicate the direction of the flow.
  4. Find every stagnation point and express the speed $|V|$ in terms of $|z|$.
  5. Let $C$ be the vertical segment from $A=(0,-1)$ to $B=(0,1)$, oriented upward. Compute the flux across $C$ both directly and from $\operatorname{Im}F(B)-\operatorname{Im}F(A)$.
Hint
  • If $F'=a+ib$, then $V=(a,-b)$.
  • Expand $(x+iy)^2$ and $(x+iy)^3$ before taking real and imaginary parts.
  • Streamlines are the level curves $\operatorname{Im}F=c$ (Prop. 1.11.2).
  • On an oriented curve, the convention is $n\,ds=(dy,-dx)$ (§1.12).
  • Your two flux calculations should agree in sign as well as size (Prop. 1.12.1).
Solution
  1. $F'(z)=z^2=(x^2-y^2)+2ixy$, so by Prop. 1.10.2 (velocity $=\overline{F'}$, with $F$ the complex potential of Def. 1.10.1) $V=\overline{F'}=(x^2-y^2,\,-2xy)$.
  2. $\operatorname{div}V=\partial_x(x^2-y^2)+\partial_y(-2xy)=2x-2x=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}V=\partial_x(-2xy)-\partial_y(x^2-y^2)=-2y+2y=0$ (Def. 1.6.1). This is no accident: it is Prop. 1.6.2 applied to the holomorphic $F'$, and by Prop. 1.6.3 the flow is incompressible and irrotational.
  3. $F=\frac13(x+iy)^3=\frac13\big(x^3-3xy^2\big)+\frac i3\big(3x^2y-y^3\big)$, so, as streamlines are the level sets of $\operatorname{Im}F$ (Def. 1.11.1, Prop. 1.11.2), they are \[ \operatorname{Im}F=x^2y-\tfrac13y^3=y\big(x^2-\tfrac13y^2\big)=c. \] For $c=0$: $y=0$ or $y=\pm\sqrt3\,x$, three lines through $0$ at angles $0°,60°,120°$. They cut the plane into six sectors, and the other streamlines are hyperbola-like curves in each sector, asymptotic to the two bounding lines. Direction: on the real axis $V=(x^2,0)$ points right, so the flow comes in along the negative real axis and leaves along the positive one; the pattern repeats with three-fold symmetry (a "monkey saddle" flow, compare the corner flow of Example 1.13.2).
  4. $V=0\iff z^2=0\iff z=0$: the only stagnation point is the origin (compare the stagnation points of Prop. 1.15.2). Speed $|V|=|F'(z)|=|z|^2$, since the speed is $|F'|$ (Prop. 1.10.2).
  5. Directly: with the convention $n\,ds=(dy,-dx)$ of §1.12, on $C$ we have $x=0$, $dx=0$, so $n\,ds=(dy,0)$ and $V\cdot n\,ds=(x^2-y^2)\,dy=-y^2\,dy$. Flux $=\int_{-1}^1-y^2\,dy=-\frac23$.
    From the stream function (Prop. 1.12.1: flux $=\operatorname{Im}F(B)-\operatorname{Im}F(A)$): $\operatorname{Im}F(0,1)=1\cdot(0-\frac13)=-\frac13$ and $\operatorname{Im}F(0,-1)=(-1)(0-\frac13)=\frac13$, so the flux is $-\frac13-\frac13=-\frac23$. ✓ (Negative: the fluid crosses $C$ from right to left, against $n$, which points right for an upward curve.)
Part I · Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem

Lecture 2 · Electrostatics, Gauss's theorem, and harmonic functions

Goal
Read holomorphic functions as charge-free electric fields; prove Gauss's theorem and its complex form; show $u$ and $v$ are harmonic; prove the Dirichlet problem has at most one solution.
Main results
Theorem 2.5.1 (Gauss) · Cor. 2.6.3 (Cauchy) · Prop. 2.7.4 (residue) · Prop. 2.8.1 (harmonic parts) · Theorem 2.9.1 (uniqueness)
Uses
Lecture 1; the divergence theorem (A.6).
Used later
Lecture 3 (existence) · Lecture 6 (Cauchy's theorem in general) · Lecture 9 (logarithmic potentials).

Slide 1 is the title slide.

L2 · Slides 2–3

2.1 Recall from last time

These two slides recap Lecture 1 (Part I). Points of the plane are written $z=x+iy$ (complex notationC.1).

DefinedDefinition 2.1.1 (holomorphic). A function $f$ on an open set $D\subseteq\mathbb C$ is holomorphic if the complex limit \[ f'(z)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(z+h)-f(z)}{h},\qquad h\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}, \] exists at every $z\in D$. This restates Def. 1.1.1.
DerivedTheorem 2.1.2 (three descriptions, from Lecture 1). Let $D\subseteq\mathbb C$ be an open disk and $u,v:D\to\R$ of class $C^1$D.1. The following are equivalent:
  1. $f=u-iv$ is holomorphic on $D$;
  2. the vector field $(u,v)$ is divergence-free and curl-free: $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}(u,v)=0$ and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}(u,v)=0$;
  3. $u$ and $v$ satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations \[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0. \]
Proof. (2)⇔(3) is the definition of div and curl (Def. 1.6.1). (1)⇔(3): $C^1$ functions are differentiable as real maps (A.1), so Theorem 1.5.2 applies to $f=u+i(-v)$ at every point, and its Cauchy–Riemann equations for the pair $(u,-v)$ are exactly (3). This is Prop. 1.6.2. ∎

(2) and (3) say the same thing, since by definition $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}(u,v)=u_x+v_y$ and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}(u,v)=v_x-u_y$ (divergence and curlA.5). The equivalence with (1) is Prop. 1.6.2. Note the minus sign in $f=u-iv$: it pairs the vector field $(u,v)$ with $f$ so that these equations come out in div/curl form. With the more common convention $f=U+iV$ one has $U=u$, $V=-v$.

In fluid terms, $(u,v)$ is the velocity field of an incompressible (divergence-free: no fluid created or destroyed) and irrotational (curl-free: no local spinning) flow.

L2 · Slides 4–5

2.2 A second interpretation: electrostatics

DefinedDefinition 2.2.1 (electric field). Think of $(u,v)$ as an electric field $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}$ confined to two dimensions: the cross-section of the field of long charged wires perpendicular to the plane. A test charge $q$ placed at $(x,y)$ feels the force \[ q\,\class{ntn-Ef}{E}(x,y)=q\,\big(u(x,y),v(x,y)\big), \] so $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}$ is the force per unit charge. (For fluids, $(u,v)$ was the velocity of the particle at $(x,y)$.)
AssumedHypothesis 2.2.2 (the laws of electrostatics). In units where $\varepsilon_0=1$, \[ \class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho},\qquad\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=0, \] where $\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho}$ is the charge density. With the electrostatic voltage (potential) $\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}$, the sign convention is $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=-\nabla\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}$.

These are physical laws (Gauss's law and the static case of Faraday's law; see Maxwell's equationsE.4), not theorems. Here $\varepsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space, unrelated to the grid size $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}$ of Lecture 3.

DerivedProposition 2.2.3 (no charge means holomorphic). In a disk with no charge ($\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho}=0$) and $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=(u,v)$ of class $C^1$, $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=0$ and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=0$, so $f=u-iv$ is holomorphic. Here $f$ represents the electric field itself.
Proof. Put $\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho}=0$ in Hypothesis 2.2.2: these are exactly condition (2) of Theorem 2.1.2, which gives (1). ∎
Remark 2.2.4 (the potential, and where Lectures 3–5 come in). If $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=-\nabla\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}$ with $\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}$ of class $C^2$, then $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=-(\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}_{yx}-\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}_{xy})=0$ automatically (mixed partials commuteA.2), and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=-(\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}_{xx}+\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}_{yy})=-\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}$. So the law $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho}$ becomes $-\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}=\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho}$, and in a charge-free region the voltage is harmonic (Def. 2.8.2): $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}=0$. Prescribing the voltage on the boundary of a region, as on the plates of a capacitor, and asking for the voltage inside is the Dirichlet problem of Lectures 3–5.
L2 · Slide 6

2.3 Where are the charges?

The condition $\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho}=0$ does not force the field to vanish: a constant electric field $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=(a,b)$ has $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=0$ and is not zero. A field is determined only after boundary conditions or behaviour at infinity are also prescribed. (Lecture 2 makes this precise in §2.9: with boundary values prescribed, there is only one field.)

The right way to think about it: our holomorphic $f$ is defined on a region $D$ (a disk, say). The charges are outside $D$: on plates and wires surrounding it, at infinity, or at points we have excluded from $D$. Inside $D$ there is no charge, so $\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho}=0$ there, and that is all the Cauchy–Riemann equations say.

DerivedExample 2.3.1 (a charge just outside). $f(z)=\dfrac1{z-a}$ is holomorphic on any disk $D$ not containing $a$. Its source is the point $a$, outside the region. Likewise $f=1/z$ is holomorphic on $D=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and the charge is at the one point we left out.
Proof. For $z\ne a$ and small $h$, \[ \frac{1}{h}\Big(\frac1{z+h-a}-\frac1{z-a}\Big)=\frac1h\cdot\frac{(z-a)-(z+h-a)}{(z+h-a)(z-a)}=\frac{-1}{(z+h-a)(z-a)}\longrightarrow\frac{-1}{(z-a)^2} \] as $h\to0$ in $\mathbb C$, by the same algebra as for real numbers. So $f'(z)=-1/(z-a)^2$ exists wherever $z\ne a$. ∎

Holomorphic functions describe the electric field away from the charges.

L2 · Slides 7–9

2.4 What does a charge contribute?

DefinedDefinition 2.4.1 (the field of a unit charge). For $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$, with $r^2=x^2+y^2$, \[ \class{ntn-E0}{E_0}:=\frac1{2\pi}\,\frac{(x,y)}{x^2+y^2},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \class{ntn-f0}{f_0}=u_0-iv_0=\frac1{2\pi}\cdot\frac1z. \]

The two forms agree: $\frac1z=\frac{\bar z}{z\bar z}=\frac{x-iy}{x^2+y^2}$, so $u_0-iv_0=\frac1{2\pi}\cdot\frac{x-iy}{r^2}$ gives $u_0=\frac{x}{2\pi r^2}$ and $v_0=\frac{y}{2\pi r^2}$. $\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}$ points straight away from the origin and has length $\frac1{2\pi r}$: it weakens like $1/r$, the two-dimensional version of Coulomb's $1/r^2$.

DefinedDefinition 2.4.2 (meaning of "$\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=\class{ntn-dlt}{\delta_0}$"). "$\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=\class{ntn-dlt}{\delta_0}$" is shorthand for: for every region $D$ with smooth boundaryC.3 not passing through $0$, \[ \oint_{\partial D}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}\cdot n\,ds=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }0\in D,\\0&\text{if }0\notin\overline D.\end{cases} \] This is what the divergence theoremA.6 would give for a unit charge concentrated at the origin: total "divergence" $1$ at the single point $0$, and none elsewhere. Similarly "$\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=0$" means: the circulation $\oint \class{ntn-E0}{E_0}\cdot t\,ds$ around every such boundary is $0$. The symbol $\class{ntn-dlt}{\delta_0}$ is the Dirac deltaE.13, a unit mass at $0$.
DerivedTheorem 2.4.3 (the claim). $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=\class{ntn-dlt}{\delta_0}$ and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=0$, in the sense of Def. 2.4.2.
Proof.
  1. Away from $0$ (slide 8). With $r^2=x^2+y^2$, the quotient rule gives $\partial_x\frac{x}{r^2}=\frac{r^2-x\cdot2x}{r^4}$ and $\partial_y\frac{y}{r^2}=\frac{r^2-2y^2}{r^4}$, so \[ 2\pi\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{x}{r^2}+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{y}{r^2}=\frac{r^2-2x^2}{r^4}+\frac{r^2-2y^2}{r^4}=\frac{2r^2-2(x^2+y^2)}{r^4}=0, \] \[ 2\pi\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{y}{r^2}-\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{x}{r^2}=\frac{-2xy+2xy}{r^4}=0. \]
  2. Regions not containing $0$. If $0\notin\overline D$, then $\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}$ is $C^1$ on $\overline D$ with zero divergence and curl, so the divergence theorem gives flux $\iint_D\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=0$, and Green's theoremA.6 gives circulation $\iint_D\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=0$.
  3. Through a circle $|z|=r$ (slide 9). The outward normal is $n=(x,y)/r$, so \[ \class{ntn-E0}{E_0}\cdot n=\frac1{2\pi}\cdot\frac{x\cdot x+y\cdot y}{r^2\cdot r}=\frac1{2\pi r},\qquad\oint_{|z|=r}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}\cdot n\,ds=\frac1{2\pi r}\cdot2\pi r=1\quad\text{for every }r. \] Because $\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}$ is radial, it is perpendicular to the circle's tangent $t$, so $\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}\cdot t=0$ and the circulation around the circle is $0$.
  4. Through any loop around $0$. Let $0\in D$ and remove a small closed disk $|z|\le\epsilon$ inside $D$. On the remaining region $D_\epsilon$ (with a hole), $\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}$ is $C^1$ with zero divergence and curl. Its boundary is $\partial D$ (traversed with outward normal) together with the small circle, whose outward normal for $D_\epsilon$ points towards $0$. The divergence theorem on $D_\epsilon$ gives \[ 0=\iint_{D_\epsilon}\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}=\oint_{\partial D}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}\cdot n\,ds-\oint_{|z|=\epsilon}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}\cdot n_{\text{away from }0}\,ds=\oint_{\partial D}\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}\cdot n\,ds-1, \] so the flux out of $\partial D$ is $1$. Green's theorem on $D_\epsilon$ gives in the same way that the circulation around $\partial D$ equals the circulation around the small circle, which is $0$ by step 3. So no curl is concentrated at the origin. ∎
Remark 2.4.4 (consequence: the singularity is the charge). Maxwell's equations are linear. So adding $q \class{ntn-f0}{f_0}=\frac{q}{2\pi}\cdot\frac1z$ to $f$ adds $q\,\class{ntn-dlt}{\delta_0}$ to $\rho$ and nothing to $\partial_tB$ (the magnetic term in Faraday's law, so the field stays static). Translating the origin to $z_0$:

A point charge $q$ at $z_0$ is the term $\dfrac{q}{2\pi}\cdot\dfrac1{z-z_0}$ in $f$. The singularity is the charge.

The voltage of the unit charge is $\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}_0=-\frac1{2\pi}\log|z|$, since $\nabla\log|z|=\frac{(x,y)}{r^2}=2\pi \class{ntn-E0}{E_0}$ and $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=-\nabla\class{ntn-Phi}{\Phi}$. Lecture 5 uses exactly this logarithm as its barrier (Def. 5.10.2; logarithmic potentialE.6).
L2 · Slides 10–11

2.5 Gauss's theorem

Suppose the charge consists of $k$ point charges $q_1,\dots,q_k$ at the points $z_1,\dots,z_k$: $\class{ntn-rhoc}{\rho}=\sum_jq_j\,\class{ntn-dlt}{\delta_{z_j}}$, so that $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=\sum_jq_j\,\class{ntn-dlt}{\delta_{z_j}}$ and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=0$. By Remark 2.4.4 this means precisely \[ \class{ntn-Ef}{E}=H+\sum_{j=1}^kq_j\,\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}(\cdot-z_j), \] where $H$ is a $C^1$ field with $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}H=\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}H=0$ on a region containing $\overline D$ (the field of the charges outside), and $\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}(\cdot-z_j)$ is the unit-charge field moved to $z_j$.

DerivedTheorem 2.5.1 (Gauss's theorem). Let $\gamma$ be a positively oriented simple closed curveC.3 bounding a region $D$, not passing through any $z_j$. Then \[ \oint_\gamma \class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot n\,ds=\sum_{z_j\in D}q_j\qquad\text{and}\qquad\oint_\gamma \class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot t\,ds=0. \]
Proof. The slide's one-line proof is \[ \oint_\gamma \class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot n\,ds=\iint_D\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}\,dA=\iint_D\sum_jq_j\,\class{ntn-dlt}{\delta_{z_j}}\,dA=\sum_{z_j\in D}q_j,\qquad\oint_\gamma \class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot t\,ds=\iint_D\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}\class{ntn-Ef}{E}\,dA=0. \] The middle steps integrate a delta, so here is the same computation term by term, using only results proved above. Both integrals are linear in $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}$.
  • For $H$: the divergence theorem and Green's theoremA.6 give flux $\iint_D\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}H=0$ and circulation $\iint_D\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}H=0$.
  • For $q_j\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}(\cdot-z_j)$: Theorem 2.4.3, moved to $z_j$, gives flux $q_j$ if $z_j\in D$ and $0$ if $z_j\notin\overline D$ (the case $z_j\in\gamma$ is excluded), and circulation $0$ in both cases.
Adding up gives $\sum_{z_j\in D}q_j$ and $0$. ∎

The shape of $\gamma$ does not matter, only which charges it encloses.

L2 · Slides 12–13

2.6 What Gauss's theorem says about complex functions

DefinedDefinition 2.6.1 (contour integral). For a closed curve $\gamma$ and $f=u-iv$, \[ \oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz:=\oint_\gamma(u-iv)(dx+i\,dy), \] a line integralA.5: parametrize $\gamma$ by $z(s)=x(s)+iy(s)$ and integrate $f(z(s))\,z'(s)\,ds$.
DerivedProposition 2.6.2 (contour integral = circulation + $i\cdot$flux). For a positively oriented closed curve, with $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}=(u,v)$, \[ \oint_\gamma f\,dz=\oint_\gamma \class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot t\,ds+i\oint_\gamma \class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot n\,ds. \] So, by Gauss's theorem, $\oint_\gamma f\,dz=\text{circulation}+i\cdot\text{flux}=i\sum_{z_j\in D}q_j$.
Proof. Multiply out, using $i^2=-1$: \[ \begin{aligned} f\,dz&=(u-iv)(dx+i\,dy)=u\,dx+iu\,dy-iv\,dx+v\,dy\\ &=\underbrace{(u\,dx+v\,dy)}_{\class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot t\,ds}+i\,\underbrace{(u\,dy-v\,dx)}_{\class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot n\,ds}. \end{aligned} \] On a curve, the tangent displacement is $t\,ds=(dx,dy)$, so $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot t\,ds=u\,dx+v\,dy$. For a positively oriented curve (region on the left), the outward normal is the tangent turned clockwise by $90°$: $n\,ds=(dy,-dx)$, so $\class{ntn-Ef}{E}\cdot n\,ds=u\,dy-v\,dx$ (curves and orientationC.3). Integrate around $\gamma$ and apply Theorem 2.5.1. ∎
DerivedCorollary 2.6.3 (Cauchy's theorem). No charge inside $\gamma$, i.e. $f$ holomorphic on $D$: $\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz=0$.
Proof. No $z_j$ lies in $D$, so the sum is empty. ∎
DerivedCorollary 2.6.4 (the residue theorem, point-charge form). If $f$ is holomorphic on $D$ except for terms $\frac{q_j}{2\pi}\cdot\frac1{z-z_j}$ at points $z_j\in D$, then $\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz=i\sum_{z_j\in D}q_j$. For example $\oint_\gamma\frac{dz}{z-z_j}=2\pi i$ for any $\gamma$ around $z_j$.
Proof. The general statement is Prop. 2.6.2. For the example, $\frac1{z-z_j}=\frac{2\pi}{2\pi}\cdot\frac1{z-z_j}$ is a charge $q=2\pi$, giving $i\cdot2\pi$. Directly on a circle: $z=z_j+re^{i\theta}$, $dz=ire^{i\theta}d\theta$, so $\oint\frac{dz}{z-z_j}=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{ire^{i\theta}}{re^{i\theta}}d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}i\,d\theta=2\pi i$. ∎

Only the enclosed charges matter, not the shape of $\gamma$.

L2 · Slides 14–15

2.7 Multipoles and the residue

DerivedProposition 2.7.1 ($1/z^2$ has zero charge). $1/z^2$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and singular at $0$, yet $\oint_{|z|=r}\frac{dz}{z^2}=0$. More generally $\oint_{|z-z_0|=r}\frac{dz}{(z-z_0)^m}=0$ for every integer $m\ge2$.
Proof. Holomorphic: as in Example 2.3.1, the derivative is $-2/z^3$ for $z\ne0$. On the circle, $z=z_0+re^{i\theta}$ and $dz=ire^{i\theta}d\theta$, so \[ \oint\frac{dz}{(z-z_0)^m}=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{ire^{i\theta}}{r^me^{im\theta}}\,d\theta=i\,r^{1-m}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(1-m)\theta}\,d\theta=0, \] since for an integer $k=1-m\ne0$, $\int_0^{2\pi}e^{ik\theta}d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}(\cos k\theta+i\sin k\theta)\,d\theta=0$. With $m=2$ and $z_0=0$ this is the slide's $\frac ir\int_0^{2\pi}e^{-i\theta}d\theta=0$. ∎

By Gauss's theorem, the net charge at $0$ is zero. What kind of singularity has zero total charge but a nonzero field?

DerivedProposition 2.7.2 (a dipole). Put a charge $+q$ at $\delta$ and $-q$ at $0$, and let $\delta\to0$ with $q\delta=1$ fixed. Then for $z\ne0$ \[ \frac{q}{2\pi}\Big(\frac1{z-\delta}-\frac1z\Big)=\frac{q}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{\delta}{z(z-\delta)}\longrightarrow\frac1{2\pi}\cdot\frac1{z^2}. \]
Proof. Common denominator: $\frac1{z-\delta}-\frac1z=\frac{z-(z-\delta)}{z(z-\delta)}=\frac{\delta}{z(z-\delta)}$. Multiply by $\frac q{2\pi}$ and use $q\delta=1$: the expression is $\frac1{2\pi}\cdot\frac1{z(z-\delta)}$, which tends to $\frac1{2\pi z^2}$ as $\delta\to0$. ∎

Two opposite charges, infinitely close and infinitely strong: total charge $0$, but a nonzero dipole charge distribution (a derivative of a delta) and hence a field nonetheless. Likewise $1/z^3$ is a quadrupole (two dipoles, merged the same way), and so on. Here $\delta$ is a small displacement, not the delta function.

DefinedDefinition 2.7.3 (the residue). A singularity of $f$ at $z_0$ can be a whole combination of multipoles, \[ \frac{\class{ntn-a1}{a_1}}{z-z_0}+\frac{a_2}{(z-z_0)^2}+\frac{a_3}{(z-z_0)^3}+\cdots, \] plus a part holomorphic near $z_0$. The coefficient $\class{ntn-a1}{a_1}$ is the residue of $f$ at $z_0$. (That every isolated singularity has such an expansion is the theory of Laurent seriesE.5.)
DerivedProposition 2.7.4 (the contour integral sees only the residue). For $\gamma$ a small circle around $z_0$ (enclosing no other singularity), $\oint_\gamma f\,dz=2\pi i\,\class{ntn-a1}{a_1}$. If $\class{ntn-a1}{a_1}=\alpha+i\beta$, the net charge (flux) is $2\pi\alpha$ and the circulation is $-2\pi\beta$. For purely electric point charges $\class{ntn-a1}{a_1}$ is real, and the enclosed charge is $2\pi \class{ntn-a1}{a_1}$.
Proof. Integrate term by term (allowed when the series converges uniformly on the circle, A.17). The holomorphic part contributes $0$ (Cor. 2.6.3); the term $\class{ntn-a1}{a_1}/(z-z_0)$ contributes $2\pi i\,\class{ntn-a1}{a_1}$ (Cor. 2.6.4); every term with $m\ge2$ contributes $0$ (Prop. 2.7.1). So $\oint f\,dz=2\pi i(\alpha+i\beta)=-2\pi\beta+i\cdot2\pi\alpha$. Comparing with Prop. 2.6.2, $\text{circulation}+i\cdot\text{flux}$, the circulation is $-2\pi\beta$ and the flux $2\pi\alpha$. A point charge $q$ has $\class{ntn-a1}{a_1}=q/2\pi$ (Remark 2.4.4), which is real, and then flux $=2\pi \class{ntn-a1}{a_1}=q$. ∎
L2 · Slides 16–17

2.8 $u$ and $v$ are harmonic

DerivedProposition 2.8.1. If $u,v\in C^2$ satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations $u_x+v_y=0$, $v_x-u_y=0$, then $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ and $v_{xx}+v_{yy}=0$.
Proof. Apply $\partial_x$ to the first equation and $\partial_y$ to the second, then subtract: \[ (u_{xx}+v_{yx})-(v_{xy}-u_{yy})=u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0. \] Apply $\partial_y$ to the first and $\partial_x$ to the second, then add: \[ (u_{xy}+v_{yy})+(v_{xx}-u_{yx})=v_{xx}+v_{yy}=0. \] In both, the mixed partials cancel because $v_{yx}=v_{xy}$ and $u_{xy}=u_{yx}$ for $C^2$ functions (equality of mixed partialsA.2). This is where $C^2$ is needed. ∎
DefinedDefinition 2.8.2 (harmonic). A $C^2$ function $h$ is harmonic if $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h:=h_{xx}+h_{yy}=0$. The operator $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}$ is the Laplacian; equivalently $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h=\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}\nabla h$.

So $u$ and $v$ are harmonic. Note that $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h=0$ is the heat equation $\partial_th=\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h$ in two dimensions, for a temperature distribution $h$ that no longer changes in time: harmonic functions are equilibrium temperatures. Examples: every linear function $a+bx+cy$, $x^2-y^2$, $e^x\cos y$ (the real part of the holomorphic $e^z$), and $\log|z|$ away from $0$ (E.6).

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 2.8.3 (charges, dipoles and contour integrals; Homework 1, Problem 2). Consider the complex electric field \[ f(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\Big(\frac2{z-1}-\frac1{z+1}\Big)+\frac1{(z-i)^2}. \] All curves are positively oriented.
  1. Locate and state the strengths of the point charges. What does the term $1/(z-i)^2$ represent, and what is its net charge?
  2. Compute $\oint_\gamma f\,dz$ for $\gamma_1:|z-1|=\frac14$, $\gamma_2:|z-i|=\frac14$, $\gamma_3:|z|=2$.
  3. For each curve, state the corresponding circulation and flux.
  4. Explain why the real and imaginary parts of $f$ are harmonic away from the three singular points.
Hint
  • A term $\frac{q}{2\pi(z-z_0)}$ represents a point charge $q$ at $z_0$ (Remark 2.4.4).
  • A second-order pole represents a dipole and has zero net charge (Prop. 2.7.1, Prop. 2.7.2).
  • $\oint_{|z-a|=r}\frac{dz}{z-a}=2\pi i$, and $\oint_{|z-a|=r}\frac{dz}{(z-a)^m}=0$ for $m\ge2$.
  • A term holomorphic on and inside a curve contributes zero (Cor. 2.6.3).
  • With $f=u-iv$, $\oint_\gamma f\,dz=\text{circulation}+i\cdot\text{flux}$ (Prop. 2.6.2).
Solution
  1. A term $\frac q{2\pi(z-z_0)}$ is the field of a charge $q$ at $z_0$ (Def. 2.4.1, Remark 2.4.4). So $\frac{2}{2\pi(z-1)}$: charge $+2$ at $z=1$; $\frac{-1}{2\pi(z+1)}$: charge $-1$ at $z=-1$. $\frac1{(z-i)^2}$ is a dipole at $i$ (Prop. 2.7.2) with net charge $0$ (Prop. 2.7.1).
  2. $\gamma_1$ encloses only $1$: the charge term gives $\frac{2}{2\pi}\cdot2\pi i=2i$ (Cor. 2.6.4: $\oint\frac{dz}{z-z_j}=2\pi i$), and the other terms are holomorphic inside, so contribute $0$ (Cor. 2.6.3): $\oint_{\gamma_1}f\,dz=2i$. $\gamma_2$ encloses only $i$: $\oint\frac{dz}{(z-i)^2}=0$ (the residue is $0$: Def. 2.7.3, Prop. 2.7.4) and the rest is holomorphic inside, so $0$. $\gamma_3$ encloses all three: by Cor. 2.6.4 and Prop. 2.7.4, $\frac1{2\pi}(2\cdot2\pi i-2\pi i)+0=i$.
  3. By Prop. 2.6.2, write each answer as circulation $+\,i\cdot$flux: $\gamma_1$: $2i$, circulation $0$, flux $2$. $\gamma_2$: circulation $0$, flux $0$. $\gamma_3$: $i$, circulation $0$, flux $1=2-1$, the total enclosed charge (Gauss, Theorem 2.5.1).
  4. Away from $1,-1,i$, $f$ is holomorphic: each term is, as in Example 2.3.1. Write $f=u-iv$. By Cauchy–Riemann (Theorem 1.5.2) $u_x=-v_y$ and $u_y=v_x$, i.e. $u_x+v_y=0$ and $v_x-u_y=0$: the field $(u,v)$ has no divergence and no curl, as in Prop. 2.2.3. Here $u,v$ are smooth, being rational functions of $x,y$ away from the poles (in general, Cor. 6.6.2). So Prop. 2.8.1 gives $\Delta u=\Delta v=0$: $u$ and $v$ are harmonic (Def. 2.8.2), and so are $\operatorname{Re}f=u$ and $\operatorname{Im}f=-v$.
L2 · Slides 18–20

2.9 Harmonic functions are determined by their boundary values

DerivedTheorem 2.9.1 (uniqueness). Let $\Omega$ be a bounded open set with piecewise $C^1$ boundaryC.3, and let $h_1,h_2\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ be harmonic on $\Omega$. If $h_1=h_2$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, then $h_1=h_2$ on all of $\Omega$.

Physically obvious for temperatures: hold the boundary of a plate at a prescribed temperature and wait; the equilibrium temperature inside is whatever it is, and nothing else. The proof is by the energy method. Here $C^2(\overline\Omega)$ means two continuous derivatives up to and including the boundary (function classesD.1); this is what the divergence theorem on $\Omega$ needs.

Proof. Let $w=h_1-h_2$. It is harmonic on $\Omega$ (the Laplacian is linear), $C^2$ up to the boundary, and zero on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  1. A product rule. For the vector field $w\nabla w=(w\,w_x,\ w\,w_y)$, \[ \operatorname{div}(w\nabla w)=\partial_x(w\,w_x)+\partial_y(w\,w_y)=(w_x^2+w\,w_{xx})+(w_y^2+w\,w_{yy})=|\nabla w|^2+w\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} w. \]
  2. The divergence theorem applied to $w\nabla w$, which is $C^1$ on $\overline\Omega$: \[ \iint_\Omega\operatorname{div}(w\nabla w)\,dA=\oint_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}w\,\nabla w\cdot n\,ds=0, \] the boundary integral vanishing because $w=0$ at every point of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  3. Combine. Integrating Step 1 over $\Omega$ and using Step 2, \[ 0=\iint_\Omega|\nabla w|^2\,dA+\iint_\Omega w\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} w\,dA=\iint_\Omega|\nabla w|^2\,dA,\qquad\text{since }\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} w=0. \]
  4. Conclude. The integrand $|\nabla w|^2$ is continuous and $\ge0$ with integral $0$, so $\nabla w\equiv0$ on $\Omega$ (zero integral forces zeroA.11). Hence $w$ is constant on each connected componentC.4 $\Omega'$ of $\Omega$: two points of $\Omega'$ can be joined by a path, and the derivative of $w$ along the path is $\nabla w\cdot(\text{velocity})=0$. Each constant is $0$: $\Omega'$ is bounded and nonempty, so it has a boundary point $p$, and $p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ (the argument of Cor. 4.4.1, step 5). By continuity $w(p)$ equals the constant, and $w(p)=0$. ∎
Remark 2.9.2 (energy). The quantity $\iint_\Omega|\nabla w|^2\,dA$ is the energy of $w$: the kinetic energy of the fluid, or the energy stored in the electric field. The proof says: a harmonic function with zero boundary values has zero energy, hence is zero. Lecture 3 builds on this: the same product rule is Prop. 3.3.3, the energy is Def. 3.13.1, and the harmonic function turns out to be the one minimizing energy (Lemma 3.13.2). Lecture 4 reproves uniqueness by the maximum principle (Cor. 4.4.2), which needs $h$ only continuous up to the boundary rather than $C^2$.
L2 · Slide 21

2.10 In practice: how does one compute the solution?

We know the boundary values determine the harmonic function. But given the boundary values, how do we find it? \[ \class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0\ \text{ in }\Omega,\qquad u=g\ \text{ on }\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}. \] The standard tool is the finite element method, in three steps: rewrite the problem in weak form; choose a finite-dimensional space of functions built on a grid; solve the resulting linear system. That is Lecture 3 (Part II, starting at §3.1), and at the end of it there is a concrete, finite-dimensional picture of why the boundary values determine everything (§3.11–§3.12).

Part I · Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem

Lecture 3 · The finite element method

Goal
Construct a candidate solution of the Dirichlet problem as the energy limit of finite element solutions.
Main results
Theorem 3.9.3 (the discrete problem is solvable) · Theorem 3.11.3 (discrete maximum principle) · Lemma 3.13.2 (energy minimization) · Theorem 3.17.2 (Poincaré) · Theorem 3.19.1 (a weak solution exists)
Uses
Lecture 2's energy; linear algebra (Appendix B); $L^2$ (Appendix D).
Used later
Lectures 4 and 5, which show the limit is a genuine solution.

3.1 The Dirichlet problem

Slide 1 is the title slide.

AssumedStanding setting 3.1.1. The slide leaves this implicit. $\Omega\subset\R^2$ is a bounded open setC.2 with boundaryC.2 $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, and $g:\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}\to\R$ is a given continuous function, the boundary data.
DefinedDefinition 3.1.2 (Dirichlet problem). Given $g$, find a harmonic function $u$, twice differentiable in $\Omega$ and continuous on $\overline\Omega$, such that \[ \class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u = 0 \ \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = g \ \text{on } \class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}. \] Here $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}$ is the Laplacian, and "harmonic" means $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ (Def. 2.8.2, Lecture 2). The regularity clause ("twice differentiable in $\Omega$, continuous on $\overline\Omega$") is not on the slide. It makes precise what "$\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ in $\Omega$" and "$u=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$" require.

The slide recalls that the previous lecture proved uniqueness: the problem has at most one solution. That is Theorem 2.9.1 (Lecture 2, by the energy method, for solutions $C^2$ up to the boundary). Lecture 4 proves it again under weaker assumptions (Cor. 4.4.2), and E.12 gives a third proof. This lecture works toward the other half, that a solution exists, and it does so constructively. The construction is a numerical method you could run on a computer.

L3 · Slide 3

3.2 The plan in three steps

Uniqueness does not say what the solution is, or that there is one. The finite element methodE.7 turns the differential equation into a finite linear system in three steps.

  1. Weak form (§3.3). Replace "$\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u = 0$ at every point" by "an integral identity holds against every test function". This uses only first derivatives of $u$, so it makes sense for functions with corners.
  2. Choose where to look (§3.4–§3.6). Replace $u$ by a function built from finitely many pieces, determined by its values at grid nodes. Replace "$u=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$" by "$U=g$ at the boundary nodes".
  3. Solve (§3.7–§3.9). The weak form restricted to these functions is an $n\times n$ linear system, and it has exactly one solution.

The slide promises two further outcomes. §3.10–§3.12 read the system as "each value is the average of its neighbours", which gives a discrete maximum principle and a concrete sense in which boundary values determine the solution. §3.13–§3.19 let the grid size tend to zero and prove that the discrete solutions converge to a function satisfying the weak form, under the grid assumptions 3.4.1 and 3.14.2.

L3 · Slide 4

3.3 The weak form

The slide says "take any function $w$ vanishing on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$". Some regularity is needed for the integrals below to exist. Throughout, "test function" means an admissible test functionD.4: continuous on $\overline\Omega$, piecewise continuously differentiable, and zero on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Hat functions (§3.4) and smooth functions both qualify.

DefinedDefinition 3.3.1 (energy form). For functions $u,w$ whose gradients are square-integrable on $\Omega$, \[ \class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w) := \iint_\Omega \nabla u\cdot\nabla w\,dA = \iint_\Omega \big(u_x w_x + u_y w_y\big)\,dA. \]
DerivedProposition 3.3.2 (properties of $a$). $a$ is a symmetric bilinear formB.1, and $\class{ntn-a}{a}(v,v)\ge 0$ for every $v$.
Proof. Linear in the first slot: $\nabla(\alpha u_1+\beta u_2)=\alpha\nabla u_1+\beta\nabla u_2$, the dot product is linear in each slot, and the integral is linear, so $\class{ntn-a}{a}(\alpha u_1+\beta u_2,w)=\alpha \class{ntn-a}{a}(u_1,w)+\beta \class{ntn-a}{a}(u_2,w)$. Symmetric: $\nabla u\cdot\nabla w=\nabla w\cdot\nabla u$ at every point. Linear in the second slot: this follows from the first two. Nonnegative: $\class{ntn-a}{a}(v,v)=\iint|\nabla v|^2\,dA$ is the integral of a nonnegative function. ∎
DerivedProposition 3.3.3 (the slide's computation). Let $u$ be twice continuously differentiable on $\overline\Omega$ with $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ in $\Omega$. Then $\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w)=0$ for every test function $w$.
Proof. Step 1 (product rule). Put $F := w\nabla u = (w u_x,\, w u_y)$. Then \[ \nabla\cdot F = \partial_x(w u_x)+\partial_y(w u_y) = (w_x u_x + w u_{xx}) + (w_y u_y + w u_{yy}) = \nabla w\cdot\nabla u + w\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u. \] Step 2 (integrate). Rearrange Step 1 as $w\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=\nabla\cdot F-\nabla w\cdot\nabla u$, integrate over $\Omega$, and apply the divergence theoremA.6 to the first term (the same computation as Steps 1–2 of Theorem 2.9.1): \[ \iint_\Omega w\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u\,dA = \oint_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}} w\,\nabla u\cdot n\,ds - \iint_\Omega \nabla w\cdot\nabla u\,dA. \] This is the "integration by parts" of the slide.
Step 3. The left side is $0$ because $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$. The boundary integral is $0$ because $w=0$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. So $0=-\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w)$, which is the slide's display.
Step 4 (piecewise smooth $w$). If $w$ is smooth only on pieces $P_1,\dots,P_m$ of $\Omega$, apply Steps 1–2 on each piece and add. A segment shared by two pieces appears in both boundary integrals with opposite outward normals and the same continuous integrand $w\nabla u$, so those contributions cancel. Only the outer boundary $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ remains, where $w=0$. ∎
DefinedDefinition 3.3.4 (weak form of the Dirichlet problem). Find $u$ with $u=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ such that \[ \class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w)=0 \quad\text{for every test function } w. \]
Remark 3.3.5. Proposition 3.3.3 proves one direction only: a smooth solution is a weak solution. The weak form asks for first derivatives only, so it also admits the functions with corners built below. The converse, that a weak solution is smooth and harmonic, is Weyl's lemma, proved in Lecture 4 (§4.6–§4.9).
L3 · Slide 5

3.4 A grid and hat functions

AssumedGrid hypothesis 3.4.1. Fix $\eps>0$ and grid lines $x_i = x_0+i\eps$, $y_j=y_0+j\eps$ with $i,j\in\mathbb Z$. $\overline\Omega$ is a finite union of closed grid squares $[x_i,x_{i+1}]\times[y_j,y_{j+1}]$, and $\Omega$ is the interior of that union.

Consequently $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is made of grid edges. An edge of a square in $\Omega$ lies on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ exactly when the square on its other side is not in $\Omega$. Call such an edge a boundary edge.

DefinedDefinition 3.4.2 (nodes). A node is a corner $(x_i,y_j)$ of some grid square contained in $\overline\Omega$.
DefinedDefinition 3.4.3 (tent and hat functions). The tent function in one variable is $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(t):=\max(0,\,1-|t|)$. The hat (basis) function at the node $(x_i,y_j)$ is \[ \class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}(x,y) := \class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}\!\Big(\frac{x-x_i}{\eps}\Big)\,\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}\!\Big(\frac{y-y_j}{\eps}\Big). \]
DerivedLemma 3.4.4 (the tent). $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}$ is continuous, $0\le\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}\le1$, $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(0)=1$, $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(m)=0$ for every nonzero integer $m$, and $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(t)=0$ for $|t|\ge1$. Away from $t\in\{-1,0,1\}$ it is differentiable, with \[ \class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}'(t)=\begin{cases} 1, & -1\lt t\lt 0,\\ -1, & 0\lt t\lt 1,\\ 0, & |t|\gt 1.\end{cases} \]
Proof. If $|t|\le1$ then $1-|t|\ge0$, so $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(t)=1-|t|$. If $|t|\ge1$ then $1-|t|\le0$, so $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(t)=0$. Every claim can be read off these two formulas; for a nonzero integer, $|m|\ge1$. The maximum of two continuous functions is continuous. ∎
DerivedProposition 3.4.5 (the hat). $\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ is continuous, equals $1$ at $(x_i,y_j)$, and vanishes outside the $2\eps\times2\eps$ block $[x_{i-1},x_{i+1}]\times[y_{j-1},y_{j+1}]$ (its supportC.7). Off the grid lines it is differentiable, with \[ \nabla\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}(x,y)=\frac1\eps\Big(\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}'\big(\tfrac{x-x_i}{\eps}\big)\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}\big(\tfrac{y-y_j}{\eps}\big),\ \class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}\big(\tfrac{x-x_i}{\eps}\big)\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}'\big(\tfrac{y-y_j}{\eps}\big)\Big). \] So $|\nabla\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}|\le\sqrt2/\eps$ and $\iint|\nabla\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}|^2\,dA\lt\infty$.
Proof. Continuity and the value $1\cdot1$ at the node follow from Lemma 3.4.4. If $|x-x_i|\ge\eps$ the first factor is $0$, and likewise in $y$, so the hat vanishes outside the block. The gradient comes from the product rule and the chain rule (inner derivative $1/\eps$). The kinks of $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}$ at $t\in\{-1,0,1\}$ correspond to $x\in\{x_{i-1},x_i,x_{i+1}\}$, which are grid lines, so off the grid lines both factors are differentiable. Each component has absolute value at most $1\cdot1/\eps$, so $|\nabla\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}|^2\le 2/\eps^2$. Integrating over the block, of area $4\eps^2$, gives at most $8$. The grid lines are finitely many segments, which have zero areaA.11, so leaving them out changes no integral. §3.10 computes the exact value, $8/3$. ∎
L3 · Slide 6

3.5 Nodal values and the space $\class{ntn-Veps}{V_\eps}$

DerivedLemma 3.5.1 (key property). $\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}(x_k,y_l)=1$ if $(k,l)=(i,j)$, and $0$ at every other node.
Proof. $(x_k-x_i)/\eps = k-i$ and $(y_l-y_j)/\eps=l-j$ are integers, so $\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}(x_k,y_l)=\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(k-i)\,\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(l-j)$. By Lemma 3.4.4 this is $1\cdot1$ when both integers are $0$, and $0$ when either is nonzero. ∎
DerivedCorollary 3.5.2 (the coefficients are the nodal values). If $U=\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ (summed over nodes), then $U(x_k,y_l)=c_{kl}$. In particular the hats are linearly independentB.2.
Proof. $U(x_k,y_l)=\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}(x_k,y_l)=c_{kl}$, since only the term with $(i,j)=(k,l)$ survives. If $U\equiv0$, evaluating at each node gives every $c_{kl}=0$. ∎
DefinedDefinition 3.5.3. $\class{ntn-Veps}{V_\eps} := \operatorname{span}\{\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}} : (x_i,y_j)\text{ a node}\}$, the set of functions $U=\sum c_{ij}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ restricted to $\overline\Omega$. (SpanB.2.)
DefinedDefinition 3.5.4 (bilinear). A function on a square is bilinear if it has the form $a+bx+cy+dxy$ there. In local coordinates $s=(x-x_i)/\eps$, $t=(y-y_j)/\eps\in[0,1]$ this is the same as the form $\alpha+\beta s+\gamma t+\delta st$, since substituting $x=x_i+\eps s$, $y=y_j+\eps t$ into one form gives the other.
DerivedLemma 3.5.5 (the four hats on one square). On the square $Q=[x_i,x_{i+1}]\times[y_j,y_{j+1}]$ with local coordinates $s,t\in[0,1]$, only the hats of the four corners are not identically zero, and \[ \class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}=(1-s)(1-t),\quad \class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{i+1,j}}=s(1-t),\quad \class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{i+1,j+1}}=st,\quad \class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{i,j+1}}=(1-s)t. \] Each is bilinear on $Q$.
Proof. For $x\in[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ we have $(x-x_i)/\eps=s\in[0,1]$, so $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(s)=1-s$. Also $(x-x_{i+1})/\eps=s-1\in[-1,0]$, so $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(s-1)=1-(1-s)=s$. The same holds in $y$; multiply. The hat of any other node has $|x-x_k|\ge\eps$ or $|y-y_l|\ge\eps$ throughout $Q$, so it vanishes on $Q$. Expanding, for example $(1-s)(1-t)=1-s-t+st$, shows each hat is bilinear. ∎
DerivedLemma 3.5.6 (a bilinear function is fixed by its corner values). Given four numbers $p_{00},p_{10},p_{01},p_{11}$, there is exactly one bilinear $p(s,t)=\alpha+\beta s+\gamma t+\delta st$ with $p(0,0)=p_{00}$, $p(1,0)=p_{10}$, $p(0,1)=p_{01}$, $p(1,1)=p_{11}$.
Proof. The conditions read $\alpha=p_{00}$, $\alpha+\beta=p_{10}$, $\alpha+\gamma=p_{01}$, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=p_{11}$. Solving in that order gives the unique answer \[ \alpha=p_{00},\quad \beta=p_{10}-p_{00},\quad \gamma=p_{01}-p_{00},\quad \delta=p_{11}-p_{10}-p_{01}+p_{00}. \] ∎
DerivedProposition 3.5.7 (the slide's description of $\class{ntn-Veps}{V_\eps}$). $\class{ntn-Veps}{V_\eps}$ is exactly the set of functions that are continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and bilinear on each grid square of $\Omega$.
Proof. (⊆) Each $\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ is continuous (Prop. 3.4.5) and bilinear on each square (Lemma 3.5.5, or identically $0$). Sums and multiples of continuous, squarewise-bilinear functions are again continuous and squarewise bilinear.
(⊇) Let $f$ be continuous and squarewise bilinear. Put $U:=\sum_{ij}f(x_i,y_j)\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}\in \class{ntn-Veps}{V_\eps}$. On any square, $f$ and $U$ are both bilinear and agree at the four corners (Cor. 3.5.2), so they agree on the whole square (Lemma 3.5.6). The squares cover $\overline\Omega$, so $f=U$. ∎
DerivedProposition 3.5.8 (linear along grid lines, not on squares). A bilinear function is linear (affine) along every horizontal and vertical segment of its square, in particular along every grid edge. It is not linear on the square when $\delta\ne0$.
Proof. Fix $t$. Then $\alpha+\beta s+\gamma t+\delta st=(\alpha+\gamma t)+(\beta+\delta t)s$, which is affine in $s$. The same argument works with $s$ fixed. Along the diagonal $s=t$ the function is $\alpha+(\beta+\gamma)s+\delta s^2$, which is not affine when $\delta\ne0$; this is the "$xy$ term" of the slide. ∎

This is also why continuity across a shared edge comes for free: the functions on the two sides are both linear on that edge and have the same endpoint values.

L3 · Slide 7

3.6 The spaces $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ and $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$

DefinedDefinition 3.6.1 (interior and boundary nodes). A node is interior if all four grid squares having it as a corner lie in $\overline\Omega$, and a boundary node otherwise. Write $I$ and $B$ for the two sets and $n:=|I|$.
DerivedLemma 3.6.2 (nodes and the boundary). (a) Every boundary node lies on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. (b) Both endpoints of every boundary edge are boundary nodes. (c) An interior node lies in $\Omega$, and its hat vanishes on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
Proof. (a) A boundary node $P$ is a corner of some square in $\overline\Omega$ (it is a node) and of some square not in $\overline\Omega$ (it is not interior). Every disc around $P$ meets the interiors of both squares, so it meets $\Omega$ and its complement. That is the definition of a boundary pointC.2.
(b) A boundary edge separates a square in $\Omega$ from a square $Q'$ not in $\Omega$. Each endpoint is a corner of $Q'$, so it is not interior, and a corner of the square in $\Omega$, so it is a node.
(c) If all four squares around $P$ are in $\overline\Omega$, the open $2\eps\times2\eps$ block around $P$ lies in $\Omega$. The hat $\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_P}$ vanishes outside that open block (Prop. 3.4.5, and $\class{ntn-Lam}{\Lambda}(\pm1)=0$ on its rim), and $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ does not meet the open block. ∎
DefinedDefinition 3.6.3. \[ \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps} := \{U\in \class{ntn-Veps}{V_\eps} : U(x_i,y_j)=g(x_i,y_j)\ \text{at every boundary node}\},\qquad \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps} := \{U\in \class{ntn-Veps}{V_\eps} : U=0\ \text{at every boundary node}\}. \] By Lemma 3.6.2(a), boundary nodes lie where $g$ is defined, so $g(x_i,y_j)$ makes sense.
DerivedProposition 3.6.4 ($\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ is affine, not linear). If $U,V\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ and $\lambda\in\R$, then $\lambda U+(1-\lambda)V\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ and $U-V\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$. $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ is not closed under addition unless $g=0$ at every boundary node.
Proof. At a boundary node, $\lambda U+(1-\lambda)V$ takes the value $\lambda g+(1-\lambda)g=g$, and $U-V$ takes $g-g=0$. The sum $U+V$ takes $2g$, which equals $g$ only where $g=0$. Closure under combinations whose coefficients add to 1 is what makes a set affineB.3; $\lambda=\tfrac12$ gives the slide's "averages". ∎
DerivedProposition 3.6.5 (the space $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$). (a) $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$ is a linear space. (b) Every $U\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$ vanishes on all of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. (c) $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}=\operatorname{span}\{\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}}:(k,l)\in \class{ntn-I}{I}\}$, so its dimensionB.2 is $n$. (d) Every $U\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ can be written $U=\class{ntn-Ug}{U_g}+W$, where $\class{ntn-Ug}{U_g}:=\sum_{\class{ntn-B}{B}}g(x_i,y_j)\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ is fixed and $W\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$.
