Proof. (a) Sums and multiples preserve the zero condition.
(b) $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is a union of boundary edges. On a boundary edge $U$ is linear (Prop. 3.5.8) and vanishes at both endpoints (Lemma 3.6.2(b)). A linear function of one variable that vanishes at two points is identically zero.
(c) By Cor. 3.5.2, $U=\sum_{\text{all nodes}}U(x_i,y_j)\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$, and the boundary coefficients are $0$, which leaves interior hats. Conversely, an interior hat is $0$ at every other node, in particular at every boundary node. Independence is Cor. 3.5.2.
(d) $\class{ntn-Ug}{U_g}\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ by Cor. 3.5.2, and $W:=U-\class{ntn-Ug}{U_g}\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$ by Prop. 3.6.4. ∎

So the search space $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ has exactly $n$ free parameters, the values at interior nodes: "finitely many unknowns, one per interior node."

L3 · Slide 8

3.7 The linear system

DefinedDefinition 3.7.1 (discrete problem). Find $U\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ such that \[ \class{ntn-a}{a}(U,w)=0\qquad\text{for every } w\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}. \] The trial function and the test functions are both restricted to finite-dimensional sets. This is an instance of the Galerkin methodE.7.

Every $w\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$ is a legitimate test function for the weak form: it is continuous, smooth on each open square, and zero on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ (Prop. 3.6.5(b)). The discrete problem gives up testing against every test function and uses only these $n$.

DefinedDefinition 3.7.2 (the matrix $A$). For nodes $(i,j),(k,l)$, \[ \class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}:=\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}},\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}})=\iint_\Omega\nabla\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}\cdot\nabla\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}}\,dA. \] In engineering this is called the stiffness matrixE.7.
DerivedProposition 3.7.3 (the equations). Make the ansatz $U=\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ with $c_{ij}=g(x_i,y_j)$ at boundary nodes. Then $U$ solves the discrete problem if and only if \[ \sum_{ij}\class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}\,c_{ij}=0\qquad\text{for every interior node }(k,l). \]
Proof. The ansatz puts $U$ in $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ (Cor. 3.5.2). By linearity of $a$ in its first slot, \[ \class{ntn-a}{a}(U,\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}})=a\Big(\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}},\,\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}}\Big)=\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\,\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}},\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}})=\sum_{ij}\class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}\,c_{ij}. \] (⇒) Each interior hat lies in $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$ and is an admissible $w$, so each sum is $0$.
(⇐) Any $w\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$ is $w=\sum_{(k,l)\in \class{ntn-I}{I}}d_{kl}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}}$ (Prop. 3.6.5(c)), and by linearity in the second slot $\class{ntn-a}{a}(U,w)=\sum d_{kl}\,\class{ntn-a}{a}(U,\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}})=0$. ∎

Count: one equation and one unknown $c_{kl}$ per interior node. The system is $n\times n$ whatever the shape of $\Omega$.

L3 · Slide 9

3.8 Block form

DefinedDefinition 3.8.1. Split the coefficient vector by node type: $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}=(c_p)_{p\in \class{ntn-I}{I}}$ is unknown and $\class{ntn-cB}{c_B}=\class{ntn-gB}{g_B}:=(g(x_q,y_q))_{q\in \class{ntn-B}{B}}$ is known. Split the matrix the same way: $\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}=(\class{ntn-A}{A_{pq}})_{p,q\in \class{ntn-I}{I}}$ and $\class{ntn-AIB}{A_{IB}}=(\class{ntn-A}{A_{pq}})_{p\in \class{ntn-I}{I},\,q\in \class{ntn-B}{B}}$. Here $p,q$ stand for node labels such as $(k,l)$ and $(i,j)$.
DerivedProposition 3.8.2. The equations of Prop. 3.7.3 are equivalent to \[ \class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}\,\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}=-\class{ntn-AIB}{A_{IB}}\,\class{ntn-gB}{g_B}. \]
Proof. For each $p\in \class{ntn-I}{I}$, split the sum over all nodes according to where $q$ lies: \[ 0=\sum_q \class{ntn-A}{A_{pq}}c_q=\sum_{q\in \class{ntn-I}{I}}\class{ntn-A}{A_{pq}}c_q+\sum_{q\in \class{ntn-B}{B}}\class{ntn-A}{A_{pq}}g_q=(\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}\class{ntn-cI}{c_I})_p+(\class{ntn-AIB}{A_{IB}}\class{ntn-gB}{g_B})_p. \] Move the known term to the right-hand side. ∎

The boundary data sits on the right and the unknowns on the left. It remains to show that $\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}$ is invertible.

L3 · Slide 10

3.9 The system has exactly one solution

DerivedLemma 3.9.1 (symmetry). $\class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}=\class{ntn-A}{A_{ij,kl}}$, so $A$ and $\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}$ are symmetric matricesB.4.
Proof. $\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}},\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}})=\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}},\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}})$ because $a$ is symmetric (Prop. 3.3.2). $\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}$ keeps the rows and columns of $A$ with the same index set $I$, so it inherits the symmetry. ∎
DerivedLemma 3.9.2 (the quadratic form is the energy). For any coefficient vector $c$ and $U=\sum c_{ij}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$, \[ c^{\mathsf T}\class{ntn-A}{A}c=\class{ntn-a}{a}(U,U)=\iint_\Omega|\nabla U|^2\,dA\ \ge 0. \]
Proof. Expand using linearity in both slots: \[ \class{ntn-a}{a}(U,U)=a\Big(\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}},\ \sum_{kl}c_{kl}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}}\Big)=\sum_{ij}\sum_{kl}c_{kl}\,\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}},\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}})\,c_{ij}=\sum_{kl,ij}c_{kl}\class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}c_{ij}=c^{\mathsf T}\class{ntn-A}{A}c. \] Nonnegativity is Prop. 3.3.2. ∎
DerivedTheorem 3.9.3 ($\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}$ is positive definite). For every nonzero $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}\in\R^n$, $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}^{\mathsf T}\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}\gt0$. So $\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}$ is positive definiteB.4, hence invertible, and the system has exactly one solution $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}$.
Proof. Extend $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}$ by zeros at the boundary nodes to get $c$ ("$c$ supported on the interior nodes"). Then $c^{\mathsf T}\class{ntn-A}{A}c=\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}^{\mathsf T}\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}$, since every term involving a boundary index is multiplied by $0$. The corresponding $U$ lies in $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$. Suppose $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}^{\mathsf T}\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}=0$; we show $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}=0$.
  1. $\nabla U\equiv0$. By Lemma 3.9.2, $\iint_\Omega|\nabla U|^2=0$. On each open square $|\nabla U|^2$ is continuous (a polynomial) and nonnegative, and a continuous nonnegative function with zero integral is zeroA.11. So $\nabla U\equiv0$ on every open square.
  2. $U$ is constant on each square. On a square, $U=\alpha+\beta s+\gamma t+\delta st$, and $\nabla U=\frac1\eps(\beta+\delta t,\ \gamma+\delta s)\equiv0$ forces $\beta=\gamma=\delta=0$.
  3. $U$ is constant on each connected piece. Two squares that share an edge have the same constant, because $U$ is continuous on the edge. So $U$ equals a single constant $\kappa$ on each cluster $C$ of squares linked through shared edges. These clusters are the slide's connected componentsC.4.
  4. Each cluster has boundary points. Pick a square $Q\in C$ whose left edge has the smallest $x$-coordinate among the squares of $C$. The square immediately left of $Q$ is not in $\Omega$: if it were, it would share an edge with $Q$ and belong to $C$, contradicting minimality. So the left edge of $Q$ is a boundary edge, its endpoints are boundary nodes (Lemma 3.6.2(b)), and $U=0$ there. Hence $\kappa=0$.
  5. So $U\equiv0$, and by Cor. 3.5.2 every $c_{kl}=0$.
This proves positive definiteness. Positive definite matrices are invertibleB.4, so $\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}=-\class{ntn-AIB}{A_{IB}}\class{ntn-gB}{g_B}$ has exactly one solution. ∎
DefinedDefinition 3.9.4 (the discrete solution). $\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}:=\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ with $\class{ntn-cB}{c_B}=\class{ntn-gB}{g_B}$ and $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}=-\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}^{-1}\class{ntn-AIB}{A_{IB}}\class{ntn-gB}{g_B}$. By Theorem 3.9.3 and Prop. 3.8.2 it is the unique solution of the discrete problem (Def. 3.7.1).
L3 · Slide 11

3.10 What the equations say: the stencil

DerivedLemma 3.10.1 (only neighbours interact). $\class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}=0$ unless the nodes $(i,j)$ and $(k,l)$ are corners of a common square, that is, $|i-k|\le1$ and $|j-l|\le1$.
Proof. On any open square only the four corner hats are nonzero (Lemma 3.5.5). If no square has both nodes as corners, then on every open square one of the two gradients is zero, so the integrand is zero except on grid lines, which have zero areaA.11. ∎
DerivedLemma 3.10.2 (integrating over one square). On one square $Q$, label its corners $1=(0,0)$, $2=(1,0)$, $3=(1,1)$, $4=(0,1)$ in local coordinates, with hats $\class{ntn-Na}{N_1},\dots,\class{ntn-Na}{N_4}$ as in Lemma 3.5.5. Then $\class{ntn-K}{K_{ab}}:=\iint_Q\nabla \class{ntn-Na}{N_a}\cdot\nabla \class{ntn-Na}{N_b}\,dA$ does not depend on $\eps$, and \[ \class{ntn-K}{K_{aa}}=\tfrac23,\qquad \class{ntn-K}{K_{ab}}=-\tfrac16\ \text{(edge-adjacent corners, e.g. 1,2)},\qquad \class{ntn-K}{K_{ab}}=-\tfrac13\ \text{(opposite corners, e.g. 1,3)}. \]
Proof. Substitute $x=x_i+\eps s$, $y=y_j+\eps t$. Then $\partial_x=\frac1\eps\partial_s$, $\partial_y=\frac1\eps\partial_t$ and $dA=\eps^2\,ds\,dt$, so \[ \class{ntn-K}{K_{ab}}=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\frac1{\eps^2}\big(\partial_s\class{ntn-Na}{N_a}\,\partial_s\class{ntn-Na}{N_b}+\partial_t\class{ntn-Na}{N_a}\,\partial_t\class{ntn-Na}{N_b}\big)\,\eps^2\,ds\,dt, \] and $\eps$ cancels. The partial derivatives are: \[ \begin{array}{c|cc} & \partial_s & \partial_t\\\hline \class{ntn-Na}{N_1}=(1-s)(1-t) & -(1-t) & -(1-s)\\ \class{ntn-Na}{N_2}=s(1-t) & 1-t & -s\\ \class{ntn-Na}{N_3}=st & t & s\\ \class{ntn-Na}{N_4}=(1-s)t & -t & 1-s\end{array} \] The one-dimensional integrals needed are $\int_0^1(1-t)^2dt=\int_0^1t^2dt=\tfrac13$ and $\int_0^1t(1-t)\,dt=\tfrac12-\tfrac13=\tfrac16$. An integrand depending only on $t$ integrates over $s\in[0,1]$ to itself, so \[ \begin{aligned} \class{ntn-K}{K_{11}}&=\iint\big[(1-t)^2+(1-s)^2\big]=\tfrac13+\tfrac13=\tfrac23,\\ \class{ntn-K}{K_{12}}&=\iint\big[-(1-t)^2+(1-s)s\big]=-\tfrac13+\tfrac16=-\tfrac16,\\ \class{ntn-K}{K_{13}}&=\iint\big[-(1-t)t-(1-s)s\big]=-\tfrac16-\tfrac16=-\tfrac13. \end{aligned} \] Rotating the square by $90°$ permutes the corners and preserves the integrals. So every diagonal entry equals $\class{ntn-K}{K_{11}}$, every edge-adjacent pair equals $\class{ntn-K}{K_{12}}$, and every opposite pair equals $\class{ntn-K}{K_{13}}$. As a check, each row sums to $\tfrac23-\tfrac16-\tfrac13-\tfrac16=0$. This must happen, because $\class{ntn-Na}{N_1}+\class{ntn-Na}{N_2}+\class{ntn-Na}{N_3}+\class{ntn-Na}{N_4}\equiv1$ has zero gradient. ∎
DerivedProposition 3.10.3 (summing over the four squares). Let $(k,l)$ be an interior node. Then \[ \class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,kl}}=\tfrac83,\qquad \class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}=-\tfrac13\ \text{for each of the 8 neighbours }(i,j),\qquad \class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}=0\ \text{otherwise}. \]
Proof. Since $(k,l)$ is interior, $\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}}$ is supported on four squares, all in $\Omega$. So $\class{ntn-A}{A_{kl,ij}}$ is the sum of the element entries over these four squares.
  • Diagonal: $(k,l)$ is a corner of all four squares, giving $4\cdot\tfrac23=\tfrac83$.
  • Edge neighbour, e.g. $(k+1,l)$: the edge joining the two nodes is shared by two of the four squares, and in each the nodes are edge-adjacent corners. This gives $2\cdot(-\tfrac16)=-\tfrac13$.
  • Diagonal neighbour, e.g. $(k+1,l+1)$: exactly one square has both as corners, as opposite corners. This gives $1\cdot(-\tfrac13)=-\tfrac13$.
  • All other nodes: Lemma 3.10.1. ∎
DerivedCorollary 3.10.4 (each interior value is the average of its eight neighbours). For every interior node, \[ c_{kl}=\frac18\sum_{\substack{(i,j)\text{ one of the}\\\text{8 neighbours of }(k,l)}}c_{ij}. \]
Proof. With Prop. 3.10.3, the equation of Prop. 3.7.3 reads $\tfrac83c_{kl}-\tfrac13\sum_{\text{nbrs}}c_{ij}=0$. Multiply by $\tfrac38$. Neighbours that are boundary nodes enter with their known values $c_{ij}=g(x_i,y_j)$. ∎

This is a discrete analogue of the mean value property of harmonic functions, Theorem 4.2.2 in Lecture 4. Other discretizations give other averaging rulesE.8.

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 3.10.5 (triangles instead of squares; Homework 1, Problem 4). Let $T$ be the triangle with corners $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(0,1)$. A linear function on $T$ has the form $a+bx+cy$.
  1. Find linear $\phi_A,\phi_B,\phi_C$, each $1$ at the corner named and $0$ at the other two, and their gradients.
  2. Compute $A_{PQ}=\iint_T\nabla\phi_P\cdot\nabla\phi_Q\,dA$ for all $P,Q\in\{A,B,C\}$, as a $3\times3$ table.
  3. Divide the unit square into four triangles by joining its centre $p_0=(\frac12,\frac12)$ to the corners $p_1=(0,0)$, $p_2=(1,0)$, $p_3=(1,1)$, $p_4=(0,1)$. Let $U$ be continuous, linear on each triangle, with $U(p_j)=g_j$ and unknown $c=U(p_0)$, and let $\phi_0$ be $1$ at the centre, $0$ at the corners, linear on each triangle. Compute $\iint\nabla U\cdot\nabla\phi_0\,dA$ one triangle at a time, and show that setting it to $0$ gives $c=\frac{g_1+g_2+g_3+g_4}4$.
  4. Two continuous piecewise-linear functions have the same boundary values and both satisfy $\iint\nabla U\cdot\nabla v=0$ for every continuous piecewise-linear $v$ vanishing on the boundary. Let $W$ be their difference; take $v=W$ and prove $W=0$.
Hint
  • Substitute the three corner values into $a+bx+cy$ and solve.
  • Gradients are constant; the area of $T$ is $\frac12$. The table is symmetric and each row sums to $0$.
  • On the bottom triangle $p_1p_2p_0$, $\phi_0=2y$. Do that triangle first; the others follow by rotation.
  • $v=W$ gives $\iint|\nabla W|^2=0$. What does that say about $W$ on a connected square? Then use the boundary values. Compare Theorem 3.9.3.
Solution
  1. $\phi_A=1-x-y$, $\phi_B=x$, $\phi_C=y$, with gradients $(-1,-1)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$. These are the triangle analogues of the hat functions of Def. 3.4.3: each is $1$ at its own node and $0$ at the others (compare Lemma 3.5.1).
  2. These are the entries of the stiffness matrix of Def. 3.7.2, restricted to one element, as in Lemma 3.10.2 for a square. Each entry is (dot product of gradients) $\times\frac12$: \[ \big(A_{PQ}\big)=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\frac12&-\frac12\\-\frac12&\frac12&0\\-\frac12&0&\frac12\end{pmatrix}\qquad(\text{rows and columns }A,B,C). \] Rows sum to $0$ because $\phi_A+\phi_B+\phi_C=1$ has gradient $0$. The table is symmetric, as in Lemma 3.9.1.
  3. Setting $\iint\nabla U\cdot\nabla\phi_0=0$ is the discrete equation of Def. 3.7.1 and Prop. 3.7.3 at the one interior node. Bottom triangle $p_1p_2p_0$ (area $\frac14$): $U=g_1+(g_2-g_1)x+\beta y$ with $U(p_0)=c$ giving $\beta=2c-g_1-g_2$. So $\nabla U=(g_2-g_1,\,2c-g_1-g_2)$ and $\nabla\phi_0=(0,2)$, and the triangle contributes $\frac14\cdot2(2c-g_1-g_2)=\frac12(2c-g_1-g_2)$. By the rotational symmetry of the configuration, the triangle with corners $p_j,p_{j+1}$ contributes $\frac12(2c-g_j-g_{j+1})$ (indices mod $4$). Summing, \[ \tfrac12\big(8c-2(g_1+g_2+g_3+g_4)\big)=4c-(g_1+g_2+g_3+g_4)=0\iff c=\tfrac{g_1+g_2+g_3+g_4}4. \] The centre value is the average of the four corners: the triangle-mesh analogue of the eight-neighbour rule, Cor. 3.10.4.
  4. $W=U_1-U_2$ is zero on the boundary and $\iint\nabla W\cdot\nabla v=0$ for all admissible $v$ (subtract the two equations). $W$ itself is admissible, so $\iint|\nabla W|^2=0$: the energy of $W$ (Lemma 3.9.2, Def. 3.13.1) is zero. $\nabla W$ is constant on each triangle, so it is $0$ on each triangle, and $W$ is constant on each; being continuous on the connected square, $W$ is one constant, which is $0$ on the boundary. So $W\equiv0$. This is the argument of Theorem 3.9.3 (zero energy forces zero coefficients), which gives uniqueness of the discrete solution (Def. 3.9.4).
L3 · Slide 12

3.11 The discrete maximum principle

DerivedLemma 3.11.1 (an average equal to the maximum). If $c_{kl}=\frac18\sum_{\text{nbrs}}c_{ij}$ and every neighbour satisfies $c_{ij}\le M=c_{kl}$, then every neighbour has $c_{ij}=M$.
Proof. $\sum_{\text{nbrs}}(M-c_{ij})=8M-8c_{kl}=0$. A sum of nonnegative terms that equals zero has every term equal to zero. ∎
DerivedLemma 3.11.2 (bilinear extrema are at corners). A bilinear function on a closed square attains its maximum and minimum at corners.
Proof. Let $(s,t)$ be any point of the square. For fixed $t$, $p$ is affine in $s$ (Prop. 3.5.8), and an affine function on $[0,1]$ is at most its larger endpoint value, so $p(s,t)\le\max\big(p(0,t),p(1,t)\big)$. Each of $p(0,t)$ and $p(1,t)$ is affine in $t$, so it is at most the larger of its values at $t=0$ and $t=1$. Hence $p(s,t)$ is at most the largest corner value. The minimum is handled the same way. ∎
DerivedTheorem 3.11.3 (discrete maximum principle). $\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}$ attains its maximum and minimum over $\overline\Omega$ at boundary nodes. Consequently \[ \min_{q\in \class{ntn-B}{B}}g(x_q,y_q)\ \le\ \class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}(x,y)\ \le\ \max_{q\in \class{ntn-B}{B}}g(x_q,y_q)\qquad\text{for all }(x,y)\in\overline\Omega. \]
Proof. Let $M$ be the largest nodal value, which exists because there are finitely many nodes.
  1. $M$ is attained at a boundary node. Suppose $M$ is attained at an interior node $P_0$. By Cor. 3.10.4 and Lemma 3.11.1, all 8 neighbours of $P_0$ have value $M$, in particular $P_1=P_0+(\eps,0)$. If $P_1$ is interior, repeat to get $P_2=P_1+(\eps,0)$ with value $M$, and so on. $\Omega$ is bounded, so this cannot continue forever, and some $P_m$ is not interior. $P_m$ is a node (a neighbour of an interior node is a corner of one of its four squares), so it is a boundary node with value $M$. This is the slide's "propagates the value to the boundary".
  2. Between the nodes. On each square $\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}$ is bilinear, so by Lemma 3.11.2 $\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}(x,y)$ is at most its largest corner value, which is at most $M$.
  3. Hence $\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}\le M=g(\text{some boundary node})\le\max_{\class{ntn-B}{B}}g$.
  4. Minimum. The equations are linear, so $-\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}$ is the discrete solution for data $-g$. Steps 1–3 give $-\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}\le\max_{\class{ntn-B}{B}}(-g)=-\min_{\class{ntn-B}{B}}g$. ∎

Boundary nodes lie on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ (Lemma 3.6.2), so in particular $\min_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}g\le \class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}g$.

L3 · Slide 13

3.12 Consequences of the maximum principle

DerivedCorollary 3.12.1 (uniqueness, again). If $g=0$ at every boundary node, then $\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}\equiv0$.
Proof. Theorem 3.11.3 gives $0\le \class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}\le0$. Applied to the difference of two discrete solutions with the same data, this reproves uniqueness without Theorem 3.9.3. ∎
DerivedCorollary 3.12.2 (a bound). $\min_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}g\le \class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}g$, and the bounds do not depend on $\eps$.
Proof. This is the last line of §3.11. The bounds involve only $g$. ∎
DerivedProposition 3.12.3 (a weighted average of the boundary data). Let $\class{ntn-W}{W}:=-\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}^{-1}\class{ntn-AIB}{A_{IB}}$, an $n\times|B|$ matrix, so that $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}=\class{ntn-W}{W}\class{ntn-gB}{g_B}$. Then \[ \class{ntn-W}{W}_{pq}\ge0\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{q\in \class{ntn-B}{B}}\class{ntn-W}{W}_{pq}=1\quad\text{for every }p\in \class{ntn-I}{I}. \] So each interior value $c_p=\sum_qW_{pq}g_q$ is a weighted average of the boundary values, and the linear system computes the weights.
Proof. Nonnegative. Take data $\class{ntn-gB}{g_B}=e_q$: 1 at boundary node $q$, 0 at the others. Then $\class{ntn-cI}{c_I}$ is the $q$-th column of $\class{ntn-W}{W}$, and Theorem 3.11.3 makes its entries $\ge\min(e_q)=0$.
Rows sum to 1. Take $\class{ntn-gB}{g_B}\equiv1$. The constant vector $c\equiv1$ satisfies every equation of Cor. 3.10.4 ($1=\frac18\cdot8$) and the boundary condition, so by uniqueness it is the solution. Hence $\class{ntn-W}{W}\mathbf 1=\mathbf 1$: every row of $\class{ntn-W}{W}$ sums to 1. ∎

The slide calls this the concrete meaning of "harmonic functions are determined by their boundary values". The weights also have a random-walk interpretationE.9, which Lecture 3 announced for later.

L3 · Slide 14

3.13 The discrete solution minimizes the energy

Up to now the argument assumed a solution of the continuous problem exists. From here on, the discrete problem is used to produce one.

DefinedDefinition 3.13.1 (energy). $\class{ntn-E}{E}(V):=\class{ntn-a}{a}(V,V)=\iint_\Omega|\nabla V|^2\,dA$.
DerivedLemma 3.13.2. Among all $V\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$, $\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}$ is the unique minimizer of $E$.
Proof. Let $V\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ and put $w:=V-\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}$, which lies in $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$ by Prop. 3.6.4. By bilinearity and symmetry (Prop. 3.3.2), \[ \class{ntn-E}{E}(V)=\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}+w,\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}+w)=\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps},\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps})+\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps},w)+\class{ntn-a}{a}(w,\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps})+\class{ntn-a}{a}(w,w)=\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps})+2\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps},w)+\class{ntn-E}{E}(w). \] The discrete equations (Def. 3.7.1) give $\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps},w)=0$, since $w\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$. So $\class{ntn-E}{E}(V)=\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps})+\class{ntn-E}{E}(w)\ge \class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps})$. If equality holds, then $\class{ntn-E}{E}(w)=0$. Writing $w=\sum d_{kl}\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{kl}}$ over interior nodes, Lemma 3.9.2 gives $d^{\mathsf T}\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}d=0$, and positive definiteness (Theorem 3.9.3) forces $d=0$, so $w=0$ and $V=\class{ntn-Ue}{U_\eps}$. ∎

The continuous version of this lemma is known as Dirichlet's principleE.10.

L3 · Slide 15

3.14 Dyadic refinement: the minima decrease

DefinedDefinition 3.14.1. $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_n}:=2^{-n}\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$. Write $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}:=U_{\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_n}}$ and $\class{ntn-mn}{m_n}:=\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n})=\min_{\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_n}}}E$ (the minimum by Lemma 3.13.2).

Each square of one grid splits into four squares of half the side in the next, so $\Omega$ is a union of squares at every level and Hypothesis 3.4.1 holds for every $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_n}$.

AssumedHypothesis 3.14.2 ("for now"). $\Omega$ is a finite union of squares of the coarsest grid ($\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}$), and $g$ is linear along each boundary edge of the coarsest grid.
DerivedLemma 3.14.3 (nesting). For $n\le k$: (a) $\class{ntn-Veps}{V_{\eps_n}}\subset \class{ntn-Veps}{V_{\eps_k}}$. (b) Under Hyp. 3.14.2, every $U\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_n}}$ equals $g$ on all of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, and $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_n}}\subset \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_k}}$. (c) $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_{\eps_n}}\subset \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_{\eps_k}}$.
Proof. It is enough to take $k=n+1$ and repeat.
(a) By Prop. 3.5.7, $U\in \class{ntn-Veps}{V_{\eps_n}}$ is continuous and bilinear on each coarse square. On a sub-square, $a+bx+cy+dxy$ still has that form. So $U$ is continuous and bilinear on each fine square, and $U\in \class{ntn-Veps}{V_{\eps_{n+1}}}$ by Prop. 3.5.7 again.
(b) Let $e$ be a boundary edge at level $n$. It lies inside a coarsest-level boundary edge, on which $g$ is linear. $U$ is linear on $e$ (Prop. 3.5.8) and equals $g$ at the endpoints of $e$. Two linear functions that agree at two points agree everywhere on $e$, so $U=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Every level-$(n+1)$ boundary node lies on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ (Lemma 3.6.2(a)), so $U$ equals $g$ there. With (a), $U\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_{n+1}}}$.
(c) $U\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_{\eps_n}}$ vanishes on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ (Prop. 3.6.5(b)), hence at the finer boundary nodes. ∎
DerivedProposition 3.14.4. $\class{ntn-mn}{m_0}\ge \class{ntn-mn}{m_1}\ge \class{ntn-mn}{m_2}\ge\dots\ge0$, so $\class{ntn-mn}{m_n}$ decreases to a limit $\class{ntn-m}{m}:=\inf_n \class{ntn-mn}{m_n}\ge0$ (written $\class{ntn-mn}{m_n}\downarrow \class{ntn-m}{m}$).
Proof. $\class{ntn-mn}{m_{n+1}}$ is the minimum of $E$ over $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_{n+1}}}$, a set that contains $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_n}}$ (Lemma 3.14.3(b)), and a minimum over a larger set is no larger. $E\ge0$ by Prop. 3.3.2. A non-increasing sequence that is bounded below converges to its infimum by the monotone convergence theoremA.15. ∎
Remark 3.14.5 (why the hypothesis is needed). Without Hyp. 3.14.2, "equals $g$ at the boundary nodes" means different things on different grids. $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ interpolates $g$ linearly between coarse nodes, which generally disagrees with $g$ at the new midpoints, so $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\notin \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_{n+1}}}$ and nesting fails. The slide's "for now" signals that the general case is handled later.
L3 · Slide 16

3.15 The parallelogram law

DefinedDefinition 3.15.1. For a scalar- or vector-valued function $F$ on $\Omega$, $\norm{F}_{L^2}^2:=\iint_\Omega|F|^2\,dA$. So $\class{ntn-E}{E}(V)=\norm{\nabla V}_{L^2}^2$. (The space of such $F$ is $L^2(\Omega)$D.2.) Convention: from here on, $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{F}}$ with no subscript always means $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{F}_{L^2}}$. No other norm appears in the rest of the lecture.
DerivedLemma 3.15.2 (parallelogram identity). $\class{ntn-E}{E}(x-y)+\class{ntn-E}{E}(x+y)=2\class{ntn-E}{E}(x)+2\class{ntn-E}{E}(y)$, and $\class{ntn-E}{E}(\lambda x)=\lambda^2\class{ntn-E}{E}(x)$ ("the energy is quadratic").
Proof. By bilinearity and symmetry, $\class{ntn-E}{E}(x\pm y)=\class{ntn-E}{E}(x)\pm2\class{ntn-a}{a}(x,y)+\class{ntn-E}{E}(y)$. Adding the two, the cross terms cancel. Also $\class{ntn-E}{E}(\lambda x)=\class{ntn-a}{a}(\lambda x,\lambda x)=\lambda^2\class{ntn-a}{a}(x,x)$. ∎
DerivedCorollary 3.15.3. \[ \norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})}_{L^2}^2=2\class{ntn-mn}{m_n}+2\class{ntn-mn}{m_k}-4E\big(\tfrac12(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}+\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})\big). \]
Proof. Take $x=\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$, $y=\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}$ in Lemma 3.15.2: \[ \class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})}}^2=\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})=2\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n})+2\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})-\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}+\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}). \] $\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n})=\class{ntn-mn}{m_n}$ and $\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})=\class{ntn-mn}{m_k}$ by Def. 3.14.1, and, since the energy is quadratic, \[ \class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}+\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})=E\big(2\cdot\tfrac12(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}+\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})\big)=4E\big(\tfrac12(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}+\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})\big). \] ∎
L3 · Slide 17

3.16 The bound tends to zero

DerivedProposition 3.16.1. For $n\le k$, $\ \norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})}_{L^2}^2\le2(\class{ntn-mn}{m_n}-\class{ntn-m}{m})+2(\class{ntn-mn}{m_k}-\class{ntn-m}{m})$. Consequently $(\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n})$ is a Cauchy sequenceD.2 in $L^2$: for every $\delta\gt0$ there is $N$ with $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})}}^2\lt\delta$ for all $n,k\ge N$.
Proof. $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_n}}\subset \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_k}}$ (Lemma 3.14.3(b)) and $\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_k}}$. Their average lies in $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_k}}$ (Prop. 3.6.4 with $\lambda=\tfrac12$: "the boundary values average to $g$"). $\class{ntn-mn}{m_k}$ is the minimum of $E$ over that set, and $\class{ntn-mn}{m_k}\ge \class{ntn-m}{m}$ (Prop. 3.14.4), so $E\big(\tfrac12(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}+\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})\big)\ge \class{ntn-mn}{m_k}\ge \class{ntn-m}{m}$. Substitute into Cor. 3.15.3: \[ \class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})}}^2\le2\class{ntn-mn}{m_n}+2\class{ntn-mn}{m_k}-4\class{ntn-m}{m}=2(\class{ntn-mn}{m_n}-\class{ntn-m}{m})+2(\class{ntn-mn}{m_k}-\class{ntn-m}{m}). \] Given $\delta\gt0$, choose $N$ with $\class{ntn-mn}{m_j}-\class{ntn-m}{m}\lt\delta/4$ for all $j\ge N$, which is possible because $\class{ntn-mn}{m_j}\to \class{ntn-m}{m}$. For $n,k\ge N$ the right side is less than $\delta$. ∎

This controls only gradients. A function can have a small gradient and still be large (add a constant). The next section closes that gap using the fact that $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}$ vanishes on the boundary.

L3 · Slides 18–19

3.17 Poincaré's inequality

DefinedDefinition 3.17.1 (width). The width $\class{ntn-L}{L}$ of $\Omega$ is a number such that, after a horizontal translation, $\Omega$ lies in the strip $\{(x,y):0\lt x\lt \class{ntn-L}{L}\}$. Such an $\class{ntn-L}{L}$ exists because $\Omega$ is bounded.
DerivedTheorem 3.17.2 (Poincaré's inequality). If $v$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$, piecewise continuously differentiable, and $v=0$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, then \[ \class{ntn-L2}{\norm{v}_{L^2}}\le \class{ntn-L}{L}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla v}_{L^2}}. \]
Proof.
  1. Extend by zero. Set $v:=0$ outside $\Omega$. The extension is continuous: at a point of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, values from inside tend to $v=0$ and values outside are $0$. It is still piecewise smooth, with $\nabla v=0$ outside $\Omega$, so integrals over the strip equal integrals over $\Omega$.
  2. Recover $v$ from its $x$-derivative. Fix $y$. The line $x=0$ lies outside $\Omega$, so $v(0,y)=0$. The function $s\mapsto v(s,y)$ is continuous and piecewise $C^1$, so by the fundamental theorem of calculusA.9 \[ v(x,y)=v(0,y)+\int_0^x\partial_xv(s,y)\,ds=\int_0^x\partial_xv(s,y)\,ds. \]
  3. Cauchy–SchwarzA.12 with the functions $1$ and $\partial_xv(\cdot,y)$ on $[0,x]$, for $0\le x\le \class{ntn-L}{L}$: \[ |v(x,y)|^2=\Big(\int_0^x1\cdot\partial_xv(s,y)\,ds\Big)^2\le\Big(\int_0^x1^2\,ds\Big)\Big(\int_0^x|\partial_xv(s,y)|^2ds\Big)\le x\int_0^{\class{ntn-L}{L}}|\partial_xv(s,y)|^2ds\le \class{ntn-L}{L}\int_0^{\class{ntn-L}{L}}|\partial_xv(s,y)|^2ds. \] The middle steps use $\int_0^x1^2=x$ and enlarge the interval of a nonnegative integrand from $[0,x]$ to $[0,\class{ntn-L}{L}]$.
  4. Integrate over $x\in(0,\class{ntn-L}{L})$. The right side does not depend on $x$, so \[ \int_0^{\class{ntn-L}{L}}|v(x,y)|^2dx\le \class{ntn-L}{L}\cdot \class{ntn-L}{L}\int_0^{\class{ntn-L}{L}}|\partial_xv(s,y)|^2ds. \]
  5. Integrate over $y$ and use $|\partial_xv|^2\le|\partial_xv|^2+|\partial_yv|^2=|\nabla v|^2$: \[ \iint|v|^2\,dA\le \class{ntn-L}{L}^2\iint|\partial_xv|^2\,dA\le \class{ntn-L}{L}^2\iint|\nabla v|^2\,dA. \] Take square roots. ∎
The constant $\class{ntn-L}{L}$ is not the best possible; see a sharper constantE.11. Any constant independent of $n$ and $k$ is enough for what follows.
DerivedCorollary 3.17.3 (it applies to $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}$). $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{U_n-U_k}_{L^2}}\le \class{ntn-L}{L}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(U_n-U_k)}_{L^2}}$, i.e. Poincaré holds with $C=\class{ntn-L}{L}$.
Proof. Take $n\le k$. Both functions lie in $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_k}}$ (Lemma 3.14.3(b)), so $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_{\eps_k}}$ (Prop. 3.6.4). It is continuous and bilinear on each square, hence piecewise smooth, and it is zero at every boundary node. On a boundary edge a bilinear function is linear (Prop. 3.5.8), and a linear function vanishing at both endpoints vanishes on the whole edge. So $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}=0$ on all of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, and Theorem 3.17.2 applies with $v=\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}$. ∎

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 3.17.4 (Poincaré's inequality; Homework 1, Problem 3). Let $\Omega$ be a finite union of grid squares in the strip $0\lt x\lt L$, and $v$ continuous, piecewise $C^1$, zero on $\partial\Omega$. Extend $v$ by zero outside $\Omega$.
  1. Explain why the extension is continuous and piecewise $C^1$.
  2. Prove $\norm{v}_{L^2(\Omega)}\le L\norm{\nabla v}_{L^2(\Omega)}$.
  3. Suppose every $v_n$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$ and $\nabla v_n$ is Cauchy in $L^2$. Prove that $v_n$ is Cauchy in $L^2$. Where was this used in Lecture 3?
Hint
  • After extending by zero, fix $y$ and write $v(x,y)=\int_0^x\partial_xv(s,y)\,ds$.
  • Apply Cauchy–SchwarzA.12 to the one-dimensional integral.
  • Use $0\lt x\lt L$, then integrate first in $x$ and afterwards in $y$.
  • Bound $|\partial_xv|$ by $|\nabla v|$ after integrating.
  • For the last part, apply the inequality to $v_n-v_m$.
Solution
  1. (This is the extension used in the proof of Theorem 3.17.2.) Continuous: inside $\Omega$ and outside $\overline\Omega$ there is nothing to check; at a point of $\partial\Omega$, $v=0$ there, $v\to0$ from inside by continuity, and $v=0$ outside. Piecewise $C^1$: the grid squares cover the plane; on each square of $\Omega$, $v$ is $C^1$ by assumption, and on every other square it is $0$.
  2. This is Theorem 3.17.2. Fix $y$. As $\Omega$ lies in $0\lt x\lt L$, $v(0,y)=0$, and by the fundamental theorem of calculusA.9 for piecewise $C^1$ functions, $v(x,y)=\int_0^x\partial_xv(s,y)\,ds$. By Cauchy–Schwarz, for $0\lt x\lt L$, \[ |v(x,y)|^2\le x\int_0^x|\partial_xv(s,y)|^2ds\le L\int_0^L|\partial_xv(s,y)|^2ds. \] Integrate over $x\in(0,L)$: $\int_0^L|v(x,y)|^2dx\le L^2\int_0^L|\partial_xv(s,y)|^2ds$. Integrate over $y$ (FubiniA.13) and use $|\partial_xv|\le|\nabla v|$: $\norm{v}^2\le L^2\norm{\partial_xv}^2\le L^2\norm{\nabla v}^2$.
  3. $v_n-v_m$ is continuous, piecewise $C^1$ and zero on $\partial\Omega$, so part 2 gives $\norm{v_n-v_m}\le L\norm{\nabla v_n-\nabla v_m}\to0$ (this is Cor. 3.17.3). In Lecture 3 this is how Prop. 3.18.1 gets the $L^2$ limit $u$: the gradients $\nabla U_n$ are Cauchy (Prop. 3.16.1), and $U_n-U_k$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$, so the $U_n$ themselves are Cauchy.
L3 · Slide 20

3.18 The limit satisfies the weak form

DerivedProposition 3.18.1 (three limits). $(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n})$, $(\partial_x\class{ntn-Un}{U_n})$ and $(\partial_y\class{ntn-Un}{U_n})$ are Cauchy in $L^2$. Call their limits $u$, $p$, $q\in L^2(\Omega)$.
Proof. Since $|\partial_xf|\le|\nabla f|$ at every point, $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\partial_x\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\partial_x\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}}}\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})}}$, and likewise for $\partial_y$. Cor. 3.17.3 gives $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k}}}\le \class{ntn-L}{L}\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_k})}}$. All three right-hand sides tend to $0$ by Prop. 3.16.1. Limits exist because $L^2$ is completeD.3. ∎
DefinedDefinition 3.18.2 (weak derivative). Let $u,p\in L^2(\Omega)$. $p$ is the weak $x$-derivative of $u$, written $p=\partial_xu$, if \[ \iint_\Omega u\,\partial_x\psi\,dA=-\iint_\Omega p\,\psi\,dA \] for every continuously differentiable $\psi$ supported inside $\Omega$C.7. The weak $y$-derivative is defined the same way. For smooth $u$, integration by parts shows the weak and classical derivatives agree, which is why the slide can say "by definition".
DerivedProposition 3.18.3. $p=\partial_xu$ and $q=\partial_yu$ weakly. Write $\nabla u:=(p,q)$.
Proof. Step 1: the identity holds for each $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$. Extend $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\psi$ by $0$ outside $\Omega$. Because $\psi$ vanishes near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, this is continuous and piecewise $C^1$ and vanishes outside a bounded set. For fixed $y$, the fundamental theorem of calculusA.9 over an interval containing that set gives $\int_{\R}\partial_x(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\psi)\,dx=0$. Off the grid lines the product rule gives $\partial_x(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\psi)=\partial_x\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\psi+\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\partial_x\psi$. Integrate in $y$: \[ \iint \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\partial_x\psi\,dA=-\iint\partial_x\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\psi\,dA. \] Step 2: pass to the limit. By Cauchy–SchwarzA.12, \[ \Big|\iint \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\partial_x\psi-\iint u\,\partial_x\psi\Big|\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u}}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\partial_x\psi}}\to0,\qquad \Big|\iint\partial_x\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\psi-\iint p\,\psi\Big|\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\partial_x\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-p}}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\psi}}\to0. \] So the two sides of Step 1 converge to $\iint u\,\partial_x\psi$ and $-\iint p\,\psi$. Equal sequences have equal limits, which is the identity of Def. 3.18.2. The same argument works in $y$. ∎
DerivedProposition 3.18.4 (test functions from a fixed grid). For every $N$ and every $w\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_{\eps_N}}$, $\ \class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w):=\iint(p\,\partial_xw+q\,\partial_yw)\,dA=0$.
Proof. For $n\ge N$, $w\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_{\eps_n}}$ (Lemma 3.14.3(c)), so $\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n},w)=0$ by Def. 3.7.1. By Cauchy–SchwarzA.12, \[ |\class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n},w)-\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w)|=\Big|\iint(\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\nabla u)\cdot\nabla w\Big|\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\nabla u}}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla w}}\to0. \] So $\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w)=\lim_n \class{ntn-a}{a}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n},w)=0$. ∎
DerivedLemma 3.18.5 (the slide's "Taylor's theorem on each square"). Let $\eta$ be twice continuously differentiable on $\overline\Omega$ with $\eta=0$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, and let $M_2$ bound $|\nabla\partial_x\eta|$ and $|\nabla\partial_y\eta|$ on $\overline\Omega$. The nodal interpolant $\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N}:=\sum_{ij}\eta(x_i,y_j)\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ at level $N$ lies in $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_{\eps_N}}$, and \[ \norm{\nabla(\eta-\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N})}_{L^2}^2\le4M_2^2\,\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_N}^2\,|\Omega|\ \longrightarrow\ 0 \quad (N\to\infty), \] where $|\Omega|$ is the area of $\Omega$.
Proof. $\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N}\in \class{ntn-Veps}{V_{\eps_N}}$, and its boundary-node values are $\eta=0$ because boundary nodes lie on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. So $\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N}\in \class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_{\eps_N}}$.
Fix a square with lower-left corner $(x_i,y_j)$ and side $h=\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_N}$, and a point $(x,y)$ inside it with $t=(y-y_j)/h$. Differentiate the formulas of Lemma 3.5.5 in $x$; each $\partial_s$ brings a factor $1/h$: \[ \partial_x\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N}(x,y)=(1-t)\,\frac{\eta(x_{i+1},y_j)-\eta(x_i,y_j)}{h}+t\,\frac{\eta(x_{i+1},y_{j+1})-\eta(x_i,y_{j+1})}{h}. \] By the mean value theoremA.3 the first quotient equals $\partial_x\eta(\xi_1,y_j)$ and the second equals $\partial_x\eta(\xi_2,y_{j+1})$, for some $\xi_1,\xi_2\in(x_i,x_{i+1})$. Both points lie in the same closed square as $(x,y)$, so each is within distance $\sqrt2h$ of it. The two-variable boundA.3 applied to $F=\partial_x\eta$ gives $|\partial_x\eta(\xi_1,y_j)-\partial_x\eta(x,y)|\le M_2\sqrt2h$, and likewise for $\xi_2$. The weights $1-t$ and $t$ are nonnegative and add to 1, so \[ |\partial_x\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N}(x,y)-\partial_x\eta(x,y)|\le(1-t)M_2\sqrt2h+tM_2\sqrt2h=\sqrt2M_2h. \] The same holds for $\partial_y$. So $|\nabla(\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N}-\eta)|^2\le2M_2^2h^2+2M_2^2h^2=4M_2^2h^2$ off the grid lines. Integrate over $\Omega$. ∎
DerivedTheorem 3.18.6 (smooth test functions). $\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,\eta)=0$ for every $\eta$ as in Lemma 3.18.5.
Proof. Split $\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,\eta)=\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N})+\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,\eta-\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N})$. The first term is $0$ by Prop. 3.18.4. The second is at most $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla u}}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\eta-\class{ntn-etaN}{\eta_N})}}$ in absolute value by Cauchy–SchwarzA.12, and this tends to $0$ as $N\to\infty$ by Lemma 3.18.5. The left side does not depend on $N$, so it is $0$. ∎
L3 · Slide 21

3.19 What has been proved

DerivedTheorem 3.19.1 (existence of a weak solution). Assume Hypothesis 3.14.2. Let $\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_0}}$ be the coarsest discrete solution and $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ the solution at level $n$; each equals $g$ on all of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Then:
  1. $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to u$ and $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to\nabla u$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. So $u$ is a square-integrable function with a square-integrable weak gradient; in the standard notation, $u$ lies in the Sobolev spaceD.6 $\class{ntn-H1}{H^1}(\Omega)$.
  2. $\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,w)=0$ for every smooth $w$ vanishing on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  3. The boundary condition is retained in this form: every $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}$ vanishes on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, while $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}\to u-\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}$ and $\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_0})\to\nabla(u-\class{ntn-Un}{U_0})$ in $L^2$.
Thus $u$ satisfies the weak form (Def. 3.3.4) of the Dirichlet problem.
Proof. Item 1 is Props. 3.18.1 and 3.18.3. Item 2 is Theorem 3.18.6. For item 3: $\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}\in \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_0}}\subset \class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_{\eps_n}}$ by Lemma 3.14.3(b), so $\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}$ and $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ both equal $g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ and their difference vanishes there. The convergence follows from item 1 by subtracting the fixed function $\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}$. ∎
Remark 3.19.2 (why item 3 is the boundary condition). An $L^2$ function can be changed on a zero-area set without changing it as an element of $L^2$, and $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ has zero area. So "$u=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$" cannot be checked point by point yet. Item 3 is the substitute: $u$ differs from $\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}$, which does equal $g$ on the boundary, by a limit of functions that vanish on the boundary. The standard formalization is the space $H^1_0$ and the trace operatorD.6.

Missing pieces

  • $u$ is smooth and $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ pointwise: Weyl's lemma. Done in Lecture 4, Cor. 4.9.6.
  • $u(x)\to g(p)$ as $x\to p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, pointwise. Done in Lecture 5, Theorem 5.11.3, by energy and comparison rather than the random walkE.9.

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 3.19.3 (equilibrium temperature and WiFi; Homework 1, optional FreeFEM++ bonus). Part A. On $\Omega=(0,4)\times(0,3)$, a radiator on $0.5\lt x\lt1.5$ of the bottom edge is held at $40°$, a window on $1.5\lt x\lt2.5$ of the top edge at $5°$, and the rest of the boundary at $15°$. Mesh $\Omega$ with separate boundary labels, solve $\Delta T=0$ with continuous $P_1$ elements, plot isotherms, and report the numerical minimum and maximum. How does the maximum principle check your result?
Part B. Run the official FreeFEM++ tutorial WiFi Propagation, which models the field by $\Delta E+\frac{k^2}{n^2}E=0$ ($n$ the refractive index, complex inside walls; $E=1$ on a small circular hotspot). (1) Submit a mesh and a signal plot. (2) Identify the outer boundary, the walls and the hotspot in the code; explain on(2,v=1). (3) The program uses $\iint_\Omega\big(\frac{k^2}{n^2}Ew-\nabla E\cdot\nabla w\big)\,dA$: explain why, starting from the equation. (4) Compare three hotspot positions with a stated coverage criterion. (5) Change the wall absorption and explain the difference.
Hint
  • Part A: split the top and bottom borders where the boundary values change; plot the mesh before solving. The core of the script is 
    fespace Vh(Th,P1);
Vh T,v;
problem heat(T,v)
    = int2d(Th)(dx(T)*dx(v)+dy(T)*dy(v))
    + on(/* wall labels */,T=15)
    + on(/* window label */,T=5)
    + on(/* radiator label */,T=40);
    This is exactly the weak form of Def. 3.3.4, solved over $P_1$ (linear-on-triangles) functions instead of bilinear ones.
  • Check that $5\le T\le40$ up to round-off.
  • Part B(3): multiply the equation by $w$ and integrate the $\Delta E$ term by parts. The test function vanishes on the hotspot; the other boundaries carry the natural zero-normal-derivative condition.
  • wall() distinguishes air from wall; wallreflexion and wallabsorption set the complex index. The hotspot has label $2$. The plotted quantity is log(real(v)^2+imag(v)^2). Keep everything else fixed when comparing.
Solution

The plots and runs are computational and not reproduced here. The mathematical parts:

  • Part A, maximum principle. The temperature is harmonic (it is the solution of the Dirichlet problem, Def. 3.1.2, and the weak solution of Theorem 3.19.1 is classical by Cor. 4.9.6), so its maximum and minimum over $\overline\Omega$ are attained on $\partial\Omega$ (Cor. 4.4.1), where the data take values $5$, $15$, $40$. So $5\le T\le40$ everywhere, and the extreme values occur on the window and the radiator. The discrete solution obeys the same bound by the discrete maximum principle (Theorem 3.11.3 and Cor. 3.12.2 are the versions for squares; for $P_1$ elements it holds on meshes without obtuse angles). A computed value outside $[5,40]$ beyond round-off signals a labelling or mesh error.
  • Part B(2). on(2,v=1) imposes the Dirichlet condition $E=1$ on the boundary with label $2$, the hotspot circle: the analogue of fixing $U=g$ at the boundary nodes in Def. 3.7.1 (the affine space $V^g_\eps$ of Def. 3.6.3).
  • Part B(3), the weak form. Multiply $\Delta E+\frac{k^2}{n^2}E=0$ by a test function $w$ vanishing on the hotspot and integrate. By Green's identity (A.6), \[ \iint_\Omega(\Delta E)w\,dA=\oint_{\partial\Omega}w\,\partial_nE\,ds-\iint_\Omega\nabla E\cdot\nabla w\,dA. \] The boundary integral vanishes: on the hotspot $w=0$, and on the outer boundary the natural condition is $\partial_nE=0$. So $\iint_\Omega\big(\frac{k^2}{n^2}Ew-\nabla E\cdot\nabla w\big)dA=0$ for all such $w$, which is what the program solves. Compare §3.3, where the same integration by parts (Prop. 3.3.3) turns $\Delta u=0$ into $a(u,w)=0$, the weak form of Def. 3.3.4.
  • Part B(4)–(5). Any clearly stated criterion is acceptable (for instance, the area where the plotted log-power is below a threshold). More absorption makes the field decay faster through walls, so rooms separated from the hotspot by more walls get weaker signal; less absorption gives more reflection and interference patterns.
Part I · Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem

Lecture 4 · The mean value property

Goal
Show that the weak solution of Lecture 3 is a smooth harmonic function, using the mean value property.
Main results
Theorem 4.2.2 (mean value property) · Theorem 4.3.1, Cor. 4.4.1, Cor. 4.4.2 (maximum principles, uniqueness) · Theorem 4.6.2 (Weyl's lemma) · Theorem 4.10.1 (converse) · Cor. 4.11.1 (uniform limits)
Uses
Lecture 3; mollifiers (D.5).
Used later
Lecture 5 · Lecture 9 (Jensen's formula uses the mean value property and the maximum principle).

Slide 1 is the title slide.

L4 · Slide 2

4.1 Where we stand

Lecture 3 worked under Hypothesis 3.14.2: $\Omega$ is a finite union of squares of the coarsest grid, and $g$ is linear on each boundary edge of that grid. $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is the finite element solution on the grid of side $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_n}=2^{-n}\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}$. Theorem 3.19.1 proved two things:

  • $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to u$ and $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to\nabla u$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ (Prop. 3.18.1 and Prop. 3.18.3);
  • $\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,\eta)=0$ for every smooth $\eta$ vanishing on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ (Theorem 3.18.6).

So $u$ is a weak solution. Its gradient exists only as a weak derivative, and the equation holds only after integrating against test functions. The goal of this lecture is to show that $u$ is in fact a classical solution in the interior: $u$ is smoothD.1 and $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ at every point of $\Omega$ (Cor. 4.9.6). The road goes through the mean value property, which describes harmonic functions without mentioning derivatives.

L4 · Slide 3

4.2 The mean value property

The lecture writes points of the plane as complex numbers, $z=x+iy$. This is only notation: no complex arithmetic beyond $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ is used. See complex notation for the planeC.1.

DefinedDefinition 4.2.1 (circles, disks, circle averages). Fix a centre $z_0$. For $t\gt0$:
  • $\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}$ is the circle of radius $t$: \[ \class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}:=\{z:|z-z_0|=t\}=\{z_0+te^{i\theta}:0\le\theta\le2\pi\}; \]
  • $\class{ntn-Dt}{D_t}:=\{z:|z-z_0|\lt t\}$ is the open disk inside it, and $\class{ntn-Dt}{\overline{D_t}}=\{|z-z_0|\le t\}$ the closed disk;
  • for a continuous $h$, $\ \class{ntn-Mt}{M}(t):=\dfrac1{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}h(z_0+te^{i\theta})\,d\theta$ is the average of $h$ over $\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}$.
The average is taken with respect to the angle; since arc length on $\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}$ is $ds=t\,d\theta$ (polar coordinatesA.8), it equals $\frac{1}{2\pi t}\oint_{\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}}h\,ds$, total over length.
DerivedTheorem 4.2.2 (mean value property). Let $h$ be $C^2$ and harmonic on an open set $\Omega$, and let the closed disk $|z-z_0|\le r$ lie in $\Omega$. Then \[ h(z_0)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}h(z_0+re^{i\theta})\,d\theta. \]
Proof. Let $\class{ntn-Mt}{M}(t)$ be the average of $h$ over $\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}$ for $0\lt t\le r$ (Def. 4.2.1). We show $M$ is constant and tends to $h(z_0)$.
  1. Differentiate under the integral. The function $(t,\theta)\mapsto h(z_0+te^{i\theta})$ has a continuous $t$-derivative on the rectangle $[0,r]\times[0,2\pi]$, because $h$ is $C^2$ on an open set containing the closed disk. So differentiation under the integral signA.4 applies: \[ \class{ntn-Mt}{M}'(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_t\big[h(z_0+te^{i\theta})\big]\,d\theta. \]
  2. Chain rule. In coordinates, $z_0+te^{i\theta}=(x_0+t\cos\theta,\ y_0+t\sin\theta)$. Its $t$-derivative is the unit vector $e^{i\theta}=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, so \[ \partial_t\big[h(z_0+te^{i\theta})\big]=h_x\cos\theta+h_y\sin\theta=\nabla h\cdot e^{i\theta}. \] At the point $z_0+te^{i\theta}$ of $\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}$, the vector $e^{i\theta}$ points straight away from the centre: it is the outward unit normal $n$ to $\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}$. So the integrand is $\nabla h\cdot n$, the outward normal derivative.
  3. Change $d\theta$ to arc length. On $\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}$, $ds=t\,d\theta$, so $d\theta=ds/t$: \[ \class{ntn-Mt}{M}'(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\nabla h\cdot n\,d\theta=\frac1{2\pi t}\oint_{\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}}\nabla h\cdot n\,ds. \]
  4. Divergence theorem. Apply the divergence theoremA.6 on $\class{ntn-Dt}{D_t}$ to $F=\nabla h$, which is $C^1$ on $\class{ntn-Dt}{\overline{D_t}}\subset\Omega$. Since $\nabla\cdot\nabla h=\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h$, \[ \oint_{\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}}\nabla h\cdot n\,ds=\iint_{\class{ntn-Dt}{D_t}}\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h\,dA=0, \] because $h$ is harmonic. So $\class{ntn-Mt}{M}'(t)=0$ for $0\lt t\le r$.
  5. $M$ is constant. A function with zero derivative on an interval is constant there, by the mean value theoremA.3. So $\class{ntn-Mt}{M}(t)=M(r)$ for all $0\lt t\le r$.
  6. Let $t\to0$. Since every $\theta$-average of a constant is that constant, \[ |\class{ntn-Mt}{M}(t)-h(z_0)|=\Big|\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\big(h(z_0+te^{i\theta})-h(z_0)\big)d\theta\Big|\le\max_{\theta}\big|h(z_0+te^{i\theta})-h(z_0)\big|. \] Given any tolerance, continuity of $h$ at $z_0$ makes the right side smaller than it once $t$ is small. So $\class{ntn-Mt}{M}(t)\to h(z_0)$.
  7. A constant function that tends to $h(z_0)$ equals $h(z_0)$. In particular $M(r)=h(z_0)$. ∎
DefinedDefinition 4.2.3 (the mean value property). A continuous function $v$ on an open set $\Omega$ has the mean value property if, for every $z$ and every $r\gt0$ with the closed disk $|\zeta-z|\le r$ inside $\Omega$, $v(z)$ equals the average of $v$ over the circle of radius $r$ about $z$.

Theorem 4.2.2 says: every $C^2$ harmonic function has the mean value property. Theorem 4.10.1 will prove the converse, so the two descriptions are equivalent. Cor. 3.10.4 in Lecture 3 was the discrete version: each nodal value is the average of its eight neighbours.

L4 · Slide 4

4.3 The strong maximum principle

DerivedTheorem 4.3.1 (strong maximum principle). Let $\Omega$ be open and connectedC.4, and let $h$ be $C^2$ and harmonic on $\Omega$. If $h(z_0)=\sup_\Omega h$ at some point $z_0\in\Omega$, then $h$ is constant on $\Omega$.
Proof. Put $M:=h(z_0)$, which is the supremumA.14 of $h$, so $h\le M$ everywhere on $\Omega$. Let $S:=\{z\in\Omega:h(z)=M\}$.
  1. $S$ is not empty: $z_0\in S$.
  2. $S$ is closed in $\Omega$C.4. If $z_k\in S$ and $z_k\to z\in\Omega$, then $h(z)=\lim h(z_k)=M$ by continuity, so $z\in S$.
  3. $S$ is open. Let $z_1\in S$. Since $\Omega$ is open, there is $r\gt0$ with the closed disk $|z-z_1|\le r$ inside $\Omega$. Fix $0\lt t\le r$. By Theorem 4.2.2 with radius $t$, \[ M=h(z_1)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}h(z_1+te^{i\theta})\,d\theta. \] So $\varphi(\theta):=M-h(z_1+te^{i\theta})$ is continuous, nonnegative (because $h\le M$), and \[ \int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(\theta)\,d\theta=2\pi M-2\pi M=0. \] A continuous nonnegative function with zero integral is identically zero (zero integral forces zeroA.11, interval version). This is the slide's argument: if $h\lt M$ at one point of $\class{ntn-Ct}{C_t}$, then $h\lt M$ on a whole arc around it, and the average would be less than $M$. So $h=M$ on the circle of radius $t$ about $z_1$. Every point $z$ with $0\lt|z-z_1|\lt r$ lies on such a circle (take $t=|z-z_1|$), and $z_1\in S$ already. So the open disk of radius $r$ about $z_1$ lies in $S$.
  4. Conclude. In a connected set, the only subsets that are both open and closed are the empty set and the whole set (C.4). $S$ is nonempty, open and closed in $\Omega$, so $S=\Omega$: $h\equiv M$. ∎
Remark 4.3.2 (why "strong"). The weak maximum principle (E.12) says the maximum over $\overline\Omega$ is reached somewhere on the boundary. The strong one says more: a harmonic function on a connected set cannot reach its maximum at an interior point at all, unless it is constant. Two things in the hypothesis matter. Connectedness: on two separate disks, $h=0$ on one and $h=1$ on the other is harmonic, reaches its supremum inside, and is not constant. And the supremum must be attained at a point of $\Omega$; the theorem says nothing if it is only approached at the boundary.
L4 · Slide 5

4.4 The maximum principle, and uniqueness

Here $C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ means: twice continuously differentiable inside $\Omega$, and continuous up to and including the boundary (function classesD.1).

DerivedCorollary 4.4.1 (maximum principle). Let $\Omega$ be bounded and open, and $h\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ harmonic. Then $\max_{\overline\Omega}h=\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}h$ and $\min_{\overline\Omega}h=\min_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}h$.
Proof.
  1. The maximum exists. $\overline\Omega$ is closed and bounded, hence compactC.5, and $h$ is continuous on it. By the extreme value theorem it attains its maximum $M$ at some $z_0\in\overline\Omega$. The boundary $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is also compact and nonempty (compact setsC.5, part (c)), so $\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}h$ exists, and it is at most $M$ because $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}\subset\overline\Omega$. It remains to find a boundary point where $h=M$.
  2. If $z_0\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, we are done.
  3. If $z_0\in\Omega$, let $\Omega'$ be the connected componentC.4 of $\Omega$ containing $z_0$. It is open and connected, $h$ is harmonic on it, and $h(z_0)=M\ge\sup_{\Omega'}h$. By Theorem 4.3.1, $h\equiv M$ on $\Omega'$.
  4. Carry the value to the boundary. $\Omega'$ is bounded and nonempty, so it has a boundary point $p$ (compact setsC.5, part (c)). Since $h$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and $p$ is a limit of points of $\Omega'$ where $h=M$, also $h(p)=M$.
  5. $p$ lies on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. $p$ is in the closure of $\Omega'$, hence of $\Omega$. Suppose $p\in\Omega$. Then a small disk $D$ about $p$ lies in $\Omega$. That disk is connected and, since $p$ is a boundary point of $\Omega'$, it meets $\Omega'$. So $\Omega'\cup D$ is connected, and by maximality of the component, $D\subset\Omega'$; then $p\in\Omega'$, which is impossible for a boundary point of the open set $\Omega'$. So $p\notin\Omega$, i.e. $p\in\overline\Omega\setminus\Omega=\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. This is the slide's "$\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}'$ is a nonempty part of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$".
  6. So $\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}h\ge h(p)=M$, and the maximum statement holds.
  7. Minimum. $-h$ is also harmonic and in the same class. Its maximum statement reads $\max_{\overline\Omega}(-h)=\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}(-h)$, which is $-\min_{\overline\Omega}h=-\min_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}h$. ∎
DerivedCorollary 4.4.2 (stability). If $h_1,h_2\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ are harmonic on a bounded open $\Omega$, then \[ \max_{\overline\Omega}|h_1-h_2|=\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}|h_1-h_2|. \] In particular, if $h_1=h_2$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ then $h_1=h_2$ on $\Omega$.
Proof. Put $w:=h_1-h_2$. The Laplacian is linear, so $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} w=\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h_1-\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h_2=0$, and $w$ is in the same class. For any $z\in\overline\Omega$, Cor. 4.4.1 gives \[ w(z)\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}w\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}|w|,\qquad -w(z)\le\max_{\overline\Omega}(-w)=\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}(-w)\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}|w|. \] So $|w(z)|\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}|w|$ for every $z$, i.e. $\max_{\overline\Omega}|w|\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}|w|$. The reverse inequality holds because $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}\subset\overline\Omega$. If $h_1=h_2$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, the right side is $0$, so $w\equiv0$. ∎

"Stability" means: boundary data that are close (within $\delta$ everywhere on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$) give solutions that are close (within $\delta$ everywhere in $\Omega$). The uniqueness half reproves Theorem 2.9.1 of Lecture 2, which used energy and needed $h_1,h_2\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$; here continuity up to the boundary is enough. Cor. 3.12.1 was its discrete version.

L4 · Slide 6

4.5 Averaging over disks

DefinedDefinition 4.5.1 (the averaging weight $\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}$). Fix a function $\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}$ on the plane that is smoothD.1, $\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}\ge0$, radial ($\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}(\zeta)$ depends only on $|\zeta|$), zero outside the unit disk, and has $\iint\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}\,dA=1$. Such a $\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}$ exists; see mollifiersD.5 for an explicit one.
DefinedDefinition 4.5.2 (rescaled weight). For $\delta\gt0$, $\ \class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(\zeta):=\delta^{-2}\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}(\zeta/\delta)$.
DerivedLemma 4.5.3. $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$ is smooth, $\ge0$, radial, zero outside the disk of radius $\delta$, and $\iint\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}\,dA=1$.
Proof. Smoothness, sign and radial symmetry pass from $\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}$ to $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$ directly. If $|\zeta|\ge\delta$ then $|\zeta/\delta|\ge1$, so $\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}(\zeta/\delta)=0$. For the integral, substitute $\zeta=\delta w$, which scales areas by $\delta^2$, so $dA(\zeta)=\delta^2\,dA(w)$ (change of variablesA.8): \[ \iint\delta^{-2}\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}(\zeta/\delta)\,dA(\zeta)=\iint\delta^{-2}\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}(w)\,\delta^2\,dA(w)=\iint\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}\,dA=1. \] The factor $\delta^{-2}$ is there exactly to cancel the area scaling: shrinking the support to radius $\delta$ while keeping total weight $1$ forces the weight to be taller. ∎
DefinedDefinition 4.5.4 (the shrunken domain and convolution). $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ is the set of $z\in\Omega$ whose closed disk of radius $\delta$ lies in $\Omega$. For a function $v$ on $\Omega$ and $z\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$, the convolution is \[ (v\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta})(z):=\iint v(\zeta)\,\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)\,dA(\zeta). \] The weight $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)$ is zero unless $|z-\zeta|\lt\delta$, so only values of $v$ on the disk of radius $\delta$ about $z$ enter, and that disk lies in $\Omega$. The weights are $\ge0$ and total $1$, so $v\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$ is a weighted average of $v$ over that disk.

Two facts about $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ are used below (compact setsC.5): it is open, and every compact $K\subset\Omega$ lies inside $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ once $\delta$ is small enough. Also, every point of $\Omega$ belongs to some $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$, because $\Omega$ is open.

DerivedLemma 4.5.5 (averaging). Let $v$ be continuous on $\Omega$ and have the mean value property (Def. 4.2.3). Then $v\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}=v$ on $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$.
Proof.
  1. Write the weight radially. Since $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$ is radial, $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(\zeta)=k(|\zeta|)$ for a one-variable function $k$ with $\class{ntn-kt}{k}(t)=0$ for $t\ge\delta$. In polar coordinatesA.8, $dA=t\,dt\,d\theta$, so the normalization of Lemma 4.5.3 reads \[ 1=\iint\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}\,dA=\int_0^\delta\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\class{ntn-kt}{k}(t)\,t\,d\theta\,dt=\int_0^\delta \class{ntn-kt}{k}(t)\,2\pi t\,dt. \]
  2. Polar coordinates about $z$. Fix $z\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ and write $\zeta=z+te^{i\theta}$. Then $|z-\zeta|=t$, so $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)=\class{ntn-kt}{k}(t)$, and \[ (v\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta})(z)=\int_0^\delta \class{ntn-kt}{k}(t)\Big(\int_0^{2\pi}v(z+te^{i\theta})\,d\theta\Big)\,t\,dt. \] Splitting the double integral into an inner $\theta$-integral and an outer $t$-integral is Fubini's theoremA.13; the integrand is continuous on a closed disk.
  3. Use the mean value property, circle by circle. For each $t\le\delta$, the closed disk of radius $t$ about $z$ lies inside the closed disk of radius $\delta$, which lies in $\Omega$. So $\int_0^{2\pi}v(z+te^{i\theta})\,d\theta=2\pi v(z)$, and \[ (v\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta})(z)=\int_0^\delta \class{ntn-kt}{k}(t)\,2\pi v(z)\,t\,dt=v(z)\int_0^\delta \class{ntn-kt}{k}(t)\,2\pi t\,dt=v(z). \]
In words: the disk average is an average of circle averages, and each circle average is $v(z)$. ∎
L4 · Slide 7

4.6 Weyl's lemma

DefinedDefinition 4.6.1 (test function, Lecture 4). A test function is a smooth function $\eta$ on $\Omega$ that vanishes outside a compactC.5 subset of $\Omega$, hence on a whole band near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. This is the class of $\psi$ in Def. 3.18.2 (weak derivative), now required to be smooth rather than $C^1$.
DerivedTheorem 4.6.2 (Weyl's lemma). Let $u\in L^2(\Omega)$ (square-integrable on $\Omega$D.2) satisfy $\iint_\Omega u\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta\,dA=0$ for every test function $\eta$. Then $u$ agrees almost everywhereA.11 with a smooth harmonic function.

The proof occupies §4.8–§4.9 (Theorem 4.9.5). First, what the hypothesis says.

DerivedProposition 4.6.3 (what the hypothesis means). If $u$ is $C^2$ on $\Omega$, then for every test function $\eta$ \[ \iint_\Omega u\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta\,dA=\iint_\Omega(\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u)\,\eta\,dA, \] and this vanishes for every test function exactly when $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ on $\Omega$.
Proof. Integrate by parts twice. Fix $y$ and work on the horizontal line through $\Omega$. The functions $u\,\partial_x\eta$ and $(\partial_xu)\,\eta$ are $C^1$ and vanish near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ (because $\eta$ does); extend them by zero, as in Prop. 3.18.3. The fundamental theorem of calculusA.9 gives $\int\partial_x(u\,\partial_x\eta)\,dx=0$ and $\int\partial_x(\partial_xu\,\eta)\,dx=0$; expanding with the product rule, \[ \int u\,\partial_x^2\eta\,dx=-\int\partial_xu\,\partial_x\eta\,dx=\int\partial_x^2u\,\eta\,dx. \] There are no boundary terms because $\eta$ vanishes near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Do the same in $y$, add, and integrate over the other variable: $\iint u\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta=\iint(\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u)\,\eta$.
"Exactly when". If $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$, the right side is $0$ for every $\eta$. Conversely, suppose $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u(z_0)\ne0$, say $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u(z_0)\gt0$. By continuity $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u\gt c\gt0$ on some disk of radius $\rho$ about $z_0$ inside $\Omega$. Take $\eta(\zeta):=\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\rho}(\zeta-z_0)$: it is a test function, $\ge0$, zero outside that disk, with integral $1$ (Lemma 4.5.3). Then $\iint(\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u)\eta\ge c\iint\eta=c\gt0$, so the integral does not vanish. The case $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u(z_0)\lt0$ is the same with signs reversed. ∎
Remark 4.6.4 (the weakest form of the equation). For $u$ only in $L^2$ (square-integrableD.2), the right side $\iint(\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u)\eta$ makes no sense, but the left side does. So the hypothesis of Weyl's lemma is "$\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ with both derivatives moved onto $\eta$". Compare the weak form of Lecture 3, $\class{ntn-a}{a}(u,\eta)=0$, which moves only one derivative. Weyl's lemma says that even this weakest version of the equation forces $u$ to be smooth. In the language of distributionsE.13, $u$ is a distributional solution of $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$.
L4 · Slide 8

4.7 Weyl's lemma applies to our $u$

DerivedProposition 4.7.1. The limit $u$ from Lecture 3 satisfies $\iint_\Omega u\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta\,dA=0$ for every test function $\eta$.
Proof.
  1. What Lecture 3 proved. $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to u$ and $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to(p,q)=\nabla u$ in $L^2$ (Prop. 3.18.1). A test function $\eta$ is smooth on $\overline\Omega$ (extended by zero near the boundary) and vanishes on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, so Theorem 3.18.6 applies to it: \[ \class{ntn-a}{a}(u,\eta)=\iint(p\,\partial_x\eta+q\,\partial_y\eta)\,dA=0. \]
  2. Integrate by parts, for each $n$. We show $\iint\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\cdot\nabla\eta\,dA=-\iint \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta\,dA$. On each closed grid square $Q$, $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is bilinear, so $F:=\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\nabla\eta$ is $C^1$ there, and by the product rule $\nabla\cdot F=\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\cdot\nabla\eta+\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta$. The divergence theoremA.6 on $Q$ gives \[ \iint_Q\big(\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\cdot\nabla\eta+\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta\big)\,dA=\oint_{\partial Q}\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\,\nabla\eta\cdot n\,ds. \] Add over all squares of $\Omega$. An edge shared by two squares appears twice, with the same integrand $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\nabla\eta$ (since $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is continuous) and opposite outward normals, so the two contributions cancel. An edge on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ contributes nothing, because $\nabla\eta=0$ there ($\eta$ vanishes near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$). The squares cover $\Omega$ up to edges of zero area. So the left sides add to $0$, which is the claim. This is the same bookkeeping as Step 4 of Prop. 3.3.3.
  3. Let $n\to\infty$. By Cauchy–SchwarzA.12, exactly as in Prop. 3.18.3, \[ \Big|\iint(\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\nabla u)\cdot\nabla\eta\Big|\le\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\nabla u}\,\norm{\nabla\eta}\to0,\qquad \Big|\iint(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u)\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta\Big|\le\norm{\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u}\,\norm{\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta}\to0. \] So the left side of Step 2 tends to $\iint(p\,\partial_x\eta+q\,\partial_y\eta)=0$, and the right side tends to $-\iint u\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta$. Equal sequences have equal limits: $\iint u\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta=0$. ∎

So the hypothesis of Weyl's lemma holds for our $u$. Note the route: Lecture 3 gave "one derivative on $u$, one on $\eta$" in the limit; Step 2 moves the last derivative onto $\eta$ before taking the limit, while $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is still a concrete piecewise-bilinear function.

L4 · Slide 9

4.8 Weyl's lemma: smoothing

From here to §4.9, $u$ is any function in $L^2(\Omega)$ satisfying the hypothesis of Weyl's lemma.

DefinedDefinition 4.8.1. $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}:=u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$, defined on $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ (Def. 4.5.4). The integral exists: it is $\iint u(\zeta)\,\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)$ over the disk of radius $\delta$ about $z$ (the weight $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\cdot)$, the function $\zeta\mapsto\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)$, is zero elsewhere), and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds it by $\norm{u}\,\norm{\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}}$.
DerivedProposition 4.8.2 ($\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ is smooth). $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ is smooth on $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$, and its derivatives are obtained by differentiating $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$: \[ \partial^\alpha \class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}(z)=\iint u(\zeta)\,\partial_z^\alpha\big[\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)\big]\,dA(\zeta)\quad\text{for every partial derivative }\partial^\alpha. \]
Proof. In $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}(z)=\iint u(\zeta)\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)$ the variable $z$ appears only inside the smooth weight. Fix $z_1\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$. Since $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ is open (C.5), there is $\rho\gt0$ such that for all $z$ within $\rho$ of $z_1$ the weight $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\cdot)$ is zero outside one fixed compact disk $B\subset\Omega$, of radius $\delta+\rho$ about $z_1$. On $B$, $u$ is integrable (Cauchy–Schwarz with the function $1$), and every $z$-derivative of $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)$ is continuous and bounded. Under these conditions differentiation under the integral signA.4 is allowed, and since the result has the same form, it can be repeated any number of times. ∎
DerivedProposition 4.8.3 ($\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ is harmonic). $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} \class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}=0$ on $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$.
Proof. Fix $z\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ and put $\eta(\zeta):=\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)$.
  1. $\eta$ is a test function. It is smooth, and it vanishes outside the closed disk of radius $\delta$ about $z$, which is a compact subset of $\Omega$ because $z\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$.
  2. $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}_z$ and $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}_\zeta$ agree on a function of $z-\zeta$. Write $\phi:=\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$ and look at $\phi(z-\zeta)$. Differentiating in the first coordinate of $z$ gives $(\partial_1\phi)(z-\zeta)$; in the first coordinate of $\zeta$ it gives $-(\partial_1\phi)(z-\zeta)$, by the chain rule. Differentiating twice, the minus sign appears twice and cancels: both give $(\partial_1^2\phi)(z-\zeta)$. The same holds in the second coordinate. So $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}_z[\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)]=\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}_\zeta[\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)]=\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta(\zeta)$.
  3. Combine. By Prop. 4.8.2 and Step 2, \[ \class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} \class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}(z)=\iint u(\zeta)\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}_z\big[\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)\big]\,dA(\zeta)=\iint u\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta\,dA=0, \] the last step being the hypothesis of Weyl's lemma applied to the test function $\eta$. ∎
CitedFact 4.8.4 (smoothing). If $u\in L^2(\Omega)$, then $u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}\to u$ in $L^2(K)$ ($L^2$ on $K$D.2) as $\delta\to0$, for every compact $K\subset\Omega$. (For small $\delta$, $K\subset\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$, so $u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$ is defined on $K$.) The slides state this as a standard fact; see mollifiersD.5.

So $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ is a smooth harmonic function that approximates $u$. The remaining question is whether these approximations settle down to a single function as $\delta\to0$. §4.9 shows they do not change at all.

L4 · Slide 10

4.9 Weyl's lemma: smoothing twice

Two facts drive the argument. (1) $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ is harmonic (Prop. 4.8.3). (2) Smoothing a harmonic function does nothing: $h\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}=h$ (Lemma 4.5.5, using Theorem 4.2.2 to get the mean value property).

DerivedLemma 4.9.1 (shrinking twice). $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{\delta+\delta'}}\subset(\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta})_{\delta'}$: if the closed disk of radius $\delta+\delta'$ about $z$ lies in $\Omega$, then the closed disk of radius $\delta'$ about $z$ lies in $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$.
Proof. Let $|w-z|\le\delta'$. Any $\zeta$ with $|\zeta-w|\le\delta$ has $|\zeta-z|\le\delta+\delta'$ by the triangle inequality, so it lies in $\Omega$. So the closed $\delta$-disk about $w$ lies in $\Omega$, i.e. $w\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$. ∎
DerivedLemma 4.9.2 (the order of two smoothings does not matter). On $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{\delta+\delta'}}$, $\ (u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta})\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}=(u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}})\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$.
Proof. Fix $z\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{\delta+\delta'}}$. Writing out both convolutions, \[ \big((u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta})\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}\big)(z)=\iint\Big(\iint u(\xi)\,\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(\zeta-\xi)\,dA(\xi)\Big)\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}(z-\zeta)\,dA(\zeta). \] Every $\xi$ that contributes is within $\delta+\delta'$ of $z$, so in $\Omega$. The integrand is absolutely integrable ($u$ is integrable on that bounded disk, the weights are bounded), so Fubini's theoremA.13 lets us integrate over $\zeta$ first: \[ =\iint u(\xi)\Big(\iint\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(\zeta-\xi)\,\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}(z-\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)\Big)dA(\xi). \] In the inner integral substitute $w=\zeta-\xi$ (a shift, which preserves area), and then $w'=(z-\xi)-w$ (a reflection and shift, also area-preserving): \[ \iint\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(w)\,\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}(z-\xi-w)\,dA(w)=\iint\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\xi-w')\,\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}(w')\,dA(w'). \] The left form is the inner integral for the order "$\delta$ then $\delta'$", the right form for "$\delta'$ then $\delta$". So both orders equal $\iint u(\xi)\,K(z-\xi)\,dA(\xi)$ with the same combined weight $K$. ∎
DerivedProposition 4.9.3 (all the $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ are one function). For all $\delta,\delta'\gt0$, $\ \class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}=\class{ntn-ud}{u_{\delta'}}$ on $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{\delta+\delta'}}$.
Proof. On $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{\delta+\delta'}}$: \[ \class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}\overset{(i)}=\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}=(u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta})\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}\overset{(ii)}=(u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}})\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}=\class{ntn-ud}{u_{\delta'}}\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}\overset{(iii)}=\class{ntn-ud}{u_{\delta'}}. \] (i) $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ is smooth and harmonic on the open set $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ (Props. 4.8.2, 4.8.3), so it has the mean value property there (Theorem 4.2.2), and Lemma 4.5.5, applied with $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ in place of $\Omega$, gives $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_{\delta'}}=\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ on $(\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta})_{\delta'}$, which contains $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{\delta+\delta'}}$ by Lemma 4.9.1. (ii) Lemma 4.9.2. (iii) The same as (i) with the roles of $\delta$ and $\delta'$ exchanged. ∎
DefinedDefinition 4.9.4 (the function $v$). For $z\in\Omega$, choose any $\delta\gt0$ with $z\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{2\delta}}$ and set $v(z):=\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}(z)$.

This is well defined. Such a $\delta$ exists because $\Omega$ is open. If $\delta$ and $\delta'$ both qualify, say $\delta\le\delta'$, then $z\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{2\delta'}}\subset\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{\delta+\delta'}}$ (a disk of radius $\delta+\delta'\le2\delta'$ fits inside one of radius $2\delta'$), so Prop. 4.9.3 gives $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}(z)=\class{ntn-ud}{u_{\delta'}}(z)$. This is the slide's "a single $v$ with $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}=v$ at all points farther than $2\delta$ from $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$".

DerivedTheorem 4.9.5 (proof of Weyl's lemma). $v$ is smooth and harmonic on $\Omega$, and $u=v$ almost everywhere.
Proof. Smooth and harmonic. Fix $\delta$. On the open set $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{2\delta}}$, $v=\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ (by definition, using this $\delta$ for every point there), and $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ is smooth and harmonic. Every point of $\Omega$ lies in some $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{2\delta}}$, so $v$ is smooth and harmonic near every point.
$v=u$ almost everywhere. Let $K\subset\Omega$ be compact. Choose $\delta_0$ with $K\subset\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{2\delta_0}}$ (C.5). For $\delta\le\delta_0$, $K\subset\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_{2\delta}}$ too, so $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}=v$ on $K$. By Fact 4.8.4, $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}\to u$ in $L^2(K)$. But $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ restricted to $K$ is the same function $v$ for every such $\delta$, so \[ \norm{v-u}_{L^2(K)}=\lim_{\delta\to0}\norm{\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}-u}_{L^2(K)}=0. \] A function with zero $L^2$ norm is zero almost everywhere, so $u=v$ almost everywhere on $K$. $\Omega$ is the union of the countably many compact sets \[ K_j:=\{z\in\Omega:\ |z|\le j\ \text{and the closed disk of radius }1/j\text{ about }z\text{ lies in }\Omega\},\qquad j=1,2,\dots, \] and a countable union of sets of measure zero has measure zero, so $u=v$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. ∎

From now on $u$ denotes $v$: we changed $u$ only on a set of area zero, which does not change it as an element of $L^2$ (D.2).

DerivedCorollary 4.9.6 (the Lecture 3 limit is a classical harmonic function). Under Hypothesis 3.14.2, the limit $u$ of the finite element solutions $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is smooth in $\Omega$ and satisfies $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ at every point of $\Omega$.
Proof. Prop. 4.7.1 verifies the hypothesis of Weyl's lemma, and Theorem 4.9.5 gives the conclusion. ∎

This settles the first of the two "missing pieces" listed in §3.19. The second, that $u(z)\to g(p)$ as $z\to p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, is the subject of Lecture 5 (Theorem 5.11.3).

L4 · Slide 11

4.10 The converse of the mean value property

DerivedTheorem 4.10.1 (converse of the mean value property). A continuous function $v$ on $\Omega$ with the mean value property is smooth and harmonic.
Proof. $v$ is smooth. By Lemma 4.5.5, $v=v\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$ on $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$. In \[ (v\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta})(z)=\iint v(\zeta)\,\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z-\zeta)\,dA(\zeta) \] the variable $z$ appears only inside $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$. As in Prop. 4.8.2, differentiate under the integral sign: every derivative falls on $\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$, which is smooth, and $v$ only needs to be continuous (so integrable on disks). So $v$ is smooth on $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$. Every point of $\Omega$ lies in some $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$, so $v$ is smooth on $\Omega$.
