$v$ is harmonic. Fix $z_0$ and let $\class{ntn-Mt}{M}(t)$ be the average of $v$ over the circle of radius $t$ about $z_0$, for $t$ small enough that the closed disk lies in $\Omega$. Steps 1–4 of Theorem 4.2.2 used only that $h$ is $C^2$, not that it is harmonic, until the last equality. Since $v$ is now smooth, they give \[ \class{ntn-Mt}{M}'(t)=\frac1{2\pi t}\iint_{\class{ntn-Dt}{D_t}}\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v\,dA. \] The mean value property says $\class{ntn-Mt}{M}(t)=v(z_0)$ for every such $t$, so $M$ is constant and $\class{ntn-Mt}{M}'(t)=0$. Hence $\iint_{\class{ntn-Dt}{D_t}}\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v\,dA=0$ for every small $t$. Divide by the area $\pi t^2$: \[ 0=\frac1{\pi t^2}\iint_{\class{ntn-Dt}{D_t}}\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v\,dA,\qquad \Big|\frac1{\pi t^2}\iint_{\class{ntn-Dt}{D_t}}\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v\,dA-\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v(z_0)\Big|\le\max_{\class{ntn-Dt}{\overline{D_t}}}|\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v-\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v(z_0)|. \] $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v$ is continuous, so the right side tends to $0$ as $t\to0$, and the disk averages (all zero) tend to $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v(z_0)$. So $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v(z_0)=0$. ∎

Together with Theorem 4.2.2: a continuous function is harmonic if and only if it has the mean value property. The right side of this equivalence mentions no derivatives.

L4 · Slide 12

4.11 Uniform limits of harmonic functions

DerivedCorollary 4.11.1 (uniform limits). Let $h_n$ be harmonic on $\Omega$ and let $h_n\to v$ uniformly on every compact subsetA.17 of $\Omega$. Then $v$ is smooth and harmonic.
Proof.
  1. $v$ is continuous. Each $z_0\in\Omega$ has a closed disk $D$ about it inside $\Omega$, which is compact. On $D$, $v$ is a uniform limit of continuous functions, hence continuous (A.17).
  2. $v$ has the mean value property. Let the closed disk $D$ of radius $r$ about $z_0$ lie in $\Omega$. Each $h_n$ is harmonic, so by Theorem 4.2.2 \[ h_n(z_0)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}h_n(z_0+re^{i\theta})\,d\theta. \] As $n\to\infty$ the left side tends to $v(z_0)$. On the right, $D$ is compact, so the convergence is uniform on the circle: \[ \Big|\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}h_n(z_0+re^{i\theta})\,d\theta-\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}v(z_0+re^{i\theta})\,d\theta\Big|\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|h_n-v|\,d\theta\le\max_D|h_n-v|\longrightarrow0. \] So both sides converge, and $v(z_0)$ equals the average of $v$ over the circle.
  3. Conclude by Theorem 4.10.1. ∎
L4 · Slide 13

4.12 Uniform limits: what just happened

Remark 4.12.1 (uniform limits are usually not smooth). Polynomials converge uniformly on $[-1,1]$ to $|x|$, which has a corner at $0$; this follows from the Weierstrass approximation theoremA.18. An explicit smooth example: $f_n(x):=\sqrt{x^2+1/n}$ is smooth and \[ 0\le f_n(x)-|x|=\frac{1/n}{\sqrt{x^2+1/n}+|x|}\le\frac{1/n}{\sqrt{1/n}}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\to0 \] uniformly in $x$. Yet the limit $|x|$ is not differentiable at $0$. Smoothness is not, in general, preserved by uniform limits.
Remark 4.12.2 (why harmonic functions escape). The slide separates two reasons.
  1. Harmonic = continuous + mean value property (Theorems 4.2.2 and 4.10.1), and the right side has no derivative in it. A statement about values and integrals survives uniform convergence (Step 2 of Cor. 4.11.1); a statement about derivatives would not, as Remark 4.12.1 shows.
  2. The smoothness of the limit is not inherited from the $h_n$. It is produced afresh by the identity $v=v\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}$ (Lemma 4.5.5): an average of a continuous function against a smooth weight is smooth (Theorem 4.10.1). The same mechanism made $\class{ntn-ud}{u_\delta}$ smooth in Weyl's lemma.

The slide closes with a preview: holomorphic functions behave the same way, for the same reason. Cauchy's integral formula (Theorem 6.3.1) is a statement about values and integrals, and Theorem 10.3.1 is the holomorphic version of Cor. 4.11.1.

Part I · Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem

Lecture 5 · Boundary values by comparison

Goal
Show the harmonic limit takes the prescribed boundary values, which completes the solution of the Dirichlet problem.
Main results
Lemma 5.6.1 (comparison) · Theorem 5.11.3 (boundary values) · Theorem 5.1.1 (existence and uniqueness)
Uses
Lectures 3 and 4; the logarithmic potential (E.6).
Used later
Part I is complete here.

Slide 1 is the title slide.

L5 · Slide 2

5.1 The theorem

DerivedTheorem 5.1.1 (the Dirichlet problem on a union of squares). Let $\Omega$ be a finite union of grid squares and $g$ continuous on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. There is exactly one $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ with $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ in $\Omega$ and $u=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.

"Finite union of grid squares" is Grid hypothesis 4.1. Note what is not assumed: $g$ need not be linear on boundary edges. $C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ is the class of twice differentiable inside, continuous up to the boundaryD.1; this is the classical Dirichlet problem of Def. 3.1.2. The proof has four steps.

StepStatementWhere
1. ReductionIt suffices to treat $g$ linear on each boundary edge of the coarsest grid.§5.2, Prop. 5.2.3
2. A candidateFor such $g$, the finite element solutions $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ converge in energy to a function $u$.Lecture 3, Theorem 3.19.1
3. Harmonic, and unique$u$ is smooth and harmonic in $\Omega$; a harmonic function in $C(\overline\Omega)$ is determined by its boundary values.Lecture 4, Cor. 4.9.6 and Cor. 4.4.2
4. Boundary values$u(z)\to g(p)$ as $z\to p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.Today: §5.4–§5.11, Theorem 5.11.3

This lecture proves step 4, by energy and a comparison of $u$ with explicit harmonic functions. Steps 1 to 3 are used as they stand; step 1 is proved in §5.2. The full proof of Theorem 5.1.1 is assembled in §5.12.

L5 · Slide 3

5.2 Step 1: reduction to piecewise linear boundary values

Suppose for now that the theorem holds for boundary data that are linear on each boundary edge of some grid (any level may play the role of the coarsest grid). We deduce it for every continuous $g$.

DefinedDefinition 5.2.1 (linearising at level $k$). Let $\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}$ be the function on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ that equals $g$ at the boundary nodes of level $k$ and is linear on each boundary edge of level $k$.

$\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}$ is well defined and continuous: $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is a union of level-$k$ boundary edges, each edge is fixed by its two endpoint values, and two edges that meet share an endpoint, where both give the value $g$ there.

DerivedLemma 5.2.2. $\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}\to g$ uniformlyA.17 on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
Proof. $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is compactC.5 and $g$ is continuous on it, so $g$ is uniformly continuousA.16: for every tolerance $\epsilon\gt0$ there is $\delta\gt0$ with $|g(q)-g(q')|\lt\epsilon$ whenever $q,q'\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ and $|q-q'|\le\delta$. Take $k$ so large that the grid side $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_k}\le\delta$. A point $q\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ lies on a level-$k$ boundary edge with endpoints $a,b$, both within $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_k}\le\delta$ of $q$. Linearity on the edge means $\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}(q)=\lambda g(a)+(1-\lambda)g(b)$ for some $\lambda\in[0,1]$, so \[ |\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}(q)-g(q)|=|\lambda(g(a)-g(q))+(1-\lambda)(g(b)-g(q))|\le\lambda|g(a)-g(q)|+(1-\lambda)|g(b)-g(q)|\lt\epsilon. \] This holds for every $q$ at once, which is uniform convergence. ∎
DerivedProposition 5.2.3 (the reduction). If Theorem 5.1.1 holds for boundary data that are linear on each boundary edge of some grid, it holds for every continuous $g$.
Proof.
  1. Solve for $\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}$. $\Omega$ is a union of level-$k$ squares too (each coarse square splits into level-$k$ squares), and $\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}$ is linear on each level-$k$ boundary edge. So Hypothesis 3.14.2 holds with level $k$ as the coarsest grid, and by assumption there is $\class{ntn-uk}{u_k}\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$, harmonic in $\Omega$, with $\class{ntn-uk}{u_k}=\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  2. The $\class{ntn-uk}{u_k}$ form a uniform Cauchy sequence. $\class{ntn-uk}{u_k}-\class{ntn-uk}{u_j}$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and continuous on $\overline\Omega$, so the stability corollary (Cor. 4.4.2) gives \[ \max_{\overline\Omega}|\class{ntn-uk}{u_k}-\class{ntn-uk}{u_j}|=\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}|\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}-\class{ntn-gk}{g_j}|\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}|\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}-g|+\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}|g-\class{ntn-gk}{g_j}|\longrightarrow0\qquad(j,k\to\infty), \] by Lemma 5.2.2 and the triangle inequality.
  3. Take the limit. A uniformly Cauchy sequence converges uniformly (A.17), so $\class{ntn-uk}{u_k}\to u$ uniformly on $\overline\Omega$ for some function $u$.
    • $u$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$: a uniform limit of continuous functions (A.17).
    • $u=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$: there $\class{ntn-uk}{u_k}=\class{ntn-gk}{g_k}\to g$.
    • $u$ is harmonic in $\Omega$: uniform convergence on $\overline\Omega$ is in particular uniform on every compact subset of $\Omega$, so Cor. 4.11.1 applies. It also makes $u$ smooth, so $u\in C^2(\Omega)$.
Uniqueness is Cor. 4.4.2 in every case. ∎

Notice the division of labour: Lecture 4's stability corollary turns uniform closeness of boundary data into uniform closeness of solutions, and its uniform-limits corollary keeps the limit harmonic.

L5 · Slide 4

5.3 Steps 2 and 3: what we may use

AssumedStanding setting 5.3.1. From now on $g$ is linear on each boundary edge of the coarsest grid (Hypothesis 3.14.2), and $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is the finite element solution on the grid of side $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_n}=2^{-n}\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}$: equal to $g$ at the boundary nodes and bilinear on each square. Points of the plane are written $z=x+iy$ (complex notationC.1).

Four facts are available.

  1. $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}=g$ on all of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. On a boundary edge, $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is linear (Prop. 3.5.8) and agrees with $g$ at both ends; $g$ is linear on the edge too, so they agree on the whole edge. (This is Lemma 3.14.3(b).)
  2. $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to u$ and $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to\nabla u$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ (Prop. 3.18.1, Prop. 3.18.3).
  3. $u$ is smooth and harmonic in $\Omega$ (Cor. 4.9.6). As agreed after Theorem 4.9.5, $u$ denotes the smooth representative; changing $u$ on a set of area zero does not affect fact 2.
  4. The maximum principle for harmonic functions in $C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ (Cor. 4.4.1).
DefinedDefinition 5.3.2 (the goal, step 4). To be proved: for every $p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, $u(z)\to g(p)$ as $z\to p$ with $z\in\Omega$.

Why this finishes the theorem: let $\tilde u:=u$ on $\Omega$ and $\tilde u:=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. At a boundary point $p$, values of $\tilde u$ at nearby interior points tend to $g(p)$ by step 4, and values at nearby boundary points tend to $g(p)$ because $g$ is continuous. So $\tilde u$ is continuous at $p$, and $\tilde u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ solves the problem.

Fact 4 cannot be applied to $u$ directly: it needs $u\in C(\overline\Omega)$, which is exactly what step 4 is meant to establish. The comparison lemma of §5.6 is the way around this.

L5 · Slide 5

5.4 Where the boundary values hide

We know $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ for every $n$, and $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to u$ in $L^2$ with $u$ harmonic. We want $u=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. This does not follow, and no argument using only these facts can prove it. Here is a counterexample.

DefinedExample 5.4.1 (a boundary layer). Take $g\equiv0$ and, for $\eps\gt0$, \[ \class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}(z):=\min\Big(1,\ \frac{\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z,\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega})}{\eps}\Big), \] where $\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z,\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega})$ is the distanceC.6 from $z$ to the boundary. (This $\class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}$ is unrelated to the discrete solution of Def. 3.9.4.)
DerivedProposition 5.4.2 (what the example does). (a) $\class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}=0$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. (b) $\class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}\to1$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as $\eps\to0$. (c) The limit $1$ is harmonic, with the wrong boundary values. (d) $\iint|\nabla \class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}|^2\,dA\approx|\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}|/\eps\to\infty$, where $|\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}|$ is the length of the boundary.
Proof. (a) On $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ the distance is $0$.
(b) $\class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}=1$ wherever $\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z,\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega})\ge\eps$. So $\class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}\ne1$ only on the layer $T_\eps:=\{z\in\Omega:\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z,\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega})\lt\eps\}$, where $0\le \class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}\le1$. Hence $\norm{\class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}-1}^2\le\operatorname{area}(T_\eps)$. $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ consists of finitely many segments of total length $|\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}|$, and the points within $\eps$ of a segment of length $\ell$ form a "stadium" of area $2\eps\ell+\pi\eps^2$. So $\operatorname{area}(T_\eps)\le2\eps|\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}|+N\pi\eps^2\to0$, with $N$ the number of segments.
(c) The constant $1$ has $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}1=0$, but it equals $1$, not $g=0$, on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
(d) In the layer, $\class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}=\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}/\eps$, and the distance function has gradient of length $1$ almost everywhere (C.6). So $|\nabla \class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}|=1/\eps$ on the layer and $0$ outside it, and $\iint|\nabla \class{ntn-Uex}{U_\eps}|^2=\operatorname{area}(T_\eps)/\eps^2$. For small $\eps$ the layer is a strip of width $\eps$ along a boundary of length $|\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}|$, of area about $\eps|\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}|$, giving about $|\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}|/\eps$. ∎
Remark 5.4.3 (the moral). The example satisfies "$U=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, $U\to u$ in $L^2$, $u$ harmonic", yet $u\ne g$ on the boundary. So those facts alone cannot prove step 4. The difference with our $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is energy: the example's energy blows up, while ours stays bounded ($\class{ntn-E}{E}(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n})=m_n\le m_0$, Prop. 3.14.4) and $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ converges in $L^2$ (fact 2 of §5.3). Any proof of step 4 must use the gradient convergence.

$L^2$ limits forget the boundary values. Energy limits remember them.

L5 · Slide 6

5.5 The plan

  1. A comparison lemma (Lemma 5.6.1), for our $u$: the harmonic $L^2$ limit of the $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$, with $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to\nabla u$ and $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. If $v$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$, harmonic in $\Omega$, and $v\ge g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, then $v\ge u$. This is a maximum principle for $v-u$ whose boundary inequality is checked against $g$, the boundary values of the $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$, because those of $u$ are not yet known to exist.
  2. Barriers (§5.10). At each $p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, explicit harmonic functions $w\ge0$: of size about $1$ at $p$, but as large as we like on the rest of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Then $\class{ntn-vpm}{v_\pm}:=g(p)\pm(\text{small}+k\,w)$ squeeze $u$ at $p$ (§5.11).

The lemma is where the energy works. The barrier is a logarithm: the potential of a point charge placed just outside $\Omega$ (logarithmic potentialE.6).

L5 · Slide 7

5.6 The comparison lemma

DerivedLemma 5.6.1 (comparison). Let $u$ be the function of Lecture 3: harmonic in $\Omega$, the $L^2$ limit of the $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$, with $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to\nabla u$ in $L^2$ and $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Let $\class{ntn-vc}{v}$ be continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and harmonic in $\Omega$. If $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\ge g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, then $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\ge u$ in $\Omega$. If $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\le g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, then $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\le u$ in $\Omega$.

Compare the maximum principle, Cor. 4.4.1: it would give $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\ge u$ from $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\ge u$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Here the boundary comparison is made with $g$ instead, because $u$ has no known boundary values yet. The proof runs through §5.6–§5.9; the complete argument is collected at the end of §5.9.

DefinedDefinition 5.6.2 (the functions $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}$ and $\class{ntn-zf}{z}$). Fix $\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}\gt0$ and put \[ \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}:=\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-\class{ntn-vc}{v},\qquad \class{ntn-zf}{z}:=u-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-\class{ntn-vc}{v}. \] Careful: in §5.6–§5.9 the letter $\class{ntn-zf}{z}$ names this function, not a point of the plane.

We show $\class{ntn-zf}{z}\le0$ in $\Omega$. Then $u\le \class{ntn-vc}{v}+\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}$, and letting $\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}\downarrow0$ gives $u\le \class{ntn-vc}{v}$. The constant $\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}$ buys a margin: on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}=g-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-\class{ntn-vc}{v}\le-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}\lt0$ strictly.

Everything rests on the positive part $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}:=\max(\class{ntn-zn}{z_n},0)$. It vanishes near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, its energy tends to zero, and it tends to $\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$. First, a list of what is needed about $t\mapsto t^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$.

L5 · Slide 8

5.7 What we need about $t\mapsto t^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$

DefinedDefinition 5.7.1 (positive part). For a real number $t$, $t^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}:=\max(t,0)$. For a function, $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}:=\max(f,0)$ pointwise. Throughout §5.7, $f$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$, $f\le-\sigma$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ for some $\sigma\gt0$, and smooth in $\Omega$ on each closed square of some grid. (In mind: $f=z_n=\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-\sigma-v$.)
DerivedProposition 5.7.2 (properties of $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$). (a) Support. $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=0$ outside the compact set $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}:=\{z\in\overline\Omega:f(z)\ge0\}$, and $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}\subset\Omega$.
(b) Contraction. $|a^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}-b^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|\le|a-b|$ for real $a,b$.
(c) Gradient. $\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=\nabla f$ where $f\gt0$, and $\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=0$ where $f\le0$, almost everywhere. So $\nabla f\cdot\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=|\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|^2$ almost everywhere.
(d) Green. $\iint_\Omega\nabla w\cdot\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\,dA=-\iint_\Omega f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} w\,dA$ for $w$ smooth in $\Omega$; so $=0$ if $w$ is harmonic.
(e) Poincaré. $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{f^+}_{L^2}}\le \class{ntn-L}{L}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla f^+}_{L^2}}$, with $\class{ntn-L}{L}$ the width of $\Omega$.
Proof.
  1. Support. $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}$ is closed (points where a continuous function is $\ge0$, inside the closed set $\overline\Omega$) and bounded, hence compactC.5. On $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, $f\le-\sigma\lt0$, so $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}$ misses $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$; hence $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}\subset\Omega$. Outside $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}$, $f\lt0$ and $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=0$. Since compact $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}$ stays a positive distance from $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ (C.5(a)), $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ vanishes on a whole band around $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, not just on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  2. Contraction. By cases. If $a,b\ge0$: $|a^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}-b^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|=|a-b|$. If $a,b\le0$: $|a^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}-b^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|=0$. If $a\gt0\ge b$: $|a^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}-b^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|=a\le a-b=|a-b|$; the case $b\gt0\ge a$ is symmetric. Geometrically, $t\mapsto t^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ has slope $0$ or $1$, so it never stretches distances: it is 1-LipschitzA.10.
  3. Gradient. Inside each open square, $f$ is smooth, so $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ is LipschitzA.10 there (by (b)) and differentiable almost everywhere. At a point of differentiability:
    • if $f\gt0$ there, then $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=f$ on a neighbourhood, so $\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=\nabla f$;
    • if $f\lt0$ there, then $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=0$ on a neighbourhood, so $\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=0$;
    • if $f=0$ there, then $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ has a minimum ($f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\ge0$ everywhere, $=0$ here), and a differentiable function has zero gradient at a minimum: $\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=0$.
    Grid lines have zero area. So almost everywhere, $\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ is either $\nabla f$ (where $f\gt0$) or $0$, and in both cases $\nabla f\cdot\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=|\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|^2$. Along any line the same reasoning applies in one variable: $f$ is piecewise $C^1$ near $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}$, $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ is Lipschitz there, and $(f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}})'=f'$ where $f\gt0$, $=0$ where $f\lt0$, and $=0$ on $\{f=0\}$ wherever it exists.
  4. Green. Fix a horizontal line. On each interval where the line crosses $\Omega$, $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ vanishes near both ends by (a). The product $w_x f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ is Lipschitz on the part of the interval where $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\ne0$ ($w$ is smooth there; $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ is Lipschitz), and zero near the ends, so the fundamental theorem of calculus for Lipschitz functionsA.10 gives $\int\partial_x(w_xf^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}})\,dx=0$. Expanding with the product rule, \[ \int w_x\,(f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}})_x\,dx=-\int w_{xx}\,f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\,dx. \] Do the same along vertical lines with $w_y$, integrate over the other variable, and add: $\iint\nabla w\cdot\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=-\iint f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} w$. There are no boundary terms because $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ vanishes near the ends. This is Step 1 of Prop. 3.18.3 with the test function $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$, which is not smooth but vanishes near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. If $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} w=0$ the right side is $0$.
  5. Poincaré. $f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and $0$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. The proof of Theorem 3.17.2 only used the fundamental theorem of calculus along horizontal lines and Cauchy–Schwarz; the first holds for Lipschitz functions (A.10), so the same proof gives $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\le \class{ntn-L}{L}\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla f^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}$. ∎

A small point on (a)–(e) as applied to $f=z_n$: $v$ is smooth inside $\Omega$ but may not be smooth on the boundary edges of squares touching $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. This does no harm, because every step above takes place on or near $\class{ntn-Kc}{K}$, which stays inside $\Omega$.

L5 · Slide 9

5.8 Proof of the lemma: the energy of $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ vanishes

DerivedProposition 5.8.1 (Step 1: $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ lives inside $\Omega$). Properties (a)–(e) of Prop. 5.7.2 apply to $f=\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}$.
Proof. Uses $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}=g\le \class{ntn-vc}{v}$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. On $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}=g$ (fact 1 of §5.3) and $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\ge g$, so $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}=g-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-\class{ntn-vc}{v}\le-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}$. Also $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$ ($\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ and $\class{ntn-vc}{v}$ are), and inside $\Omega$ it is smooth on each closed square of the level-$n$ grid ($\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is bilinear there and $\class{ntn-vc}{v}$ is smooth, being harmonic). These are the hypotheses of §5.7. ∎
DerivedProposition 5.8.2 (Step 2: its energy tends to zero). $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u)}}\to0$, and $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\to0$.
Proof. Uses $u$ harmonic and $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to\nabla u$.
  1. By Prop. 5.7.2(c), $|\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|^2=\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}\cdot\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ almost everywhere.
  2. Split $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}=(\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}-\class{ntn-zf}{z})+\class{ntn-zf}{z}$, where $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}-\class{ntn-zf}{z}=\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u$ (the $-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-\class{ntn-vc}{v}$ cancels): \[ \iint_\Omega|\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|^2\,dA=\iint_\Omega\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u)\cdot\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\,dA+\underbrace{\iint_\Omega\nabla \class{ntn-zf}{z}\cdot\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\,dA}_{=\,0}. \]
  3. The last integral is $0$ by Prop. 5.7.2(d): $\class{ntn-zf}{z}=u-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-\class{ntn-vc}{v}$ is smooth and harmonic in $\Omega$, since $u$ and $\class{ntn-vc}{v}$ are harmonic, $\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}$ is a constant, and $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}$ is linear.
  4. By Cauchy–SchwarzA.12, the first integral is at most $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u)}}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}$. So \[ \class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}^2\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u)}}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}. \] If $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}=0$ the claim is trivial; otherwise divide by it: $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla(\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u)}}$, which tends to $0$ by fact 2 of §5.3.
  5. By Prop. 5.7.2(e), $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\le \class{ntn-L}{L}\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\nabla \class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\to0$. ∎

The point of Step 2: the energy of $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ is controlled by how far $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ is from $\nabla u$. This is exactly where gradient convergence enters, the ingredient Example 5.4.1 lacked.

5.9 Proof of the lemma: identify the limit

DerivedProposition 5.9.1 (Step 3: $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\to \class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ in $L^2$). $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}-\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u}}\to0$, and consequently $\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=0$ almost everywhere in $\Omega$.
Proof. Uses $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to u$ in $L^2$. By Prop. 5.7.2(b), at every point of $\Omega$, \[ |\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}-\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}|\le|\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}-\class{ntn-zf}{z}|=|\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u|. \] Square and integrate: $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}-\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}-u}}\to0$. So $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\to \class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$ in $L^2$, while $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\to0$ by Prop. 5.8.2. Limits in $L^2$ are unique: \[ \class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}-\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}+\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}\to0, \] so $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}}}=0$, and $\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}=0$ almost everywhereA.11. ∎
DerivedProposition 5.9.2 (Step 4: almost everywhere to everywhere). $\class{ntn-zf}{z}\le0$ at every point of $\Omega$, that is, $u\le \class{ntn-vc}{v}+\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}$.
Proof. $\class{ntn-zf}{z}=u-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-\class{ntn-vc}{v}$ is continuous in $\Omega$. If $\class{ntn-zf}{z}\gt0$ at some point, continuity gives a disk around it on which $\class{ntn-zf}{z}\gt0$, so $\class{ntn-zf}{z}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}\gt0$ on a set of positive area. That contradicts Prop. 5.9.1. So $\class{ntn-zf}{z}\le0$ everywhere. ∎
Proof of Lemma 5.6.1. Let $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\ge g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. For each $\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}\gt0$, Props. 5.8.1–5.9.2 give $u\le \class{ntn-vc}{v}+\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}$ in $\Omega$. Let $\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}\downarrow0$: $u\le \class{ntn-vc}{v}$.
For the mirror statement, suppose $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\le g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ and take $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}:=\class{ntn-vc}{v}-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ and $\class{ntn-zf}{z}:=\class{ntn-vc}{v}-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-u$. On $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}=\class{ntn-vc}{v}-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}-g\le-\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}$; $\class{ntn-zf}{z}$ is harmonic; and $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}-\class{ntn-zf}{z}=u-\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$. The same four steps apply word for word and give $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\le u+\class{ntn-sig}{\sigma}$, hence $\class{ntn-vc}{v}\le u$. ∎

5.10 The barrier: a point charge outside $\Omega$

DerivedLemma 5.10.1 (an empty coarse square at $p$). Fix $p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Some closed square $\class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$ of the coarsest grid contains $p$ and is not a square of $\Omega$. Its interior misses $\overline\Omega$, and it contains a closed square $\class{ntn-Qp}{Q_p}$ of side $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/2$ with a corner at $p$.
Proof. The closed coarse squares containing $p$ (one, two or four of them, depending on whether $p$ is inside a square, on an edge, or at a node) together cover a disk around $p$. If all of them were squares of $\Omega$, that disk would lie in their union, and $p$ would be in the interior of $\overline\Omega$, which is $\Omega$ (Hypothesis 3.4.1). But $p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ and $\Omega$ is open, so $p\notin\Omega$. So one of them, $\class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$, is not a square of $\Omega$.
Distinct grid squares overlap only along edges, so no closed square of $\Omega$ meets the interior of $\class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$; since $\overline\Omega$ is the union of those squares, $\overline\Omega$ misses the interior of $\class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$.
Finally, $p\in \class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$ is within $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/2$ of the centre of $\class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$ in each coordinate, so the square of side $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/2$ with corner $p$ that extends towards the centre of $\class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$ lies inside $\class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$. Call it $\class{ntn-Qp}{Q_p}$. ∎
DefinedDefinition 5.10.2 (the barrier). Let $\class{ntn-yp}{y}$ be the point on the diagonal of $\class{ntn-Qp}{Q_p}$ through $p$ at distance $d\le\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/4$ from $p$, and \[ \class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(z):=\log\frac{|z-\class{ntn-yp}{y}|}{\class{ntn-dd}{d}/2}. \] This is the potential of a point chargeE.6 at $\class{ntn-yp}{y}$ (Lecture 2, Remark 2.4.4). Here $z$ is again a point of the plane, and $\class{ntn-yp}{y}$ is a point, not a coordinate.
DerivedLemma 5.10.3 (properties of the barrier). (i) $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and smooth on $\overline\Omega$, since $\class{ntn-yp}{y}\notin\overline\Omega$.
(ii) $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}\ge0$ on $\overline\Omega$.
(iii) $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(p)=\log2$.
(iv) $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(z)\ge\log(|z-p|/\class{ntn-dd}{d})$ whenever $|z-p|\ge2\class{ntn-dd}{d}$.
Proof. Write $\class{ntn-yp}{y}=p+\frac{\class{ntn-dd}{d}}{\sqrt2}(\pm1,\pm1)$, with signs pointing into $\class{ntn-Qp}{Q_p}$.
  1. $\log|z-\class{ntn-yp}{y}|$ is harmonic away from $\class{ntn-yp}{y}$ (E.6), and $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}$ differs from it by the constant $-\log(\class{ntn-dd}{d}/2)$. The point $\class{ntn-yp}{y}$ is at distance $\class{ntn-dd}{d}/\sqrt2\gt0$ from the two sides of $\class{ntn-Qp}{Q_p}$ through $p$, and at distance at least $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/2-\class{ntn-dd}{d}/\sqrt2\ge\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/2-\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/(4\sqrt2)\gt0$ from the other two, so $\class{ntn-yp}{y}$ is in the interior of $\class{ntn-Qp}{Q_p}\subset \class{ntn-Ssq}{S}$, which misses $\overline\Omega$ (Lemma 5.10.1). So $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}$ is smooth on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$.
  2. $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}\lt0$ exactly when $|z-\class{ntn-yp}{y}|\lt \class{ntn-dd}{d}/2$. The disk of radius $\class{ntn-dd}{d}/2$ about $\class{ntn-yp}{y}$ lies inside $\class{ntn-Qp}{Q_p}$: its radius $\class{ntn-dd}{d}/2$ is less than $\class{ntn-dd}{d}/\sqrt2$, the distance to the near sides, and less than $\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/2-\class{ntn-dd}{d}/\sqrt2\approx0.32\,\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}$, the distance to the far sides (since $\class{ntn-dd}{d}/2\le\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/8$). So that disk misses $\overline\Omega$, and $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}\ge0$ on $\overline\Omega$.
  3. $|p-\class{ntn-yp}{y}|=\class{ntn-dd}{d}$, so $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(p)=\log\frac{\class{ntn-dd}{d}}{\class{ntn-dd}{d}/2}=\log2$.
  4. If $|z-p|\ge2\class{ntn-dd}{d}$ then $d\le\frac12|z-p|$, and by the triangle inequality \[ |z-\class{ntn-yp}{y}|\ge|z-p|-|p-\class{ntn-yp}{y}|=|z-p|-d\ge\tfrac12|z-p|. \] Since $\log$ is increasing, $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(z)\ge\log\frac{|z-p|/2}{\class{ntn-dd}{d}/2}=\log\frac{|z-p|}{\class{ntn-dd}{d}}$. ∎

So the barrier is small at $p$ (exactly $\log2$) and large everywhere else as $d\to0$: at a fixed distance $r$ from $p$ it is at least $\log(r/\class{ntn-dd}{d})\to\infty$. Placing the charge outside $\Omega$ is what keeps $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}$ harmonic and nonnegative on all of $\overline\Omega$; this is possible because every boundary point of a union of squares has an empty square next to it.

L5 · Slide 12

5.11 Squeezing $u$ at $p$

DefinedDefinition 5.11.1 (the squeezing functions). Fix $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}\le\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/2$ and $d\le\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}/2$. Let \[ \class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}:=\max\{|g(q)-g(p)|:q\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega},\ |q-p|\le\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}\} \] (the oscillation of $g$ within $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}$ of $p$), and put \[ \class{ntn-vpm}{v_\pm}:=g(p)\pm\big(\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}+\class{ntn-kk}{k}\,\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}\big),\qquad \class{ntn-kk}{k}:=\frac{2\max|g|}{\log(\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}/\class{ntn-dd}{d})}. \]

The maximum defining $\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}$ exists because it is taken over a compact set ($\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ intersected with a closed disk) of values of a continuous function. Since $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}/d\ge2$, $\log(\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}/\class{ntn-dd}{d})\ge\log2\gt0$, so $\class{ntn-kk}{k}$ is a well-defined nonnegative number. Also $d\le\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}/2\le\class{ntn-epsn}{\eps_0}/4$, as Def. 5.10.2 requires.

DerivedLemma 5.11.2 (boundary comparison). $\class{ntn-vpm}{v_-}\le g\le \class{ntn-vpm}{v_+}$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, and $\class{ntn-vpm}{v_\pm}$ are continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and harmonic in $\Omega$.
Proof. $\class{ntn-vpm}{v_\pm}$ is a constant plus a constant multiple of $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}$, which is smooth on $\overline\Omega$ and harmonic in $\Omega$ (Lemma 5.10.3(i)). Let $q\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  • Within $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}$ of $p$ ($|q-p|\le\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}$): $\class{ntn-kk}{k}\,\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(q)\ge0$ by Lemma 5.10.3(ii), so \[ \class{ntn-vpm}{v_+}(q)\ge g(p)+\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}\ge g(p)+|g(q)-g(p)|\ge g(q). \]
  • Farther than $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}$ from $p$: $|q-p|\gt\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}\ge2\class{ntn-dd}{d}$, so Lemma 5.10.3(iv) gives $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(q)\ge\log(|q-p|/\class{ntn-dd}{d})\ge\log(\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}/\class{ntn-dd}{d})$, hence $\class{ntn-kk}{k}\,\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(q)\ge2\max|g|$. Since $\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}\ge0$ and $g(p)\ge-\max|g|$, \[ \class{ntn-vpm}{v_+}(q)\ge g(p)+2\max|g|\ge\max|g|\ge g(q). \]
So $\class{ntn-vpm}{v_+}\ge g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. The same two cases, with all signs reversed, give $\class{ntn-vpm}{v_-}\le g$. ∎
DerivedTheorem 5.11.3 (step 4: boundary values). For every $p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, $u(z)\to g(p)$ as $z\to p$ with $z\in\Omega$.
Proof.
  1. Squeeze. By Lemma 5.11.2 and the comparison lemma (Lemma 5.6.1, both halves), $\class{ntn-vpm}{v_-}\le u\le \class{ntn-vpm}{v_+}$ in $\Omega$. Subtracting $g(p)$: \[ |u(z)-g(p)|\le\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}+\class{ntn-kk}{k}\,\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(z)\qquad\text{for all }z\in\Omega. \]
  2. Let $z\to p$. $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}$ is continuous at $p$ with $\class{ntn-wd}{w_d}(p)=\log2$, so taking the limit superiorA.14, \[ \limsup_{z\to p}|u(z)-g(p)|\le\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}+\class{ntn-kk}{k}\log2=\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}+\frac{2\max|g|\log2}{\log(\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}/\class{ntn-dd}{d})}. \]
  3. Remove $\class{ntn-dd}{d}$ and $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}$. The left side involves neither $\class{ntn-dd}{d}$ nor $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}$, so the inequality holds for every admissible choice. Let $d\to0$ with $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}$ fixed: $\log(\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}/\class{ntn-dd}{d})\to\infty$, so the second term vanishes, and $\limsup|u(z)-g(p)|\le\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}$. Then let $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}\to0$: $\class{ntn-osc}{\operatorname{osc}_\rho}\to0$ by continuity of $g$ at $p$.
  4. So $\limsup_{z\to p}|u(z)-g(p)|=0$, which means $u(z)\to g(p)$. ∎

The two parameters do different jobs. $\class{ntn-rho}{\rho}$ controls how much $g$ itself varies near $p$; $\class{ntn-dd}{d}$ controls how sharply the barrier rises away from $p$, and sending $d\to0$ makes the barrier's cost at $p$ (the term $\class{ntn-kk}{k}\log2$) negligible.

DerivedTheorem 5.12.1 (step 4, restated). For $g$ linear on the coarse boundary edges, the energy limit $u$ of Lecture 3 satisfies $u(z)\to g(p)$ as $z\to p$, for every $p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
Proof of Theorem 5.1.1.
  1. Linear-edge data. Let $g$ be linear on each boundary edge of some grid, and take that grid as the coarsest. Lecture 3 gives the energy limit $u$ (Theorem 3.19.1); Lecture 4 makes it smooth and harmonic in $\Omega$ (Cor. 4.9.6); Theorem 5.11.3 gives the boundary values. As explained after Def. 5.3.2, $u$ extended by $g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ lies in $C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ and solves the problem.

Remark 5.12.2 (what went in).
  • Lecture 3: the two limits $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to u$ and $\nabla \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\to\nabla u$, and $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}=g$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  • Lecture 4: Weyl's lemma and the maximum principle.
  • Today: integration by parts against $\class{ntn-zn}{z_n}^{\class{ntn-pos}{+}}$, and the logarithmic barrier.
Remark 5.12.3 (beyond grids). The comparison lemma used nothing about the $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ except the three properties above. Stripped of the grid, it says:

A harmonic function that is an energy limit of functions with boundary values $\le v$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is $\le v$ in $\Omega$.

With "$H^1$" and "trace"D.6 put in, this is the weak maximum principleE.14 of the modern theory of elliptic equations. The grid was used in only two places: to build the $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ (Lecture 3), and to find an empty square next to each boundary point for the barrier (Lemma 5.10.1). On general domains the second can fail; see barriers and regular pointsE.15.
Part II

Cauchy's theory

One complex derivative, with continuous real and imaginary parts, forces a function to be a power series. Lecture 6 derives this from Cauchy's theorem and integral formula, then turns residues into a tool for counting, as far as the Hardy–Ramanujan formula for partitions. Lecture 7 counts zeros and poles with the argument principle.
