L7 · Slide 2

7.1 Zeros, poles and $f'/f$

The residue theorem counts residues. Applied to $f'/f$, it counts zeros and poles. First, the two local pictures side by side.

DefinedDefinition 7.1.1 (zero of order $m$). $f$ has a zero of order $m\ge1$ at $a$ if $f$ is holomorphic near $a$ and its Taylor coefficients at $a$ satisfy $a_0=\dots=a_{m-1}=0\ne a_m$. (This is Def. 6.7.2.)
DefinedDefinition 7.1.2 (pole of order $m$). $f$ has a pole of order $m\ge1$ at $a$ if, for some $\rho\gt0$, $f=g/(z-a)^m$ on $0\lt|z-a|\lt\rho$, with $g$ holomorphic on $|z-a|\lt\rho$ and $g(a)\ne0$. (This is Def. 6.8.1, with an open disk.)

In both cases $f(z)$ behaves like a constant times $(z-a)^{\pm m}$ near $a$: a zero is a "pole of negative order". The lemma below makes this precise through the logarithmic derivative $f'/f$, so called because it is $(\log f)'$ wherever a branch of $\log f$ exists.

DerivedLemma 7.1.3 (logarithmic derivative). Let $f$ be holomorphic and $\ne0$ on $0\lt|z-a|\lt r$, with a zero or a pole of order $m$ at $a$. Then for every $\epsilon\in(0,r)$, \[ \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-a|=\epsilon}\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=\begin{cases}\ \ m&\text{at a zero},\\-m&\text{at a pole}.\end{cases} \]

Test case: $f(z)=(z-a)^m$ has $\frac{f'}{f}=\frac{m}{z-a}$, whose integral is $m$ (Cor. 2.6.4); $f=(z-a)^{-m}$ gives $-m$. The lemma says that only this leading behaviour matters.

L7 · Slide 3

7.2 The logarithmic derivative: proof

Proof of Lemma 7.1.3.
  1. Rewrite as an average. Let $\class{ntn-Gld}{G}(z):=(z-a)\,f'(z)/f(z)$. With $z=a+\epsilon e^{i\theta}$, $dz=i\epsilon e^{i\theta}d\theta=i(z-a)\,d\theta$, so \[ \class{ntn-Ieps}{I}(\epsilon):=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-a|=\epsilon}\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,i(z-a)\,d\theta=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\class{ntn-Gld}{G}(a+\epsilon e^{i\theta})\,d\theta. \]
  2. $\class{ntn-Ieps}{I}(\epsilon)$ is constant. $f'$ is holomorphic where $f$ is (Cor. 6.6.2), so $f'/f$ is holomorphic on $0\lt|z-a|\lt r$, where $f\ne0$. For $0\lt\epsilon_1\lt\epsilon_2\lt r$, Lemma 6.2.1 with $C:|z-a|=\epsilon_2$ and the single inner circle $|z-a|=\epsilon_1$ gives $\class{ntn-Ieps}{I}(\epsilon_1)=\class{ntn-Ieps}{I}(\epsilon_2)$.
  3. Reduce to a limit. Writing $\pm m=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}(\pm m)\,d\theta$, \[ |\class{ntn-Ieps}{I}(\epsilon)\mp m|=\Big|\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\big(\class{ntn-Gld}{G}(a+\epsilon e^{i\theta})\mp m\big)\,d\theta\Big|\le\max_\theta|\class{ntn-Gld}{G}(a+\epsilon e^{i\theta})\mp m|. \] So if $\class{ntn-Gld}{G}(z)\to\pm m$ as $z\to a$, then $\class{ntn-Ieps}{I}(\epsilon)\to\pm m$ as $\epsilon\to0$; and since $I$ is constant, $\class{ntn-Ieps}{I}(\epsilon)=\pm m$ for every $\epsilon$. It remains to show $\class{ntn-Gld}{G}(z)\to\pm m$.
  4. At a zero. The Taylor coefficients of $f'$ at $a$ are those of $f$ shifted: the $k$-th one is $\frac{(f')^{(k)}(a)}{k!}=\frac{f^{(k+1)}(a)}{k!}=(k+1)\,a_{k+1}$ (Theorem 6.6.1). It is $0$ for $k\lt m-1$ and $m\,a_m$ for $k=m-1$. The Taylor remainder (Cor. 6.5.1), for $f$ with $N=m+1$ and for $f'$ with $N=m$, gives, as $z\to a$, \[ f(z)=(z-a)^m\big(a_m+O(|z-a|)\big),\qquad f'(z)=(z-a)^{m-1}\big(m\,a_m+O(|z-a|)\big). \] So \[ \class{ntn-Gld}{G}(z)=\frac{(z-a)\,(z-a)^{m-1}(m\,a_m+O(|z-a|))}{(z-a)^m(a_m+O(|z-a|))}=\frac{m\,a_m+O(|z-a|)}{a_m+O(|z-a|)}\longrightarrow m, \] since $a_m\ne0$.
  5. At a pole. Near $a$, $g\ne0$ (it is continuous with $g(a)\ne0$). From $f=g\,(z-a)^{-m}$, the product rule gives $f'=g'(z-a)^{-m}-m\,g\,(z-a)^{-m-1}$, so \[ \frac{f'}f=\frac{g'}g-\frac m{z-a},\qquad \class{ntn-Gld}{G}(z)=(z-a)\frac{g'(z)}{g(z)}-m\longrightarrow-m, \] because $g'/g$ is continuous, hence bounded, near $a$. ∎
L7 · Slide 4

7.3 The argument principle

DerivedTheorem 7.3.1 (argument principle). Let $f$ be holomorphic near $\{|z|\le R\}\setminus\{\zeta_1,\dots,\zeta_p\}$, with poles at $\zeta_1,\dots,\zeta_p\in\{|z|\lt R\}$, and $f\ne0$ on $C:=\{|z|=R\}$. Let $\class{ntn-ZP}{Z}$ and $\class{ntn-ZP}{P}$ be the numbers of zeros and of poles of $f$ in $|z|\lt R$, counted with multiplicity (each zero or pole counted as often as its order). Then \[ \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=\class{ntn-ZP}{Z}-\class{ntn-ZP}{P}. \]

The name: along $C$, $\frac{f'}{f}dz$ is the change in a logarithm of $f(z)$, whose imaginary part is the argument. So the integral is the number of times $f(z)$ winds around $0$ as $z$ goes once around $C$; see winding numbersE.17.

Proof, part 1: $\class{ntn-ZP}{Z}$ is finite.
  1. $\Omega:=\{|z|\lt R\}\setminus\{\zeta_1,\dots,\zeta_p\}$ is open, and connectedC.4 (any two of its points can be joined by a path in the disk that detours around the finitely many $\zeta_j$).
  2. $f\not\equiv0$ on $\Omega$: $f$ is continuous and nonzero on $C$, so it is nonzero at points of $\Omega$ close to $C$.
  3. By the isolated zeros theorem (Theorem 6.7.1) each zero of $f$ in $\Omega$ is isolated, and its Taylor coefficients are not all $0$ (step 1 of that proof), so it has a finite order. Otherwise $f\equiv0$ near it.
  4. Suppose there were infinitely many distinct zeros $z_k$. They lie in the compact disk $|z|\le R$, so a subsequence converges to some $w$ with $|w|\le R$ (Bolzano–Weierstrass, C.5). Then:
    • $w$ is not a pole: near a pole, $|f|=|g|/|z-\zeta|^m\to\infty$, but $f(z_k)=0$;
    • so $f$ is continuous at $w$, and $f(w)=\lim f(z_k)=0$; in particular $w\notin C$;
    • so $w\in\Omega$ is a zero that is a limit of other zeros, i.e. not isolated. This contradicts step 3.
So there are finitely many zeros, each of finite order, and $\class{ntn-ZP}{Z}$ is a finite number. ∎
L7 · Slide 5

7.4 The argument principle: counting

Proof, part 2: counting.
  1. List the special points. Let $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_q$ be the zeros and the poles of $f$ in $|z|\lt R$, with orders $m_1,\dots,m_q$. Take $\delta\gt0$ so small that the disks $|z-\xi_j|\lt2\delta$ are pairwise disjoint, lie in $|z|\lt R$, and contain no zero or pole other than $\xi_j$.
  2. Where $f'/f$ is holomorphic. $f'/f$ is holomorphic on the open set where $f$ is holomorphic and $\ne0$ (Cor. 6.6.2 and the quotient rule). That set contains each punctured disk $0\lt|z-\xi_j|\lt2\delta$, and the closed region $A$ inside $C$ and outside the circles $|z-\xi_j|=\delta$: $A$ contains no zero or pole (those inside are the $\xi_j$, and $f\ne0$ on $C$).
  3. Move the circle, then apply the lemma. Lemma 6.2.1, then Lemma 7.1.3 with $r=2\delta$ and $\epsilon=\delta$: \[ \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f'}f\,dz=\sum_{j=1}^q\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-\xi_j|=\delta}\frac{f'}f\,dz=\sum_{\xi_j\text{ a zero}}m_j-\sum_{\xi_j\text{ a pole}}m_j=\class{ntn-ZP}{Z}-\class{ntn-ZP}{P}. \]
∎

In the language of the residue theorem: $f'/f$ has a simple pole at each zero and each pole of $f$, with residue $+m$ or $-m$ (step 4 and step 5 of Lemma 7.1.3 show $f'/f=\frac{\pm m}{z-a}+$ (bounded)), and no other singularities. The theorem is Theorem 6.9.1 applied to $f'/f$.

L7 · Slide 6

7.5 Example: rational functions

DerivedExample 7.5.1 (rational functions). Let $f(z)=\lambda\prod_j(z-a_j)^{m_j}\big/\prod_k(z-b_k)^{n_k}$, with $\lambda\ne0$, the $a_j,b_k$ distinct, and none of them on $|z|=R$. Then \[ \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=R}\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=\sum_{|a_j|\lt R}m_j-\sum_{|b_k|\lt R}n_k, \] and this is $\class{ntn-ZP}{Z}-\class{ntn-ZP}{P}$, as Theorem 7.3.1 predicts.
Proof.
  1. Logarithmic derivative of a product. By the product rule, $(gh)'/(gh)=g'/g+h'/h$, and similarly for quotients with a minus sign; also $\frac{((z-a)^m)'}{(z-a)^m}=\frac m{z-a}$. So \[ \frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}=\sum_j\frac{m_j}{z-a_j}-\sum_k\frac{n_k}{z-b_k}. \]
  2. Integrate each term. For $|a|\ne R$: \[ \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=R}\frac{dz}{z-a}=\begin{cases}1,&|a|\lt R\quad\text{(Theorem 6.3.1 with }f\equiv1\text{, }w=a),\\0,&|a|\gt R\quad\text{(Theorem 6.1.2: }\tfrac1{z-a}\text{ is holomorphic near }|z|\le R).\end{cases} \]
  3. Identify $\class{ntn-ZP}{Z}-\class{ntn-ZP}{P}$. Near $a_j$, $f=(z-a_j)^{m_j}h$ with $h$ holomorphic and $h(a_j)\ne0$ (the other factors do not vanish at $a_j$). By Leibniz's rule for the $k$-th derivative of a product, $f^{(k)}(a_j)=\sum_i\binom ki\big((z-a_j)^{m_j}\big)^{(i)}h^{(k-i)}\big|_{a_j}$, and $\big((z-a_j)^{m_j}\big)^{(i)}$ vanishes at $a_j$ unless $i=m_j$. So $f^{(k)}(a_j)=0$ for $k\lt m_j$ and $f^{(m_j)}(a_j)=m_j!\,h(a_j)\ne0$: a zero of order $m_j$. Near $b_k$, $f=g/(z-b_k)^{n_k}$ with $g(b_k)\ne0$: a pole of order $n_k$. There are no other zeros or poles. ∎

For rational functions the argument principle is therefore just bookkeeping. Its power is that it holds for every $f$ that is holomorphic apart from poles (a meromorphic function), whose zeros usually cannot be listed in advance. Rouché's theorem (Theorem 11.10.1) is the main application in the course.

Part III

Contour integrals and Fourier analysis

Real integrals and Fourier transforms are evaluated by closing the line of integration in the complex plane. The same contour moves show that the width of the strip where $f$ is holomorphic governs the decay of $\hat f$, and that band-limited signals are determined by their samples.

Part III · Contour integrals and Fourier analysis

Lecture 8 · Integrals, Fourier transforms and sampling

Goal
Evaluate real integrals and Fourier transforms by contour integration; match analyticity of $f$ with decay of $\hat f$; prove the sampling theorem.
Main results
Prop. 8.2.2, Prop. 8.3.1 (two transforms) · Theorem 8.5.2 (strips and decay) · Theorem 8.7.1 (Paley–Wiener) · Cor. 8.9.2 (time- or band-limited) · Theorem 8.10.1 (sampling)
Uses
Theorems 6.1.2 and 6.9.1, extended in Prop. 8.1.1; Theorem 6.7.1; Fourier inversion (D.7); Poisson summation (E.16).
Used later
Cor. 11.9.1 supplies the Gaussian integral used here.

Slide 1 is the title slide.

L8 · Slide 2

8.1 Warm-up: $\int dx/(1+x^2)$

The idea of the lecture: a real integral $\int_{-\infty}^\infty$ is the limit of $\int_{-R}^R$; close the segment $[-R,R]$ into a loop in $\mathbb C$, evaluate the loop integral by residues, and show the added piece vanishes as $R\to\infty$. The loops used are half-disks, rectangles and sectors, not circles, so we first extend Part II's two theorems to them.

DerivedProposition 8.1.1 (other contours). Theorem 6.1.2 and Theorem 6.9.1 hold for every bounded closed region $D$ whose boundary consists of finitely many piecewise $C^1$ closed curves (a half-disk, a rectangle, a circular sector), oriented with $D$ on the left: if $f$ is holomorphic near $D$ then $\oint_{\partial D}f\,dz=0$; and if $f$ is holomorphic near $D$ except for poles $\zeta_j$ in the interior of $D$, then $\oint_{\partial D}f\,dz=2\pi i\sum_j\class{ntn-res}{\operatorname{Res}}_{\zeta_j}f$.
Proof. Green's theoremA.6 holds for such regions, and the proof of Theorem 6.1.2 used nothing else. For the residue form, remove from $D$ small open disks $|z-\zeta_j|\lt\delta$ (disjoint, inside the interior of $D$). Cauchy's theorem on what remains gives $\oint_{\partial D}f\,dz=\sum_j\oint_{|z-\zeta_j|=\delta}f\,dz$, exactly as in Lemma 6.2.1, and step 3 of the proof of Theorem 6.9.1 evaluates each small circle as $\delta\to0$. ∎

The slides use this without comment ("by the residue theorem").

DerivedProposition 8.1.2. $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\pi$.
Proof.
  1. Poles. $f(z)=\frac1{1+z^2}=\frac1{(z-i)(z+i)}$ has simple poles at $\pm i$. For $R\gt1$ close $[-R,R]$ by the semicircle $\class{ntn-SR}{S_R}$ of radius $R$ in the upper half-plane, traversed anticlockwise. Only $i$ is inside, and $\class{ntn-res}{\operatorname{Res}}_if=\frac1{2i}$ (Prop. 6.8.4: $A=1$, $B=1+z^2$, $B'(i)=2i$).
  2. Residue theorem (Prop. 8.1.1): \[ \int_{-R}^R\frac{dx}{1+x^2}+\int_{\class{ntn-SR}{S_R}}\frac{dz}{1+z^2}=2\pi i\cdot\frac1{2i}=\pi. \]
  3. The arc vanishes. On $\class{ntn-SR}{S_R}$, $|1+z^2|\ge|z|^2-1=R^2-1$, and $\class{ntn-SR}{S_R}$ has length $\pi R$. By the ML estimateA.25, \[ \Big|\int_{\class{ntn-SR}{S_R}}f\,dz\Big|\le\frac{\pi R}{R^2-1}\longrightarrow0\qquad(R\to\infty). \]
  4. So $\int_{-R}^R\frac{dx}{1+x^2}\to\pi$. The integrand is positive and integrable ($\le1/x^2$ for large $|x|$), so this limit is the improper integralA.22. ∎

The answer is no surprise ($\arctan x$ runs from $-\pi/2$ to $\pi/2$), but the method needs no antiderivative, and the next sections apply it where none is available.

L8 · Slide 3

8.2 A Fourier transform

DefinedDefinition 8.2.1 (Fourier transform). The Fourier transform of an integrable function $f$ on $\R$ (one with $\int|f|\lt\infty$) is \[ \class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi):=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\,e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx\qquad(\xi\in\R). \]

The integral converges absolutely because $|e^{-2\pi ix\xi}|=1$. $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)$ measures how much of the frequency $\xi$ (oscillations $e^{2\pi ix\xi}$, $\xi$ per unit length) is present in $f$. Background and the inversion theorem are in D.7.

DerivedProposition 8.2.2. For $f(x)=\dfrac1{1+x^2}$, $\ \class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=\pi e^{-2\pi|\xi|}$.
Proof.
  1. Which half-plane? For $z=x+iy$, $|e^{-2\pi iz\xi}|=e^{\operatorname{Re}(-2\pi i(x+iy)\xi)}=e^{2\pi\xi y}$. If $\xi\ge0$ this is $\le1$ exactly when $y=\operatorname{Im}z\le0$. So close $[-R,R]$ by a semicircle in the lower half-plane, where the exponential is harmless.
  2. Orientation. Going along $[-R,R]$ left to right and back along the lower arc keeps the half-disk on the right: the loop is clockwise, so the residue theorem carries a factor $-2\pi i$. The only pole inside is $-i$.
  3. The arc. As in §8.1, the arc contributes at most $\frac{\pi R}{R^2-1}\cdot1\to0$.
  4. The residue. At $-i$, $\frac{e^{-2\pi iz\xi}}{(z+i)(z-i)}$ has a simple pole with residue $\frac{e^{-2\pi i(-i)\xi}}{-i-i}=\frac{e^{-2\pi\xi}}{-2i}$. So \[ \class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=-2\pi i\class{ntn-res}{\operatorname{Res}}_{-i}\frac{e^{-2\pi iz\xi}}{(z+i)(z-i)}=-2\pi i\cdot\frac{e^{-2\pi\xi}}{-2i}=\pi e^{-2\pi\xi}. \]
  5. $\xi\lt0$. Now $|e^{-2\pi iz\xi}|\le1$ for $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$: close in the upper half-plane, anticlockwise, around $i$, with residue $\frac{e^{2\pi\xi}}{2i}$, giving $2\pi i\cdot\frac{e^{2\pi\xi}}{2i}=\pi e^{2\pi\xi}=\pi e^{-2\pi|\xi|}$. ∎

The rule of thumb: the sign of $\xi$ decides the half-plane in which $e^{-2\pi iz\xi}$ decays, and the contour must be closed there.

L8 · Slide 4

8.3 Shifting the line: the Gaussian

A second technique: no poles at all, but the line of integration is moved.

DerivedProposition 8.3.1 (the Gaussian is its own transform). For every $\xi\in\R$, \[ \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\pi x^2}e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx=e^{-\pi\xi^2}. \]

We use $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\pi x^2}dx=1$: this is the Gaussian integral, proved in §11.9 (substitute $u=\sqrt\pi\,x$ in $\int e^{-u^2}du=\sqrt\pi$; or see polar coordinatesA.8).

Proof.
  1. Complete the square. \[ -\pi x^2-2\pi ix\xi=-\pi(x^2+2ix\xi-\xi^2)-\pi\xi^2=-\pi(x+i\xi)^2-\pi\xi^2. \] So the claim is $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\pi(x+i\xi)^2}dx=1$: the integral of the entire function $e^{-\pi z^2}$ along the horizontal line $\operatorname{Im}z=\xi$ equals its integral along $\R$.
  2. Cauchy on a rectangle. Take $\xi\gt0$ (for $\xi\lt0$ use the mirror rectangle below the axis; $\xi=0$ is the known integral). By Prop. 8.1.1, the integral of $e^{-\pi z^2}$ around the rectangle with corners $\pm R$, $\pm R+i\xi$ is $0$: \[ \int_{-R}^Re^{-\pi x^2}dx+\int_{\text{right}}-\int_{-R}^Re^{-\pi(x+i\xi)^2}dx-\int_{\text{left}}=0, \] the top side being traversed from right to left.
  3. The vertical sides vanish. On them $z=\pm R+iy$ with $0\le y\le\xi$, and $\operatorname{Re}\big((\pm R+iy)^2\big)=R^2-y^2$, so $|e^{-\pi z^2}|=e^{-\pi(R^2-y^2)}\le e^{-\pi(R^2-\xi^2)}$. Each side has length $\xi$, so each integral is at most $\xi e^{-\pi(R^2-\xi^2)}\to0$.
  4. Letting $R\to\infty$ (both horizontal integrals converge absolutely, as $|e^{-\pi(x+i\xi)^2}|=e^{-\pi(x^2-\xi^2)}$), the two horizontal integrals are equal. ∎
L8 · Slide 5

8.4 Fourier transforms and analyticity

DefinedDefinition 8.4.1 (sinc). $\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}\xi:=\dfrac{\sin\pi\xi}{\pi\xi}$ for $\xi\ne0$, and $\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}0:=1$.

sinc is continuous (since $\sin\pi\xi/\pi\xi\to1$), entire (its power series $\sum_k(-1)^k(\pi\xi)^{2k}/(2k+1)!$ converges everywhere), and $|\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}\xi|\le1$ on $\R$ (as $|\sin x|\le|x|$). Its zeros are the nonzero integers.

DerivedLemma 8.4.2 (the box). $\displaystyle\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx=\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}\xi$; that is, $\widehat{\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}}=\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}$. Since sinc is even, also $\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{2\pi ix\xi}dx=\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}\xi$.
Proof. For $\xi=0$ the integral is $1$. For $\xi\ne0$, \[ \int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{-2\pi ix\xi}dx=\Big[\frac{e^{-2\pi ix\xi}}{-2\pi i\xi}\Big]_{-1/2}^{1/2}=\frac{e^{-\pi i\xi}-e^{\pi i\xi}}{-2\pi i\xi}=\frac{-2i\sin\pi\xi}{-2\pi i\xi}=\frac{\sin\pi\xi}{\pi\xi}. \] ∎

Three transforms side by side ($\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ is $1$ on that interval and $0$ outside):

$f(x)$$\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)$Largest strip where $f$ is holomorphicWhere
$e^{-\pi x^2}$$e^{-\pi\xi^2}$$\mathbb C$Prop. 8.3.1
$\dfrac1{1+x^2}$$\pi e^{-2\pi|\xi|}$$|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt1$ (poles at $\pm i$)Prop. 8.2.2
$\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}(x)$$\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}\xi$none: $f$ jumps at $\pm\frac12$Lemma 8.4.2

The pattern: the wider the strip where $f$ is holomorphic, the faster $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ decays. Entire: faster than any exponential. Strip of half-width $1$: like $e^{-2\pi|\xi|}$. Not even continuous: like $1/|\xi|$. And in the other direction, if $f$ vanishes outside a bounded interval, $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ is entire (sinc is). The next two theorems make both statements precise.

L8 · Slide 6

8.5 Analyticity in a strip is exponential decay

CitedFact 8.5.1 (Fourier inversion). If $f$ and $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ are continuous and integrable on $\R$, then $f(x)=\int\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)\,e^{2\pi ix\xi}\,d\xi$ for all $x\in\R$. Applied to $F$: if $F$ and $f(x):=\int F(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$ are continuous and integrable, then $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}=F$.

A standard theorem, used without proof; see D.7. The second form follows from the first applied to $\xi\mapsto F(-\xi)$.

DerivedTheorem 8.5.2 (strips and decay). Let $f$ be continuous and integrable on $\R$, and $a\gt0$.
(a) If $f$ extends holomorphically to the strip $|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt a$, with $|f(x+iy)|\le\dfrac{C}{1+x^2}$ for $|y|\lt a$, then $|\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)|\le\pi C\,e^{-2\pi a|\xi|}$.
(b) Conversely, if $|\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)|\le C\,e^{-2\pi a|\xi|}$ for all $\xi\in\R$, then $f$ extends holomorphically to $|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt a$.

Check (a) on $\frac1{1+x^2}$: it is holomorphic for $|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt1$, and the theorem predicts decay at every rate $a\lt1$, consistent with $\pi e^{-2\pi|\xi|}$. (The bound $\frac{C}{1+x^2}$ holds only on narrower strips $|y|\le a'\lt1$, which is why $a\lt1$.)

L8 · Slide 7

8.6 Analyticity in a strip: proof

Proof of Theorem 8.5.2(a). Let $\xi\ge0$ and $0\lt b\lt a$.
  1. Shift the line down by $b$. The function $f(z)e^{-2\pi iz\xi}$ is holomorphic near the rectangle with corners $\pm R$, $\pm R-ib$ (it lies in the strip, as $b\lt a$). On its vertical sides, $|e^{-2\pi iz\xi}|=e^{2\pi\xi\operatorname{Im}z}\le1$ (since $\operatorname{Im}z\le0$) and $|f|\le\frac C{1+R^2}$, over a length $b$. So the vertical sides contribute at most $\frac{2bC}{1+R^2}\to0$, and Cauchy's theorem (Prop. 8.1.1) with $R\to\infty$ gives \[ \class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x-ib)\,e^{-2\pi i(x-ib)\xi}\,dx=e^{-2\pi b\xi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x-ib)\,e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx, \] using $e^{-2\pi i(-ib)\xi}=e^{-2\pi b\xi}$. Both integrals converge absolutely, since $|f(x-ib)|\le\frac C{1+x^2}$.
  2. Estimate. $|\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)|\le e^{-2\pi b\xi}\int\frac{C\,dx}{1+x^2}=\pi C\,e^{-2\pi b\xi}$ (Prop. 8.1.2).
  3. Let $b\to a$. The bound holds for every $b\lt a$, hence for $b=a$. For $\xi\lt0$, shift up instead. ∎
Proof of Theorem 8.5.2(b). Let $0\lt b\lt a$, and define $F(z):=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)\,e^{2\pi iz\xi}\,d\xi$ for $|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt b$.
  1. Domination. For $z=x+iy$ with $|y|\lt b$: $|e^{2\pi iz\xi}|=e^{-2\pi y\xi}\le e^{2\pi b|\xi|}$. So the integrand is at most $Ce^{-2\pi(a-b)|\xi|}$, and its $z$-derivative $2\pi i\xi\,\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)e^{2\pi iz\xi}$ is at most $2\pi C|\xi|e^{-2\pi(a-b)|\xi|}$. Both bounds are integrable in $\xi$ and do not depend on $z$.
  2. $F$ is holomorphic. By differentiation under the integral signA.4 (version 3), $F$ has continuous partial derivatives $F_x=\int2\pi i\xi\,\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}e^{2\pi iz\xi}d\xi$ and $F_y=iF_x$, which are the Cauchy–Riemann equations; so $F$ is holomorphic on $|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt b$ (Theorem 1.5.2). As $b\lt a$ was arbitrary, on $|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt a$.
  3. $F$ extends $f$. $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ is continuous (A.22) and integrable (by the hypothesis), and so is $f$. By Fourier inversion (Fact 8.5.1), $F(x)=\int\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi=f(x)$ for real $x$. ∎
L8 · Slide 8

8.7 The Paley–Wiener theorem

The second half of the pattern of §8.4: vanishing outside an interval corresponds to $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ being entire with controlled growth.

DerivedTheorem 8.7.1 (Paley–Wiener, a simple form). Let $A\gt0$.
(a) If $f$ is continuous and vanishes outside $[-A,A]$, then $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\zeta):=\int_{-A}^Af(x)e^{-2\pi ix\zeta}dx$ is an entire function of $\zeta$. If moreover $f$ is $C^2$ (on all of $\R$), then \[ (1+|\zeta|^2)\,|\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\zeta)|\le C\,e^{2\pi A|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|}\qquad\text{on }\mathbb C. \] (b) Conversely, if $F$ is entire and $(1+|\zeta|^2)|F(\zeta)|\le C\,e^{2\pi A|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|}$ on $\mathbb C$, then $F=\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ for a continuous $f$ vanishing outside $[-A,A]$.

Notation: $\class{ntn-n1}{\norm{f}_1}:=\int|f(x)|\,dx$. The constant in (a) can be taken as $C=\class{ntn-n1}{\norm{f}_1}+\class{ntn-n1}{\norm{f''}_1}$.

Proof of (a).
  1. Entire. The integral runs over the bounded interval $[-A,A]$, and $\zeta\mapsto f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\zeta}$ is entire with $\zeta$-derivative $-2\pi ix\,f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\zeta}$, continuous in $(x,\zeta)$. Differentiating under the integral sign (A.4) shows $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ has continuous partial derivatives satisfying Cauchy–Riemann, so it is entire.
  2. Growth. For $|x|\le A$, $|e^{-2\pi ix\zeta}|=e^{2\pi x\operatorname{Im}\zeta}\le e^{2\pi A|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|}$. So $|\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\zeta)|\le\class{ntn-n1}{\norm{f}_1}e^{2\pi A|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|}$.
  3. Decay from smoothness. If $f$ is $C^2$, then $f$ and $f'$ are continuous and vanish outside $[-A,A]$, hence vanish at $\pm A$. Integrating by parts twice, the boundary terms vanish: \[ \int_{-A}^Af''(x)e^{-2\pi ix\zeta}dx=2\pi i\zeta\int_{-A}^Af'(x)e^{-2\pi ix\zeta}dx=(2\pi i\zeta)^2\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\zeta). \] As in step 2, the left side is at most $\class{ntn-n1}{\norm{f''}_1}e^{2\pi A|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|}$, so $4\pi^2|\zeta|^2|\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\zeta)|\le\class{ntn-n1}{\norm{f''}_1}e^{2\pi A|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|}$.
  4. Add steps 2 and 3: $(1+4\pi^2|\zeta|^2)|\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}|\le(\class{ntn-n1}{\norm{f}_1}+\class{ntn-n1}{\norm{f''}_1})e^{2\pi A|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|}$, and $1+|\zeta|^2\le1+4\pi^2|\zeta|^2$. ∎
L8 · Slide 9

8.8 Paley–Wiener: proof of (b)

Proof of Theorem 8.7.1(b). Put $f(x):=\int_{-\infty}^\infty F(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$. On $\R$, $|F(\xi)|\le\frac{C}{1+\xi^2}$, so the integral converges absolutely and $f$ is continuous (A.22).
  1. $f(x)=0$ for $x\gt A$. Fix such $x$ and $t\gt0$, and apply Cauchy's theorem (Prop. 8.1.1) to the entire function $F(\zeta)e^{2\pi ix\zeta}$ on the rectangle with corners $\pm R$, $\pm R+it$. For $0\le\operatorname{Im}\zeta\le t$, \[ |F(\zeta)e^{2\pi ix\zeta}|\le\frac{Ce^{2\pi A\operatorname{Im}\zeta}}{1+|\zeta|^2}\,e^{-2\pi x\operatorname{Im}\zeta}=\frac{Ce^{-2\pi(x-A)\operatorname{Im}\zeta}}{1+|\zeta|^2}\le\frac{C}{1+|\zeta|^2}, \] which is at most $\frac C{1+R^2}$ on the vertical sides. So they vanish as $R\to\infty$, and \[ |f(x)|=\Big|\int_{-\infty}^\infty F(\xi+it)\,e^{2\pi ix(\xi+it)}\,d\xi\Big|\le Ce^{-2\pi(x-A)t}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{d\xi}{1+\xi^2}=\pi C\,e^{-2\pi(x-A)t}, \] using $|\xi+it|^2\ge\xi^2$.
  2. Let $t\to\infty$. As $x-A\gt0$, the bound tends to $0$: $f(x)=0$. For $x\lt-A$, shift down ($t\lt0$) instead.
  3. $F=\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$. On $\R$, $F$ and $f$ are continuous and integrable ($f$ vanishes outside $[-A,A]$), so Fourier inversion (Fact 8.5.1, second form) gives $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}=F$ on $\R$. By part (a), $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ is entire, so $F-\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ is entire and vanishes on $\R$. Its zeros are not isolated, so $F-\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}\equiv0$ (Theorem 6.7.1). ∎

The trick in step 1 is the same as in Theorem 8.5.2(a), run in reverse: the more room there is to push the line, the more decay one gets; here there is unlimited room, so $f$ is not just small but zero.

L8 · Slide 10

8.9 Time-limited or band-limited, not both

DefinedDefinition 8.9.1. A function $f$ on $\R$ is time-limited if it vanishes outside a bounded interval, and band-limited if $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ does.
DerivedCorollary 8.9.2. If $f$ is continuous and time-limited, and $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ vanishes on an interval of positive length, then $f\equiv0$. In particular, a continuous $f\not\equiv0$ is not both time-limited and band-limited.
Proof. By Paley–Wiener (a), $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ is entire. Every point of the interval is a limit of other zeros, so the zeros are not isolated and $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}\equiv0$ (Theorem 6.7.1). Then $f$ and $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}=0$ are continuous and integrable, and Fourier inversion gives $f=\int0\cdot e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi=0$. For the second statement: if $f$ is band-limited, $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ vanishes outside a bounded interval, in particular on an interval of positive length. ∎

This is a form of the uncertainty principle: a signal cannot be confined both in time and in frequency. It is the identity theorem in disguise. Every real signal is time-limited, so "band-limited" in the next sections is always an idealization.

L8 · Slide 11

8.10 The sampling theorem

DerivedTheorem 8.10.1 (Whittaker, Kotelnikov, Shannon). Let $g$ be $C^2$ on $\R$ and vanish outside $[-\frac12,\frac12]$, and let $f(x):=\int g(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$. Then for every $x\in\R$, with absolutely convergent series, \[ f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f(n)\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}(x-n)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f(n)\,\frac{\sin\pi(x-n)}{\pi(x-n)}. \]

So $f$ is band-limited ($\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}=g$ vanishes outside $[-\frac12,\frac12]$, Step 1 below), and it is completely determined by its values at the integers. Each term $f(n)\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}(x-n)$ equals $f(n)$ at $x=n$ and $0$ at the other integers, so the series interpolates the samples. The proof (§8.12–§8.13) needs one more tool.

L8 · Slide 12

8.11 The Poisson summation formula

CitedTheorem 8.11.1 (Poisson summation). Let $a\gt0$, and let $F$ be holomorphic in the strip $|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt a$, with $|F(x+iy)|\le\dfrac{C}{1+x^2}$ for $|y|\lt a$. Then, both sums converging absolutely, \[ \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}F(n)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(m). \]

The slides refer to Homework 1, Problem 3 for the proof. A complete proof by residues, with the contour and the estimates, is in E.16. Absolute convergence: $|F(n)|\le\frac C{1+n^2}$, and $|\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(m)|\le\pi C'e^{-2\pi b|m|}$ for any $b\lt a$ by Theorem 8.5.2(a).

The formula says that sampling at the integers in "time" and summing equals sampling the transform at the integers in "frequency" and summing. The sampling theorem uses it with $F(x)=f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}$.

L8 · Slide 13

8.12 The sampling theorem: proof

Proof of Theorem 8.10.1, Step 1: $f$ is entire, summable at the integers, and $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}=g$. Define $f(z):=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}g(\xi)e^{2\pi iz\xi}d\xi$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$; this is $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat g}(-z)$. By Paley–Wiener (a) with $A=\frac12$, it is entire and \[ (1+|z|^2)\,|f(z)|\le C\,e^{\pi|\operatorname{Im}z|}. \] On $\R$ this gives $|f(x)|\le\frac{C}{1+x^2}$. Hence $\sum_n|f(n)|\le\sum_n\frac C{1+n^2}\lt\infty$, $f$ is integrable on $\R$, and since $f$ and $g$ are continuous and integrable, Fourier inversion (Fact 8.5.1, second form) gives $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}=g$. ∎
Step 2: for $|\xi|\lt\frac12$, $\ \sum_nf(n)e^{-2\pi in\xi}=g(\xi)$. Fix such $\xi$ and let $F(z):=f(z)\,e^{-2\pi iz\xi}$.
  1. $F$ meets the hypotheses of Poisson summation with $a=1$. $F$ is entire. As $|\xi|\lt\frac12$, $|e^{-2\pi iz\xi}|=e^{2\pi\xi\operatorname{Im}z}\le e^{\pi|\operatorname{Im}z|}$. With Step 1 and $|z|^2\ge x^2$, for $|y|\lt1$: \[ |F(x+iy)|\le\frac{Ce^{\pi|y|}e^{\pi|y|}}{1+|z|^2}\le\frac{Ce^{2\pi}}{1+x^2}. \]
  2. Its transform. \[ \class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(m)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}e^{-2\pi ixm}dx=\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(m+\xi)=g(m+\xi). \] For $m\ne0$, $|m+\xi|\ge|m|-|\xi|\gt1-\frac12=\frac12$, so $g(m+\xi)=0$. Only $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(0)=g(\xi)$ survives.
  3. Poisson summation (Theorem 8.11.1): \[ \sum_nf(n)e^{-2\pi in\xi}=\sum_nF(n)=\sum_m\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(m)=g(\xi). \] ∎

Step 2 says that $g$ (restricted to $(-\frac12,\frac12)$) is the Fourier series whose coefficients are the samples $f(n)$. This is where the band limit is used: if $g$ were nonzero beyond $\pm\frac12$, other terms $g(m+\xi)$ would survive and mix into the sum (§8.14).

L8 · Slide 14

8.13 The sampling theorem: end of proof

Step 3: the interpolation formula. Let $x\in\R$. Multiply Step 2 by $e^{2\pi ix\xi}$ and integrate over $[-\frac12,\frac12]$ (Step 2 fails at most at the two endpoints, which do not affect the integral). The series $\sum_nf(n)e^{-2\pi in\xi}$ converges uniformly in $\xi$, since its terms are bounded by $|f(n)|$ and $\sum|f(n)|\lt\infty$ (Step 1 and the M-testA.21), so it may be integrated term by term. By Lemma 8.4.2, $\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{2\pi it\xi}d\xi=\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}t$. Therefore \[ f(x)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}g(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi=\sum_nf(n)\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{2\pi i(x-n)\xi}d\xi=\sum_nf(n)\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}(x-n). \] The series converges absolutely because $|\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}|\le1$ and $\sum|f(n)|\lt\infty$. ∎
Remark 8.13.1 (the proof in one line). $f$ and $g$ are a Fourier pair. Sampling $f$ at the integers turns $g$ into its periodic version $\sum_mg(\xi+m)$ (Poisson). If $g$ lives in a window of width $1$, the periodic version shows $g$ unchanged on the window, so the samples determine $g$, and hence $f$.
L8 · Slide 15

8.14 Why the band limit: aliasing

At every integer $n$, $e^{2\pi i(\xi+1)n}=e^{2\pi i\xi n}e^{2\pi in}=e^{2\pi i\xi n}$. Frequencies $\xi$ and $\xi+1$ give the same samples. So samples at the integers can only tell apart the frequencies in a band of width $1$, such as $[-\frac12,\frac12]$.

DefinedExample 8.14.1 (aliasing). $\cos(2\pi\cdot0.3\,x)$ and $\cos(2\pi\cdot0.7\,x)$ agree at every integer, as $0.7=1-0.3$: \[ \cos(2\pi\cdot0.7n)=\cos(2\pi n-2\pi\cdot0.3n)=\cos(2\pi\cdot0.3n). \]

In signal processing this is aliasing: a frequency outside the band masquerades as one inside it. It is why the wheels of a car in a film can seem to turn backwards.

L8 · Slide 16

8.15 Sampling at rate $T$

DerivedCorollary 8.15.1 (sampling at rate $T$). Let $T\gt0$, let $g$ be $C^2$ on $\R$ and vanish outside $[-\frac T2,\frac T2]$, and let $f(x):=\int g(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$. Then, the series converging absolutely, \[ f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f\Big(\frac nT\Big)\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}(Tx-n)\qquad(x\in\R). \]
Proof. Substituting $\xi=T\eta$, \[ f(x/T)=\int g(\xi)e^{2\pi i(x/T)\xi}d\xi=\int Tg(T\eta)\,e^{2\pi ix\eta}\,d\eta. \] The function $\eta\mapsto Tg(T\eta)$ is $C^2$ and vanishes outside $[-\frac12,\frac12]$ (as $|T\eta|\le\frac T2\iff|\eta|\le\frac12$). So Theorem 8.10.1 applies to $f_T(y):=f(y/T)$: $f_T(y)=\sum_nf_T(n)\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}(y-n)$. Take $y=Tx$: $f_T(Tx)=f(x)$ and $f_T(n)=f(n/T)$. ∎

So $T$ samples per unit length determine a signal whose frequencies lie in $[-\frac T2,\frac T2]$: the sampling rate must be twice the largest frequency $\frac T2$. This rate is the Nyquist rate. (Audio CDs sample at 44.1 kHz to capture frequencies up to about 22 kHz, just above human hearing.)

L8 · Slide 17

8.16 Exercises

The slide lists five exercises with answers. Full solutions are below; try each one first.

Exercise 8.16.1 (a double pole). Show $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)^2}=\frac\pi2$.
Solution

Close in the upper half-plane as in §8.1. Now $\frac1{(1+z^2)^2}=\frac{h(z)}{(z-i)^2}$ with $h(z)=(z+i)^{-2}$, a pole of order $2$ at $i$, so the residue is $h'(i)=-2(z+i)^{-3}\big|_{z=i}=\frac{-2}{(2i)^3}=\frac{-2}{-8i}=\frac1{4i}$ (Def. 6.8.3). The arc is at most $\frac{\pi R}{(R^2-1)^2}\to0$. So the integral is $2\pi i\cdot\frac1{4i}=\frac\pi2$.

Exercise 8.16.2. Show $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{2+\cos\theta}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt3}$. Hint: $z=e^{i\theta}$, $d\theta=\frac{dz}{iz}$.
Solution

As $\theta$ runs over $[0,2\pi]$, $z=e^{i\theta}$ runs once around $|z|=1$, with $\cos\theta=\frac12(z+z^{-1})$ and $d\theta=\frac{dz}{iz}$. So \[ \int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{2+\cos\theta}=\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{1}{2+\frac12(z+z^{-1})}\cdot\frac{dz}{iz}=\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{2\,dz}{i(z^2+4z+1)}. \] The roots of $z^2+4z+1$ are $-2\pm\sqrt3$; only $z_1=-2+\sqrt3\approx-0.27$ is inside. It is a simple pole with residue $\frac{2}{i(z_1-z_2)}=\frac2{i\cdot2\sqrt3}=\frac1{i\sqrt3}$. The integral is $2\pi i\cdot\frac1{i\sqrt3}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt3}$.

Exercise 8.16.3 (a sector). Show $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{dx}{1+x^3}=\frac{2\pi}{3\sqrt3}$, using the sector $0\le\arg z\le\frac{2\pi}3$.
Solution

Let $\omega:=e^{2\pi i/3}$, so $\omega^3=1$. The sector of radius $R$ has three sides: $[0,R]$; the arc; and the ray from $R\omega$ back to $0$. On the ray $z=r\omega$, $z^3=r^3$ and $dz=\omega\,dr$, so that side contributes $-\omega\int_0^R\frac{dr}{1+r^3}$. The arc has length $\frac{2\pi R}3$ and $|1+z^3|\ge R^3-1$, so it vanishes as $R\to\infty$. The only pole inside is $\alpha:=e^{i\pi/3}$ (a root of $z^3=-1$), with residue $\frac1{3\alpha^2}=\frac{\alpha}{3\alpha^3}=-\frac\alpha3$ (Prop. 6.8.4). Writing $I$ for the integral, as $R\to\infty$: \[ (1-\omega)I=2\pi i\Big(-\frac\alpha3\Big). \] Now $1-\omega=\alpha(\bar\alpha-\alpha)=\alpha\cdot(-2i\sin\frac\pi3)=-i\sqrt3\,\alpha$, using $\alpha^2=\omega$. So $I=\frac{-2\pi i\alpha/3}{-i\sqrt3\,\alpha}=\frac{2\pi}{3\sqrt3}$.

Exercise 8.16.4. Show that $f(x)=(1+x^2)^{-2}$ has $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=\frac\pi2\big(1+2\pi|\xi|\big)e^{-2\pi|\xi|}$.
Solution

For $\xi\ge0$ close in the lower half-plane, clockwise, as in Prop. 8.2.2: $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=-2\pi i\class{ntn-res}{\operatorname{Res}}_{-i}$. Write the integrand as $\frac{k(z)}{(z+i)^2}$ with $k(z)=\frac{e^{-2\pi iz\xi}}{(z-i)^2}$; the residue is $k'(-i)$. Now \[ k'(z)=e^{-2\pi iz\xi}\Big(\frac{-2\pi i\xi}{(z-i)^2}-\frac{2}{(z-i)^3}\Big), \] and at $z=-i$: $e^{-2\pi iz\xi}=e^{-2\pi\xi}$, $(z-i)^2=-4$, $(z-i)^3=8i$. So $k'(-i)=e^{-2\pi\xi}\big(\frac{\pi i\xi}2+\frac{i}4\big)=ie^{-2\pi\xi}\big(\frac{\pi\xi}2+\frac14\big)$, and $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=-2\pi i\cdot ie^{-2\pi\xi}\big(\frac{\pi\xi}2+\frac14\big)=\frac\pi2(1+2\pi\xi)e^{-2\pi\xi}$. By symmetry ($f$ is even, so $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ is even) the formula holds with $|\xi|$. Check: $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(0)=\frac\pi2=\int f$, matching Exercise 8.16.1.

Exercise 8.16.5. Find $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ for the triangle $f(x)=\max(0,1-|x|)$. Is $\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^2$ band-limited?
Solution

$f$ is even and vanishes outside $[-1,1]$, so $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=2\int_0^1(1-x)\cos(2\pi x\xi)\,dx$. For $\xi\ne0$, integrating by parts (the boundary term $\big[(1-x)\frac{\sin2\pi x\xi}{2\pi\xi}\big]_0^1$ vanishes), \[ \class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=2\int_0^1\frac{\sin2\pi x\xi}{2\pi\xi}\,dx=\frac{1-\cos2\pi\xi}{2\pi^2\xi^2}=\frac{2\sin^2\pi\xi}{2\pi^2\xi^2}=\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^2\xi, \] and $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(0)=\int f=1=\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^20$. Both $f$ and $\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^2$ are continuous and integrable, so Fourier inversion gives $f(x)=\int\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^2(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$; that is, the transform of $\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^2$ is $f(-x)=f(x)$, which vanishes outside $[-1,1]$. So yes: $\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^2$ is band-limited, to $[-1,1]$. (Consistent with Cor. 8.9.2: $\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^2$ is not time-limited.)

Exercise 8.16.6 (a trigonometric integral; Practice midterm 1, Problem 1). Compute $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{5+3\cos\theta}$.
Hint Write it as a contour integral over $|z|=1$ with $z=e^{i\theta}$, $\cos\theta=\frac12(z+z^{-1})$, $d\theta=\frac{dz}{iz}$, as in Exercise 8.16.2.
Solution The integral becomes (as in Exercise 8.16.2) $\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{2\,dz}{i(3z^2+10z+3)}=\oint\frac{2\,dz}{3i(z+\frac13)(z+3)}$. Only $-\frac13$ is inside, a simple pole with residue $\frac{2}{3i(-\frac13+3)}=\frac{2}{8i}=\frac1{4i}$ (Prop. 6.8.4). By the residue theorem (Theorem 6.9.1), the integral is $2\pi i\cdot\frac1{4i}=\frac\pi2$. (Check: $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{a+b\cos\theta}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}=\frac{2\pi}4$.)
Exercise 8.16.7 (a trigonometric integral; Practice midterm 2, Problem 1). Compute $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{5-4\sin\theta}$.
Hint $\sin\theta=\frac1{2i}(z-z^{-1})$, $d\theta=\frac{dz}{iz}$. Find which root of the denominator is inside $|z|=1$.
Solution $5-4\sin\theta=5+2i(z-z^{-1})$, and multiplying by $iz$: $i(5z+2iz^2-2i)=-(2z^2-5iz-2)$. So the integral is $-\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{dz}{2z^2-5iz-2}$. The roots of $2z^2-5iz-2$ are $\frac{5i\pm3i}4=2i,\frac i2$; only $\frac i2$ is inside. With $2z^2-5iz-2=2(z-2i)(z-\frac i2)$, the residue of $\frac{-1}{2(z-2i)(z-i/2)}$ at the simple pole $\frac i2$ is $\frac{-1}{2(-\frac{3i}2)}=\frac1{3i}$ (Prop. 6.8.4). By Theorem 6.9.1 the integral is $2\pi i\cdot\frac1{3i}=\frac{2\pi}3$. (Check: $\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{25-16}}$.)
Exercise 8.16.8 (a trigonometric integral; Practice midterm 3, Problem 1). Compute $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{3+2\sin\theta}$.
Hint As in the previous exercise; the roots of the denominator involve $\sqrt5$.
Solution $3+2\sin\theta=3-i(z-z^{-1})$; multiplying by $iz$ gives $z^2+3iz-1$. So the integral is $\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{dz}{z^2+3iz-1}$, with roots $z_{1,2}=\frac{(-3\pm\sqrt5)i}2$. Only $z_1=\frac{(-3+\sqrt5)i}2\approx-0.38i$ is inside; the residue at this simple pole is $\frac1{z_1-z_2}=\frac1{i\sqrt5}$ (Prop. 6.8.4). By Theorem 6.9.1 the integral is $2\pi i\cdot\frac1{i\sqrt5}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt5}$. (Check: $\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{9-4}}$.)
Part IV

Entire functions

A polynomial is determined by its zeros up to a constant factor. Lectures 9 and 10 extend this to entire functions: Jensen's formula bounds the number of zeros by the growth, and infinite products rebuild a function from its zeros, the sine first. Lecture 11 continues functions beyond where they are first defined, constructs the Gamma function on the whole plane, and closes with Rouché's theorem.

Part IV · Entire functions

Lecture 9 · Jensen's formula and the zeros of entire functions

Goal
Relate the zeros of a holomorphic function to its size: Jensen's formula, and the order of an entire function.
Main results
Lemma 9.1.1 (removable singularities) · Prop. 9.2.1 (factoring out zeros) · Theorem 9.5.1 (Jensen) · Cor. 9.6.2 (counting zeros) · Theorem 9.10.1 (zeros versus order)
Uses
Theorem 4.2.2 and Cor. 4.4.1 from Part I; Theorems 6.3.1, 6.4.1, 6.7.1; the logarithmic potential (E.6).
Used later
Lecture 10: Lemma 9.1.1 in Euler's product, Theorem 9.10.1 in Hadamard's theorem.

Slide 1 is the title slide.

L9 · Slide 2

9.1 Removable singularities

DerivedLemma 9.1.1 (removable singularities). If $g$ is holomorphic on $0\lt|z-a|\lt r$ and bounded near $a$, then $g$ extends holomorphically to $|z-a|\lt r$.

Compare Theorem 4.10.1 and Lecture 4's moral: for harmonic and holomorphic functions, mild-looking hypotheses force full regularity. Here mere boundedness near $a$ rules out a singularity.

Proof. Fix $w$ and $r'$ with $0\lt|w-a|\lt r'\lt r$. Let $B$ bound $|g|$ on some punctured disk $0\lt|z-a|\le\epsilon_0$.
  1. Three circles. For small $\epsilon\gt0$ and $\delta\gt0$, the closed disks $|z-a|\le\epsilon$ and $|z-w|\le\delta$ are disjoint and inside $|z-a|\lt r'$. The function $\frac{g(z)}{z-w}$ is holomorphic near the region inside $|z-a|=r'$ and outside both small circles, so Lemma 6.2.1 gives \[ \oint_{|z-a|=r'}\frac{g(z)\,dz}{z-w}=\oint_{|z-w|=\delta}\frac{g(z)\,dz}{z-w}+\oint_{|z-a|=\epsilon}\frac{g(z)\,dz}{z-w}. \]
  2. The circle around $w$. $g$ is holomorphic near $|z-w|\le\delta$, so Cauchy's formula (Theorem 6.3.1, centred at $w$) makes the first integral on the right $2\pi i\,g(w)$.
  3. The circle around $a$ is $O(\epsilon)$. For $\epsilon\le\min(\epsilon_0,\frac12|w-a|)$, on $|z-a|=\epsilon$ we have $|g|\le B$ and $|z-w|\ge|w-a|-\epsilon\ge\frac12|w-a|$, so by the ML estimate the integral is at most $2\pi\epsilon\cdot\frac{2B}{|w-a|}\to0$. Here boundedness is used.
  4. Let $\epsilon\to0$. The other two terms do not depend on $\epsilon$, so \[ g(w)=G(w):=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-a|=r'}\frac{g(z)\,dz}{z-w}. \]
  5. $G$ is holomorphic on the whole disk $|w-a|\lt r'$, including at $w=a$: this is the case $n=0\to1$ of the proof of Theorem 6.6.1, which only used that $g$ is continuous on the circle $|z-a|=r'$.
So setting $g(a):=G(a)$ makes $g=G$ on $|z-a|\lt r'$, holomorphic there. As $r'\lt r$ was arbitrary, $g$ is holomorphic on $|z-a|\lt r$. ∎

The point $a$ is then called a removable singularity. With Def. 6.8.1 this sorts the isolated singularities of a holomorphic function near $a$: bounded (removable), $|g|\to\infty$ like a power (a pole), or neither (an essential singularity, such as $e^{1/z}$ at $0$; see Laurent seriesE.5).

L9 · Slide 3

9.2 Factoring out zeros

DerivedProposition 9.2.1 (factorization in a disk). Let $f$ be holomorphic near $|z|\le R$, with no zeros on $|z|=R$. Then $f$ has finitely many zeros $a_1,\dots,a_N$ in $|z|\lt R$ (repeated by multiplicity), and \[ f(z)=(z-a_1)\cdots(z-a_N)\,g(z), \] with $g$ holomorphic and zero-free near $|z|\le R$.
Proof.
  1. No zeros near the circle. The set where $f\ne0$ is open (by continuity) and contains the compact circle $|z|=R$, so it contains an annulus $R-\eta\lt|z|\lt R+\eta$ (C.5(a), applied to the circle inside that open set). Shrinking the open set on which $f$ is holomorphic, we may assume it is a disk $|z|\lt R+\eta$, which is connected, and $f\not\equiv0$ there.
  2. $N\lt\infty$. All zeros lie in the compact disk $|z|\le R-\eta$. Infinitely many would have a limit point there (Bolzano–Weierstrass), which would be a non-isolated zero, contradicting Theorem 6.7.1. Each zero has finite order (step 1 of that proof).
  3. Define $g$. Let $g:=f/\prod_j(z-a_j)$ off the zeros. It is holomorphic there, and nonzero there (as $f$ is).
  4. At a zero $a$ of order $m$. By the Taylor remainder (Cor. 6.5.1), $f(z)=c(z-a)^m+O(|z-a|^{m+1})$ with $c=a_m\ne0$. Exactly $m$ of the $a_j$ equal $a$, so $\prod_j(z-a_j)=(z-a)^mq(z)$ with $q$ a polynomial and $q(a)\ne0$. Hence \[ g(z)=\frac{c+O(|z-a|)}{q(z)}\longrightarrow\frac c{q(a)}\ne0\qquad(z\to a). \] So $g$ is bounded near $a$, Lemma 9.1.1 extends it holomorphically to $a$, and by continuity $g(a)=c/q(a)\ne0$. ∎
L9 · Slide 4

9.3 $\log|f|$ after factoring out the zeros

With $f=(z-a_1)\cdots(z-a_N)\,g$ as in Prop. 9.2.1, off the zeros, \[ \log|f(z)|=\sum_{j=1}^N\log|z-a_j|+\log|g(z)|. \] In the language of Part I, $\log|f|$ is the potential of unit point charges at the zeros (each $\log|z-a_j|$ is a logarithmic potentialE.6), plus a harmonic function:

DerivedLemma 9.3.1. If $g$ is holomorphic and zero-free near $|z|\le R$, then $\log|g|$ is harmonic near $|z|\le R$.
Proof.
  1. A slightly bigger disk. The open set where $g$ is holomorphic and zero-free contains the compact disk $|z|\le R$, hence a disk $|z|\lt R'$ with $R'\gt R$ (C.5(a)).
  2. A primitive of $g'/g$. $g'/g$ is holomorphic on $|z|\lt R'$. By Theorem 6.4.1 (applied on every closed disk $|z|\le r$, $r\lt R'$; the coefficients do not depend on $r$, by Theorem 6.6.1) it is a power series $\sum_nc_nz^n$ converging on $|z|\lt R'$. Then $G(z):=\sum_n\frac{c_n}{n+1}z^{n+1}$ converges on the same disk and $G'=g'/g$ (power seriesA.19 may be differentiated term by term). The slide phrases this as "Cauchy's theorem on a disk"; either way, a holomorphic function on a disk has a primitive there.
  3. $g$ is an exponential. \[ (ge^{-G})'=g'e^{-G}-gG'e^{-G}=e^{-G}(g'-g\cdot g'/g)=0. \] A holomorphic function with zero derivative on a connected open set is constant (its real and imaginary parts have zero gradient, by Theorem 1.5.2). So $g=c\,e^G$, and $c\ne0$ as $g\ne0$.
  4. Take $\log|\cdot|$. $|g|=|c|\,e^{\operatorname{Re}G}$, so $\log|g|=\log|c|+\operatorname{Re}G$, the real part of a holomorphic function plus a constant: harmonic, by Cor. 6.6.2. ∎
L9 · Slide 5

9.4 The mean of $\log|Re^{i\theta}-a|$

DerivedLemma 9.4.1 (the mean of a logarithmic potential). For $R\gt0$ and $|a|\ne R$, \[ \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|Re^{i\theta}-a|\,d\theta=\log\max(R,|a|). \]
Proof. By the mean value property for harmonic functions, Theorem 4.2.2.
  1. $|a|\gt R$ (charge outside). $z\mapsto\log|z-a|$ is harmonic away from $a$ (E.6), in particular near $|z|\le R$. So its mean over the circle $|z|=R$ is its value at the centre: $\log|0-a|=\log|a|$.
  2. $|a|\lt R$ (charge inside). Factor out $R$: \[ |Re^{i\theta}-a|=|e^{i\theta}|\,|R-ae^{-i\theta}|=|\overline{R-ae^{-i\theta}}|=|R-\bar ae^{i\theta}|=R\,\Big|1-\frac{\bar a}Re^{i\theta}\Big|. \] So the mean is $\log R$ plus the mean over $|w|=1$ of $h(w):=\log|1-\frac{\bar a}{R}w|$. If $a=0$, $h\equiv0$. Otherwise $h(w)=\log\frac{|a|}R+\log|w-\frac R{\bar a}|$ is harmonic away from $\frac R{\bar a}$, which lies outside $|w|\le1$ since $|\frac R{\bar a}|\gt1$. So $h$ is harmonic near $|w|\le1$, and its mean over $|w|=1$ is $h(0)=\log1=0$. The total is $\log R$. ∎

Physically: the average of a point charge's potential over a circle is the potential at the centre if the charge is outside, and as if the charge sat on the circle ($\log R$) if it is inside. This is Newton's shell theorem in two dimensions.

L9 · Slide 6

9.5 Jensen's formula

DerivedTheorem 9.5.1 (Jensen's formula). Let $f$ be holomorphic near $|z|\le R$, with $f(0)\ne0$, zeros $a_1,\dots,a_N$ in $|z|\lt R$ (repeated by multiplicity) and none on $|z|=R$. Then \[ \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|f(Re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta=\log|f(0)|+\sum_{j=1}^N\log\frac{R}{|a_j|}. \]
Proof. Average \[ \log|f|=\sum_j\log|z-a_j|+\log|g| \] (§9.3) over $|z|=R$:
  • each $\log|z-a_j|$ gives $\log R$, by Lemma 9.4.1, since $|a_j|\lt R$;
  • $\log|g|$ is harmonic near $|z|\le R$ (Lemma 9.3.1), so by the mean value property (Theorem 4.2.2) it gives $\log|g(0)|$. From $f(0)=\prod_j(0-a_j)\cdot g(0)$, $\log|g(0)|=\log|f(0)|-\sum_j\log|a_j|$. (Each $a_j\ne0$, as $f(0)\ne0$.)
The total is \[ N\log R+\log|f(0)|-\sum_j\log|a_j|=\log|f(0)|+\sum_j\log\frac R{|a_j|}. \] ∎

Each term $\log\frac R{|a_j|}$ is positive. So zeros inside the disk raise the average of $\log|f|$ on the circle above its value $\log|f(0)|$ at the centre, and the closer a zero is to $0$, the more it raises it. With no zeros, Jensen's formula is the mean value property for $\log|f|$. Read backwards, the formula bounds the number of zeros by the size of $f$; that is the next corollary.

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 9.5.2 (Mahler measure; Homework 2, Problem 2(b)). For $p(z)=a_d\prod_{j=1}^d(z-\alpha_j)$ with $a_d\ne0$, the Mahler measure is $M(p):=|a_d|\prod_j\max(1,|\alpha_j|)$. Show that if no $\alpha_j$ lies on $|z|=1$, then $\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|p(e^{i\theta})|\,d\theta=\log M(p)$. Deduce that if $p$ has integer coefficients, the geometric mean of $|p|$ on the unit circle is at least $1$.
Hint Take logarithms of the product and use Lemma 9.4.1 with $R=1$ on each factor.
Solution $\log|p(e^{i\theta})|=\log|a_d|+\sum_j\log|e^{i\theta}-\alpha_j|$. By Lemma 9.4.1 with $R=1$ (allowed, as $|\alpha_j|\ne1$), each factor averages to $\log\max(1,|\alpha_j|)$. Summing gives $\log|a_d|+\sum_j\log\max(1,|\alpha_j|)=\log M(p)$. (When $p(0)\ne0$ this is Jensen's formula, Theorem 9.5.1, for $p$ on $|z|=1$.) The geometric mean is $\exp$ of the average of $\log|p|$, i.e. $M(p)\ge|a_d|\ge1$ when $a_d$ is a nonzero integer.

Remark: for monic $p\in\mathbb Z[z]$ with $p(0)\ne0$, $M(p)=1$ exactly when $p$ is a product of cyclotomic polynomials (Kronecker). Whether $M(p)\ge1+\delta$ for some absolute $\delta\gt0$ otherwise is Lehmer's open problem (1933); the smallest known value is $1.17628\ldots$, for $z^{10}+z^9-z^7-z^6-z^5-z^4-z^3+z+1$.

L9 · Slide 7

9.6 Counting zeros

For $f$ holomorphic near $|z|\le R$, let $\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R):=\max_{|z|=R}|f|$, and let $\class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)$ be the number of zeros of $f$ in $|z|\le r$, counted with multiplicity.

DerivedLemma 9.6.1 (maximum modulus). If $f$ is holomorphic near $|z|\le R$, then $|f(w)|\le \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)$ for $|w|\le R$. In particular $\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R')\le \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)$ for $R'\lt R$.
Proof. Fix $w$ and choose a real $\alpha$ with $e^{-i\alpha}f(w)=|f(w)|$. The function $u:=\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\alpha}f)$ is harmonic (Cor. 6.6.2), so by the maximum principle (Cor. 4.4.1) on the disk, \[ |f(w)|=u(w)\le\max_{|z|=R}u\le\max_{|z|=R}|e^{-i\alpha}f|=\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R). \] ∎

The slide's "(maximum principle)" refers to this lemma.

DerivedCorollary 9.6.2 (counting zeros). Let $f$ be holomorphic near $|z|\le R$, $f(0)\ne0$, and $0\lt r\lt R$. Then \[ \class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)\le\frac{\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)-\log|f(0)|}{\log(R/r)}. \]
Proof.
  1. If $f\ne0$ on $|z|=R$. In Jensen's formula, each of the $\class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)$ zeros with $|a_j|\le r$ contributes $\log\frac R{|a_j|}\ge\log\frac Rr$, and the others contribute $\gt0$. The left side is at most $\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)$, as $\log|f(Re^{i\theta})|\le\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)$. So $\class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)\log\frac Rr\le\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)-\log|f(0)|$.
  2. Otherwise. $f$ is holomorphic on a disk $|z|\lt R''$ with $R''\gt R$ (C.5(a)), which is connected, and $f\not\equiv0$ there as $f(0)\ne0$. So its zeros cannot accumulate (Theorem 6.7.1), and only finitely many lie in the compact disk $|z|\le R$. Hence $f\ne0$ on $|z|=R'$ for all $R'$ close to $R$ except finitely many. For such $R'\in(r,R)$, step 1 and Lemma 9.6.1 give \[ \class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)\le\frac{\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R')-\log|f(0)|}{\log(R'/r)}\le\frac{\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)-\log|f(0)|}{\log(R'/r)}. \] Let $R'\uparrow R$. ∎

So a function that is not too big cannot have too many zeros. A polynomial of degree $d$ is the model: $\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)\approx d\log R$, and taking $R$ huge recovers $\class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)\le d$.

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 9.6.3 (zeros at the integers force slow growth; Homework 2, Problem 2(a)). Let $f$ be entire with $f(n)=0$ for $n=1,2,3,\dots$ and $|f(z)|\le Ce^{c|z|}$ for all $z$, where $c\lt1$. Show $f\equiv0$.
Hint If $f\not\equiv0$, divide by a power of $z$ so that $f(0)\ne0$, and apply Jensen's formula (Theorem 9.5.1) on $|z|=R$ with $N\lt R\lt N+1$, $f\ne0$ on $|z|=R$. Show $N\log N-\log N!\ge N-1-\log N$ by comparing $\log N!$ with $\int_1^N\log t\,dt$.
Solution
  1. Normalize. If $f\not\equiv0$, let $k$ be the order of its zero at $0$ (Def. 6.7.2; $k=0$ if $f(0)\ne0$) and write $f=z^kg$ with $g$ entire, $g(0)\ne0$ (Theorem 6.7.1); $g$ still vanishes at $1,2,\dots$, and $|g(z)|\le Ce^{c|z|}$ for $|z|\ge1$.
  2. Jensen. For $N\lt R\lt N+1$ with $g\ne0$ on $|z|=R$ (all but finitely many such $R$: by Theorem 10.1.1 there are only finitely many zeros in $|z|\le N+1$), Jensen's formula (Theorem 9.5.1) applies. Every zero in $|z|\lt R$ contributes a positive term $\log\frac R{|a_j|}$, so keeping only $1,\dots,N$, and bounding the mean of $\log|g|$ by its maximum (compare Cor. 9.6.2): \[ \log|g(0)|+\sum_{n=1}^N\log\frac Rn\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|g(Re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta\le\log C+cR\le\log C+c(N+1). \]
  3. Stirling-type bound. $\sum_{n\le N}\log\frac Rn\ge N\log N-\log N!$, and since $\log$ is increasing, $\log N!=\sum_{n=2}^N\log n\le\int_1^N\log t\,dt+\log N=N\log N-N+1+\log N$. So $\sum\ge N-1-\log N$.
  4. Contradiction. Combining, $(1-c)N\le\log C-\log|g(0)|+1+c+\log N$ for all large $N$. The left side grows linearly and the right side logarithmically, impossible as $c\lt1$. So $f\equiv0$.

Remark: $\sin\pi z$ vanishes on $\mathbb Z$ and satisfies the bound with $c=\pi$; Carlson's theorem shows $c\lt\pi$ already forces $f\equiv0$. Jensen alone gives $c\lt1$.

Exercise 9.6.4 (the Blaschke condition; Homework 2, Problem 2(c)). Let $f$ be holomorphic and bounded on $D(0,1)$, $f\not\equiv0$, with zeros $a_1,a_2,\dots$ (listed by multiplicity). Show $\sum_k(1-|a_k|)\lt\infty$.
Hint Assume $f(0)\ne0$. Apply Jensen on $|z|=r\lt1$, then let $r\to1$. Use $\log\frac1x\ge1-x$ for $0\lt x\le1$.
Solution
  1. Normalize. If $f$ has a zero of order $k$ at $0$, replace $f$ by $f/z^k$: still holomorphic (Def. 6.7.2, or Lemma 9.1.1, the singularity at $0$ being removable) and bounded (bounded by $2^kM$ for $|z|\ge\frac12$, and continuous on $|z|\le\frac12$), and it drops only finitely many terms from the sum. So assume $f(0)\ne0$ and $|f|\le M$.
  2. Jensen. For $r\lt1$ with no zero on $|z|=r$ (all but countably many $r$: by Theorem 10.1.1, only finitely many zeros lie in each $|z|\le r'\lt1$), Theorem 9.5.1 gives \[ \sum_{|a_k|\lt r}\log\frac r{|a_k|}=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|f(re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta-\log|f(0)|\le\log M-\log|f(0)|=:K. \]
  3. Let $r\to1$. Fix $n$. For $r\gt\max_{k\le n}|a_k|$, all terms are $\ge0$, so $\sum_{k\le n}\log\frac r{|a_k|}\le K$; letting $r\to1$, $\sum_{k\le n}\log\frac1{|a_k|}\le K$ for every $n$.
  4. As $\log\frac1x\ge1-x$, $\sum_k(1-|a_k|)\le K\lt\infty$.
L9 · Slide 8

9.7 A check: $\sin\pi z$

Test Jensen's formula on $f(z):=\dfrac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}$ (with $f(0):=1$; it is entire, by its power series), with $R:=K+\frac12$ for an integer $K\ge1$. Then $f(0)=1$, and the zeros in $|z|\lt R$ are $\pm1,\dots,\pm K$, all simple. (The radius is a half-integer so that no zero lies on the circle.)

DerivedProposition 9.7.1 (both sides of Jensen for $\sin\pi z/\pi z$). As $R\to\infty$, both sides of Jensen's formula equal $2R-\log(2\pi R)+O(1/R)$.
Proof.
  1. The zeros. \[ \sum_{0\lt|n|\lt R}\log\frac R{|n|}=2(K\log R-\log K!). \] Stirling's formulaA.23 gives $\log K!=K\log K-K+\frac12\log(2\pi K)+O(\frac1K)$, and \[ K\log R-K\log K=K\log(1+\frac1{2K})=\frac12+O(\frac1K). \] So \[ 2(K\log R-\log K!)=2K+1-\log(2\pi K)+O(\tfrac1K)=2R-\log(2\pi R)+O(\tfrac1R), \] using $2K+1=2R$ and $\log(2\pi R)-\log(2\pi K)=\log\frac RK=O(\frac1R)$.
  2. The circle: a formula for $|\sin|$. For $z=x+iy$, \[ \sin\pi z=\sin\pi x\cosh\pi y+i\cos\pi x\sinh\pi y, \] so \[ |\sin\pi z|^2=\sin^2\pi x\cosh^2\pi y+\cos^2\pi x\sinh^2\pi y=\sin^2\pi x+\sinh^2\pi y. \]
  3. The circle: $\log|f|$. On $|z|=R$ we claim \[ \log|f(z)|=\pi|y|-\log(2\pi R)+O(e^{-2\pi|y|}) \] with an absolute constant. Since $\log|f|=\log|\sin\pi z|-\log(\pi R)$, this says $\log|\sin\pi z|=\pi|y|-\log2+O(e^{-2\pi|y|})$. For $|y|\ge1$: $\sinh^2\pi y\le|\sin\pi z|^2\le\cosh^2\pi y$, and both $\log\sinh\pi|y|$ and $\log\cosh\pi y$ equal $\pi|y|-\log2+O(e^{-2\pi|y|})$. For $|y|\lt1$ (and $R\ge3$): $x^2=R^2-y^2$ puts $|x|$ within $1/R$ of $R=K+\frac12$, so $|\sin\pi x|\ge\cos(\pi/R)\ge\frac12$, and $\log|\sin\pi z|$ lies between $\log\frac12$ and $\log\cosh\pi$: bounded, as is $\pi|y|-\log2$. A bounded difference is $O(e^{-2\pi|y|})$ when $|y|\lt1$.
  4. Average over the circle. With $y=R\sin\theta$: \[ \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\pi R|\sin\theta|\,d\theta=\frac{\pi R}{2\pi}\cdot4=2R. \] For the error, \[ \int_0^{2\pi}e^{-2\pi R|\sin\theta|}d\theta=4\int_0^{\pi/2}e^{-2\pi R\sin\theta}d\theta\le4\int_0^{\pi/2}e^{-4R\theta}d\theta\le\frac1R, \] using $\sin\theta\ge\frac{2\theta}\pi$. So the mean of $\log|f|$ is $2R-\log(2\pi R)+O(\frac1R)$. ∎
$R$$\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|f(Re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta$$\sum_{0\lt|n|\lt R}\log\frac R{|n|}$$2R-\log(2\pi R)$
10.516.818716.818716.8107
100.5194.5528194.5528194.5520

The first two columns agree to all digits shown, as Jensen's formula says they must. The third column, the common asymptotic value, is off by $O(1/R)$.

L9 · Slide 9

9.8 Polynomials with coefficients $\pm1$

DerivedProposition 9.8.1. Let $f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^n\varepsilon_kz^k$ with all $\varepsilon_k=\pm1$, and $0\lt\delta\lt1$. At most $\frac2\delta\log\frac2\delta$ zeros of $f$ lie in $|z|\le1-\delta$, whatever $n$ is.
Proof. Apply Cor. 9.6.2 with $r=1-\delta$ and $R=1-\frac\delta2$.
  • $|f(0)|=|\varepsilon_0|=1$, so $\log|f(0)|=0$.
  • On $|z|=R$: $|f(z)|\le\sum_kR^k\lt\frac1{1-R}=\frac2\delta$, so $\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(R)\lt\log\frac2\delta$.
  • \[ \log\frac Rr=-\log\frac{1-\delta}{1-\delta/2}=-\log\Big(1-\frac{\delta/2}{1-\delta/2}\Big)=-\log\Big(1-\frac\delta{2R}\Big)\gt\frac\delta{2R}\gt\frac\delta2, \] using $-\log(1-x)\gt x$ for $0\lt x\lt1$ and $R\lt1$.
So $\class{ntn-nr}{n}(1-\delta)\lt\log\frac2\delta\big/\frac\delta2=\frac2\delta\log\frac2\delta$. ∎
DerivedCorollary 9.8.2 (zeros hug the unit circle). All but at most $\frac4\delta\log\frac2\delta$ zeros of $f$ lie in the annulus $1-\delta\lt|z|\lt\frac1{1-\delta}$.
Proof. $z^nf(1/z)=\sum_k\varepsilon_kz^{n-k}$ is again a $\pm1$ polynomial (of degree $n$, as $\varepsilon_0\ne0$). Its zeros are the $1/a$ for the zeros $a$ of $f$ (all nonzero, as $f(0)\ne0$), with the same multiplicities. A zero $a$ with $|a|\ge\frac1{1-\delta}$ gives a zero $1/a$ with $|1/a|\le1-\delta$, and Prop. 9.8.1 allows at most $\frac2\delta\log\frac2\delta$ of those. Add the at most $\frac2\delta\log\frac2\delta$ zeros in $|z|\le1-\delta$. ∎

Example: for $n=200$ and $\delta=0.1$, the bound allows $\frac2{0.1}\log20\approx59.9$, so at most $59$ zeros in $|z|\le0.9$; the random sample in the figure has $6$. The bound does not depend on $n$, so as $n$ grows almost all the $n$ zeros crowd towards the unit circle.

L9 · Slide 10

9.9 The order of an entire function

An entire function is one that is holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$. By Theorem 6.4.1, its Taylor series at $0$ converges everywhere.

DefinedDefinition 9.9.1 (order). For $f$ entire, let $\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(r):=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$. If $\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(r)\le e^{r^\lambda}$ for all large $r$, for some $\lambda\gt0$, then $f$ has finite order; its order $\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}$ is the infimum of such $\lambda$.

The order measures growth on a doubly exponential scale: $\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{\log\log \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(r)}{\log r}$.

$f$OrderWhyZeros
polynomial$0$$\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(r)\le Cr^d\le e^{r^\lambda}$ for large $r$, for every $\lambda\gt0$finitely many
$e^{az+b}$, $a\ne0$$1$$\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(r)=e^{|a|r+\operatorname{Re}b}$none
$\sin\pi z$$1$$\sinh\pi r\le \class{ntn-Mr}{M}(r)\le e^{\pi r}$ (by §9.7, step 2)$\mathbb Z$: about $2r$ in $|z|\le r$
$\cos\sqrt z=\sum_k\frac{(-z)^k}{(2k)!}$$\frac12$$|\cos w|\le e^{|w|}$ gives $\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(r)\le e^{\sqrt r}$; at $z=-r$ it is $\cosh\sqrt r$$\pi^2(n-\frac12)^2$, $n\ge1$: about $\sqrt r/\pi$ in $|z|\le r$
$e^{z^2}$$2$$\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(r)=e^{r^2}$none

The power series defines $\cos\sqrt z$ without choosing a square root: it is $\cos w$ for either root $w$ of $z$, since $\cos$ is even. Its zeros are the $z=w^2$ with $\cos w=0$, i.e. $w=\pi(n-\frac12)$. The table suggests that order controls the number of zeros: order $1$, about $r$ zeros; order $\frac12$, about $\sqrt r$. The next theorem proves one direction.

L9 · Slide 11

9.10 Zeros versus order

DerivedTheorem 9.10.1 (zeros versus order). Let $f$ be entire of finite order $\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}$, with $f(0)\ne0$ and zeros $a_1,a_2,\dots$ (repeated by multiplicity). Then:
(1) for every $\epsilon\gt0$, $\class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)=O(r^{\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon})$ as $r\to\infty$;
(2) for every $\sigma\gt\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}$, $\sum_k|a_k|^{-\sigma}\lt\infty$.
Proof.
  1. (1). By definition of the order, $\class{ntn-Mr}{M}(2r)\le e^{(2r)^{\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon}}$ for large $r$. Cor. 9.6.2 with $R=2r$ (so $\log\frac Rr=\log2$) gives \[ \class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)\le\frac{(2r)^{\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon}-\log|f(0)|}{\log2}=O(r^{\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon}). \]
  2. (2), dyadic shells. Let $\epsilon:=(\sigma-\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho})/2\gt0$. By (1) there is $C$ with $\class{ntn-nr}{n}(r)\le Cr^{\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon}$ for all $r\ge1$ (for small $r$ enlarge $C$). The zeros with $2^j\lt|a_k|\le2^{j+1}$ number at most $\class{ntn-nr}{n}(2^{j+1})\le C2^{\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon}\,2^{j(\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon)}$, and each contributes $|a_k|^{-\sigma}\lt2^{-j\sigma}$. Since $\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon-\sigma=-\epsilon$, \[ \sum_{|a_k|\gt1}|a_k|^{-\sigma}\le C2^{\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon}\sum_{j\ge0}2^{j(\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon)}2^{-j\sigma}=C2^{\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}+\epsilon}\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j\epsilon}\lt\infty. \] Only finitely many $a_k$ have $|a_k|\le1$ (zeros cannot accumulate). ∎
Remark 9.10.2 ($\sigma=\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}$ can fail). $\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}$ has order $1$ and zeros $\pm1,\pm2,\dots$, and $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac2n=\infty$. So (2) is sharp.

Theorem 9.10.1(2) is exactly what is needed to build a convergent product with prescribed zeros (Hadamard's theorem, Theorem 10.13.1). Lecture 10 develops infinite products.
