L10 · Slide 2

10.1 The identity theorem

Two tools from Part II's toolbox are proved in full first: the identity theorem (announced in Lecture 1 as Theorem 1.3.1) and the stability of holomorphy under uniform limits.

Notation: $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(x,r):=\{z:|z-x|\lt r\}$, the open disk.

DerivedTheorem 10.1.1 (identity theorem). Let $f,g$ be holomorphic on a connectedC.4 open set $U$, and let $x_n\in U\setminus\{x\}$ with $x_n\to x\in U$. If $f(x_n)=g(x_n)$ for every $n$, then $f=g$ on $U$.

This contains Theorem 1.3.1 (a nonempty open set contains such a sequence) and Cor. 1.3.2 (take $g=0$). Let $h:=f-g$; the hypothesis says $h(x_n)=0$.

Proof, Step 1. If zeros $x_n\ne x$ of $h$ tend to $x\in U$, then $h\equiv0$ on every disk $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(x,r)\subset U$.
  1. Fix $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(x,r)\subset U$. On each closed disk $|z-x|\le r'$ with $r'\lt r$, Theorem 6.4.1 gives $h(z)=\sum_ka_k(z-x)^k$, with coefficients $a_k=h^{(k)}(x)/k!$ that do not depend on $r'$. So the expansion holds on all of $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(x,r)$.
  2. Suppose some $a_k\ne0$, and let $a_m$ be the first. By the Taylor remainder (Cor. 6.5.1 with $N=m+1$), $h(z)=a_m(z-x)^m+O(|z-x|^{m+1})$, that is, \[ \frac{h(z)}{(z-x)^m}=a_m+O(|z-x|)\qquad(z\to x). \]
  3. Put $z=x_n$ (allowed, as $x_n\ne x$, and $x_n\in \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(x,r)$ for large $n$): $a_m=\lim_n\frac{h(x_n)}{(x_n-x)^m}=\lim_n0=0$, a contradiction. So all $a_k=0$, and $h\equiv0$ on $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(x,r)$. ∎

Compare the proof of Theorem 6.7.1, which ran the same argument through derivatives; this version is the one the slides use.

L10 · Slide 3

10.2 The identity theorem: proof

Proof, Step 2: $h\equiv0$ on $U$. Let $S:=\{z\in U:h\equiv0\text{ on some disk }\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z,r)\subset U\}$.
  • $x\in S$, by Step 1 ($U$ is open, so some disk $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(x,r)$ lies in $U$).
  • $S$ is open: if $h\equiv0$ on $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z,r)$, every $w\in \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z,r)$ has the disk $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(w,r-|w-z|)\subset \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z,r)$ on which $h\equiv0$, so $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z,r)\subset S$.
  • $S$ is closed in $U$: let $z\in U$ be a limit of points $z_n\in S\setminus\{z\}$. Then $h(z_n)=0$, so $z$ is a limit of zeros $z_n\ne z$, and Step 1 (with $z$ in place of $x$) gives $h\equiv0$ on a disk $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z,r)\subset U$: $z\in S$.
As $U$ is connected, the nonempty, open and closed set $S$ is all of $U$. ∎
DefinedExample 10.2.1. $\sin2z=2\sin z\cos z$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$. Here $\sin z:=\frac{e^{iz}-e^{-iz}}{2i}$ and $\cos z:=\frac{e^{iz}+e^{-iz}}2$ are entire (power series with infinite radius, A.19). Both sides are entire, and they agree on $\R$, which contains a sequence such as $\frac1n\to0$. Theorem 10.1.1 does the rest.

This is how every real identity between entire functions (addition formulas, $\sin^2+\cos^2=1$, and so on) passes to $\mathbb C$ at no cost; Prop. 11.1.2 says it again.

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 10.2.2 (prescribed values at $1/n$; Practice midterm 1, Problem 2(b)). Is there an entire function $f$ with $f(\frac1n)=\frac1{n^2}$ for all integers $n\ge1$, and $f(2)=2$?
Hint Which entire function takes the values $\frac1{n^2}$ at $\frac1n$? Use the identity theorem (Theorem 10.1.1).
Solution No. $f$ and $z^2$ are entire and agree at the points $\frac1n\to0\in\mathbb C$, so $f=z^2$ on the connected (C.4) set $\mathbb C$ by the identity theorem, Theorem 10.1.1 (the limit point $0$ lies in $\mathbb C$, and $\frac1n\ne0$). Then $f(2)=4\ne2$.
Exercise 10.2.3 (zeros at $1/n$ or at $n$; Practice midterm 2, Problem 2(b)). Is there an entire function $f\not\equiv0$ with $f(\frac1n)=0$ for all integers $n\ge1$? Is there one with $f(n)=0$ for all integers $n\ge1$?
Hint Where do the zeros accumulate in each case?
Solution First: no. The zeros $\frac1n$ accumulate at $0\in\mathbb C$, so $f\equiv0$ by the identity theorem, Theorem 10.1.1 (with $g=0$; compare Cor. 1.3.2). Second: yes, for example $\sin\pi z$. The zeros $1,2,3,\dots$ have no limit point in $\mathbb C$, so the identity theorem says nothing. (Any sequence $|a_k|\to\infty$ is the zero set of an entire function: Theorem 10.11.1.)
Exercise 10.2.4 (holomorphic on the disk but not entire; Practice midterm 3, Problem 2(b)). Is there a holomorphic $f:D(0,1)\to\mathbb C$ with $f(\frac1n)=\frac1{n+1}$ for all integers $n\ge2$? Is there an entire one?
Hint Write $\frac1{n+1}$ as a function of $\frac1n$. For the entire question, where would that function have to be singular?
Solution
  • On the disk: yes. $\frac1{n+1}=\frac{1/n}{1+1/n}$, so $f(z)=\frac z{1+z}$ works; its only pole, $-1$, is outside $D(0,1)$. (It is the only one, by Theorem 10.1.1 on the connected set $D(0,1)$.)
  • Entire: no. If $F$ were entire with these values, then $F$ and $\frac z{1+z}$ are holomorphic on the connected (C.4) open set $\mathbb C\setminus\{-1\}$ and agree at the points $\frac1n\to0$, so $F=\frac z{1+z}$ on all of $\mathbb C\setminus\{-1\}$ by the identity theorem (Theorem 10.1.1). But $\frac z{1+z}\to\infty$ as $z\to-1$, while $F$ is continuous at $-1$. Contradiction.
L10 · Slide 4

10.3 Uniform limits

DerivedTheorem 10.3.1 (uniform limits). Let $f_N$ be holomorphic on an open set $U$, and $f_N\to f$ uniformlyA.17 on every closed disk contained in $U$. Then $f$ is holomorphic on $U$.
Proof. Let $\overline{\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z_0,r)}\subset U$, let $\gamma$ be the circle $|z-z_0|=r$, and $w\in \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z_0,r)$.
  1. $f$ is continuous on the closed disk: a uniform limit of continuous functions (A.17).
  2. By Cauchy's formula (Theorem 6.3.1), $f_N(w)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f_N(z)}{z-w}dz$. On $\gamma$, $|z-w|\ge r-|w-z_0|\gt0$, so by the ML estimate \[ \Big|\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f_N(z)-f(z)}{z-w}\,dz\Big|\le\frac{r\max_\gamma|f_N-f|}{r-|w-z_0|}\longrightarrow0. \] Letting $N\to\infty$ on both sides, \[ f(w)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f_N(z)}{z-w}\,dz=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f(z)}{z-w}\,dz. \]
  3. The right side is holomorphic in $w\in \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(z_0,r)$: differentiate under the integral sign, exactly as in the proof of Theorem 6.6.1, which only needed $f$ continuous on $\gamma$.
Every point of $U$ is the centre of such a disk, so $f$ is holomorphic on $U$. ∎

Lecture 4 proved the same for harmonic functions (Cor. 4.11.1), by the same mechanism: an integral formula survives uniform limits. In real analysis this fails badly: by the Weierstrass approximation theoremA.18, polynomials converge uniformly on $[-1,1]$ to $|x|$, which is not differentiable.

L10 · Slide 5

10.4 Infinite products

A polynomial is determined, up to a constant factor, by its zeros: $c\prod(z-a_j)$. The goal of the lecture is the analogue for entire functions, which may have infinitely many zeros. That needs infinite products.

DerivedLemma 10.4.1 (products). Let $u_1,u_2,\dots$ be holomorphic on an open set $U$, with $\sum_n\max_D|u_n|\lt\infty$ for every closed disk $D\subset U$. Then $F_N:=\prod_{n\le N}(1+u_n)$ converges uniformly on every closed disk $D\subset U$ to a holomorphic function $F$ on $U$. For $z\in U$: $F(z)=0$ if and only if some factor $1+u_n(z)=0$; only finitely many factors vanish at $z$; and the order of the zero of $F$ at $z$ is the sum of their orders.
Proof of convergence. Fix $D$ and let $s_n:=\max_D|u_n|$, so $\sum s_n\lt\infty$.
  1. A uniform bound. On $D$, using $1+s\le e^s$: $|F_N|\le\prod_{n\le N}(1+s_n)\le e^{\sum_ns_n}=:B$.
  2. Successive differences. $F_{N+1}-F_N=F_N\,u_{N+1}$, so $|F_{N+1}-F_N|\le B\,s_{N+1}$ on $D$.
  3. Telescoping. $F_N=F_1+\sum_{n\lt N}(F_{n+1}-F_n)$. The series has terms bounded on $D$ by $Bs_{n+1}$, which are summable, so it converges uniformly on $D$ (M-testA.21).
  4. Each $F_N$ is holomorphic, so the limit $F$ is holomorphic on $U$ by Theorem 10.3.1. ∎
L10 · Slide 6

10.5 Infinite products: zeros

Proof of the statement about zeros. Fix $D$, and $M$ with $s_n\le\frac12$ for $n\gt M$ (possible as $s_n\to0$).
  1. Split off a finite product. By the first part (applied to $u_{M+1},u_{M+2},\dots$), $T:=\prod_{n\gt M}(1+u_n)$ is holomorphic on $U$, and $F=F_M\,T$, as a limit of $F_M\prod_{M\lt n\le N}(1+u_n)$.
  2. The tail has no zeros on $D$. For $n\gt M$, on $D$: $|1+u_n|\ge1-s_n\ge e^{-2s_n}$, by the inequality below. Hence \[ |T|=\lim_{N\to\infty}\prod_{M\lt n\le N}|1+u_n|\ge e^{-2\sum_{n\gt M}s_n}\gt0\qquad\text{on }D. \]
  3. The inequality. $1-t\ge e^{-2t}$ for $0\le t\le\frac12$: the function $\varphi(t):=1-t-e^{-2t}$ is concave ($\varphi''=-4e^{-2t}\lt0$), with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi(\frac12)=\frac12-e^{-1}\gt0$. A concave function lies above its chord, so $\varphi\ge0$ on $[0,\frac12]$.
  4. Conclude. On $D$, $F=F_M\,T$ with $T$ holomorphic and nonzero. So $F$ has the same zeros as the finite product $F_M$, with the same orders (multiplying by a nonzero holomorphic function does not change the order: $(z-z_0)^mh\cdot T$ with $h(z_0)T(z_0)\ne0$). The order of a zero of a finite product is the sum of the orders of the factors, by the same reasoning. And $1+u_n\ne0$ on $D$ for $n\gt M$.
Every $z\in U$ lies in such a closed disk $D$ (as $U$ is open), which proves all three claims. ∎

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 10.5.1 (Blaschke products; Homework 2, Problem 2(d) (optional)). Let $0\lt|a_k|\lt1$ with $\sum_k(1-|a_k|)\lt\infty$. Show that $B(z):=\prod_k\frac{|a_k|}{a_k}\cdot\frac{a_k-z}{1-\bar a_kz}$ converges uniformly on each $\overline{D(0,r)}$, $r\lt1$, to a holomorphic function on $D(0,1)$ with $|B|\le1$, whose zeros are exactly the $a_k$.
Hint For $|z|\le r$, the factor differs from $1$ by at most $(1-|a_k|)\frac{1+r}{1-r}$. Then use Lemma 10.4.1.
Solution
  1. The factor minus one. With $b_k(z):=\frac{|a_k|}{a_k}\cdot\frac{a_k-z}{1-\bar a_kz}$, \[ b_k(z)-1=\frac{|a_k|(a_k-z)-a_k(1-\bar a_kz)}{a_k(1-\bar a_kz)}=\frac{-(1-|a_k|)\,(a_k+|a_k|z)}{a_k(1-\bar a_kz)}. \] For $|z|\le r$: $|a_k+|a_k|z|\le|a_k|(1+r)$ and $|1-\bar a_kz|\ge1-r$, so $|b_k-1|\le(1-|a_k|)\frac{1+r}{1-r}$.
  2. Products. These bounds are summable, so Lemma 10.4.1 (with $U=D(0,1)$ and $u_k=b_k-1$) gives uniform convergence on each $\overline{D(0,r)}$ to a holomorphic $B$ whose zeros are those of the factors: $b_k$ vanishes only at $a_k$, simply.
  3. $|B|\le1$. Each factor is $\frac{|a_k|}{a_k}\varphi_{a_k}$, a rotation of the automorphism of Def. 12.13.1, so it maps the disk into itself (Lemma 12.13.2, Lecture 12). Directly, each factor has modulus $\lt1$ on the disk: $|1-\bar az|^2-|a-z|^2=(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)\gt0$ for $|a|,|z|\lt1$ (expand both sides). So partial products have modulus $\lt1$, and so does their limit (at most $1$).

With the previous exercise: the zero sets of bounded holomorphic functions on the disk are exactly the sequences with $\sum(1-|a_k|)\lt\infty$.

L10 · Slide 7

10.6 Entire functions without zeros

A product with the right zeros determines $f$ only up to a factor without zeros. This lemma pins such factors down by their growth.

DerivedLemma 10.6.1 (no zeros). Let $F$ be entire with no zeros, and $\class{ntn-Ar}{A}(r):=\max_{|z|=r}\log|F(z)|$. Then $F=e^G$ with $G(z)=\sum_nc_nz^n$ entire, and \[ |c_n|\,r^n\le2\class{ntn-Ar}{A}(r)-2\log|F(0)|\qquad\text{for all }r\gt0,\ n\ge1. \] If $\class{ntn-Ar}{A}(r_j)\le\varepsilon_jr_j^{k+1}$ with $r_j\to\infty$ and $\varepsilon_j\to0$, then $G$ is a polynomial of degree $\le k$.
Proof.
  1. $F=e^G$. $F'/F$ is entire (as $F\ne0$), so it is a power series converging on all of $\mathbb C$ (Theorem 6.4.1 on every disk); integrating term by term gives an entire primitive $G$ (A.19). Adjust the constant so that $e^{G(0)}=F(0)$ (choose $G(0)$ to be any logarithm of $F(0)\ne0$). Then $(Fe^{-G})'=e^{-G}(F'-FG')=0$, so $Fe^{-G}$ is constant, equal to its value $1$ at $0$.
  2. A nonnegative function on the circle. $|F|=e^{\operatorname{Re}G}$, so $\operatorname{Re}G=\log|F|$. Fix $r$; then $\varphi(\theta):=\class{ntn-Ar}{A}(r)-\operatorname{Re}G(re^{i\theta})\ge0$, by definition of $\class{ntn-Ar}{A}(r)$ as a maximum.
  3. Fourier coefficients of $\operatorname{Re}G$. Since $\operatorname{Re}w=\frac12(w+\bar w)$, \[ \operatorname{Re}G(re^{i\theta})=\operatorname{Re}c_0+\tfrac12\sum_{n\ge1}\big(c_nr^ne^{in\theta}+\bar c_nr^ne^{-in\theta}\big), \] uniformly convergent in $\theta$ (power series converge uniformly on circles inside their disk, A.19). Multiply by $e^{-in\theta}$ ($n\ge1$) and integrate term by term: $\int_0^{2\pi}e^{ik\theta}e^{-in\theta}d\theta$ is $2\pi$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise, and the terms $\bar c_ke^{-ik\theta}e^{-in\theta}$ ($k\ge1$) and the constant all integrate to $0$. So $\int_0^{2\pi}\operatorname{Re}G(re^{i\theta})e^{-in\theta}d\theta=\pi c_nr^n$, and similarly $\int_0^{2\pi}\operatorname{Re}G\,d\theta=2\pi\operatorname{Re}c_0$.
  4. Estimate. As $\int_0^{2\pi}\class{ntn-Ar}{A}(r)e^{-in\theta}d\theta=0$, \[ \pi|c_n|r^n=\Big|\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(\theta)e^{-in\theta}d\theta\Big|\le\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(\theta)\,d\theta=2\pi\big(\class{ntn-Ar}{A}(r)-\operatorname{Re}c_0\big), \] where $\varphi\ge0$ was used to drop the absolute value. Finally $\operatorname{Re}c_0=\operatorname{Re}G(0)=\log|F(0)|$.
  5. Polynomial. For $n\gt k$, i.e. $n\ge k+1$, and $r_j\ge1$: \[ |c_n|\le2r_j^{-n}\big(\varepsilon_jr_j^{k+1}-\log|F(0)|\big)\le2\varepsilon_j+2r_j^{-n}\big|\log|F(0)|\big|\longrightarrow0. \] So $c_n=0$ for all $n\gt k$. ∎

The key idea is step 4: a bound on $\operatorname{Re}G$ from above only controls all of $G$, because $\varphi\ge0$ turns the absolute value of an integral into an integral. With $k=0$ it says a zero-free entire function with $\log|F|=o(r)$ along a sequence of circles is constant.

L10 · Slide 8

10.7 Euler's sine product

DerivedTheorem 10.7.1 (Euler). For every $z\in\mathbb C$, \[ \sin\pi z=\class{ntn-Ps}{P}(z):=\pi z\prod_{n\ge1}\Big(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\Big). \]

Euler's heuristic: $\sin\pi z$ vanishes exactly at the integers, like a "polynomial of infinite degree", so it should factor over its zeros. The proof below makes this honest in three steps.

Step 1: $f:=\sin\pi z/\class{ntn-Ps}{P}$ is entire and zero-free, so $f=e^G$.
  1. $\class{ntn-Ps}{P}$ is entire, with simple zeros exactly at the integers. On $|z|\le R$, $|z^2/n^2|\le R^2/n^2$, which is summable over $n$. So the product lemma (Lemma 10.4.1, with $u_n=-z^2/n^2$) makes $\class{ntn-Ps}{P}$ entire. Its zeros: $\pi z$ vanishes (simply) at $0$, and $1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}=(1-\frac zn)(1+\frac zn)$ vanishes simply at $\pm n$; by the lemma, the zeros of $\class{ntn-Ps}{P}$ are exactly these, each simple.
  2. So is $\sin\pi z$. $\sin\pi z=0$ iff $e^{2\pi iz}=1$ iff $z\in\mathbb Z$. At $m\in\mathbb Z$ the derivative $\pi\cos\pi m=\pm\pi\ne0$, so the zero is simple.
  3. The quotient. Off $\mathbb Z$, $f$ is holomorphic and nonzero. At $m\in\mathbb Z$, both are $(z-m)$ times a function holomorphic and nonzero at $m$, so $f$ is a quotient of two such functions: bounded near $m$, hence holomorphic there by Lemma 9.1.1, and nonzero at $m$. So $f$ is entire with no zeros, and $f=e^G$ by Lemma 10.6.1.
  4. $f$ is even, and $f(0)=1$. $\sin\pi z$ and $\class{ntn-Ps}{P}$ are both odd, so their quotient is even. As $z\to0$, $\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}\to1$ and $\frac{\class{ntn-Ps}{P}(z)}{\pi z}=\prod_n(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2})\to1$ (the product is continuous, with value $1$ at $0$). So $f(0)=1$. ∎
L10 · Slide 9

10.8 Euler's sine product: growth on circles

Step 2: on $|z|=r:=N+\frac12$ $(N=0,1,2,\dots)$, $\ \log|f(z)|\le O(r\log r)$.
  1. $z$ stays away from the integers. For $n\in\mathbb Z$, $|z-n|\ge\big||z|-|n|\big|=|r-|n||\ge\frac12$, as $r$ is a half-integer.
  2. Factors with $1\le n\le2r$ (at most $2r$ of them): $\big|1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\big|=\frac{|n-z|\,|n+z|}{n^2}\ge\frac{1/4}{n^2}\ge\frac1{16r^2}$.
  3. Factors with $n\gt2r$: $\frac{r^2}{n^2}\le\frac14\le\frac12$, so by the inequality of §10.5, $\big|1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\big|\ge1-\frac{r^2}{n^2}\ge e^{-2r^2/n^2}$.
  4. Lower bound for $|\class{ntn-Ps}{P}|$. $\sum_{n\gt2r}\frac{2r^2}{n^2}\le2r^2\int_{2r}^\infty\frac{dt}{t^2}=r$ (the sum starts at $n=2r+1$, as $2r=2N+1$ is an integer, and $\frac1{n^2}\le\int_{n-1}^n\frac{dt}{t^2}$), and $|\pi z|=\pi r\gt1$. So \[ \log|\class{ntn-Ps}{P}(z)|\ge\log(\pi r)-2r\log(16r^2)-r\ge-2r\log(16r^2)-r. \]
  5. Upper bound for $|\sin|$. $|\sin w|=\frac12|e^{iw}-e^{-iw}|\le e^{|w|}$, so $\log|\sin\pi z|\le\pi r$.
  6. So \[ \log|f|=\log|\sin\pi z|-\log|\class{ntn-Ps}{P}|\le\pi r+2r\log(16r^2)+O(r)=O(r\log r). \] ∎
Step 3: $f\equiv1$. By Step 2, $\class{ntn-Ar}{A}(r)=\max_{|z|=r}\log|f|\le Cr\log r$ on the circles $r_j=j+\frac12$. As $r\log r=o(r^2)$, take $\varepsilon_j:=C\log r_j/r_j\to0$: the no-zeros lemma with $k=1$ shows $G(z)=a+bz$. As $f$ is even, $e^{a+bz}=e^{a-bz}$, so $e^{2bz}=1$ for all $z$; differentiating at $0$ gives $2b=0$. As $f(0)=1$, $e^a=1$. So $f\equiv1$, i.e. $\sin\pi z=\class{ntn-Ps}{P}(z)$. ∎

Notice why the circles were chosen with half-integer radii: on them $|\sin\pi z|$ is not small and the factors of $\class{ntn-Ps}{P}$ are not small, so the ratio can be controlled. And the no-zeros lemma only needs control on some sequence of circles.

A first dividend: comparing the coefficients of $z^2$ on both sides of $\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}=\prod(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2})$ gives $\sum1/n^2=\pi^2/6$, the Basel sumE.18 used in Lemma 6.13.2.

L10 · Slide 10

10.9 The partial products

  • No polynomial is the sine. $\class{ntn-PN}{P_N}(x):=\pi x\prod_{n\le N}(1-x^2/n^2)$ is a polynomial of degree $2N+1$, so $|\class{ntn-PN}{P_N}(x)|\to\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$, while $|\sin\pi x|\le1$. The partial products follow the sine only on a bounded window, which grows with $N$.
  • The convergence is slow. For fixed $x\notin\mathbb Z$, as $N\to\infty$, \[ \frac{\class{ntn-PN}{P_N}(x)}{\sin\pi x}=\prod_{n\gt N}\Big(1-\frac{x^2}{n^2}\Big)^{-1}=\exp\Big(\sum_{n\gt N}-\log\Big(1-\frac{x^2}{n^2}\Big)\Big)=e^{x^2/N+O(N^{-2})}, \] since $-\log(1-t)=t+O(t^2)$ and $\sum_{n\gt N}\frac1{n^2}=\frac1N+O(\frac1{N^2})$ (compare with $\int_N^\infty dt/t^2$). So the relative error is about $x^2/N$: halving it costs doubling $N$. At $x=1.5$, $N=10$ the ratio is $1.24$ (the leading term predicts $e^{0.225}\approx1.25$).
L10 · Slide 11

10.10 Convergence factors

Euler's product worked because the factors for $\pm n$ pair up as $1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}$, whose deviations from $1$ are summable. In general the naive product over the zeros diverges. For $a_k=k$: at $z=-1$, $\prod_{k\le N}(1+\frac1k)=\prod_{k\le N}\frac{k+1}k=N+1\to\infty$ (telescoping). The cure is to multiply each factor by an exponential, which has no zeros.

DefinedDefinition 10.10.1 (Weierstrass factors). \[ \class{ntn-Ep}{E_0}(w):=1-w,\qquad \class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}(w):=(1-w)\exp\Big(w+\frac{w^2}2+\dots+\frac{w^p}p\Big)\quad(p\ge1). \] Each $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}$ is entire, and its only zero is $w=1$, a simple one ($\exp$ never vanishes).
DerivedLemma 10.10.2 (convergence factors). For $p\ge0$ and $|w|\le\frac12$, $\ |1-\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}(w)|\le4|w|^{p+1}$.
Proof.
  1. $1-w$ as an exponential. For $|w|\lt1$ let $L(w):=-\sum_{k\ge1}w^k/k$. Then $L'(w)=-\sum_{k\ge1}w^{k-1}=-\frac1{1-w}$, so $\big((1-w)e^{-L}\big)'=e^{-L}\big(-1+(1-w)\frac{1}{1-w}\big)=0$; the function is constant on the disk, equal to $1$ at $w=0$. So $1-w=e^{L(w)}$.
  2. $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}$ as an exponential. Hence $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}(w)=e^{L(w)+w+\dots+w^p/p}=e^u$ with $u:=-\sum_{k\gt p}w^k/k$: the factor $\exp(w+\dots+w^p/p)$ cancels the first $p$ terms of $L$.
  3. Estimate $u$. For $|w|\le\frac12$: $|u|\le\sum_{k\gt p}|w|^k=\frac{|w|^{p+1}}{1-|w|}\le2|w|^{p+1}\le1$.
  4. Estimate $e^u-1$. For $|u|\le1$: \[ |e^u-1|\le\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{|u|^j}{j!}\le|u|\sum_{j\ge1}\frac1{j!}=(e-1)|u|\le2|u|\le4|w|^{p+1}. \] ∎

So $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}(w)$ is within $O(|w|^{p+1})$ of $1$ for small $w$, instead of $O(|w|)$ for $1-w$: the larger $p$, the faster the factors approach $1$.

L10 · Slide 12

10.11 The Weierstrass product

DerivedTheorem 10.11.1 (Weierstrass). Let $a_1,a_2,\dots$ be nonzero, with $|a_k|\to\infty$ (repetitions allowed). Then \[ \class{ntn-Wz}{W}(z):=\prod_k\class{ntn-Ep}{E_k}(z/a_k) \] converges uniformly on every closed disk to an entire function. Its zeros are the $a_k$, and the order of the zero at $a$ is $\#\{k:a_k=a\}$.
Proof. Fix $R\gt0$. As $|a_k|\to\infty$, all but finitely many $k$ have $|a_k|\ge2R$. For these, $|z/a_k|\le\frac12$ on $|z|\le R$, so Lemma 10.10.2 (with $p=k$) gives \[ \max_{|z|\le R}|1-\class{ntn-Ep}{E_k}(z/a_k)|\le4\cdot2^{-k-1}, \] which is summable. The finitely many other terms are finite. So the product lemma (Lemma 10.4.1) applies to $u_k:=\class{ntn-Ep}{E_k}(z/a_k)-1$. The only zero of $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_k}(z/a_k)$ is $z=a_k$, a simple one, so by the lemma the zero of $W$ at $a$ has order equal to the number of $k$ with $a_k=a$. ∎

Using $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_k}$ with $k$ growing is crude but always works. Hadamard's theorem (§10.13) shows that a fixed $p$ suffices when the zeros come from a function of finite order.

L10 · Slide 13

10.12 Factoring an entire function

DerivedCorollary 10.12.1 (Weierstrass factorization). Every entire $f\not\equiv0$ can be written \[ f(z)=z^m\,e^{h(z)}\prod_k\class{ntn-Ep}{E_k}\Big(\frac z{a_k}\Big), \] with $h$ entire, $m\ge0$ the order of the zero of $f$ at $0$, and $a_k$ the zeros of $f$ other than $0$, each listed as often as its order.
Proof.
  1. The zeros are a legitimate list. By the identity theorem, the zeros of $f\not\equiv0$ have no limit point in $\mathbb C$, so each disk $|z|\le R$ contains finitely many (else Bolzano–Weierstrass would give one). Each zero has finite order (otherwise $f\equiv0$ near it, hence on $\mathbb C$). So the $a_k$ are finitely many, or $|a_k|\to\infty$.
  2. A function with the same zeros. $Q(z):=z^m\prod_k\class{ntn-Ep}{E_k}(z/a_k)$ is entire (Theorem 10.11.1, or a finite product) with the same zeros as $f$, with the same orders.
  3. The quotient. As in Step 1 of §10.7, $f/Q$ extends to an entire function without zeros: at a common zero $a$ of order $p$, $f=(z-a)^ph_1$ and $Q=(z-a)^ph_2$ with $h_1,h_2$ nonzero near $a$. By Lemma 10.6.1, $f/Q=e^h$ with $h$ entire. ∎
L10 · Slide 14

10.13 Hadamard's theorem

CitedTheorem 10.13.1 (Hadamard). Let $f\not\equiv0$ be entire of finite order $\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}$, with a zero of order $m\ge0$ at $0$ and other zeros $a_k$, each listed as often as its order. Let $p:=\lfloor\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}\rfloor$. Then \[ f(z)=z^m\,e^{h(z)}\prod_k\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}(z/a_k),\qquad h\text{ a polynomial of degree}\le\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}. \]

The slides state this without proof; the idea is in E.20. What can be checked here is that the product converges:

Why the product converges. $f/z^m$ is entire of the same order, with nonzero value at $0$ and zeros $a_k$. As $p+1\gt\class{ntn-rhoo}{\rho}$, Theorem 9.10.1(2) with $\sigma=p+1$ gives $\sum_k|a_k|^{-p-1}\lt\infty$. On $|z|\le R$, for the $k$ with $|a_k|\ge2R$, Lemma 10.10.2 gives $|1-\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}(z/a_k)|\le4R^{p+1}|a_k|^{-p-1}$, which is summable; so Lemma 10.4.1 applies. ∎

Compared with Weierstrass, Hadamard gains two things for functions of finite order: one fixed $p$ for all factors, and $h$ a polynomial, not just entire. The proof of the second uses Lemma 10.6.1 together with lower bounds for the product away from its zeros.

L10 · Slide 15

10.14 Hadamard's theorem: examples

DefinedExample 10.14.1 (the sine again). $\sin\pi z$ has order $1$ (table of §9.9), so $p=1$. List its nonzero zeros as $1,-1,2,-2,\dots$ and pair consecutive factors (grouping factors of a convergent product does not change its limit, as it only selects a subsequence of partial products): \[ \class{ntn-Ep}{E_1}\Big(\frac zn\Big)\class{ntn-Ep}{E_1}\Big(-\frac zn\Big)=\Big(1-\frac zn\Big)e^{z/n}\Big(1+\frac zn\Big)e^{-z/n}=1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}. \] So $\sin\pi z=z\,e^{a+bz}\prod_{n\ge1}(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2})$. Here $e^{a+bz}$ is even, as a quotient of odd functions, so $b=0$; and letting $z\to0$, $e^a=\lim\frac{\sin\pi z}z=\pi$. This is Euler's product again (Theorem 10.7.1).
DefinedExample 10.14.2 ($\cos\sqrt z$). $\cos\sqrt z:=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-z)^n}{(2n)!}$ has order $\frac12$ (§9.9), so $p=0$ and $h$ is a constant. Its zeros $\pi^2(n-\frac12)^2$, $n\ge1$, are simple (the derivative, $-\frac{\sin w}{2w}$ at $w=\sqrt z$, is nonzero there), and $\cos\sqrt0=1$ fixes $e^h=1$. So, with $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_0}(w)=1-w$, \[ \cos\sqrt z=\prod_{n\ge1}\Big(1-\frac{z}{\pi^2(n-\frac12)^2}\Big). \] Replacing $z$ by $z^2$ gives the companion of Euler's product: $\cos z=\prod_{n\ge1}\big(1-\frac{4z^2}{\pi^2(2n-1)^2}\big)$.

L11 · Slide 2

11.1 Analytic continuation

DefinedDefinition 11.1.1 (continuation). Let $U\subset W$ be open, and $f$ holomorphic on $U$. A continuation of $f$ to $W$ is a holomorphic $F$ on $W$ with $F=f$ on $U$.
DerivedProposition 11.1.2 (gluing and uniqueness). Let $U$, $V$, $W$ be open.
(1) Gluing. If $f$ is holomorphic on $U$, $g$ on $V$, and $f=g$ on $U\cap V$, then $F:=f$ on $U$, $F:=g$ on $V$ defines a holomorphic function on $U\cup V$.
(2) Uniqueness. If $W$ is connected, and $F,G$ are holomorphic on $W$ and agree on a nonempty open set or on a real interval $[a,b]$ $(a\lt b)$ in $W$, then $F=G$ on $W$.
Proof. (1) On $U\cap V$ the two definitions agree, so $F$ is well defined. Holomorphy is a local property (a limit of difference quotients at each point), and near each point of $U\cup V$, $F$ coincides with $f$ or with $g$ on an open set.
(2) Either set contains a point $x$ and points $x_n\ne x$ with $x_n\to x$: for $[a,b]$, take $x:=a$ and $x_n:=a+\frac{b-a}n$; an open set contains a small disk around any of its points. Apply the identity theorem (Theorem 10.1.1) to $F$ and $G$. ∎

Consequences. If $W$ is connected and $U\ne\emptyset$, a continuation of $f$ to $W$ is unique, if it exists; so it makes sense to speak of the continuation. And identities continue: $\sin^2z+\cos^2z-1$ is entire and vanishes on $\R$, hence on $\mathbb C$.

L11 · Slide 3

11.2 A natural boundary

Continuation is not always possible: a function can be holomorphic on a disk and impossible to continue across any point of its boundary circle.

DefinedDefinition 11.2.1 (natural boundary). Let $f$ be holomorphic on $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(0,1)$, where $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(a,r):=\{z:|z-a|\lt r\}$. The unit circle is a natural boundary of $f$ if $f$ continues to $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(0,1)\cup \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(w_0,\delta)$ for no $|w_0|=1$ and no $\delta\gt0$.
DerivedProposition 11.2.2. The unit circle is a natural boundary of $f(z):=\sum_{n\ge0}z^{2^n}$ $(|z|\lt1)$.

The series converges for $|z|\lt1$, since its terms are among those of $\sum_m|z|^m$; so $f$ is holomorphic there (A.19).

Proof. Suppose $F$ continues $f$ to $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(0,1)\cup \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(w_0,\delta)$, with $|w_0|=1$ and $\delta\gt0$.
  1. A dyadic root of unity near $w_0$. The points $e^{2\pi ij/2^k}$ ($j,k\ge0$) are dense in the unit circle: for each $k$ they are $2^k$ equally spaced points, so every arc longer than $2\pi/2^k$ contains one. The arc of the circle inside $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(w_0,\delta)$ has positive length, so it contains such a point $w=e^{2\pi ij/2^k}$.
  2. $F(w)$ is a radial limit of $f$. For $r\lt1$ close to $1$, $rw\in \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(0,1)\cap \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(w_0,\delta)$, where $F=f$. As $F$ is continuous at $w$, $F(w)=\lim_{r\to1^-}f(rw)$.
  3. But $f$ blows up along that radius. $w^{2^n}=e^{2\pi ij2^{n-k}}=1$ for $n\ge k$. So \[ f(rw)=\sum_{n\lt k}(rw)^{2^n}+\sum_{n\ge k}r^{2^n}. \] The first $k$ terms have modulus $\lt1$ each; the others are positive reals. Keeping only $M$ of them, for every integer $M\ge1$, \[ |F(w)|=\lim_{r\to1^-}|f(rw)|\ge\lim_{r\to1^-}\Big(\sum_{k\le n\lt k+M}r^{2^n}-k\Big)=M-k. \]
As $M$ is arbitrary, $|F(w)|=\infty$, a contradiction. ∎

The gaps in the exponents $2^n$ ("lacunary series") make $f$ behave the same way near a dense set of boundary points. Compare $\sum z^n=\frac1{1-z}$, which is singular only at $z=1$ and continues to $\mathbb C\setminus\{1\}$.

L11 · Slide 4

11.3 Euler's integral

DerivedProposition 11.3.1 (the Gamma function). For $\operatorname{Re}z\gt0$, the integral \[ \Gamma(z):=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt\qquad\big(t^{z-1}:=e^{(z-1)\log t}\big) \] converges absolutely, $\Gamma$ is holomorphic, and $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$. So $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$ for integers $n\ge0$.
Proof. Let $0\lt a\le\operatorname{Re}z\le b$.
  1. Domination. $|t^{z-1}|=|e^{(z-1)\log t}|=e^{(\operatorname{Re}z-1)\log t}=t^{\operatorname{Re}z-1}$. On $(0,1]$, $\log t\le0$, so this is at most $t^{a-1}$; on $[1,\infty)$ it is at most $t^{b-1}$. Since $\int_0^1t^{a-1}dt=\frac1a$ and $\int_1^\infty t^{b-1}e^{-t}dt\lt\infty$, the integral converges absolutely.
  2. Truncations are entire. $I_N(z):=\int_{1/N}^Nt^{z-1}e^{-t}dt$ is entire: the interval is compact and $\partial_zt^{z-1}=(\log t)\,t^{z-1}$ is continuous, so differentiation under the integral sign (A.4) applies.
  3. Uniform convergence on strips. \[ |\Gamma(z)-I_N(z)|\le\int_0^{1/N}t^{a-1}dt+\int_N^\infty t^{b-1}e^{-t}dt=\frac{N^{-a}}a+\int_N^\infty t^{b-1}e^{-t}dt\longrightarrow0, \] uniformly in the strip $a\le\operatorname{Re}z\le b$.
  4. Holomorphic. Each closed disk in $\{\operatorname{Re}z\gt0\}$ lies in such a strip, so $\Gamma$ is holomorphic by Theorem 10.3.1.
  5. Functional equation. Integrating by parts on $[\epsilon,N]$, with $\frac{d}{dt}t^z=zt^{z-1}$, \[ \int_\epsilon^Nt^ze^{-t}dt=\big[-t^ze^{-t}\big]_\epsilon^N+z\int_\epsilon^Nt^{z-1}e^{-t}dt. \] As $\epsilon\to0^+$ and $N\to\infty$, the boundary terms vanish ($|t^z|=t^{\operatorname{Re}z}\to0$ at $0$, and $t^{\operatorname{Re}z}e^{-t}\to0$ at $\infty$), giving $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$.
  6. Factorials. $\Gamma(1)=\int_0^\infty e^{-t}dt=1$, and by induction $\Gamma(n+1)=n\Gamma(n)=n!$. ∎

So $\Gamma$ interpolates the factorials: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$. The integral diverges at $t=0$ when $\operatorname{Re}z\le0$; the next section continues $\Gamma$ there using the functional equation instead.

L11 · Slide 5

11.4 Continuing $\Gamma$ by the functional equation

DefinedDefinition 11.4.1. For $n\ge0$ let \[ \class{ntn-Wn}{W_n}:=\{\operatorname{Re}z\gt-n\}\setminus\{0,-1,\dots,-n+1\},\qquad\class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_n}(z):=\frac{\Gamma(z+n)}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+n-1)}. \] $\class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_n}$ is holomorphic on $\class{ntn-Wn}{W_n}$: there $\operatorname{Re}(z+n)\gt0$, and the denominator does not vanish. $\class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_0}=\Gamma$ (empty product), and $\class{ntn-Wn}{W_0}=\{\operatorname{Re}z\gt0\}$.
DerivedProposition 11.4.2 (the continuation of $\Gamma$). $\class{ntn-Wn}{W_n}\subset \class{ntn-Wn}{W_{n+1}}$ and $\class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_{n+1}}=\class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_n}$ on $\class{ntn-Wn}{W_n}$. So $\Gamma:=\class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_n}$ on $\class{ntn-Wn}{W_n}$ continues $\Gamma$ to \[ \class{ntn-Wset}{W}:=\bigcup_n\class{ntn-Wn}{W_n}=\mathbb C\setminus\{0,-1,-2,\dots\}, \] uniquely, and $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$ on $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$.
Proof.
  1. Consistency. $\class{ntn-Wn}{W_n}\subset \class{ntn-Wn}{W_{n+1}}$ is clear. For $z\in \class{ntn-Wn}{W_n}$, $\operatorname{Re}(z+n)\gt0$, so the functional equation (Prop. 11.3.1) gives $\Gamma(z+n+1)=(z+n)\Gamma(z+n)$, and \[ \class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_{n+1}}(z)=\frac{(z+n)\,\Gamma(z+n)}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+n)}=\frac{\Gamma(z+n)}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+n-1)}=\class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_n}(z). \]
  2. Gluing. By induction and Prop. 11.1.2(1), these define one holomorphic function on $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$. It is unique because $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$ is connected (a path between two of its points can detour around the isolated points $0,-1,-2,\dots$) and Prop. 11.1.2(2).
  3. Functional equation on $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$. If $z\in \class{ntn-Wset}{W}$ then $z+1\in \class{ntn-Wset}{W}$ (if $z+1=-m$ with $m\ge0$, then $z=-m-1\notin \class{ntn-Wset}{W}$). So both $\Gamma(z+1)$ and $z\Gamma(z)$ are holomorphic on $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$, and they agree on $\{\operatorname{Re}z\gt0\}$; by uniqueness they agree on $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$. ∎

The functional equation is used backwards: $\Gamma(z)=\Gamma(z+1)/z$ defines $\Gamma$ one strip further left, then $\Gamma(z+1)/z$ again, and so on. Division by $z,z+1,\dots$ produces the poles.

L11 · Slide 6

11.5 The poles of $\Gamma$

Recall (Def. 6.8.1 with $m=1$, and Def. 6.8.3): $f$ has a simple pole at $a$ with residue $c$ if $f(z)=\frac{g(z)}{z-a}$ near $a$, with $g$ holomorphic near $a$ and $g(a)=c\ne0$.

DerivedProposition 11.5.1 (poles of $\Gamma$). For each integer $n\ge0$, $\Gamma$ has a simple pole at $-n$, with residue $\dfrac{(-1)^n}{n!}$.
Proof. On $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(-n,1)\setminus\{-n\}$: every point has real part $\gt-n-1$, and the only non-positive integer in $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(-n,1)$ is $-n$. So this punctured disk lies in $\class{ntn-Wn}{W_{n+1}}$, where $\Gamma=\class{ntn-Gn}{\Gamma_{n+1}}$: \[ \Gamma(z)=\frac{\Gamma(z+n+1)}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+n)}=\frac{g(z)}{z+n},\qquad g(z):=\frac{\Gamma(z+n+1)}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+n-1)}. \] $g$ is holomorphic on all of $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(-n,1)$: there $\operatorname{Re}(z+n+1)\gt0$, and $z\ne0,-1,\dots,-n+1$ (these are at distance $\ge1$ from $-n$). And \[ g(-n)=\frac{\Gamma(1)}{(-n)(-n+1)\cdots(-1)}=\frac1{(-1)^nn!}=\frac{(-1)^n}{n!}\ne0. \] ∎
L11 · Slide 7

11.6 $1/\Gamma$ is entire

DerivedTheorem 11.6.1 (Weierstrass product for $1/\Gamma$). Let $\class{ntn-gam}{\gamma}:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\class{ntn-aN}{a_N}$, where $\class{ntn-aN}{a_N}:=\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n-\log N$ (Euler's constant, $\class{ntn-gam}{\gamma}\approx0.5772$). Then \[ \class{ntn-Rg}{R}(z):=z\,e^{\class{ntn-gam}{\gamma} z}\prod_{n\ge1}\Big(1+\frac zn\Big)e^{-z/n} \] is entire, with zeros exactly at $0,-1,-2,\dots$ (all simple), and $\Gamma(z)\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(z)=1$ for $z\in \class{ntn-Wset}{W}$. Hence $\Gamma$ has no zeros, and $1/\Gamma$ extends to the entire function $R$.

Idea. For $x\gt0$, the integrals $\int_0^Nt^{x-1}(1-\frac tN)^Ndt$ tend to $\Gamma(x)$, since $(1-\frac tN)^N\to e^{-t}$, and they can be computed exactly. Their reciprocals are the partial products of $R$.

Proof, part 1: $\class{ntn-gam}{\gamma}$ exists. Since $\log(N+1)=\sum_{n\le N}\log(1+\frac1n)$ (telescoping: $\log\frac{n+1}n=\log(n+1)-\log n$), \[ \class{ntn-aN}{a_N}-\log\Big(1+\frac1N\Big)=\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n-\log(N+1)=\sum_{n\le N}\Big(\frac1n-\log\Big(1+\frac1n\Big)\Big). \] From $x-\frac{x^2}2\le\log(1+x)\le x$ for $x\ge0$, the terms lie in $[0,\frac1{2n^2}]$: they are $O(n^{-2})$, so the series converges. As $\log(1+\frac1N)\to0$, $\class{ntn-aN}{a_N}$ converges. ∎
Part 2: $R$ is entire, with the stated zeros. On each disk $|z|\le\rho$, for $n\ge2\rho$ we have $|z/n|\le\frac12$, and $(1+\frac zn)e^{-z/n}=\class{ntn-Ep}{E_1}(-\frac zn)$ (Def. 10.10.1), so by Lemma 10.10.2 \[ \Big|\Big(1+\frac zn\Big)e^{-z/n}-1\Big|=\Big|1-\class{ntn-Ep}{E_1}\Big(-\frac zn\Big)\Big|\le4\frac{\rho^2}{n^2}, \] which is summable. By the product lemma (Lemma 10.4.1), $R$ is entire, and its zeros are those of its factors: $z=0$, and $z=-n$ from $1+\frac zn$; each simple. ∎
L11 · Slide 8

11.7 $1/\Gamma$ is entire: Gauss's limit

Part 3: $\Gamma R=1$ on $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$. $\Gamma R$ is holomorphic on the connected set $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$, so by uniqueness (Prop. 11.1.2(2)) it suffices to show $\Gamma(x)\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(x)=1$ for real $x\gt0$. Fix $x\gt0$ and let \[ \class{ntn-gN}{g_N}:=\int_0^Nt^{x-1}\Big(1-\frac tN\Big)^Ndt. \]
  1. $\class{ntn-gN}{g_N}\to\Gamma(x)$. Write $\class{ntn-gN}{g_N}=\int_0^\infty\mathbf 1_{[0,N]}(t)\,t^{x-1}(1-\frac tN)^Ndt$. Since $\log(1-u)\le-u$, $0\le(1-\frac tN)^N=e^{N\log(1-t/N)}\le e^{-t}$ on $[0,N]$; so the integrand is dominated by $t^{x-1}e^{-t}$, which is integrable. For fixed $t$, $N\log(1-\frac tN)\to-t$, so the integrand tends to $t^{x-1}e^{-t}$. By dominated convergenceA.22, $\class{ntn-gN}{g_N}\to\Gamma(x)$.
  2. $\class{ntn-gN}{g_N}$ is explicit. Substitute $t=Ns$: $\class{ntn-gN}{g_N}=N^x\int_0^1s^{x-1}(1-s)^Nds$. For $y\gt0$ and $k\ge1$, integration by parts (the boundary term $\big[\frac{s^y}y(1-s)^k\big]_0^1$ vanishes) gives \[ \int_0^1s^{y-1}(1-s)^kds=\frac ky\int_0^1s^y(1-s)^{k-1}ds. \] Applying this $N$ times, with $y=x,x+1,\dots,x+N-1$ and $k=N,N-1,\dots,1$: \[ \class{ntn-gN}{g_N}=N^x\cdot\frac{N!}{x(x+1)\cdots(x+N-1)}\int_0^1s^{x+N-1}ds=\frac{N^x\,N!}{x(x+1)\cdots(x+N)}. \]
  3. $1/\class{ntn-gN}{g_N}$ is a partial product of $R$. \[ N^{-x}=e^{-x\log N}=e^{x \class{ntn-aN}{a_N}}e^{-x\sum_{n\le N}1/n}=e^{x\class{ntn-aN}{a_N}}\prod_{n\le N}e^{-x/n}. \] And \[ \frac{x(x+1)\cdots(x+N)}{N!}=x\prod_{n\le N}\frac{n+x}n=x\prod_{n\le N}(1+\frac xn). \] So \[ \frac1{\class{ntn-gN}{g_N}}=x\,e^{x\class{ntn-aN}{a_N}}\prod_{n\le N}\Big(1+\frac xn\Big)e^{-x/n}\longrightarrow x\,e^{\class{ntn-gam}{\gamma} x}\prod_{n\ge1}\Big(1+\frac xn\Big)e^{-x/n}=\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(x). \]
  4. Hence $\Gamma(x)\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(x)=\lim \class{ntn-gN}{g_N}\cdot\lim\frac1{\class{ntn-gN}{g_N}}=1$. ∎
Finally, $\Gamma R=1$ on $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$ shows $\Gamma(z)\ne0$ there, and $1/\Gamma=R$ on $\class{ntn-Wset}{W}$; $R$ is the entire extension (with value $0$ at the poles of $\Gamma$).
DerivedCorollary 11.7.1 (Gauss's limit). For $x\gt0$, $\displaystyle\Gamma(x)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{N^x\,N!}{x(x+1)\cdots(x+N)}$.

This is step 2 combined with step 1. The same limit holds for complex $z\in \class{ntn-Wset}{W}$: the algebra of step 3 works verbatim for complex $z$ (with $N^{z}:=e^{z\log N}$), so the reciprocals of the right side are the partial products of $\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(z)$, which converge to $\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(z)=1/\Gamma(z)\ne0$.

L11 · Slide 9

11.8 The reflection formula

DerivedTheorem 11.8.1 (Euler's reflection formula). For $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Z$, \[ \Gamma(z)\,\Gamma(1-z)=\frac\pi{\sin\pi z}. \]
Proof. Let $z\notin\mathbb Z$. Then $z,-z,1-z\in \class{ntn-Wset}{W}$, so $\frac1{\Gamma(\pm z)}=\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(\pm z)$ by Theorem 11.6.1, and $\Gamma(1-z)=-z\,\Gamma(-z)$ by the functional equation. Multiplying the products for $\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(z)$ and $\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(-z)$ factor by factor (the product of two convergent products is the limit of the products of partial products): \[ \class{ntn-Rg}{R}(z)\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(-z)=z e^{\class{ntn-gam}{\gamma} z}(-z)e^{-\class{ntn-gam}{\gamma} z}\prod_{n\ge1}\Big(1+\frac zn\Big)e^{-z/n}\Big(1-\frac zn\Big)e^{z/n}=-z^2\prod_{n\ge1}\Big(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\Big). \] Hence, by Euler's product (Theorem 10.7.1), \[ \frac1{\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)}=\frac1{\Gamma(z)\cdot(-z)\Gamma(-z)}=\frac{\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(z)\class{ntn-Rg}{R}(-z)}{-z}=z\prod_{n\ge1}\Big(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\Big)=\frac{\sin\pi z}\pi. \] ∎

Both sides have simple poles exactly at the integers: on the left, the poles of $\Gamma(z)$ at $0,-1,\dots$ and of $\Gamma(1-z)$ at $1,2,\dots$.

L11 · Slide 10

11.9 Consequences of the reflection formula

DerivedCorollary 11.9.1 (the value at $\frac12$, and the Gaussian integral). $\Gamma(\frac12)=\sqrt\pi$, and $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2}du=\sqrt\pi$, $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\pi x^2}dx=1$.
Proof. With $z=\frac12$ the reflection formula gives $\Gamma(\frac12)^2=\frac\pi{\sin(\pi/2)}=\pi$. Also $\Gamma(\frac12)=\int_0^\infty t^{-1/2}e^{-t}dt\gt0$, so $\Gamma(\frac12)=\sqrt\pi$. Substituting $t=u^2$, $dt=2u\,du$: \[ \sqrt\pi=\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-u^2}}{u}\,2u\,du=2\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}du=\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2}du. \] Finally substitute $u=\sqrt\pi\,x$: $\int e^{-\pi x^2}dx=\frac1{\sqrt\pi}\int e^{-u^2}du=1$. ∎

These are the facts used in Prop. 8.3.1 and Prop. 6.18.1.

DerivedCorollary 11.9.2 (on the line $\operatorname{Re}z=\frac12$). For real $y$, \[ \Big|\Gamma\Big(\frac12+iy\Big)\Big|^2=\frac\pi{\cosh\pi y},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\Big|\Gamma\Big(\frac12+iy\Big)\Big|\sim\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-\pi|y|/2}\quad(|y|\to\infty). \]
Proof.
  1. Conjugate symmetry. For $\operatorname{Re}z\gt0$, $\Gamma(\bar z)=\overline{\Gamma(z)}$: conjugate the integrand, using $\overline{t^{z-1}}=\overline{e^{(z-1)\log t}}=e^{(\bar z-1)\log t}=t^{\bar z-1}$ for real $t\gt0$.
  2. For $z=\frac12+iy$: $1-z=\frac12-iy=\bar z$, and $\sin(\frac\pi2+i\pi y)=\cos(i\pi y)=\cosh\pi y$. So \[ \Big|\Gamma\Big(\frac12+iy\Big)\Big|^2=\Gamma(z)\,\overline{\Gamma(z)}=\Gamma(z)\Gamma(\bar z)=\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\frac\pi{\sin\pi z}=\frac\pi{\cosh\pi y}. \]
  3. As $|y|\to\infty$, $\cosh\pi y=\frac12e^{\pi|y|}(1+e^{-2\pi|y|})\sim\frac12e^{\pi|y|}$, so $|\Gamma|^2\sim2\pi e^{-\pi|y|}$. Take square roots. ∎

So $\Gamma$ decays exponentially along vertical lines, unlike its factorial growth along the real axis. This kind of estimate is what makes $\Gamma$ useful in the theory of the Riemann zeta function.

L11 · Slide 11

11.10 Rouché's theorem

The final slide returns to the argument principle (Lecture 7) and draws its most useful consequence: zeros are stable under small perturbations.

DerivedTheorem 11.10.1 (Rouché). Let $f$, $g$ be holomorphic on an open set containing $\overline{\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(a,r)}$, and $C:=\partial \class{ntn-Dar}{D}(a,r)$. If $|f-g|\lt|f|$ on $C$, then $f$ and $g$ have equally many zeros in $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(a,r)$, counted with multiplicity.

Picture: $g$ is $f$ plus a perturbation that is smaller than $f$ on the circle. A dog ($g$) on a leash shorter than its owner's ($f$) distance from a tree ($0$) circles the tree as often as its owner does (winding numbersE.17).

Proof.
  1. Interpolate. For $t\in[0,1]$ let $\class{ntn-ft}{f_t}:=f+t(g-f)$, so $f_0=f$ and $f_1=g$. On $C$, $|\class{ntn-ft}{f_t}|\ge|f|-t|g-f|\ge|f|-|g-f|\gt0$. So no $\class{ntn-ft}{f_t}$ vanishes on $C$.
  2. Count. By the argument principle (Theorem 7.3.1, moved to the centre $a$; $\class{ntn-ft}{f_t}$ is holomorphic, so $P=0$), \[ \class{ntn-Nt}{N}(t):=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{\class{ntn-ft}{f_t}'(z)}{\class{ntn-ft}{f_t}(z)}\,dz \] is the number of zeros of $\class{ntn-ft}{f_t}$ in $\class{ntn-Dar}{D}(a,r)$: an integer.
  3. $N$ is continuous. The integrand $h(t,z):=\frac{f'(z)+t(g'(z)-f'(z))}{f(z)+t(g(z)-f(z))}$ is continuous on the compactC.5 set $[0,1]\times C$, as the denominator does not vanish there. So it is uniformly continuousA.16, and by the ML estimate \[ |\class{ntn-Nt}{N}(t)-\class{ntn-Nt}{N}(s)|\le\frac{2\pi r}{2\pi}\max_{z\in C}|h(t,z)-h(s,z)|=r\max_{z\in C}|h(t,z)-h(s,z)|\longrightarrow0\quad(s\to t). \]
  4. Integer-valued and continuous means constant. If $\class{ntn-Nt}{N}(0)\ne \class{ntn-Nt}{N}(1)$, the intermediate value theoremA.24 would give a $t$ with $\class{ntn-Nt}{N}(t)$ equal to a non-integer between them. So $\class{ntn-Nt}{N}(0)=\class{ntn-Nt}{N}(1)$. ∎
DefinedExample 11.10.2 (a typical use). How many zeros does $g(z)=z^5+3z+1$ have in $|z|\lt2$? Take $f(z)=z^5$. On $|z|=2$: $|g-f|=|3z+1|\le7\lt32=|f|$. So $g$, like $f$, has $5$ zeros in $|z|\lt2$, without solving anything. (Not from the slides; an illustration.)

Rouché's theorem gives a second proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra: for a polynomial of degree $d$ with leading term $f=cz^d$, the rest is smaller than $|f|$ on a large circle, so the polynomial has $d$ zeros inside.

Exercises

From the homework and the practice midterms. Each has a hint and a full solution; open them only after trying.

Exercise 11.10.3 (one solution in the disk; Homework 2, Problem 1(a); Practice midterm 1, Problem 3). Let $\lambda\gt1$. Show that $z\,e^{\lambda-z}=1$ has exactly one solution in $D(0,1)$, and that this solution is real and lies in $(0,1)$.
Hint Compare $z\,e^{\lambda-z}-1$ with $z\,e^{\lambda-z}$ on $|z|=1$ using Theorem 11.10.1. For "real", use the intermediate value theorem on $[0,1]$.
Solution
  1. Rouché. Let $f(z):=z\,e^{\lambda-z}$ and $g:=f-1$, both entire. On $|z|=1$, $|f(z)|=|z|\,|e^{\lambda-z}|=e^{\lambda-\operatorname{Re}z}\ge e^{\lambda-1}\gt1=|f-g|$, as $\operatorname{Re}z\le1$ and $\lambda\gt1$. By Theorem 11.10.1, $g$ has as many zeros in $D(0,1)$ as $f$, counted with multiplicity. $f$ has exactly one: $e^{\lambda-z}\ne0$, so its only zero is at $0$, of order $1$ (Def. 7.1.1).
  2. It is real. $\phi(x):=x\,e^{\lambda-x}-1$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ with $\phi(0)=-1\lt0$ and $\phi(1)=e^{\lambda-1}-1\gt0$, so it vanishes at some $x_0\in(0,1)$ by the intermediate value theorem (A.24). That is a solution in $D(0,1)$, and by step 1 there is only one, so it is $x_0$.
Exercise 11.10.4 (Hurwitz's theorem; Homework 2, Problem 1(b)). Let $U$ be a connected open set, and $f_N\to f$ uniformly on every closed disk in $U$, each $f_N$ holomorphic on $U$ with no zeros in $U$. Show that either $f\equiv0$ or $f$ has no zeros in $U$.
Hint $f$ is holomorphic by Theorem 10.3.1. Suppose $f\not\equiv0$ and fix $a\in U$. Choose $r\gt0$ with $\overline{D(a,r)}\subset U$ and $f\ne0$ on $|z-a|=r$ (why is this possible?), and count the zeros of $f$ in $D(a,r)$ with Rouché.
Solution
  1. $f$ is holomorphic on $U$ (Theorem 10.3.1). Suppose $f\not\equiv0$ and fix $a\in U$.
  2. Choosing $r$. Take $\overline{D(a,r_0)}\subset U$. As $U$ is connected and $f\not\equiv0$, only finitely many zeros of $f$ lie in the compact disk $\overline{D(a,r_0)}$: infinitely many would have a limit point in that disk (C.5), hence in $U$, and the identity theorem (Theorem 10.1.1 with $g=0$) would give $f\equiv0$. Pick $r\in(0,r_0)$ different from all their distances to $a$: then $f\ne0$ on the circle $|z-a|=r$, and $\mu:=\min_{|z-a|=r}|f|\gt0$.
  3. Rouché. By uniform convergence on $\overline{D(a,r)}$, for large $N$, $|f_N-f|\lt\mu\le|f|$ on the circle (A.17). Rouché, Theorem 11.10.1, applied to $f$ and $f_N$: $f$ and $f_N$ have equally many zeros in $D(a,r)$, namely none. In particular $f(a)\ne0$. As $a$ was arbitrary, $f$ has no zeros.
Exercise 11.10.5 (limits of injective maps; Homework 2, Problem 1(c)). Under the hypotheses of the previous exercise, but with each $f_N$ injective instead of zero-free, show that $f$ is injective or constant.
Hint Fix $b\in U$ and apply the previous exercise to $f_N(z)-f_N(b)$ on $U\setminus\{b\}$. Is $U\setminus\{b\}$ connected?
Solution Suppose $f$ is not constant, and fix $b\in U$. On $U':=U\setminus\{b\}$, the functions $g_N(z):=f_N(z)-f_N(b)$ have no zeros ($f_N$ is injective), and converge uniformly on closed disks in $U'$ to $g(z):=f(z)-f(b)$ (a closed disk in $U'$ is one in $U$, and $f_N(b)\to f(b)$). $U'$ is open, and connected: a path in $U$ between two points of $U'$ can be rerouted around the single point $b$ (C.4). By Hurwitz (Exercise 11.10.4), $g\equiv0$ on $U'$ or $g$ has no zeros on $U'$. The first would make $f\equiv f(b)$ on $U'$, hence on $U$ by continuity: constant, excluded. So $f(z)\ne f(b)$ for every $z\ne b$. As $b$ is arbitrary, $f$ is injective.
Exercise 11.10.6 (zeros of partial sums of the exponential; Homework 2, Problem 1(d)–(e)). Let $s_N(z):=\sum_{n=0}^N\frac{z^n}{n!}$. (d) Show that for every $R\gt0$ there is $N_0$ such that $s_N$ has no zeros in $\overline{D(0,R)}$ for $N\ge N_0$. (e) (Optional) Plot the zeros of $s_N(Nz)$ for $N=20,50,100$; they approach the Szegő curve $|z\,e^{1-z}|=1$, $|z|\le1$. Root-finding needs high precision (about 30 digits for $N=100$, e.g. mpmath).
Hint (d) $s_N\to e^z$ uniformly on compact sets, and $e^z$ has no zeros. You don't need Rouché: compare $|s_N|$ with $|e^z|$ directly. (e) Use mpmath.polyroots with mp.dps = 30.
Solution (d) The power series of $e^z$ converges uniformly on $\overline{D(0,R)}$ (A.19), so $\max_{|z|\le R}|s_N-e^z|\to0$. Let $\mu:=\min_{|z|\le R}|e^z|=e^{-R}\gt0$, and take $N_0$ with $|s_N-e^z|\lt\mu$ on the disk for $N\ge N_0$. Then $|s_N(z)|\ge|e^z|-|s_N(z)-e^z|\gt0$ there. (This is Hurwitz's theorem, Exercise 11.10.4, in a quantitative form; the same comparison is the hypothesis of Rouché, Theorem 11.10.1, with $e^z$ having no zeros.)
(e) A script: 
from mpmath import mp, polyroots, factorial, exp
mp.dps = 30
N = 50
coeffs = [N**n/factorial(n) for n in range(N, -1, -1)]   # s_N(Nz), highest power first
roots = polyroots(coeffs, maxsteps=200, extraprec=200)
Plot the roots with the curve $|z|e^{1-\operatorname{Re}z}=1$ in $|z|\le1$. Why that curve: by Stirling, $s_N(Nz)\approx e^{Nz}$ inside it and $\approx\frac{(Nz)^N}{N!}\approx\frac{(ze)^N}{\sqrt{2\pi N}}$ outside; zeros sit where the two sizes balance, $|e^{z}|=|ze|$, i.e. $|z\,e^{1-z}|=1$.
Exercise 11.10.7 (counting solutions with Rouché; Practice midterm 2, Problem 3). Let $n\ge1$ and $|a|\gt e$. Show that $e^z=az^n$ has exactly $n$ solutions in $D(0,1)$, counted with multiplicity.
Hint Which of $az^n$ and $e^z$ is bigger on $|z|=1$?
Solution On $|z|=1$: $|az^n|=|a|\gt e\ge e^{\operatorname{Re}z}=|e^z|$. Take $f=az^n$ and $g=az^n-e^z$ in Theorem 11.10.1: $|f-g|=|e^z|\lt|f|$, so $g$ has as many zeros in $D(0,1)$ as $az^n$, namely $n$ (a zero of order $n$ at $0$, Def. 7.1.1). The zeros of $g$ are exactly the solutions of $e^z=az^n$.
Exercise 11.10.8 (one real zero; Practice midterm 3, Problem 3). Show that $p(z)=z^4+6z+3$ has exactly one zero in $D(0,1)$, counted with multiplicity, and that this zero is real.
Hint Compare $p$ with $6z$ on $|z|=1$. For "real": coefficients are real, so non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
Solution
  1. Rouché. On $|z|=1$, $|p-6z|=|z^4+3|\le4\lt6=|6z|$. By Theorem 11.10.1 (with $f=6z$, $g=p$), $p$ has as many zeros in $D(0,1)$ as $6z$: exactly one.
  2. Real. $p(-1)=1-6+3=-2\lt0$ and $p(0)=3\gt0$, so $p$ has a real zero in $(-1,0)\subset D(0,1)$ (intermediate value theorem, A.24). It is the only one. (Alternatively: $p$ has real coefficients, so $\overline{p(z)}=p(\bar z)$; a non-real zero $z_0$ in the disk would bring $\bar z_0\ne z_0$, giving two.)
Part V

Conformal maps

A holomorphic bijection between two regions carries harmonic functions on one to harmonic functions on the other, so a Dirichlet problem on a complicated region can be moved to the disk. Lecture 12 develops the tools: harmonic conjugates, the open mapping and inverse theorems, angle preservation, examples, the automorphisms of the disk and the Schwarz lemma. Lecture 13 runs the logic the other way: it builds the conformal map onto the disk out of the solution of a Dirichlet problem, so Part I's existence theorem becomes the Riemann mapping theorem for regions made of squares.

Part V · Conformal maps

Lecture 12 · Conformal maps

Goal
Transport harmonic functions between regions by holomorphic bijections; build the local theory of holomorphic maps (local behaviour, open mapping, inverse theorem); classify the automorphisms of the disk with the Schwarz lemma.
Main results
Lemma 12.2.1 (harmonic conjugates) · Theorem 12.3.1 (harmonic under holomorphic maps) · Prop. 12.4.1 (Cayley map) · Theorem 12.6.1 (local behaviour) · Theorem 12.7.1 (open mapping) · Theorem 12.9.1 (inverse) · Theorem 12.14.1 (Schwarz lemma) · Theorem 12.15.1 (automorphisms of the disk) · Theorem 12.16.1 (Liouville)
Uses
Rouché's theorem (Theorem 11.10.1); the identity theorem (Theorem 10.1.1); removable singularities and maximum modulus (Lemma 9.1.1, Lemma 9.6.1); Cauchy's estimate (Cor. 6.5.2).
Used later
Lecture 13 · Problem 4 of the practice midterms (conformal maps, the Schwarz lemma).
