Appendix A

Calculus and analysis

Background the slides use without stating. Short results are proved here from standard first-year facts. Deeper standard theorems are cited, with a link to a full treatment.

A.1

Real differentiability and little-$o$

DefinedCited

Cited inL1 · Slides 6–10 · Thm. 1.5.2L1 · Slides 11–14 · Prop. 1.6.2L1 · Slide 16 · Prop. 1.8.1L2 · Slides 2–3 · Thm. 2.1.2Appendix A.20

$o(|h|)$ ("little-$o$ of $|h|$") stands for any quantity $\epsilon(h)$ with $\epsilon(h)/|h|\to0$ as $h\to0$: an error that is small even compared with $|h|$.

A function $u:\R^2\to\R$ is differentiable at $(x_0,y_0)$ if \[ u(x_0+h_1,\,y_0+h_2)=u(x_0,y_0)+h_1u_x+h_2u_y+o(|h|),\qquad|h|=\sqrt{h_1^2+h_2^2}, \] that is, $u$ is well approximated near the point by a linear function (its tangent plane). A map $f=(u,v)$ is differentiable if both components are. Having both partial derivatives is not enough: $u=\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ (with $u(0,0)=0$) has $u_x=u_y=0$ at the origin but is not even continuous there.

Theorem (cited). If the partial derivatives exist near a point and are continuous at it (in particular if $u$ is $C^1$), then $u$ is differentiable there.

Further reading: Differentiability in several variables · Little-o notation

A.2

Equality of mixed partials

Cited

Cited inL1 · Slides 17–18 · Prop. 1.9.1L2 · Slides 4–5 · Rem. 2.2.4L2 · Slides 16–17 · Prop. 2.8.1L13 · Slide 8 · Lemma 13.7.2

Theorem (Schwarz / Clairaut). If $h$ is $C^2$ on an open set, then $h_{xy}=h_{yx}$ there: the order of differentiation does not matter.

Without continuity of the second derivatives this can fail; the standard counterexample is $h=xy\frac{x^2-y^2}{x^2+y^2}$ at the origin. Prop. 2.8.1 needs the theorem to cancel $v_{yx}$ against $v_{xy}$.

Further reading: Symmetry of second derivatives

A.3

Mean value theorem and a two-variable bound

CitedProved here

Cited inL1 · Slide 20 · Prop. 1.11.2L3 · Slide 20 · Lemma 3.18.5L4 · Slide 3 · Thm. 4.2.2

Theorem (cited). If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, there is $\xi\in(a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a)=f'(\xi)(b-a)$.
Corollary (proved). Let $F$ be continuously differentiable on a convex set $K\subset\R^2$ with $|\nabla F|\le M$ on $K$. Then $|F(P)-F(Q)|\le M\,|P-Q|$ for all $P,Q\in K$.
Proof. The segment from $Q$ to $P$ lies in $K$ by convexity. Put $f(t):=F(Q+t(P-Q))$ for $t\in[0,1]$. By the chain rule $f'(t)=\nabla F(Q+t(P-Q))\cdot(P-Q)$. The mean value theorem gives some $\tau$ with \[ |F(P)-F(Q)|=|f(1)-f(0)|=|f'(\tau)|\le|\nabla F|\,|P-Q|\le M|P-Q|, \] using the vector inequalityA.12 $|a\cdot b|\le|a||b|$. ∎

This is the first-order case of Taylor's theorem that the slide invokes. Lemma 3.18.5 uses it with $K$ a grid square and $F=\partial_x\eta$ or $\partial_y\eta$.

Further reading: Mean value theorem · Taylor's theorem

A.4

Differentiation under the integral sign

Cited

Cited inL4 · Slide 3 · Thm. 4.2.2L4 · Slide 9 · Prop. 4.8.2L8 · Slide 7L8 · Slide 8 · Thm. 8.7.1L11 · Slide 4 · Prop. 11.3.1Appendix A.7L12 · Slide 3 · Lemma 12.2.1

Theorem (two versions).
  1. Continuous version. If $f(t,\theta)$ and $\partial_tf(t,\theta)$ are continuous on a rectangle $[a,b]\times[0,2\pi]$, then $F(t)=\int_0^{2\pi}f(t,\theta)\,d\theta$ is differentiable and $F'(t)=\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_tf(t,\theta)\,d\theta$.
  2. Integrable version. Let $u$ be integrable over a bounded set $B$, and let $k(z,\zeta)$ be zero for $\zeta\notin B$, with every $z$-derivative continuous and bounded. Then $z\mapsto\iint u(\zeta)\,k(z,\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)$ is smooth, and each derivative may be taken inside the integral, on $k$.
  3. Unbounded intervals, complex parameter. Let $h(z,\xi)$ be continuous for $z$ in an open set $U\subset\mathbb C$ and $\xi$ in an interval $J$ (possibly infinite), holomorphic in $z$ for each $\xi$, with $\partial_zh$ continuous, and suppose $|h|\le H(\xi)$ and $|\partial_zh|\le H(\xi)$ on $U\times J$ for an integrable $H$. Then $F(z)=\int_Jh(z,\xi)\,d\xi$ is holomorphic on $U$, with $F'=\int_J\partial_zh\,d\xi$. (The partial derivatives in $x$ and $y$ pass under the integral by dominated convergence, A.22, and satisfy Cauchy–Riemann because $h$ does.)

Version 1 is used in Theorem 4.2.2; version 2, with $k(z,\zeta)=\chi_\delta(z-\zeta)$, in Prop. 4.8.2 and Theorem 4.10.1; version 3 in Lectures 8 and 11 (Theorem 8.5.2, Theorem 8.7.1, Prop. 11.3.1). Version 2 is a consequence of the dominated convergence theorem, applied to difference quotients.

Further reading: Leibniz integral rule · Dominated convergence theorem

A.5

Divergence, curl, flux and circulation

Defined

Cited inL1 · Slides 11–14 · Def. 1.6.1L1 · Slide 21L2 · Slides 2–3 · Thm. 2.1.2L2 · Slides 12–13 · Def. 2.6.1Appendix E.4

Lecture 1 defines divergence and curl (Def. 1.6.1); this entry adds their meaning, flux, circulation and line integrals.

For a vector field $F=(F_1,F_2)$ in the plane:

  • $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}F:=\partial_xF_1+\partial_yF_2$ (also written $\nabla\cdot F$): the rate at which $F$ spreads out from a point, the "source density".
  • $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}F:=\partial_xF_2-\partial_yF_1$: the rate at which $F$ swirls around a point. (In three dimensions the curl is a vector; in the plane only its component perpendicular to the plane survives, a scalar.)

Along an oriented curve $\gamma$ with unit tangent $t$ and unit normal $n$ (pointing to the right of the direction of travel, so outward for a positively oriented boundary):

  • flux $\oint_\gamma F\cdot n\,ds$ measures how much of $F$ crosses $\gamma$;
  • circulation $\oint_\gamma F\cdot t\,ds$ measures how much of $F$ runs along $\gamma$.

In coordinates, $t\,ds=(dx,dy)$ and $n\,ds=(dy,-dx)$, so flux $=\oint F_1\,dy-F_2\,dx$ and circulation $=\oint F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy$. A line integral $\oint P\,dx+Q\,dy$ is computed from a parametrization $s\mapsto(x(s),y(s))$ as $\int(P\,x'+Q\,y')\,ds$. The divergence theorem and Green's theorem (A.6) turn flux and circulation into area integrals of $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{div}}F$ and $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}F$.

Further reading: Divergence · Curl · Line integral · Flux

A.6

The divergence theorem

Cited

Cited inL1 · Slides 11–14 · Prop. 1.6.3L1 · Slide 29L2 · Slides 7–9 · Def. 2.4.2L2 · Slides 7–9 · Thm. 2.4.3L2 · Slides 10–11 · Thm. 2.5.1L3 · Slide 4 · Prop. 3.3.3L4 · Slide 3 · Thm. 4.2.2L4 · Slide 8 · Prop. 4.7.1L5 · Slide 13 · Rem. 5.12.3L6 · Slide 2 · Thm. 6.1.2L8 · Slide 2 · Prop. 8.1.1Appendix A.5Appendix C.3L3 · Slide 21 · Exercise 3.19.3

Theorem. Let $D\subset\R^2$ be a bounded region whose boundary is a piecewise smooth curve, with outward unit normal $n$. If $F=(F_1,F_2)$ is continuously differentiable on $\overline D$, then \[ \iint_D \nabla\cdot F\,dA=\oint_{\partial D}F\cdot n\,ds,\qquad \nabla\cdot F=\partial_xF_1+\partial_yF_2. \]
Green's theorem (circulation form, cited). Under the same hypotheses, with $t$ the unit tangent for the positive orientation (region on the left), \[ \iint_D\operatorname{curl}F\,dA=\oint_{\partial D}F\cdot t\,ds,\qquad\operatorname{curl}F=\partial_xF_2-\partial_yF_1. \] The divergence form is this one applied to the field turned by $90°$, since $F\cdot n=(F_2,-F_1)\cdot t$ when $n$ is $t$ turned clockwise.
Regions with holes. Both theorems hold for a region bounded by several curves, such as a disk with a smaller disk removed, provided each boundary curve is traversed with the region on its left: the outer curve anticlockwise, each inner curve clockwise. On an inner circle the outward normal of the region points towards the centre of the hole. Theorem 2.4.3 uses this.

In two dimensions this is a restatement of Green's theorem. Applied to $F=w\nabla u$ it gives Green's first identity, $\iint w\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=\oint w\,\partial_nu-\iint\nabla w\cdot\nabla u$, which is how Prop. 3.3.3 uses it. That identity is the two-dimensional form of integration by parts. The grid regions of this lecture have boundaries made of finitely many segments, so they meet the hypothesis.

Further reading: Divergence theorem · Green's theorem · Green's identities

A.7

The Poincaré lemma on a disk

Proved here

Cited inL1 · Slide 15 · Fact 1.7.1L12 · Slide 3 · Lemma 12.2.1

Theorem. Let $D$ be an open disk and $W=(W_1,W_2)$ a $C^1$ field on $D$ with $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}W=\partial_xW_2-\partial_yW_1=0$. Then $W=\nabla\varphi$ for some $\varphi$, unique up to an additive constant.
Proof. Shift so the centre of $D$ is the origin. For $p=(x,y)\in D$, the segment from $0$ to $p$ lies in $D$; integrate $W$ along it: \[ \varphi(x,y):=\int_0^1W(tx,ty)\cdot(x,y)\,dt=\int_0^1\big(x\,W_1(tx,ty)+y\,W_2(tx,ty)\big)\,dt. \] Differentiate under the integral sign (A.4) in $x$, using the chain rule ($\partial_x[W_j(tx,ty)]=t\,(\partial_xW_j)(tx,ty)$): \[ \varphi_x=\int_0^1\Big(W_1+t\,x\,\partial_xW_1+t\,y\,\partial_xW_2\Big)(tx,ty)\,dt. \] Now use $\class{ntn-divc}{\operatorname{curl}}W=0$, i.e. $\partial_xW_2=\partial_yW_1$: \[ \varphi_x=\int_0^1\Big(W_1+t\,(x\,\partial_xW_1+y\,\partial_yW_1)\Big)(tx,ty)\,dt=\int_0^1\frac{d}{dt}\Big[t\,W_1(tx,ty)\Big]\,dt=W_1(x,y), \] since $\frac{d}{dt}[tW_1(tx,ty)]=W_1+t(x\partial_xW_1+y\partial_yW_1)$ by the product and chain rules, and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $1\cdot W_1(x,y)-0$. The same computation gives $\varphi_y=W_2$.
Uniqueness: if $\nabla\varphi_1=\nabla\varphi_2$, the difference has zero gradient on the connected set $D$, so it is constant (the argument of Theorem 2.9.1, step 4). ∎

The proof needs every segment from the centre to stay in the domain ("star-shaped"). On $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ this fails, and so does the lemma (Prop. 1.14.3).

Further reading: Poincaré lemma · Conservative vector field

A.8

Polar coordinates and change of variables

CitedProved here

Cited inL4 · Slide 3 · Def. 4.2.1L4 · Slide 6 · Lemma 4.5.3L4 · Slide 6 · Lemma 4.5.5L8 · Slide 4 · Prop. 8.3.1

Change of variables (cited). If $\Phi$ maps a region one-to-one and smoothly onto another, then $\iint f(\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)=\iint f(\Phi(w))\,|\det D\Phi(w)|\,dA(w)$.
Consequences (proved).
  • Polar coordinates. $\Phi(t,\theta)=(x_0+t\cos\theta,\ y_0+t\sin\theta)$ has $\det D\Phi=\cos\theta\cdot t\cos\theta-(-t\sin\theta)\sin\theta=t$. So $dA=t\,dt\,d\theta$.
  • Arc length on a circle. $\theta\mapsto z_0+te^{i\theta}$ has velocity $t(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$, of length $t$. So $ds=t\,d\theta$, and the circle has length $2\pi t$.
  • Scaling. $\zeta=\delta w$ has $\det D\Phi=\delta^2$, so $dA(\zeta)=\delta^2\,dA(w)$.
  • Shifts and reflections $\zeta=w+c$, $\zeta=c-w$ have $|\det D\Phi|=1$: they preserve area.

Further reading: Polar coordinates · Change of variables

A.9

Fundamental theorem of calculus, piecewise version

CitedProved here

Cited inL1 · Slide 21 · Prop. 1.12.1L3 · Slides 18–19 · Thm. 3.17.2L3 · Slide 20 · Prop. 3.18.3L4 · Slide 7 · Prop. 4.6.3L6 · Slide 7 · Thm. 6.6.1Appendix A.10L12 · Slide 3 · Lemma 12.2.1L3 · Slides 18–19 · Exercise 3.17.4

Theorem (cited). If $f$ is continuously differentiable on $[a,b]$, then $f(b)-f(a)=\int_a^bf'(s)\,ds$.
Corollary (proved). If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and continuously differentiable on each piece $[t_{k-1},t_k]$ of a partition $a=t_0\lt t_1\lt\dots\lt t_m=b$, then $f(b)-f(a)=\int_a^bf'(s)\,ds$, where $f'$ may be left undefined at the finitely many $t_k$.
Proof. Apply the theorem on each piece and add: \[ \sum_{k=1}^m\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}f'=\sum_{k=1}^m\big(f(t_k)-f(t_{k-1})\big)=f(t_m)-f(t_0). \] The sum telescopes because $f$ is continuous, so each $f(t_k)$ is the same number from both sides. The values of $f'$ at finitely many points do not affect the integral. ∎

Poincaré's inequality applies this to $s\mapsto v(s,y)$; Prop. 3.18.3 applies it to $x\mapsto \class{ntn-Un}{U_n}\psi$. Both are continuous, and smooth between grid lines.

Further reading: Fundamental theorem of calculus

A.10

Lipschitz functions

DefinedCited

Cited inL5 · Slide 8 · Prop. 5.7.2

A function $F$ is Lipschitz with constant $C$ if $|F(a)-F(b)|\le C|a-b|$ for all $a,b$; "1-Lipschitz" means $C=1$. Examples: $t\mapsto t^+$ and $t\mapsto|t|$ (1-Lipschitz), any $C^1$ function on a closed interval ($C=\max|F'|$), the distance function (C.6). Composing with a Lipschitz function keeps Lipschitz: if $f$ is $C$-Lipschitz, so is $f^+$. Products of bounded Lipschitz functions are Lipschitz.

Facts (cited).
  1. Rademacher's theorem. A Lipschitz function on an open set of $\R^2$ (or an interval) is differentiable almost everywhere, with gradient bounded by $C$.
  2. Fundamental theorem of calculus. A Lipschitz function $F$ on $[a,b]$ satisfies $F(b)-F(a)=\int_a^bF'(x)\,dx$, the derivative existing almost everywhere. (Lipschitz functions are absolutely continuous.)

Fact 2 is what Lecture 5 needs. $f^+$ can have infinitely many corners on a line (if $f$ crosses zero infinitely often), so the piecewise version A.9 does not apply, but the Lipschitz version does. Lipschitz is the right replacement for "continuous and piecewise smooth": the step function of earlier discussions, which jumps, is not Lipschitz.

Further reading: Lipschitz continuity · Rademacher's theorem · Absolute continuity

A.11

Sets of zero area and vanishing integrals

DefinedProved hereCited

Cited inL2 · Slides 18–20 · Thm. 2.9.1L3 · Slide 5 · Prop. 3.4.5L3 · Slide 10 · Thm. 3.9.3L3 · Slide 11 · Lemma 3.10.1L4 · Slide 4 · Thm. 4.3.1L4 · Slide 7 · Thm. 4.6.2L5 · Slide 10 · Prop. 5.9.1Appendix D.4

Definition. A set $Z\subset\R^2$ has zero area if for every $\delta\gt0$ it can be covered by finitely many rectangles whose total area is less than $\delta$.
(a) A line segment has zero area (proved). A horizontal or vertical segment of length $\ell$ fits in an $\ell\times\delta/\ell$ rectangle, of area $\delta$; take a slightly smaller height. A finite union of zero-area sets has zero area, since the covers can be combined. So the grid lines inside a bounded region, and $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ itself, have zero area.
(b) Changing a bounded integrand on a zero-area set does not change the integral (cited). This is a standard property of the Riemann (and Lebesgue) integral. It is why gradients defined only off grid lines can be integrated.
(c) Zero integral forces zero (proved). If $f$ is continuous and nonnegative on an open set $Q$ and $\iint_Qf\,dA=0$, then $f\equiv0$ on $Q$. The same holds for a continuous nonnegative function on an interval, such as $\theta\mapsto\varphi(\theta)$ on $[0,2\pi]$, with an interval around the point in place of a disc.
Proof of (c). Suppose $f(P)=2\mu\gt0$ at some $P\in Q$. By continuity there is $r\gt0$ such that the disc $D_r(P)$ lies in $Q$ and $f\gt\mu$ on it. Since $f\ge0$ everywhere, $\iint_Qf\ge\iint_{D_r(P)}f\ge\pi r^2\mu\gt0$, a contradiction. ∎
(d) "Almost everywhere" (defined). A statement holds almost everywhere (a.e.) if the set where it fails has zero area, in the Lebesgue sense: it can be covered by countably many rectangles of arbitrarily small total area. Two functions equal a.e. are the same element of $L^2$ (D.2). A countable union of such sets again has zero area, which is how Theorem 4.9.5 passes from compact pieces to all of $\Omega$. A function with $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{f}_{L^2}}=0$ is zero a.e. (cited).

Further reading: Almost everywhere · Null set · Jordan measure

A.12

Cauchy–Schwarz inequality

Proved here

Cited inL3 · Slides 18–19 · Thm. 3.17.2L3 · Slide 20 · Prop. 3.18.3L3 · Slide 20 · Prop. 3.18.4L3 · Slide 20 · Thm. 3.18.6L4 · Slide 8 · Prop. 4.7.1L5 · Slide 9 · Prop. 5.8.2Appendix A.3L3 · Slides 18–19 · Exercise 3.17.4

Theorem. (i) For vectors, $|a\cdot b|\le|a|\,|b|$. (ii) For square-integrable scalar or vector-valued $F,G$ on a region $D$, \[ \Big|\iint_DF\cdot G\,dA\Big|\le\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{F}_{L^2}}\,\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{G}_{L^2}}. \] The one-variable version $\big(\int fh\big)^2\le\int f^2\int h^2$ is proved the same way.
Proof. Write $\langle F,G\rangle$ for either $a\cdot b$ or $\iint F\cdot G$; the argument uses only that it is symmetric, bilinear and $\langle F,F\rangle\ge0$. For every real $\lambda$, \[ 0\le\langle F+\lambda G,F+\lambda G\rangle=\langle F,F\rangle+2\lambda\langle F,G\rangle+\lambda^2\langle G,G\rangle. \] If $\langle G,G\rangle\gt0$, this quadratic in $\lambda$ never goes negative, so its discriminant is $\le0$: $4\langle F,G\rangle^2-4\langle F,F\rangle\langle G,G\rangle\le0$. Take square roots. If $\langle G,G\rangle=0$, the expression is linear in $\lambda$ and bounded below, which forces $\langle F,G\rangle=0$, and the inequality holds trivially. ∎

Further reading: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality

A.13

Fubini's theorem

Cited

Cited inL4 · Slide 6 · Lemma 4.5.5L4 · Slide 10 · Lemma 4.9.2Appendix A.21L3 · Slides 18–19 · Exercise 3.17.4

Theorem. If $\iint\!\iint|F(\xi,\zeta)|\,dA(\xi)\,dA(\zeta)\lt\infty$, then the double integral of $F$ can be computed as an iterated integral in either order, with the same result. The same holds for a continuous integrand on a bounded region split into $t$ and $\theta$.

Used to split disk integrals into circles (Lemma 4.5.5) and to swap the order of two convolutions (Lemma 4.9.2).

Further reading: Fubini's theorem

A.14

Supremum and infimum

Defined

Cited inL4 · Slide 4 · Thm. 4.3.1L5 · Slide 12 · Thm. 5.11.3

The supremum $\sup_\Omega h$ is the least upper bound of the values of $h$: $h\le\sup h$ everywhere, and no smaller number has that property. It exists (possibly $+\infty$) by the completeness of the real numbers (A.15). Unlike a maximum, it need not be attained: $\sup_{(0,1)}x=1$, but no point of $(0,1)$ has $x=1$. The infimum is the greatest lower bound. Theorem 4.3.1 assumes the supremum is attained at an interior point.

The limit superior $\limsup_{z\to p}F(z)$ is the largest value that $F$ keeps coming close to as $z$ approaches $p$: precisely, $\lim_{r\to0}\sup\{F(z):0\lt|z-p|\lt r\}$. It always exists (possibly infinite), even when $\lim F$ does not. For a nonnegative $F$, $\limsup_{z\to p}F(z)=0$ is the same as $\lim_{z\to p}F(z)=0$; Theorem 5.11.3 uses this with $F=|u-g(p)|$.

Further reading: Infimum and supremum

A.15

Monotone convergence for sequences

Proved here

Cited inL3 · Slide 15 · Prop. 3.14.4L6 · Slide 13 · Prop. 6.12.2Appendix A.14

Theorem. A non-increasing sequence of reals that is bounded below converges to its infimum.
Proof. The set $\{m_n\}$ is nonempty and bounded below, so it has a greatest lower bound $m$. This is the completeness axiom of the real numbers (cited). Given $\delta\gt0$, $m+\delta$ is not a lower bound, so $m_N\lt m+\delta$ for some $N$. For $n\ge N$, $m\le m_n\le m_N\lt m+\delta$. So $|m_n-m|\lt\delta$ for all $n\ge N$. ∎

Further reading: Monotone convergence theorem · Least-upper-bound property

A.16

Uniform continuity

DefinedCited

Cited inL5 · Slide 3 · Lemma 5.2.2L11 · Slide 11 · Thm. 11.10.1L13 · Slide 5

$g$ is uniformly continuous on a set $T$ if for every tolerance $\epsilon\gt0$ there is one $\delta\gt0$ that works everywhere: $|g(q)-g(q')|\lt\epsilon$ whenever $q,q'\in T$ and $|q-q'|\le\delta$. Plain continuity allows $\delta$ to depend on the point.

Theorem (Heine–Cantor, cited). A continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

Without compactness this fails: $g(x)=1/x$ is continuous on $(0,1]$ but needs ever smaller $\delta$ near $0$. Lemma 5.2.2 uses the theorem on the compact set $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.

Further reading: Uniform continuity · Heine–Cantor theorem

A.17

Uniform convergence

DefinedProved here

Cited inL2 · Slides 14–15 · Prop. 2.7.4L4 · Slide 12 · Cor. 4.11.1L5 · Slide 3 · Lemma 5.2.2L5 · Slide 3 · Prop. 5.2.3L6 · Slide 7 · Thm. 6.6.1L10 · Slide 4 · Thm. 10.3.1L11 · Slide 11 · Exercise 11.10.4

Definitions. $f_n\to f$ uniformly on a set $S$ if $\max_S|f_n-f|\to0$ (a supremum, if the maximum is not attained): one rate of convergence works at every point of $S$ at once. $f_n\to f$ uniformly on every compact subset of $\Omega$ if this holds for each compact $K\subset\Omega$ separately; the rate may get worse near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
Proposition. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
Proof. Let $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $S$, fix $z_0\in S$ and a tolerance $\epsilon\gt0$. Choose $n$ with $|f_n-f|\lt\epsilon/3$ on all of $S$, then (by continuity of $f_n$) a radius $\rho$ with $|f_n(z)-f_n(z_0)|\lt\epsilon/3$ for $|z-z_0|\lt\rho$. For such $z$, \[ |f(z)-f(z_0)|\le|f(z)-f_n(z)|+|f_n(z)-f_n(z_0)|+|f_n(z_0)-f(z_0)|\lt\tfrac\epsilon3+\tfrac\epsilon3+\tfrac\epsilon3. \] Uniformity is what lets one $n$ serve for both $z$ and $z_0$. ∎
Proposition (uniformly Cauchy sequences converge uniformly). If $\max_S|f_k-f_j|\to0$ as $j,k\to\infty$, then $f_k$ converges uniformly on $S$ to some $f$.
Proof. At each point $z$, the numbers $f_k(z)$ form a Cauchy sequence of reals, which converges (completeness of $\R$, cited); call the limit $f(z)$. Given $\epsilon\gt0$, pick $N$ with $|f_k-f_j|\lt\epsilon$ on $S$ for $j,k\ge N$. Letting $j\to\infty$ at each point gives $|f_k-f|\le\epsilon$ on $S$ for $k\ge N$: one $N$ for all points, which is uniform convergence. ∎

Pointwise convergence is not enough: $x^n\to0$ for $0\le x\lt1$ but $1^n=1$, so the limit on $[0,1]$ jumps at $x=1$.

Further reading: Uniform convergence · Compact convergence

A.18

Weierstrass approximation theorem

Cited

Cited inL4 · Slide 13 · Rem. 4.12.1L10 · Slide 4 · Thm. 10.3.1

Theorem. Every continuous function on a closed interval $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

Applied to $|x|$ on $[-1,1]$: smooth functions (polynomials) can converge uniformly to a function with a corner. Remark 4.12.1 gives an explicit smooth sequence with the same behaviour.

Further reading: Weierstrass approximation theorem

A.19

Power series

DefinedCited

Cited inL1 · Slide 2 · Def. 1.1.2L6 · Slide 5 · Thm. 6.4.1L9 · Slide 4 · Lemma 9.3.1L10 · Slide 3 · Ex. 10.2.1L10 · Slide 7 · Lemma 10.6.1L11 · Slide 3 · Prop. 11.2.2Appendix C.8Appendix E.2L11 · Slide 11 · Exercise 11.10.6L6 · Slide 12 · Exercise 6.11.5

A power series about $z_0$ is $\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-z_0)^n$ with complex coefficients.

Theorem (cited). There is a radius of convergence $\rho\in[0,\infty]$, namely $1/\rho=\limsup_n|c_n|^{1/n}$, such that:
  1. the series converges absolutely for $|z-z_0|\lt\rho$ and diverges for $|z-z_0|\gt\rho$;
  2. it converges uniformly on every closed disk $|z-z_0|\le r$ with $r\lt\rho$;
  3. its sum $f$ is holomorphic on $|z-z_0|\lt\rho$, and may be differentiated term by term: $f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}nc_n(z-z_0)^{n-1}$, a series with the same radius. Likewise $\sum_n\frac{c_n}{n+1}(z-z_0)^{n+1}$ has the same radius and is a primitive of $f$.

Part (b) follows from the Weierstrass M-test (A.21): if $r\lt r_1\lt\rho$, the terms are eventually bounded by $(r/r_1)^n$. Part (c) says analytic functions (Def. 1.1.2) are holomorphic; Theorem 6.4.1 gives the converse. A series with $\rho=\infty$ defines an entire function. Examples: $e^z=\sum z^n/n!$, $\sin z=\sum(-1)^kz^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$, $\cos z=\sum(-1)^kz^{2k}/(2k)!$, all with $\rho=\infty$, and $\sum z^n=\frac1{1-z}$ with $\rho=1$.

Further reading: Power series · Radius of convergence

A.20

Asymptotic notation: $O$, $o$, $\sim$

Defined

Cited inL6 · Slide 6 · Cor. 6.5.1L6 · Slide 16 · Lemma 6.15.1L6 · Slide 18 · Thm. 6.17.1

Let $F$ and $G\ge0$ be functions of a variable tending to a limit (such as $w\to z_0$, or $n\to\infty$).

  • $F=O(G)$ ("big-$O$"): $|F|\le CG$ for some constant $C$, for all values close enough to the limit. An absolute constant is one that does not depend on any other parameter in sight. Inside a formula, $O(G)$ stands for some quantity of this size: $f(w)=a_m(w-z_0)^m+O(|w-z_0|^{m+1})$ means the difference is at most $C|w-z_0|^{m+1}$.
  • $F=o(G)$ ("little-$o$"): $F/G\to0$; for instance $o(1)$ is a quantity tending to $0$. (A.1 uses $o(|h|)$ in the same sense.)
  • $F\sim G$ ("asymptotic to"): $F/G\to1$. Equivalently $F=G(1+o(1))$.

Rules used freely: $O(G)+O(G)=O(G)$; $O(G_1)O(G_2)=O(G_1G_2)$; if $|w|\le C$ then $e^{O(|w|)}=1+O(|w|)$; and $\frac{a+O(\epsilon)}{b+O(\epsilon)}\to\frac ab$ when $b\ne0$ and $\epsilon\to0$.

Further reading: Big O notation · Asymptotic analysis

A.21

Series: absolute convergence, the M-test, double series

CitedProved here

Cited inL6 · Slide 11 · Lemma 6.10.2L6 · Slide 11 · Prop. 6.10.3L6 · Slide 14 · Lemma 6.13.1L8 · Slide 14L10 · Slide 5 · Lemma 10.4.1Appendix A.19L6 · Slide 12 · Exercise 6.11.5L6 · Slide 12 · Exercise 6.11.6

Facts.
  1. Absolute convergence. If $\sum|a_n|\lt\infty$, then $\sum a_n$ converges, and any rearrangement or regrouping of its terms converges to the same sum (cited).
  2. Weierstrass M-test. If $|f_n|\le M_n$ on a set $S$ and $\sum M_n\lt\infty$, then $\sum f_n$ converges uniformly on $S$. Proof: the tails satisfy $|\sum_{n\gt N}f_n|\le\sum_{n\gt N}M_n\to0$, a bound independent of the point. In particular a uniformly convergent series of continuous functions on a curve may be integrated term by term: $|\int\sum_{n\gt N}f_n|\le\text{length}\cdot\sum_{n\gt N}M_n\to0$.
  3. Double series. If $\sum_{j,k}|a_{jk}|\lt\infty$ (summed in any order), then $\sum_j\sum_ka_{jk}=\sum_k\sum_ja_{jk}$, and the double series may be summed in any grouping (cited; Fubini's theorem for sums, compare A.13). In particular the product of two absolutely convergent series is $\big(\sum_ja_j\big)\big(\sum_kb_k\big)=\sum_{j,k}a_jb_k$.

Further reading: Absolute convergence · Weierstrass M-test · Fubini for sums

A.22

Improper integrals and dominated convergence

DefinedCited

Cited inL6 · Slide 19 · Prop. 6.18.1L8 · Slide 2 · Prop. 8.1.2L8 · Slide 7L8 · Slide 9L11 · Slide 8Appendix A.4Appendix D.7

A function $f$ on $\R$ (or on $(0,\infty)$) is integrable if $\int|f|\lt\infty$. Then $\int_{-\infty}^\infty f=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R}^Rf$, and the limit does not depend on how the endpoints go to infinity. For a merely convergent limit such as $\lim_R\int_{-R}^R$ this independence can fail, which is why the lectures check integrability.

Dominated convergence theorem (cited). If $f_n\to f$ pointwise (or almost everywhere) and $|f_n|\le g$ for one integrable $g$, then $\int f_n\to\int f$.

Typical consequences: if $|f(x,\xi)|\le g(x)$ with $g$ integrable and $f$ continuous in $\xi$, then $\xi\mapsto\int f(x,\xi)\,dx$ is continuous; so the Fourier transform of an integrable function is continuous. Theorem 6.17.1 (Prop. 6.18.1) and Theorem 11.6.1 (§11.7) use the theorem directly, with dominating functions $2e^{-u^2/2}$ and $t^{x-1}e^{-t}$.

Further reading: Dominated convergence theorem · Improper integral

A.23

Stirling's formula

Cited

Cited inL9 · Slide 8 · Prop. 9.7.1Appendix E.19

Theorem (cited). As $K\to\infty$, \[ \log K!=K\log K-K+\tfrac12\log(2\pi K)+O\big(\tfrac1K\big),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad K!\sim\sqrt{2\pi K}\Big(\frac Ke\Big)^K. \]

The main term $K\log K-K$ is $\int_1^K\log t\,dt$ up to a constant: compare the sum $\log K!=\sum_{k\le K}\log k$ with the integral. The constant $\sqrt{2\pi}$ can be found from Wallis's product, or from $\Gamma(\frac12)=\sqrt\pi$ (Cor. 11.9.1). Used in §9.7, and in the outline of Lemma 6.15.1 (E.19).

Further reading: Stirling's approximation

A.24

The intermediate value theorem

Cited

Cited inL11 · Slide 11 · Thm. 11.10.1L13 · Slide 6 · Prop. 13.5.1L11 · Slide 11 · Exercise 11.10.3L11 · Slide 11 · Exercise 11.10.8

Theorem (cited). A continuous real function on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.

Consequence used in Theorem 11.10.1: a continuous function $[0,1]\to\R$ that takes only integer values is constant. If $N(0)\ne N(1)$, it would take the non-integer value halfway between them. In the language of C.4: $[0,1]$ is connected.

Further reading: Intermediate value theorem

A.25

The ML estimate for contour integrals

Proved here

Cited inL6 · Slide 5 · Thm. 6.4.1L8 · Slide 2 · Prop. 8.1.2

Proposition. If $\gamma$ is a piecewise $C^1$ curve of length $L$ and $|f|\le M$ on $\gamma$, then $\Big|\displaystyle\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz\Big|\le ML$.
Proof. Parametrize $\gamma$ by $z(s)$, $a\le s\le b$ (Def. 2.6.1). For a complex-valued integral, $|\int h|\le\int|h|$: write $\int h=|\int h|e^{i\alpha}$; then $|\int h|=\int\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\alpha}h)\le\int|h|$. So \[ \Big|\int_a^bf(z(s))\,z'(s)\,ds\Big|\le\int_a^b|f(z(s))|\,|z'(s)|\,ds\le M\int_a^b|z'(s)|\,ds=ML, \] since $\int|z'(s)|\,ds$ is the length. ∎

The name comes from "$M$ times $L$". Every "the arc contributes at most…" in Parts II–IV is this estimate. Typical shapes: a circle of radius $r$ has $L=2\pi r$; a semicircle, $\pi R$; a vertical side of a rectangle, its height.

Further reading: Estimation lemma

Appendix B

Linear algebra

B.1

Bilinear forms

Defined

Cited inL3 · Slide 4 · Prop. 3.3.2

Let $V$ be a real vector space. A bilinear form is a map $a:V\times V\to\R$ that is linear in each argument when the other is held fixed: \[ a(\alpha u_1+\beta u_2,w)=\alpha a(u_1,w)+\beta a(u_2,w),\qquad a(u,\alpha w_1+\beta w_2)=\alpha a(u,w_1)+\beta a(u,w_2). \] It is symmetric if $a(u,w)=a(w,u)$, and positive semidefinite if $a(v,v)\ge0$ for all $v$. If also $a(v,v)=0$ only for $v=0$, it is an inner product. The energy form $a$ is positive definite on each $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$ (Theorem 3.9.3), but not on all functions, since constants have zero energy.

Further reading: Bilinear form · Inner product space

B.2

Span, linear independence, dimension

Defined

Cited inL3 · Slide 6 · Cor. 3.5.2L3 · Slide 6 · Def. 3.5.3L3 · Slide 7 · Prop. 3.6.5

The span of functions $\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_N$ is the set of all linear combinations $\sum c_k\varphi_k$ with real $c_k$. They are linearly independent if $\sum c_k\varphi_k\equiv0$ only when every $c_k=0$. Independent functions spanning a space form a basis, and the number of basis elements is the dimension. It is a standard fact (cited) that every basis of a given space has the same size.

Further reading: Linear span · Linear independence · Dimension

B.3

Affine sets

Defined

Cited inL3 · Slide 7 · Prop. 3.6.4

A subset $S$ of a vector space is affine if $\lambda U+(1-\lambda)V\in S$ whenever $U,V\in S$ and $\lambda\in\R$. A nonempty affine set is a translate of a linear subspace: fixing any $U_*\in S$, $S=U_*+\{U-U_*:U\in S\}$, and the set of differences is linear. For $S=\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ the difference space is $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$, as Prop. 3.6.4 and 3.6.5(d) show. A line not through the origin is the basic picture.

Further reading: Affine space · Affine combination

B.4

Symmetric and positive definite matrices

DefinedProved here

Cited inL3 · Slide 10 · Lemma 3.9.1L3 · Slide 10 · Thm. 3.9.3

Definitions. A square matrix $M$ is symmetric if $M^{\mathsf T}=M$, i.e. $M_{pq}=M_{qp}$. A symmetric $M$ is positive definite if $c^{\mathsf T}Mc\gt0$ for every nonzero vector $c$. A principal submatrix keeps the rows and columns with the same index set, as $\class{ntn-AII}{A_{II}}$ does.
Proposition. A positive definite matrix is invertible.
Proof. If $Mc=0$ then $c^{\mathsf T}Mc=0$, so $c=0$. So the kernel of $M$ is $\{0\}$. For a square $n\times n$ matrix, the rank–nullity theorem (cited) gives rank $n$, so $M$ is onto as well as one-to-one, hence invertible. ∎

Positive definite systems are also the ones solved well in practice: conjugate gradients and Cholesky factorization both require this property.

Further reading: Symmetric matrix · Definite matrix · Rank–nullity theorem

B.5

Bézout's identity

Cited

Cited inL6 · Slide 12 · Lemma 6.11.1

Theorem (cited). If the integers $a,b\ge1$ are coprime (their only common divisor is $1$), there are integers $x,y$ (one of them usually negative) with $xa+yb=1$.

The Euclidean algorithm finds them: for $a=3$, $b=5$, $2\cdot3-1\cdot5=1$. Lemma 6.11.1 uses it to show that $1$ is the only common root of $z^a=1$ and $z^b=1$.

Further reading: Bézout's identity

Appendix C

Sets and topology

C.1

Complex notation for the plane

Defined

Cited inL1 · Slide 2L2 · Slides 2–3L4 · Slide 3L5 · Slide 4 · Setting 5.3.1

Lecture 4 writes the point $(x,y)$ as $z=x+iy$. Nothing about complex multiplication is used except the following translations.

  • $|z-z_0|=\sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2}$ is the distance between two points.
  • $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ is the unit vector $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ at angle $\theta$.
  • $z_0+te^{i\theta}=(x_0+t\cos\theta,\ y_0+t\sin\theta)$ traces the circle of radius $t$ about $z_0$ as $\theta$ runs over $[0,2\pi]$.
  • $\nabla h\cdot e^{i\theta}$ is the dot product of the gradient with that unit vector: the rate of change of $h$ in direction $\theta$.
  • $\zeta$ ("zeta") and $\xi$ ("xi") are further names for points, used as integration variables.

Further reading: Complex plane · Euler's formula

C.2

Open, bounded, closure, boundary

Defined

Cited inL1 · Slide 2 · Def. 1.1.1L3 · Slide 2 · Setting 3.1.1L3 · Slide 7 · Lemma 3.6.2L6 · Slide 2 · Conv. 6.1.1Appendix E.12

Let $\Omega\subset\R^2$ and write $D_r(P)$ for the open disc of radius $r$ about $P$.

  • $\Omega$ is open if every $P\in\Omega$ has some $D_r(P)\subset\Omega$.
  • $\Omega$ is bounded if it lies in some disc $D_R(0)$.
  • $P$ is a boundary point of $\Omega$ if every disc $D_r(P)$ meets both $\Omega$ and its complement. The set of boundary points is $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  • The closure is $\overline\Omega=\Omega\cup\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.

For an open $\Omega$, $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is disjoint from $\Omega$. A bounded closed set such as $\overline\Omega$ is compact, so continuous functions on it attain a maximum and a minimum (the extreme value theorem, cited).

Further reading: Open set · Boundary · Closure · Extreme value theorem

C.3

Curves, orientation, piecewise $C^1$ boundaries

DefinedCited

Cited inL2 · Slides 7–9 · Def. 2.4.2L2 · Slides 10–11 · Thm. 2.5.1L2 · Slides 12–13 · Prop. 2.6.2L2 · Slides 18–20 · Thm. 2.9.1L6 · Slide 2 · Thm. 6.1.2

  • A closed curve is a continuous map $\gamma:[a,b]\to\R^2$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$; it is simple if it does not cross itself (injective on $[a,b)$). A circle is simple; a figure eight is not.
  • Jordan curve theorem (cited): a simple closed curve splits the plane into a bounded inside $D$ and an unbounded outside, with the curve as their common boundary.
  • The curve is positively oriented if $D$ lies on the left as you travel along it: anticlockwise for a circle. Then the outward normal $n$ is the unit tangent $t$ turned clockwise by $90°$: if $t=(t_1,t_2)$, $n=(t_2,-t_1)$.
  • A boundary is piecewise $C^1$ (or piecewise smooth) if it consists of finitely many curves, each continuously differentiable with nonzero velocity, joined at finitely many corners. Polygons, disks and unions of grid squares qualify. This is what the divergence theorem (A.6) needs.

Further reading: Jordan curve theorem · Curve orientation

C.4

Connected sets and components

DefinedCited

Cited inL1 · Slide 4 · Thm. 1.3.1L2 · Slides 18–20 · Thm. 2.9.1L3 · Slide 10 · Thm. 3.9.3L4 · Slide 4 · Thm. 4.3.1L4 · Slide 5 · Cor. 4.4.1L6 · Slide 8 · Thm. 6.7.1L7 · Slide 4 · Thm. 7.3.1L10 · Slide 2 · Thm. 10.1.1Appendix A.24L12 · Slide 18 · Def. 12.17.1L11 · Slide 11 · Exercise 11.10.5L10 · Slide 3 · Exercise 10.2.2L10 · Slide 3 · Exercise 10.2.4

Let $S\subset\Omega$. $S$ is closed in $\Omega$ if every limit of points of $S$ that lies in $\Omega$ is itself in $S$. (Limits outside $\Omega$, on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, don't count.)

An open set $\Omega$ is connected if it cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open sets. Equivalently, the only subsets of $\Omega$ that are both open and closed in $\Omega$ are $\emptyset$ and $\Omega$. This is the form used in Theorem 4.3.1. For open sets in $\R^2$ it is equivalent (cited) to being path-connected: any two points can be joined by a continuous path inside $\Omega$. Disks are connected.

A connected component is a maximal connected subset. Every open set is the disjoint union of its components, and each component is open: a small disk about a point of the component lies in $\Omega$, is connected, and meets the component, so by maximality it lies in the component.

For a grid region the components are exactly the clusters used in Theorem 3.9.3: squares chained through shared edges. The proof there works with clusters directly, so it needs no general topology.

Further reading: Connected space

C.5

Compact sets

DefinedCitedProved here

Cited inL4 · Slide 5 · Cor. 4.4.1L4 · Slide 6 · Def. 4.5.4L4 · Slide 7 · Def. 4.6.1L4 · Slide 9 · Prop. 4.8.2L4 · Slide 10 · Thm. 4.9.5L5 · Slide 3 · Lemma 5.2.2L5 · Slide 8 · Prop. 5.7.2L6 · Slide 5 · Thm. 6.4.1L7 · Slide 4 · Thm. 7.3.1L9 · Slide 3 · Prop. 9.2.1L9 · Slide 4 · Lemma 9.3.1L9 · Slide 7 · Cor. 9.6.2L11 · Slide 11 · Thm. 11.10.1L13 · Slide 2 · Prop. 13.1.2L13 · Slide 6 · Prop. 13.5.1L11 · Slide 11 · Exercise 11.10.4

A subset of $\R^2$ is compact if it is closed and bounded (for subsets of $\R^2$ this agrees with the general definition, by the Heine–Borel theorem, cited). Closed disks, $\overline\Omega$ for bounded $\Omega$, and $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ are compact. A compact subset of $\Omega$ is a compact set contained in the open set $\Omega$; it stays a positive distance away from $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. On a compact set, a continuous function attains its maximum and minimum (extreme value theorem, cited).

Facts (proved). Let $\Omega$ be open.
  1. Compact sets sit inside some $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$. For compact $K\subset\Omega$ there is $\delta\gt0$ with $K\subset\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$. Proof: $d(z):=$ distance from $z$ to the complement of $\Omega$ is continuous (it changes by at most $|z-z'|$ between $z$ and $z'$) and positive on $\Omega$ (which is open). On compact $K$ it attains a positive minimum $d_0$; any $\delta\lt d_0$ works.
  2. $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ is open. If the closed $\delta$-disk about $z$ lies in $\Omega$, apply (a) to that disk: some slightly larger closed disk, of radius $\delta+\rho$, still lies in $\Omega$. Then every $w$ with $|w-z|\lt\rho$ has its closed $\delta$-disk inside it, so $w\in\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$.
  3. A nonempty bounded open set has a boundary point. Take $P\in\Omega$ and move right: $T:=\sup\{t:P+(s,0)\in\Omega\text{ for all }0\le s\le t\}$ is finite because $\Omega$ is bounded. The point $P+(T,0)$ is a limit of points of $\Omega$, but is not in $\Omega$ (else, $\Omega$ being open, we could go further). So it lies on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.
  4. Every point of $\Omega$ lies in some $\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$ (since $\Omega$ is open), so $\Omega=\bigcup_{\delta\gt0}\class{ntn-Omd}{\Omega_\delta}$.
  5. Bolzano–Weierstrass (cited). Every sequence in a compact set has a subsequence converging to a point of the set. Lectures 7, 9 and 10 use it to show that a holomorphic $f\not\equiv0$ has only finitely many zeros in a compact set: infinitely many would accumulate, contradicting Theorem 6.7.1.

Further reading: Compact space · Heine–Borel theorem · Extreme value theorem · Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem

C.6

The distance function

DefinedProved hereCited

Cited inL5 · Slide 5 · Ex. 5.4.1L5 · Slide 5 · Prop. 5.4.2Appendix A.10

For a nonempty closed set $A$, $\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z,A):=\min\{|z-a|:a\in A\}$, the distance from $z$ to the nearest point of $A$.

Proposition. $\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(\cdot,A)$ is 1-Lipschitz: $|\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z,A)-\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z',A)|\le|z-z'|$.
Proof. Let $a\in A$ be nearest to $z'$. Then \[ \class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z,A)\le|z-a|\le|z-z'|+|z'-a|=|z-z'|+\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z',A). \] Swap $z$ and $z'$. ∎

Near a straight piece of boundary, $\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}(z,\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega})$ is the distance to a line, a linear function whose gradient is a unit normal. In general $|\nabla\class{ntn-dist}{\operatorname{dist}}|=1$ almost everywhere off $A$ (cited). Example 5.4.1 uses this to compute the energy of its boundary layer.

Further reading: Distance function · Distance to a set

C.7

Support; "supported inside $\Omega$"

Defined

Cited inL3 · Slide 5 · Prop. 3.4.5L3 · Slide 20 · Def. 3.18.2Appendix D.4

The support of a function $f$ is the closure of the set where $f\ne0$. The hat $\class{ntn-phi}{\varphi_{ij}}$ has support $[x_{i-1},x_{i+1}]\times[y_{j-1},y_{j+1}]$.

A function is supported inside $\Omega$ (or compactly supported in $\Omega$) if its support is a closed bounded set contained in $\Omega$. Such a function vanishes on a whole neighbourhood of $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$, not just on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ itself. This is the class of $\psi$ used to define weak derivatives (Def. 3.18.2).

Further reading: Support · Bump function

C.8

The principal logarithm, powers and roots

DefinedCited

Cited inL6 · Slide 14 · Lemma 6.13.1L6 · Slide 16 · Cor. 6.15.2L6 · Slide 12 · Exercise 6.11.7L12 · Slide 12 · Exercise 12.11.3

For $z\ne0$ write $z=re^{i\theta}$ with $r=|z|$ and $-\pi\lt\theta\le\pi$; this $\theta$ is the principal argument $\operatorname{Arg}z$. The principal logarithm is $\log z:=\log r+i\theta$ (one branch of E.3). It satisfies $e^{\log z}=z$, and it is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$ with derivative $1/z$.

  • Series. For $|w|\lt1$, $1-w$ lies in the right half-plane, and $-\log(1-w)=\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{w^m}m$. Proof: both sides are holomorphic on $|w|\lt1$, with derivative $\frac1{1-w}=\sum w^{m-1}$ (A.19), and both vanish at $w=0$.
  • Powers. For $t\gt0$ and complex $z$, $t^z:=e^{z\log t}$ with the real logarithm; then $|t^z|=t^{\operatorname{Re}z}$. For complex $\tau$ off $(-\infty,0]$, the principal square root is $\sqrt\tau:=e^{\frac12\log\tau}$; it has positive real part.
  • Caution. $\log(zw)=\log z+\log w$ can fail by $2\pi i$ when the arguments add up beyond $(-\pi,\pi]$. In §6.18, $\sqrt{t(1-is)}=\sqrt t\sqrt{1-is}$ is safe because $t\gt0$ adds nothing to the argument.

Further reading: Principal value of the logarithm · Principal square root

Appendix D

Function spaces

D.1

Function classes: $C^k$, smooth

Defined

Cited inL2 · Slides 2–3 · Thm. 2.1.2L2 · Slides 18–20 · Thm. 2.9.1L4 · Slide 2L4 · Slide 5L4 · Slide 6 · Def. 4.5.1L5 · Slide 2 · Thm. 5.1.1

  • $C(\overline\Omega)$: continuous on $\overline\Omega$, boundary included.
  • $C^k(\Omega)$: all partial derivatives up to order $k$ exist and are continuous in $\Omega$. "$h$ is $C^2$" means $C^2(\Omega)$.
  • Smooth ($C^\infty$): $C^k$ for every $k$.
  • $C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$: twice continuously differentiable inside, continuous up to the boundary. This is the natural class for the classical Dirichlet problem (Def. 3.1.2): enough derivatives inside to state $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} h=0$, enough continuity at the edge to state $h=g$.

Further reading: Smoothness

D.2

The space $L^2(\Omega)$ and Cauchy sequences

Defined

Cited inL3 · Slide 16 · Def. 3.15.1L3 · Slide 17 · Prop. 3.16.1L4 · Slide 7 · Thm. 4.6.2L4 · Slide 7 · Rem. 4.6.4L4 · Slide 9 · Fact 4.8.4L4 · Slide 10 · Thm. 4.9.5Appendix A.11

$L^2(\Omega)$ is the space of functions $f$ on $\Omega$ with $\norm{f}_{L^2}^2=\iint_\Omega|f|^2\,dA\lt\infty$. Functions that differ only on a zero-area set are treated as the same element. Distance is $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{f-h}_{L^2}}$, and $f_n\to f$ in $L^2$ means $\class{ntn-L2}{\norm{f_n-f}_{L^2}}\to0$. Vector-valued functions such as gradients are handled componentwise.

In words: $u\in L^2(\Omega)$ says only that $u$ is square-integrable, that $|u|^2$ has a finite integral over $\Omega$. It says nothing about continuity or derivatives; $u$ may jump, and its values on a set of zero area are irrelevant. This is why Weyl's lemma (Theorem 4.6.2) is surprising: from this weak information it concludes that $u$ is smooth. For a set $K\subset\Omega$, $L^2(K)$ is the same with the integral taken over $K$ only, so "$f_n\to f$ in $L^2(K)$" means $\iint_K|f_n-f|^2\,dA\to0$.

A sequence $(f_n)$ is Cauchy if for every $\delta\gt0$ there is $N$ with $\norm{f_n-f_k}\lt\delta$ for all $n,k\ge N$: its terms eventually become arbitrarily close to each other. A convergent sequence is always Cauchy. The converse is the content of D.3.

Further reading: $L^p$ space · Cauchy sequence

D.3

Completeness of $L^2$ (Riesz–Fischer)

Cited

Cited inL3 · Slide 20 · Prop. 3.18.1Appendix D.2

Theorem. Every Cauchy sequence in $L^2(\Omega)$ converges in $L^2(\Omega)$ to some $f\in L^2(\Omega)$.

This is the step that produces the limit function $u$ from nothing but estimates. It needs the Lebesgue integral: with Riemann-integrable functions alone, the limit may fail to exist in the space. The slides use it without comment in "call their limits $u,p,q$".

Further reading: Riesz–Fischer theorem · Complete metric space

D.4

Test functions: three versions

Defined

Cited inL3 · Slide 4

A function $w:\overline\Omega\to\R$ is piecewise continuously differentiable if $\overline\Omega$ can be cut by finitely many line segments into pieces, and on each piece $w$ extends to a continuously differentiable function. It is an admissible test function if, in addition, it is continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and $w=0$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$.

This is the precise meaning this guide gives to the slide's "any function $w$ vanishing on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$". It is broad enough to include hat functions (cut along grid lines) and smooth functions (no cuts). Its gradient exists off the cuts, which have zero areaA.11, so $a(u,w)$ is defined.

The lectures use three classes of test function, each fitted to what it is tested against:

NameWhereSmoothnessAt the boundary
admissible $w$weak form, Def. 3.3.4continuous, piecewise $C^1$$=0$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$
$\psi$weak derivative, Def. 3.18.2$C^1$$=0$ near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$
$\eta$Weyl's lemma, Def. 4.6.1smooth$=0$ near $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$

The weak form only moves one derivative and tests a function ($u$) whose boundary values are known, so vanishing on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is enough. The other two test an $L^2$ function with no boundary values at all, so they must vanish on a whole band (C.7). Weyl's lemma moves two derivatives, so it asks for smoothness.

Further reading: Weak formulation · Piecewise functions

D.5

Mollifiers and the smoothing fact

DefinedCited

Cited inL1 · Slide 4 · Cor. 1.3.3L3 · Slide 21 · Rem. 3.19.2L4 · Slide 6 · Def. 4.5.1L4 · Slide 9 · Fact 4.8.4

A weight $\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}$ as in Def. 4.5.1 is called a mollifier. An explicit one: \[ \class{ntn-chi}{\chi}(\zeta)=c\,\exp\!\Big(\frac{-1}{1-|\zeta|^2}\Big)\ \text{ for }|\zeta|\lt1,\qquad\class{ntn-chi}{\chi}(\zeta)=0\ \text{ otherwise}, \] with $c$ chosen so the integral is $1$. It is smooth even across the unit circle, because $e^{-1/s}$ and all its derivatives tend to $0$ as $s\downarrow0$. It is radial and nonnegative.

Theorem (cited). If $u\in L^2(\Omega)$ and $K\subset\Omega$ is compact, then $\norm{u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}-u}_{L^2(K)}\to0$ as $\delta\to0$.

The idea: for continuous $u$ this is easy, since $u\class{ntn-conv}{*}\class{ntn-chid}{\chi_\delta}(z)$ is an average of values within $\delta$ of $z$. A general $L^2$ function is an $L^2$-limit of continuous ones, and averaging never increases the $L^2$ norm, so the estimate passes to the limit.

Further reading: Mollifier · Bump function · Convolution

D.6

Sobolev spaces $\class{ntn-H1}{H^1}$, $\class{ntn-H1}{H^1_0}$ and the trace

DefinedCited

Cited inL3 · Slide 21 · Thm. 3.19.1L3 · Slide 21 · Rem. 3.19.2L5 · Slide 13 · Rem. 5.12.3Appendix E.14

$\class{ntn-H1}{H^1}(\Omega)$ is the set of $u\in L^2(\Omega)$ whose weak derivatives $\partial_xu,\partial_yu$ (Def. 3.18.2) exist and lie in $L^2(\Omega)$. $\class{ntn-H1}{H^1_0}(\Omega)$ is the set of limits, in the sense of item 1 of Theorem 3.19.1 (function and gradient both converge in $L^2$), of piecewise smooth functions vanishing on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. Item 3 of that theorem says exactly $u-\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}\in \class{ntn-H1}{H^1_0}(\Omega)$.

The trace theorem (cited) says that, for reasonable domains, restriction to $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ extends from smooth functions to a well-defined map on $\class{ntn-H1}{H^1}(\Omega)$, whose kernel is $\class{ntn-H1}{H^1_0}(\Omega)$. So $u-\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}\in \class{ntn-H1}{H^1_0}$ means "$u$ has the same boundary trace as $\class{ntn-Un}{U_0}$", namely $g$.

Further reading: Sobolev space · Trace operator · Weak derivative

D.7

The Fourier transform and Fourier inversion

DefinedCited

Cited inL7 · Slide 6 · Ex. 7.5.1L8 · Slide 3 · Def. 8.2.1L8 · Slide 6 · Fact 8.5.1

For integrable $f$ on $\R$, $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}dx$ (Def. 8.2.1). With the $2\pi$ inside the exponent, the transform and its inverse are symmetric, and $e^{-\pi x^2}$ is its own transform (Prop. 8.3.1). $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ is continuous (A.22) and bounded by $\int|f|$.

Inversion theorem (cited). If $f$ and $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ are both integrable, then $f(x)=\int\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$ at every point where $f$ is continuous; in particular everywhere, if $f$ is continuous. This is Fact 8.5.1.

Rules that make the examples of Lecture 8 quick: shifting $f(x-a)$ multiplies $\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ by $e^{-2\pi ia\xi}$; scaling $f(x/T)$ gives $T\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}(T\xi)$ (used in Cor. 8.15.1); $\class{ntn-hat}{\widehat{f'}}=2\pi i\xi\class{ntn-hat}{\hat f}$ (the integration by parts of Theorem 8.7.1); and convolution becomes multiplication, which is why the triangle, the convolution of two boxes, has transform $\class{ntn-sinc}{\operatorname{sinc}}^2$ (Exercise 8.16.5).

Further reading: Fourier transform · Fourier inversion theorem · Sampling theorem

Appendix E

Context and previews

Remarks that go beyond the slides: history, connections, outlines of omitted proofs, and a few complete proofs of results the slides cite.

E.1

Sign conventions: $u+iv$ versus $u-iv$

Context

Cited inL1 · Slides 11–14 · Prop. 1.6.2L6 · Slide 2 · Thm. 6.1.2

The lectures attach a vector field to a complex function in two ways, and it is easy to mix them up.

ConventionWhereCauchy–Riemann reads
$f=u+iv$, $f\leftrightarrow(u,v)$ as a map $\R^2\to\R^2$Def. 1.5.1, Theorem 1.5.2$u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$
$f=u-iv$, $(u,v)$ a velocity or electric field§1.6, §1.10, Lecture 2$\operatorname{div}(u,v)=0$, $\operatorname{curl}(u,v)=0$

The second is the first applied to the pair $(u,-v)$ (Prop. 1.6.2). In flow language: if $f=\class{ntn-vphi}{\varphi}+i\class{ntn-spsi}{\psi}$ is the complex potential, the velocity field is $V=\overline{f'}$ (Prop. 1.10.2), and $f'=u-iv$ with $(u,v)=V$. Lecture 2's $f$ is Lecture 1's complex velocity $f'$, not its complex potential: both lectures attach $\frac1z$ to the radial field $(x,y)/r^2$ (Example 1.14.1, Def. 2.4.1).

Further reading: Two-dimensional potential flow · Cauchy–Riemann equations

E.2

Holomorphic, analytic, smooth: how the definitions meet

Context

Cited inL1 · Slide 2 · Def. 1.1.2L6 · Slide 2 · Conv. 6.1.1

The course uses three conditions on a function $f$ on an open set:

  1. a complex derivative at every point (Def. 1.1.1);
  2. a complex derivative at every point, with $C^1$ real and imaginary parts (Convention 6.1.1);
  3. locally a convergent power series (Def. 1.1.2).

Lecture 6 proves (2) ⇒ (3): Theorem 6.4.1, through Cauchy's theorem, whose proof by Green's theorem needs the $C^1$ parts. Power series give (3) ⇒ (2) (A.19), and Cor. 6.6.2 adds that such functions are $C^\infty$. Clearly (2) ⇒ (1).

The remaining step, (1) ⇒ (2), is Goursat's theorem: Cauchy's theorem holds for every $f$ with a complex derivative at each point, with no continuity assumed. The proof avoids Green's theorem: it subdivides a triangle into four, picks the piece with the largest integral, and repeats; the nested triangles shrink to a point where $f$ is differentiable, and that forces the integral to be $0$. So all three conditions are equivalent, and the $C^1$ requirement of Convention 6.1.1 is a convenience, not a restriction. A converse, Morera's theorem, says a continuous $f$ whose integral around every small circle vanishes is holomorphic.

Further reading: Goursat's theorem · Analytic function · Morera's theorem

E.3

The complex logarithm and its branches

DefinedContext

Cited inL1 · Slides 24–26 · Ex. 1.14.1Appendix C.8Appendix E.17

Write $z\ne0$ in polar form $z=re^{i\theta}$. A logarithm should satisfy $e^{\log z}=z$, which gives $\log z=\log r+i\theta$, but the angle $\theta$ is only determined up to adding $2\pi k$. A branch of $\log$ on a region is a choice of $\theta$ that varies continuously there. On any disk not containing $0$ (more generally, on $\mathbb C$ cut along a ray from $0$) a branch exists, and it is holomorphic with derivative $1/z$. Going once around the origin increases $\theta$ by $2\pi$, so no branch exists on all of $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ (Prop. 1.14.3). The function $\log|z|=\log r$, the real part, is single-valued and harmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$: it is the logarithmic potential of E.6.

Further reading: Complex logarithm · Branch point

E.4

Maxwell's equations in the plane

Context

Cited inL2 · Slides 4–5 · Hyp. 2.2.2

In three dimensions, the static part of Maxwell's equations reads $\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ (Gauss's law) and $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B$ (Faraday's law), which is $0$ when nothing changes in time. For long straight wires perpendicular to the plane, the field does not depend on the coordinate along the wires and has no component in that direction, so it is a planar field $(u,v)$. The 3-D curl then has only one nonzero component, the scalar $\operatorname{curl}$ of A.5. Choosing units with $\varepsilon_0=1$ gives Hypothesis 2.2.2. In these units a unit line charge produces the field $\class{ntn-E0}{E_0}$ of Def. 2.4.1, of strength $\frac{1}{2\pi r}$: its flux through any circle around it is $1$.

Further reading: Maxwell's equations · Gauss's law · Electric potential

E.5

Laurent series and the residue theorem

Cited

Cited inL2 · Slides 14–15 · Def. 2.7.3L6 · Slide 10 · Thm. 6.9.1L9 · Slide 2 · Lemma 9.1.1

Theorem (Laurent). If $f$ is holomorphic on a punctured disk $0\lt|z-z_0|\lt R$, then $f(z)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}c_m(z-z_0)^m$ there, converging uniformly on every smaller closed annulus. The terms with $m\lt0$ form the principal part; $c_{-1}$ is the residue.

In Lecture 2's notation, $a_m=c_{-m}$ for $m\ge1$, and the terms with $m\ge0$ are the "part holomorphic near $z_0$". Uniform convergence on the circle is what justifies integrating term by term in Prop. 2.7.4. The residue theorem says $\oint_\gamma f\,dz=2\pi i\sum\class{ntn-res}{\operatorname{Res}}$ over the singularities enclosed by $\gamma$; Cor. 2.6.4 is the case of simple charges, and Theorem 6.9.1 proves it for poles of any order, where the principal part is finite (Prop. 6.8.2). Laurent series are needed only for essential singularities, where infinitely many negative powers occur, such as $e^{1/z}=\sum_{m\ge0}z^{-m}/m!$ at $0$; the residue theorem holds there too, with $c_{-1}$ as the residue.

Further reading: Laurent series · Residue theorem · Multipole expansion

E.6

The logarithmic potential

Proved here

Cited inL2 · Slides 7–9 · Rem. 2.4.4L2 · Slides 16–17 · Def. 2.8.2L4 · Slide 13 · Rem. 4.12.2L5 · Slide 6L5 · Slide 11 · Def. 5.10.2L5 · Slide 11 · Lemma 5.10.3L8 · Slide 17 · Exercise 8.16.5L9 · Slide 4L9 · Slide 5 · Lemma 9.4.1Appendix E.3L12 · Slide 3 · Rem. 12.2.2L13 · Slide 9 · Rem. 13.8.2

Proposition. For a fixed point $y$, the function $z\mapsto\log|z-y|$ is harmonic on the plane minus $y$.
Proof. $\nabla\log|z-y|=\frac{z-y}{|z-y|^2}$ (as a vector) is $2\pi$ times the unit-charge field $E_0$ of Def. 2.4.1, moved to $y$. So $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\log|z-y|=\operatorname{div}\nabla\log|z-y|=2\pi\operatorname{div}E_0(\cdot-y)$, which is $0$ away from $y$ by Theorem 2.4.3, step 1. ∎

Physically, $\log|z-y|$ is (up to a constant factor) the electrostatic potential of a point charge at $y$ in the plane, and the fundamental solution of the Laplacian: $\frac1{2\pi}\log|z|$ satisfies $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}=\delta_0$ in the sense of distributions. It grows slowly, like $\log$ of the distance, and is $-\infty$ only at $y$ itself. Lecture 5 uses it as a barrier by putting the charge just outside $\Omega$. Its gradient is $\nabla\log|z|=2\pi E_0$, the field of a unit charge from Lecture 2 (Def. 2.4.1).

Further reading: Fundamental solution · Logarithmic potential

E.7

Terminology: finite elements, Galerkin, stiffness

Context

Cited inL3 · Slide 3L3 · Slide 8 · Def. 3.7.1L3 · Slide 8 · Def. 3.7.2

  • Finite element method: approximate the solution by functions built from simple pieces on a mesh (here, bilinear pieces on squares), then impose the weak form on those functions.
  • Galerkin method: impose a weak form using the same finite-dimensional space (up to boundary data) for trial and test functions. Def. 3.7.1 is Galerkin with $\class{ntn-Vg}{V^g_\eps}$ and $\class{ntn-Vz}{V^0_\eps}$.
  • Stiffness matrix: the matrix $A$ of Def. 3.7.2. The name comes from structural mechanics, where the same construction relates forces to displacements. The per-square matrix $K$ of Lemma 3.10.2 is the element stiffness matrix, and summing over squares (Prop. 3.10.3) is called assembly.
  • Bilinear interpolation: filling in a square from its four corner values by the unique bilinear function (Lemma 3.5.6). $\class{ntn-Veps}{V_\eps}$ is exactly the set of such interpolants.

Further reading: Finite element method · Galerkin method · Stiffness matrix · Bilinear interpolation

E.8

Other averaging stencils

Context

Cited inL3 · Slide 11 · Cor. 3.10.4

A harmonic function equals its average over every circle inside its domain (Theorem 4.2.2, Lecture 4). Cor. 3.10.4 is a discrete analogue: each nodal value is the average of its eight neighbours.

Different discretizations give different averaging rules. Finite differences, which replace $u_{xx}$ by $(u(x+\eps)-2u(x)+u(x-\eps))/\eps^2$, give the five-point stencil: each value is the average of its four edge neighbours. Bilinear finite elements give the nine-point rule of Prop. 3.10.3.

Further reading: Mean value property · Five-point stencil · Nine-point stencil

E.9

Random walks and harmonic measure

Preview

Cited inL3 · Slide 13 · Prop. 3.12.3L3 · Slide 21 · Rem. 3.19.2

Start a random walk at an interior node $p$. At each step, move to one of the 8 neighbours with probability $\tfrac18$ each, and stop on reaching a boundary node. Let $h_q(p)$ be the probability that the walk stops at the boundary node $q$.

Conditioning on the first step gives $h_q(p)=\tfrac18\sum_{\text{nbrs}}h_q(\text{nbr})$, the equation of Cor. 3.10.4, with boundary data $e_q$. By uniqueness, $h_q(p)=\class{ntn-W}{W}_{pq}$, the weight of Prop. 3.12.3. (This uses the fact that the walk reaches $B$ with probability 1, which is not proved here.) The continuum limit is Brownian motion, and the limiting weights form the harmonic measure. Lecture 3 announced this as the route to $u(x)\to g(p)$ at boundary points. Lecture 5 proves that fact a different way, with energy and a barrier (Theorem 5.11.3), so the random walk is not needed.

Further reading: Harmonic measure · Random walk

E.10

Dirichlet's principle

Context

Cited inL3 · Slide 14 · Lemma 3.13.2L13 · Slide 9 · Rem. 13.8.1

The continuous version of Lemma 3.13.2: the harmonic function with boundary values $g$ minimizes $\iint|\nabla v|^2$ among all $v$ with those boundary values. Riemann used it in the 1850s by assuming a minimizer exists. Weierstrass showed that an energy-type functional can have a positive infimum that no admissible function attains, so the assumption needed proof. Hilbert rehabilitated the principle around 1900.

The slides avoid the gap: they never assume a minimizer. They build the minimizers $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ over finite-dimensional sets, where existence is linear algebra, and obtain $u$ as a limit.

Further reading: Dirichlet's principle

E.11

A sharper Poincaré constant

Proved here

Cited inL3 · Slides 18–19 · Thm. 3.17.2

In step 3 of Theorem 3.17.2, keep the factor $x$ instead of replacing it by $\class{ntn-L}{L}$: \[ \int_0^{\class{ntn-L}{L}}|v(x,y)|^2dx\le\int_0^Lx\,dx\cdot\int_0^{\class{ntn-L}{L}}|\partial_xv|^2ds=\frac{\class{ntn-L}{L}^2}2\int_0^{\class{ntn-L}{L}}|\partial_xv|^2ds. \] This gives $\norm{v}\le\frac{\class{ntn-L}{L}}{\sqrt2}\norm{\nabla v}$. The best constant for a strip of width $\class{ntn-L}{L}$ is $\class{ntn-L}{L}/\pi$, from the first eigenvalue of $-d^2/dx^2$ on $(0,\class{ntn-L}{L})$ with zero boundary values. For the existence proof any constant independent of $n,k$ is enough.

Further reading: Poincaré inequality · Wirtinger's inequality

E.12

Uniqueness via the weak maximum principle

Proved here

Cited inL3 · Slide 2 · Def. 3.1.2L4 · Slide 4 · Rem. 4.3.2

Theorem (weak maximum principle). Let $\Omega$ be bounded and open, and let $u$ be twice continuously differentiable in $\Omega$, continuous on $\overline\Omega$, with $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$. Then $\max_{\overline\Omega}u=\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}u$.
Proof. Fix $\delta\gt0$ and put $v:=u+\delta(x^2+y^2)$. Then $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v=\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u+4\delta=4\delta\gt0$. $v$ is continuous on the compact set $\overline\Omega$, so it attains a maximum there (extreme value theoremC.2). Suppose the maximum is at an interior point $P$. Then $x\mapsto v(x,P_y)$ has a local maximum at $P_x$, so its second derivative there is $\le0$; likewise in $y$. So $\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} v(P)\le0$, a contradiction. The maximum of $v$ is therefore on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. With $R$ such that $x^2+y^2\le R^2$ on $\overline\Omega$, \[ u\le v\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}v\le\max_{\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}}u+\delta R^2. \] Let $\delta\to0$. ∎
Corollary (uniqueness). The Dirichlet problem has at most one solution.
Proof. If $u_1,u_2$ both solve it, $w=u_1-u_2$ is harmonic with $w=0$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$. The theorem gives $w\le0$, and applied to $-w$ it gives $w\ge0$. ∎

This is a third proof of uniqueness, alongside the energy method of Lecture 2 (Theorem 2.9.1) and the strong maximum principle of Lecture 4 (Cor. 4.4.2). Theorem 3.11.3 is the discrete counterpart, proved by the averaging property rather than second derivatives. Lecture 4 reproves this result the same way, through the mean value property: Theorem 4.3.1 and Cor. 4.4.1, 4.4.2.

Further reading: Maximum principle · Dirichlet problem

E.13

Three strengths of "$\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$" and distributions

Context

Cited inL2 · Slides 7–9 · Def. 2.4.2L4 · Slide 7 · Rem. 4.6.4

The two lectures meet the equation in three forms, each moving more derivatives off $u$ onto a test function $\eta$:

FormStatementNeeds of $u$
Classical (Def. 3.1.2)$\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta} u=0$ at every pointtwo derivatives
Weak (Def. 3.3.4)$\iint\nabla u\cdot\nabla\eta=0$one (weak) derivative
Very weak (Theorem 4.6.2)$\iint u\,\class{ntn-Delta}{\Delta}\eta=0$none: $u\in L^2$

The last form treats $u$ as a distribution: an object known only through its integrals against test functions. Each form implies the next when $u$ is smooth enough (integration by parts). Weyl's lemma goes the other way, all the way back: for the Laplacian, the weakest form already forces the strongest. This is the simplest case of elliptic regularity.

The Dirac delta $\delta_0$ of Lecture 2 is the basic example of a distribution that is not a function: it is known only through $\eta\mapsto\eta(0)$. "$\operatorname{div}E_0=\delta_0$" (Def. 2.4.2) means $-\iint E_0\cdot\nabla\eta\,dA=\eta(0)$ for every test function $\eta$: the divergence moved onto $\eta$, exactly as in the weak forms above. Def. 2.4.2 states the same thing with fluxes through curves instead of test functions.

Further reading: Distributions · Weyl's lemma · Elliptic regularity

E.14

The weak maximum principle in $\class{ntn-H1}{H^1}$

Context

Cited inL5 · Slide 13 · Rem. 5.12.3

Remark 5.12.3 says the comparison lemma is a grid-free statement in disguise. In Sobolev language (D.6) it reads: if $u\in \class{ntn-H1}{H^1}(\Omega)$ is weakly harmonic and $(u-v)^+\in \class{ntn-H1}{H^1_0}(\Omega)$, then $u\le v$ almost everywhere. The proof is the one of §5.8–§5.9: test the weak equation with $(u-v-\sigma)^+$, whose energy then vanishes. The condition $(u-v)^+\in \class{ntn-H1}{H^1_0}$ is "$u\le v$ on $\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ in the trace sense", exactly what the $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}$ supplied through $\class{ntn-Un}{U_n}=g\le v$. This is the starting point of the $L^2$ theory of elliptic equations with variable coefficients, where no mean value property is available.

Further reading: Maximum principle for elliptic PDE · Sobolev space

E.15

Barriers and regular boundary points

Context

Cited inL5 · Slide 13 · Rem. 5.12.3

A barrier at $p\in\class{ntn-dOm}{\partial\Omega}$ is a function harmonic (or superharmonic) in $\Omega$, continuous on $\overline\Omega$, positive on $\overline\Omega$ except at $p$ where it is smallest. A boundary point with a barrier is called regular: at such points every Dirichlet solution takes its boundary value continuously, by an argument like §5.11.

For a union of squares every boundary point is regular, thanks to the empty square of Lemma 5.10.1. More generally, an exterior cone or exterior disk at $p$ is enough. Not every domain qualifies: a punctured disk (the boundary point $0$ is isolated) admits no solution with $u(0)$ prescribed independently of the outer circle, and Lebesgue's "spike" in three dimensions has an irregular tip. In the plane, any boundary point lying on a nontrivial connected piece of the boundary is regular.

Further reading: Barrier function · Perron's method · Dirichlet problem

E.16

A proof of Poisson summation by residues

Proved here

Cited inL7 · Slide 6 · Ex. 7.5.1L8 · Slide 12 · Thm. 8.11.1Index

The slides refer Theorem 8.11.1 to a homework problem. Here is a complete proof with the tools of Lectures 6 and 8. Let $F$ be holomorphic on $|\operatorname{Im}z|\lt a$ with $|F(x+iy)|\le\frac C{1+x^2}$ there, and fix $0\lt b\lt a$.

Proof.
  1. A kernel with residue $\frac1{2\pi i}$ at each integer. Let $k(z):=\frac1{e^{2\pi iz}-1}$. Its poles are the zeros of $e^{2\pi iz}-1$, the integers, all simple, and $\class{ntn-res}{\operatorname{Res}}_nk=\frac1{2\pi ie^{2\pi in}}=\frac1{2\pi i}$ by Prop. 6.8.4 with $A=1$, $B=e^{2\pi iz}-1$. ($B$ is not a polynomial, but the proof still works: by Theorem 6.4.1, $B(n)=0$ gives $B=(z-n)B_1$ with $B_1$ holomorphic.)
  2. Rectangle. Let $Q_N$ be the rectangle with vertical sides $\operatorname{Re}z=\pm(N+\frac12)$ and horizontal sides $\operatorname{Im}z=\pm b$, anticlockwise. It encloses the integers $|n|\le N$, so by Prop. 8.1.1 \[ \oint_{Q_N}F(z)k(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{|n|\le N}\frac{F(n)}{2\pi i}=\sum_{|n|\le N}F(n). \]
  3. Vertical sides. On $\operatorname{Re}z=\pm(N+\frac12)$, $e^{2\pi iz}=-e^{-2\pi y}$ is negative, so $|e^{2\pi iz}-1|=1+e^{-2\pi y}\ge1$ and $|k|\le1$. With $|F|\le\frac C{1+N^2}$ and height $2b$, these sides are $O(N^{-2})$.
  4. Bottom side ($\operatorname{Im}z=-b$, left to right). There $|e^{2\pi iz}|=e^{2\pi b}\gt1$, so $k(z)=\frac{e^{-2\pi iz}}{1-e^{-2\pi iz}}=\sum_{m\ge1}e^{-2\pi imz}$, uniformly convergent on the line (ratio $e^{-2\pi b}$). Integrating term by term over the whole line (the bound $\frac{C}{1+x^2}\sum_me^{-2\pi bm}$ is integrable), \[ \int_{\operatorname{Im}z=-b}F(z)k(z)\,dz=\sum_{m\ge1}\int_{-\infty}^\infty F(x-ib)e^{-2\pi im(x-ib)}dx=\sum_{m\ge1}\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(m), \] the last step being the line shift of Theorem 8.5.2(a), step 1.
  5. Top side ($\operatorname{Im}z=b$, traversed right to left). There $|e^{2\pi iz}|=e^{-2\pi b}\lt1$, so $k(z)=-\frac1{1-e^{2\pi iz}}=-\sum_{m\ge0}e^{2\pi imz}$. The minus sign cancels against the reversed direction, so this side contributes \[ \sum_{m\ge0}\int_{-\infty}^\infty F(x+ib)\,e^{2\pi im(x+ib)}\,dx=\sum_{m\ge0}\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(-m), \] shifting the line back to $\R$ as before ($|e^{2\pi imz}|\le1$ for $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$).
  6. Let $N\to\infty$. The truncated horizontal integrals converge to the full ones (the integrands are dominated by integrable functions), and the vertical sides vanish. So \[ \sum_nF(n)=\sum_{m\ge1}\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(m)+\sum_{m\ge0}\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(-m)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\class{ntn-hat}{\hat F}(m). \] ∎

The usual real-variable proof expands the periodic function $\sum_nF(x+n)$ in a Fourier series and evaluates at $x=0$.

Further reading: Poisson summation formula

E.17

The argument principle and winding numbers

Context

Cited inL7 · Slide 4 · Thm. 7.3.1L11 · Slide 11 · Thm. 11.10.1

Why "argument"? Along a small arc of $C$ where $f\ne0$, choose a branch of $\log f$ (E.3); then $\frac{f'}f=(\log f)'$, and $\int\frac{f'}fdz$ is the change of $\log f=\log|f|+i\arg f$ along the arc. Around the closed curve $C$, $\log|f|$ returns to its starting value, while $\arg f$ may increase by a multiple of $2\pi$. So \[ \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f'}f\,dz=\frac{\text{total change of }\arg f(z)}{2\pi}=\text{the number of times }f(C)\text{ winds around }0. \] This number is the winding number of the image curve $f(C)$ about $0$. Theorem 7.3.1 says it equals $Z-P$. Rouché's theorem (Theorem 11.10.1) then says: if $|g-f|\lt|f|$ on $C$, the curves $f(C)$ and $g(C)$ wind around $0$ equally often, because the segment from $f(z)$ to $g(z)$ never passes through $0$ (the "dog on a leash").

Further reading: Argument principle · Winding number · Rouché's theorem

E.18

The Basel sum $\sum1/n^2=\pi^2/6$

Proved here

Cited inL6 · Slide 14 · Lemma 6.13.2L9 · Slide 11 · Rem. 9.10.2L10 · Slide 9

Lemma 6.13.2 uses this; it follows from Euler's product, proved later (Theorem 10.7.1). There is no circularity: Lecture 10 does not use Lecture 6's partition estimates.

Proof. On $|z|\lt1$, $\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}=\prod_{n\ge1}\big(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\big)$, and the partial products $Q_N$ converge uniformly on $|z|\le\frac12$ (Lemma 10.4.1). The $z^2$-coefficient of a holomorphic function near $|z|\le\frac12$ is $\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=1/2}(\cdot)\,z^{-3}dz$ (Theorem 6.4.1), which passes to uniform limits. The $z^2$-coefficient of $Q_N$ is $-\sum_{n\le N}\frac1{n^2}$ (expand the finite product), and that of $\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}=1-\frac{\pi^2z^2}6+\dots$ is $-\frac{\pi^2}6$. So $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n^2}=\frac{\pi^2}6$. ∎

Further reading: Basel problem

E.19

The circle method, and where Lemma A comes from

Context

Cited inL6 · Slide 15 · Prop. 6.14.1L6 · Slide 16 · Lemma 6.15.1Appendix A.23

§6.14–§6.19 is the simplest instance of the circle method of Hardy and Ramanujan (1918), later developed by Hardy–Littlewood for Waring's problem and by Vinogradov. Its ingredients: a generating function, Cauchy's coefficient formula on a circle close to the radius of convergence, a major arc near the dominant singularity where the function has an explicit approximation, and minor arcs where it is shown to be small.

Lemma 6.15.1, outline. Write $\log P(e^{-\tau})=\sum_{k\ge1}\phi(k\tau)$ with $\phi(u):=-\log(1-e^{-u})$. For small $\tau$ the sum is a Riemann sum with step $\tau$: \[ \sum_{k\ge1}\phi(k\tau)\approx\frac1\tau\int_0^\infty\phi(u)\,du+\text{correction}=\frac{\pi^2}{6\tau}+\dots, \] since \[ \int_0^\infty-\log(1-e^{-u})\,du=\sum_m\frac1m\int_0^\infty e^{-mu}du=\sum\frac1{m^2}=\frac{\pi^2}6. \] The correction comes from the singularity of $\phi(u)\approx-\log u$ at $u=0$; the Euler–Maclaurin formula, together with Stirling's formula (A.23) for $\sum\log k$, produces the term $\frac12\log\frac\tau{2\pi}$. A cleaner route is the modular transformation of Dedekind's eta function, which gives the formula with an exponentially small error.

Further reading: Partition function · Circle method · Euler–Maclaurin formula · Dedekind eta function

E.20

Hadamard's theorem: the idea of the proof

Context

Cited inL10 · Slide 14 · Thm. 10.13.1

Theorem 10.13.1 is stated without proof. By Cor. 10.12.1 (with $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}$ instead of $\class{ntn-Ep}{E_k}$, which converges by the argument of §10.13), $f=z^me^hQ$ with $Q:=\prod_k\class{ntn-Ep}{E_p}(z/a_k)$. It remains to show $h$ is a polynomial of degree $\le\rho$. By Lemma 10.6.1 with $k=\lfloor\rho\rfloor$, it is enough to bound $\operatorname{Re}h=\log|f|-m\log|z|-\log|Q|$ from above by $o(r^{k+1})$ on a sequence of circles. The term $\log|f|\le r^{\rho+\epsilon}$ is fine. The difficulty is a lower bound for $|Q|$, which is small near its zeros: one shows that $\log|Q(z)|\ge-r^{\rho+\epsilon}$ outside small disks around the $a_k$ (of total radius much less than $r$), so that suitable circles avoid them. This uses Theorem 9.10.1 to control how many zeros there are.

Further reading: Hadamard factorization theorem · Weierstrass factorization theorem
